en: Vālmīki: Having heard the words spoken by Hanumān exactly as they were addressed, [Rāma... Rāmāyaṇa, 6. Yuddhakāṇḍa 6.001.001a.
6.001.001c Rāma, filled with joy, spoke these further words:

6.001.002a "Hanumān has accomplished a task on this earth that is truly great and difficult to perform— 6.001.002c a deed which no one else on the surface of the earth could even conceive of in their mind."
6.001.003a Indeed, I do not see anyone who could cross the great ocean, 6.001.003c other than Garuḍa, Vāyu, or Hanumān;
6.001.004a among the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas.

Who indeed could enter the unassailable city of Laṅkā, so well-guarded by Rāvaṇa, and emerge alive, relying on his own strength? Who could enter that city, which is extremely difficult to assail and well-protected by the Rākṣasas?
6.001.005e He who is endowed with the power of valor would not be equal to Hanumān; 6.001.006a a great service to Sugrīva has been performed by Hanumān,
6.001.006c having thus displayed his own strength in accordance with his prowess.
For that servant who, having been appointed by his master to a difficult task,
performs it out of devotion to him— him they call the best of men. But he who, though appointed, does not perform the king’s business with a concentrated mind, [is not so].
6.001.008c A servant who is diligent yet capable—him they call the lowest of men.
6.001.009a By Hanūmat, appointed to that very task, the duty was accomplished;
6.001.009c neither was his own dignity diminished, nor was Sugrīva left unsatisfied.
"I, the lineage of Raghu, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa have today been protected by righteousness through the sight of Vaidehī. Yet,
this thought draws my wretched mind even further into distress."
6.001.011c If I do not perform a fitting act of kindness here for this messenger of pleasant news,
6.001.012a then this embrace, which constitutes my very all, offered by Hanumān—
6.001.012c having reached this moment, I shall bestow it upon that high-souled one.
In every respect, the search for Sītā has been well-conducted;
yet, having reached the ocean, my mind is once again lost.
How indeed can one cross the great waters of the sea, so difficult to traverse?

6.001.014c The monkeys, with concentrated minds, will go to the southern shore. 6.001.015a Even though this account was told to me by Vaidehī regarding the crossing of the ocean by the monkeys, what further [response] could there be?
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, agitated by grief, then entered into meditation regarding Hanumān. [Then,
seeing] that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, consumed by sorrow...
The illustrious Sugrīva spoke these words that dispel sorrow:
"O hero, why do you grieve like some other common man? Do not be thus; cast off your grief as one who is ungrateful casts off friendship."
"O Raghava, I see no ground for your distress,
since the enemy's activity has been observed and his dwelling place is known.
You are steadfast, learned in the scriptures, wise, and a scholar, O Raghava."
Abandon this wicked resolve which, like a thief, ruins one's own welfare. Having leaped across the ocean teeming with great crocodiles,
we shall ascend Laṅkā and slay your enemy.
For one who lacks enthusiasm, who is dejected, and whose mind is overwhelmed by grief,
all undertakings fail and he encounters calamity.
These leaders of our monkey hosts are all brave and capable.
"Having exerted their efforts for the sake of your welfare, they would even enter the fire;
by their joy, I know this, and my conviction in this matter is firm. I shall recover Sītā through valor, having slain the enemy."

"O Rāghava, act in such a way that a bridge may be built here so that we might see that city; for once we have seen that city of Laṅkā situated upon the peak of Mount Trikūṭa," [we shall know our course].
6.002.010c Consider Rāvaṇa as already slain in battle from this very sight. 6.002.011a The bridge has been built across the ocean as far as the vicinity of Laṅkā;
6.002.011c let it be understood that the entire army has crossed over and victory is won.
"For these tawny monkeys in battle are heroes who can assume any form at will.
Therefore, O King, enough of this despondent mindset which destroys all one's goals;
for in this world, grief in a man is a detractor from his valor."
But whatever task must be performed by a man who maintains his dignity—
for among heroic men such as yourself, O high-souled ones,
grief destroys all purpose when one is ruined or lost.

But you, O Raghava, are the best among the wise and are skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures; therefore, you ought to conquer the enemy here together with ministers such as myself. Indeed, I do not see anyone in the three worlds who could oppose you.

If anyone, with bow grasped, should stand facing you in battle, your mission will not fail while you are occupied with the monkeys. Before long, having crossed the inexhaustible ocean, you shall behold Sītā.

Therefore, O King, enough of resorting to grief; resort instead to anger. All dull-witted Kṣatriyas remain inactive when they fear a fierce man, even for the sake of crossing the terrible ocean, the lord of rivers.
"Accompanied by us here, you of subtle intellect, deliberate upon this:
for these heroic monkeys, capable of assuming any form at will,
shall scatter those enemies with showers of rocks and trees."
"By some means we have somehow found your abode, O Varuṇa.
What more need be said? In every way, you are victorious.
Having heard these reasoned words of Sugrīva, the knower of the ultimate truth—
Kākutstha received Hanumān and then said:
"Whether by my speed, by the construction of a bridge, or by the drying up of the ocean,
I am in every way fully capable of leaping across this sea."

"O monkey, tell me how many fortifications there are in that inaccessible Laṅkā; I wish to know all of it as if by direct sight. Also, [tell me] the measure of the army and the construction of the gates and fortresses."
6.003.004c You have seen the defensive works of Laṅkā and the dwellings of the Rākṣasas; 6.003.005a You have observed everything in Laṅkā exactly as it is and according to your pleasure.
6.003.005c Tell me truly about Saramā, for you are in every way capable.

Having heard Rāma’s words, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god and the best among those skilled in speech, then spoke these words again to Rāma: "Listen; I shall relate everything according to the methods for constructing fortifications."
Just as the city of Laṅkā is guarded and protected by its forces, [he described] the supreme prosperity of Laṅkā, the terrifying nature of the ocean,
the distribution of the flood of troops, and the disposition of the vehicles.
6.003.009a Laṅkā was thrilled and rejoicing, crowded with rutting elephants;
6.003.009c it was vast, filled with chariots, and teeming with hosts of Rākṣasas.
6.003.010a Its gates were firmly fastened and provided with great iron bolts.
It has four vast and exceedingly great gates;
and upon its ramparts are powerful and massive stone engines,
by which an approaching enemy army is repelled.
At the gates, hundreds of formidable, sharp *śataghnīs* made of black iron had been prepared and deployed by the hosts of heroic Rākṣasas.
And its great golden rampart was difficult to assail.
Its interior was strewn with gems, coral, lapis lazuli, and pearls;
and on all sides were great, formidable, and most auspicious moats filled with cool water, unfathomable, infested with crocodiles, and frequented by fish.
At their gates were four extremely long drawbridges,
equipped with many large machines and strong joints;
those drawbridges protected them when the enemy forces arrived.
By those machines, they were scattered everywhere into the moats. But there was one bridge, unshakable, strong, and exceedingly firm,
adorned with many golden pillars and altars.

O Rāma, Rāvaṇa himself is naturally endowed with prowess and is eager for battle; he has risen up and remains vigilant in surveying his forces. The city of Laṅkā is self-sustained, difficult even for the gods to assail, and terrifying.
[Water] is of four kinds: that which comes from rivers, from mountains, from the forest, and that which is artificial.
O Raghava, they stand on the far shore of the ocean, whose further shore is distant;
there is no path for boats here, and it is inaccessible from all sides.
On the mountain peak was built that fortress, Durgā, resembling the city of the gods; filled with horses and elephants, Laṅkā was exceedingly difficult to conquer.
There were iron bars, *śataghnī* weapons, and various kinds of mechanical engines.
They beautify the city of Laṅkā belonging to the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
Ten thousand Rākṣasas here occupy the western gate;
they are unassailable, bearing spears in their hands, and all are warriors who fight with the tips of swords.
6.003.024a A hundred thousand *niyutas* of *rākṣasas* are stationed here at the southern gate;
6.003.024c with a fourfold army, the warriors there are likewise unsurpassed.
6.003.025a A million *prayutas* of *rākṣasas* are stationed here at the eastern gate.
All of them bore shields and swords and were likewise experts in all weapons.
Ten billion *arbudas* of *rākṣasas* took their positions at the northern gate;
there were chariot-warriors and horsemen, well-born sons who were highly honored.

A hundred times a hundred thousand have taken refuge in the central division; there are invincible Yātudhānas and more than ten million Rākṣasas. Those bridges have been destroyed by me, and the moats have been filled up.
Lanka has been burned and its ramparts destroyed;
by whatever path we may cross the abode of Varuṇa,
let it be understood by the monkeys that the city of Lanka has been slain.
"Aṅgada, Dvivida, Mainda, Jāmbavat, Panasa, Nala,
and the commander-in-chief Nīla— if these remain with the rest of the army, what need have you for anything else?
For once we have leaped and reached that great city of Rāvaṇa,"
"They shall bring Maithilī back along with her attendants and her palace. "Therefore, give orders immediately for the mobilization of all the forces;
set out at an auspicious moment."
Having heard Hanumān’s words exactly as they were and in due order,
the immensely radiant Rāma, whose prowess is truth, then spoke:
"As for that city of Laṅkā belonging to the terrible Rākṣasa which you describe..."
"I shall slay her quickly; I tell you this truly.
Sugrīva, I favor setting out at this very moment. The hour for victory is joined, and the sun has reached the meridian."
"Today is indeed the day of Uttarā-phalgunī, and tomorrow it will be joined with Hasta. O Sugrīva, let us set forth, surrounded by our entire army.
Moreover, auspicious omens are appearing before me."
"Having slain Rāvaṇa, I shall bring back Sītā, the daughter of Janaka;
for this throbbing of my left eye above proclaims, as it were,
that my heart's desire has attained victory."
"Let Nīla go at the head of this army to scout the path,
surrounded by a hundred thousand swift monkeys,
with fruits and roots, and with cool forest waters."
"O General, lead the army swiftly along a path rich in honey.
Wicked-minded Rākṣasas might defile the roots, fruits, and water on the way; therefore, you must always remain vigilant and protect them from them."
6.004.010a Let the forest-dwellers, leaping into low-lying places, forest fastnesses, and woods,
6.004.010c behold the enemy's army destroyed. 6.004.011a Let those of great strength look upon that formidable vanguard, which resembles the surging tide of the ocean.
Let the monkey-lions lead the way by the hundreds and thousands;
let Gaja, who resembles a mountain, and the mighty Gavaya,
as well as Gavākṣa, go at the front like proud bulls among cattle.
Let the monkey Ṛṣabha, the bull among monkeys, go with the monkey army as the lord of leapers, protecting the right flank;
and let the swift Gandhamādana, as unassailable as a scent-elephant, proceed.
"Let me mount Hanumān, like the Lord [Indra] upon Airāvata, and stationed on the left flank of the monkey army, I shall proceed through the midst of the forces, gladdening the host."
Let this Lakṣmaṇa, who resembles the God of Death, march together with Aṅgada,
just as the Lord of Beings (Śiva) is joined by the Sovereign of All (Viṣṇu), or the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) by the Lord of the Earth (Yama).
And let Jāmbavān, Suṣeṇa, and the monkey Vegadarśin [also go].
"May those three great beings, the lords of the bears, protect your belly.
Having heard the words of Rāghava, Sugrīva, the lord of the army and bull among monkeys,
commanded the monkeys of great prowess.
6.004.019a All those hosts of monkeys, eager for battle, leapt up together; 6.004.019c they then swiftly sprang forth from their caves and mountain peaks.
6.004.020a Then he was honored by the king of the monkeys and by Lakṣmaṇa.
The righteous Rāma, accompanied by his army, departed for the southern direction;
surrounded then by hundreds, hundreds of thousands, crores, and even tens of thousands of elephants and monkeys, he proceeded.
As he went, that great army of monkeys followed him;
all of them, protected by Sugrīva, were joyful and exceedingly delighted. Leaping, bounding, and roaring, the monkeys pressed forward.
6.004.023e Laughter and shouting, they indeed went toward the southern direction;
6.004.024a eating fragrant honey and fruits,
and carrying great trees laden with clusters of blossoms.
Seeing one another suddenly, they strike and hurl each other down;
some fall and spring up again, while others knock their opponents to the ground.
"Rāvaṇa must be slain, as must all these night-stalkers! they cried.
Thus the monkeys roared in the presence of Rāghava.
In front, the heroic Ṛṣabha, as well as Nīla and Kumuda,
cleared the path along with many other monkeys.
In the center, however, were King Sugrīva, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa—
those destroyers of enemies— surrounded by many powerful and formidable [monkeys].
The heroic monkey Śatabali was surrounded by ten *koṭis*.
For alone, having taken hold of the entire army of monkeys, he protected it;
Kesari with a retinue of a hundred crores, Panasa, Gaja,
and the exceedingly powerful Arka guarded one of his flanks.
Suṣeṇa and Jāmbavat, surrounded by many bears,
placed Sugrīva at their head and protected the rear. Their heroic commander was Nīla, the bull among monkeys.
6.004.032c Saṃpāti, the best of those who fly, protected that force.
6.004.033a Darīmukha, Prajaṅgha, Jambha, and the monkey Rabhasa—
6.004.033c these heroes went everywhere, urging on the monkeys.
Thus those tigers among monkeys, proceeding with pride in their strength,
beheld the Sahya mountain, the best of peaks, covered with trees and creepers;
that great army of monkeys was as formidable as the surging tide of the ocean.
It issued forth with a great roar, like the ocean in its terrible surge.
At the side of that son of Daśaratha, all those heroic elephant-like monkeys leaped forward swiftly, like well-bred horses urged on by their riders.
Carried by the two monkeys, those two bulls among men shone like the moon and the sun joined together with two massive crocodiles.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, seated upon Aṅgada, addressed Rāma with auspicious words.
6.004.038c Having achieved his purpose, the mindful and eloquent one spoke: 6.004.039a "Having recovered Vaidehī who was carried away, and having swiftly slain Rāvaṇa,
you shall return to the prosperous city of Ayodhyā with your goals fulfilled."
"O Rāghava, I see great and auspicious omens both in the sky and upon the earth, all of which portend the accomplishment of your purpose. A pleasant,
gentle, and beneficial breeze blows favorably behind the army."
These beasts and birds are crying out with full and melodious voices;
all the quarters of the sky are serene, and the sun is stainless. Furthermore, Uśanas Bhārgava, his radiance clear, has followed after you.
The pure mass of Brahman and the purified supreme ṛṣis,
all radiant, shine while perpetually circumambulating Dhruva. The stainless royal sage Triśaṅku shines forth together with his domestic priest.
The boon-granting Grandfather [Brahmā] belongs to us, the high-souled Ikṣvākus.
And the two Viśākhās shine forth stainless and free from affliction;
this is the supreme lunar mansion of us, the high-souled Ikṣvākus.
The constellation of the Nairṛtas is being oppressed by the planet Nairṛta;
Mūla, touched by the root-dwelling [planet], is being scorched by a comet. This omen has appeared for the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
The lunar mansion of those who have met their end at the proper time is afflicted by a planet; yet the waters are clear and delicious, the forests are laden with fruit,
fragrances blow intensely, and the trees bear flowers according to the season.
"O Lord, these marshaled monkey armies appear even more magnificent,
like the armies of the gods in the battle against Tāraka.
Having observed them thus, O Noble One, you ought to be pleased."
Having thus consoled his brother, the joyful son of Sumitrā spoke;
then, having covered the entire earth, the great army set forth,
surrounded by tigers among bears and monkeys who had claws and fangs for weapons.
The dust raised from the earth by the monkeys with the tips of their hands and the tips of their feet obscured the world,
blocking out the radiance of the sun.
That great army of monkeys marched on, day and night.
6.004.053c The army, protected by Sugrīva, was joyful and exultant. 6.004.054a All the forest-dwellers, rejoicing in the prospect of battle, marched swiftly;
6.004.054c Desiring to liberate Sītā, they did not tarry anywhere for even a moment.
Then they reached the Sahya mountain and the Malaya range, which were dense with trees and teeming with various wild animals;
there they beheld diverse forests, rivers, and waterfalls.
Even as he looked on, Rāma proceeded past the Sahya and Malaya mountains; meanwhile,
the monkeys were breaking off campaka, tilaka, mango, aśoka, sinduvāraka,
karavīra, and timiśa trees.
There, the monkeys, fierce in their strength, feasted upon the fruits, roots, and flowers of the trees, which possessed the fragrance of nectar.
The monkeys ate those hanging down, measuring as much as a *droṇa* in size.
6.004.059c Drunk and joyful, those monkeys, tawny as honey, went along drinking the honeys.
6.004.060a Breaking down trees and likewise dragging away creepers,
those bulls among monkeys proceeded, shattering the great mountains.
But other monkeys, intoxicated by the honey and roaring, [acted] differently from those on the trees;
some leaped toward the trees while others fell down as well.
The earth became completely filled with those foremost of monkeys.
6.004.062c Just as the earth appears with fields of lotuses when they have ripened,
6.004.063a Then, having reached Mount Mahendra, the lotus-eyed Rāma, the mighty-armed one, ascended its peak adorned with trees.
Then, having ascended the peak, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
beheld a reservoir of water teeming with tortoises and fish. Having traversed the Sahya and the great Malaya mountains, they [proceeded further].
6.004.065c They reached the ocean of terrifying roar in due order.
6.004.066a Having disembarked, Rāma— the best among those who give delight— along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, quickly went to the unsurpassed forest on the shore.
Then, having reached the vast shore whose surface was like polished stone due to the suddenly surging floods of water, Rāma spoke these words:
"O Sugrīva, we have arrived at the abode of Varuṇa."
6.004.068c Now, this reflection has arisen here which did not arise before. 6.004.069a Beyond this point lies the shoreless ocean, the lord of rivers;
6.004.069c and this sea cannot be crossed by one who lacks the proper means.
"Let our encampment be right here; let a plan be proposed so that this army of monkeys may reach the opposite shore.
Thus spoke the mighty-armed one, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā.
6.004.071c Having reached the ocean, Rāma then ordered them to halt.
6.004.072a "The time for counsel has arrived for us here regarding the crossing of the ocean.
6.004.072c Leaving each your respective divisions, let no one go anywhere."
"Let the heroic monkeys go; we must ascertain what is hidden and the danger that threatens us.
Having heard Rāma's words, Sugrīva, together with Lakṣmaṇa, encamped the army on the shore of the ocean, which was thick with trees.
That army, stationed near the ocean,
shone like a second glorious ocean with its honey-colored, pale waters.
Then those bulls among monkeys approached the forest on the shore.
6.004.075c Intent upon reaching the further shore, they longed for the great ocean.
6.004.076a Having reached the vast sea, that army of monkeys was filled with joy as it beheld the great ocean, tossed by the force of the wind.
Beholding the abode of Varuṇa, which has a far-reaching shore, is unconfined, and is frequented by hosts of Rākṣasas, the leaders of the monkey troops sat down at the beginning of the night,
when the day had ended, amidst the terrible presence of fierce crocodiles and sea-monsters.
At the rising of the moon, it was tossed about and filled with counter-moons;
strewn with fierce winds as its great sea-monsters and with *timi* and *timimigila* fish,
it resembled the abode of Varuṇa crowded with serpents of blazing coils.
It was plunged into by great beings, crowded with various mountains, difficult to traverse, impassable, trackless, and bottomless— that abode of the Asuras.
It was infested by sea-monsters and the coils of serpents, and its waters were reddened by blood.
Masses of water surged upward and fell back down;

like scattered sparks of fire, the sun, water, and serpents made that terrible realm of the enemies of the gods— always as treacherous as the netherworld— appear as if it were the very underworld itself.
The ocean appeared like the sky, and the sky was like the ocean;
the ocean and the sky were seen without distinction.
For the water was joined with the sky, and the sky was joined with the water.
In such a form they appeared, filled with stars and jewels;
between the sky, with its rising clouds, and the ocean, with its garlands of waves, there was no distinction between the two.
Striking one another and clashing together, the waves of the king of rivers roared with a terrifying sound, like great kettledrums in battle;
they resounded with the noise of the massed jewels and waters, as if held fast by the wind.
Those great-souled ones beheld it like a lake struck by the wind, rising up as if in fury and teeming with hosts of aquatic creatures;
tossed by the breeze in the sky, it seemed to be leaping with its waves.
Resounding with the noise of agitated waves like a surging ocean,
that army was properly stationed on the northern shore of the sea by Nīla, who had himself been well-guarded and remained perfectly composed.
Both Mainda and Dvivida, those two bulls among monkeys,
roamed throughout that army in every direction for the sake of its protection. When the army had encamped on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, they remained there.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa standing by his side, Rāma spoke these words:
"It is said that grief indeed departs with the passing of time;
yet for me, as I do not behold my beloved, it increases day by day."
"It is not my grief that my beloved is far away, nor is it my grief that she has been carried off;
this alone I lament: her youth is passing away.
Blow, O Wind, from where that maiden is; having touched her, touch me as well."
"The touch of your limbs upon me and the meeting of our eyes with the moon—
that burns my limbs like poison swallowed into the stomach. Alas, my lord!"— these were the words my beloved spoke as she was being carried away.
"With separation from her as its fuel and the vast flames of thoughts of her as its fire,
my body is consumed day and night by the fire of passion. O Saumitri, I shall go and sleep after plunging into the ocean, without you."
How might the blazing fire of desire burn one who is fast asleep in water?
For one who yearns so intensely, it is possible to live by this [means]:
that both she and I, O lady of beautiful thighs, have resorted to the same earth.
6.005.011 Just as a dry field depends on a watered one,

so do I live by the moisture [of her presence], for I hear that she is still living. 6.005.012 But when indeed shall I see that lady of beautiful thighs, whose eyes are as long as a hundred-petaled lotus?

6.005.012c Having conquered my enemies, I shall behold Sītā like the fullness of prosperity. 6.005.013a When indeed shall I, lifting her face slightly— her lotus-like countenance with its lovely bimba-red lips— drink from it as a sick man drinks an elixir?
"When will those two joined, full breasts of hers, resembling palm fruits and trembling,
come to touch me as she laughs?
Surely that woman with dark-cornered eyes, though virtuous, is now situated in the midst of Rākṣasas."
Like a woman whose husband has perished, she finds no protector;
when will she, having agitated the Rākṣasas and shaken them off, fly up into the air—
just as the crescent moon, having dispersed the dark clouds, rises in the autumn?

Surely Sītā’s natural form has been thinned by grief and by fasting; it has become even more attenuated due to the adversity of place and time. When, indeed, will she see the arrows fixed in the chest of the lord of the Rākṣasas?
"I shall recover Sītā, casting off the grief in my mind. When indeed will the virtuous Sītā, who resembles the daughter of the gods, longingly embrace my neck and shed tears born of joy?"
"When shall I suddenly cast off this terrible grief born of separation from Maithilī, just as one discards a soiled garment? While the wise Rāma was thus lamenting there, [the sun set].
At the end of the day, the sun, its body dimmed, went to its setting.
Comforted by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma performed the twilight worship,
overwhelmed with grief as he remembered Sītā, whose eyes were like lotus petals.
Having seen the terrible deed committed in Laṅkā, which brings about worldly existence,
the Lord of the Rākṣasas— by Hanumān, as if by the high-souled Śakra—
spoke to all the Rākṣasas with his face somewhat cast down in shame.
6.006.002a He has both assaulted and entered Laṅkā, that city difficult to withstand;
6.006.002c by that mere monkey, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, has been seen.
6.006.003a The sanctuary has been defiled and the foremost Rākṣasas have been slain.
The entire city of Laṅkā has been thrown into turmoil by Hanumān.
What shall I do? May it be well with you; what is appropriate for the next step?
Tell me that which is effective and would be a well-performed deed.
"For the wise and noble say that victory is rooted in counsel;
therefore, O mighty ones, I favor employing counsel against Rāma.
There are three kinds of men in this world: the superior, the inferior, and the middling."
6.006.006c But regarding those who have assembled together, I shall declare their merits and defects.
6.006.007a [One should consult] with ministers who are intent on one's welfare and capable in determining counsel,
or also with friends who share the same purpose, or even with kinsmen who are well-wishers.
He who, having deliberated together with others, undertakes his undertakings, and exerts effort in matters concerning the divine—he is called the best of men.
He alone should reflect upon his purpose; he alone should fix his mind upon dharma.
6.006.009c He who accomplishes his tasks alone is called a man of middling character.
6.006.010a Without discerning merits and defects, and having abandoned reliance on destiny,
he who neglects a task thinking "I shall do it" is the lowest of men.
6.006.011 Just as these men are always classified as superior, inferior, or middling,
so too should counsel be understood as superior, inferior, or middling.
6.006.012 Having reached a consensus through the eye provided by the vision of the scriptures—
6.006.012c Where ministers have cast aside [their differences], they call that counsel supreme.
6.006.013a When many opinions have been exchanged by the ministers in determining a matter,
yet they again reach a state of unity, that counsel is considered middling.
6.006.014 When counsel is spoken while relying on mutual opinions,
and no single consensus exists, that advice is called inferior.
6.006.015 Therefore, O best of ministers, may you deliberation well.
"Let them undertake this task, for it is my most urgent duty.
Surrounded by thousands of heroic monkeys,
Rāma approaches the city of Laṅkā as our assailant."

And it is quite evident that Rāghava, together with his younger brother, his army, and his followers, will easily cross the ocean by means of a suitable display of prowess. Since this matter has thus turned out, [it must be dealt with] in opposition to the monkeys.
"Let everything that is beneficial for both the city and the army be deliberated upon with me.
Having been addressed thus by the Lord of the Rākṣasas,
all those mighty Rākṣasas spoke with joined palms to Rāvaṇa, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas.
"O King, our army is vast and crowded with clubs, spears, double-edged swords, tridents, and sharp-edged missiles; why do you yield to despondency?
[For you are] a dweller on the peak of Kailāsa, surrounded by many yakṣas."

Having caused a great slaughter, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) was brought under your control. O Lord, that mighty world-protector, boasting of his friendship with Maheśvara, was defeated in battle by you out of wrath.
"Having struck down the hosts of yakṣas, having agitated and subdued them,
this celestial chariot was brought from the peak of Kailāsa by you, while Maya, the lord of the dānavas, desiring friendship out of fear of you, [offered it]."
"O bull among rākṣasas, your daughter was given to him as his wife.
Madhu, the lord of the Dānavas, who was arrogant in his prowess and difficult to approach,
was subdued and brought under control by Kumbhīnasī for her own comfort."
"O mighty-armed one, those nāgas have been conquered by you after you went to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Śaṅkha, and Jaṭī have been brought under your control—
those who are indestructible, powerful, heroic, and who had obtained boons."
"O Lord, O subduer of enemies, having fought with you in battle for a year,
the Dānavas have been brought under your control by relying on their own strength; and there, O lord of the Rākṣasas, many illusions were mastered."

O mighty-armed one, those sons of Varuṇa, though brave and powerful, were defeated in battle along with their fourfold forces. [They entered] that ocean which has the staff of Death for its great crocodile and is adorned by Śālmalidvīpa.
"O King, having plunged into the ocean of Yama's power,
you have achieved vast victory and Death itself has been repelled. By your noble combat, all the worlds there have been thoroughly gratified."
The earth was filled with many heroic Kṣatriyas whose prowess equaled that of Śakra, like the ground covered by great trees;
yet Rāghava was not their equal in battle, owing to his own heroism, virtues, and energy.
"O King, those who were exceedingly difficult to conquer have been slain by you through sheer force. O King, this calamity has not come upon you as it does upon common folk;
you should not harbor such anxiety in your heart, for you shall slay Rāghava."
Then the heroic general named Prahasta, who resembled a dark blue cloud, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents— "
They are not even able to overpower you, much less the monkeys in battle.
We have all been negligent, trusting, and deceived by Hanumān;
for as long as I live, that forest-dweller shall not depart alive while I remain alive.

"I shall make the entire earth, bounded by the ocean and including its mountains, forests, and groves, free of monkeys; may your lordship command me. Furthermore, O night-stalker, I shall provide protection from the monkeys."
"Not even a slight suffering born of your own transgression shall come upon you.
Then the Rākṣasa named Durmukha, highly incensed, said:
"Indeed, this assault upon us all is not to be tolerated."
This further humiliation of the city and the inner apartments,
and this assault by the lord of monkeys upon the illustrious lord of the Rākṣasas—
killing [him] alone at this very moment, I shall turn back from the monkeys.
Whether they have entered the fearsome ocean, the sky, or the subterranean realm,
then the immensely powerful Vajradaṃṣṭra, filled with great rage,
seized a terrible iron club smeared with flesh and blood and spoke.
"What need have you for the wretched and pitiable Hanumān,
while the invincible Rāma stands here with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa?
Today, I shall [strike] Rāma, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, with my iron club."
"I shall return alone after slaying him and throwing the monkey host into turmoil.
Then the heroic and powerful son of Kumbhakarna, named Nikumbha,
being exceedingly enraged, spoke to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out.
"6.008.013a All of you, remain here united with the great king.
6.008.013c I alone shall slay Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa.
6.008.014a Then there was a Rākṣasa named Vajrahanu, who resembled a mountain.
Enraged, he licked his mouth with his tongue and spoke these words:
"Let you all perform your tasks at ease, free from anxiety;
I alone shall devour all those leaders of the monkey hosts."
"Let them remain at ease and play without anxiety; let them drink the honey-wine of Varuṇa.
I alone shall slay Sugrīva along with Lakṣmaṇa, as well as Aṅgada, Hanumān, and Rāma, that elephant among warriors."
Then there were the impetuous Nikumbha, the mighty Sūryaśatru,
Suptaghna, Yajñakopa, Mahāpārśva, Mahodara,
the invincible Agniketu, and the Rākṣasa Raśmiketu.
And Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, possessed of great splendor and strength;
then Prahasta, Virūpākṣa, the exceedingly powerful Vajradaṃṣṭra,
Dhūmrākṣa, Atikāya, and the Rākṣasa Durmukha.
Seizing iron clubs, cloth-bands, spears, javelins, tridents,
axes, bows with arrows, and large, sharp swords,
the Rākṣasas, filled with supreme rage, leapt up.
All of them, as if blazing with energy, said to Rāvaṇa:
"Today we shall slay Rāma, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa,
and the wretched Hanumān by whom Laṅkā was violated."
Having restrained all of them who had taken up their weapons, Vibhīṣaṇa made them sit down again and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
"O dear one, that purpose which cannot be attained even by the three means..."
6.009.008c The wise say that those are the opportune times for valorous action: 6.009.009a when [the enemy] is negligent, when they are attacked, and when they have been struck down by fate.
6.009.009c O dear one, such actions succeed when undertaken after careful examination and according to the proper method.
"How can you wish to assail him who is vigilant, desirous of victory, established in his strength, who has conquered anger, and is invincible—
after having crossed the terrible ocean, the lord of rivers and streams?"
Who could possibly conceive of the difficult feat accomplished by Hanumān?
O night-stalkers, the strengths and heroic powers of others are immeasurable; one must never, under any circumstances, treat them with sudden contempt.
6.009.013a Moreover, what wrong was previously done by Rāma to the king of the rākṣasas?
6.009.013c He carried off the wife of that illustrious one from Janasthāna.
6.009.014a If Khara, having acted with transgression, was slain by Rāma in battle—

"The lives of living beings must certainly be protected according to one's power. For this reason, Vaidehī might cause us very great danger. Was she not brought here for the sake of a quarrel, and should she not be abandoned?"
"It is not fitting for us to engage in a pointless enmity with that powerful one who follows the path of righteousness. Let Maithilī be given back to him, before he seizes this city,
along with its elephants, horses, and abundant treasures."

"He tears the city apart with his arrows; let Maithilī be given to him, before the most terrible, great, and unassailable army of monkeys attacks Laṅkā. Let Sītā be surrendered while it is not yet too late."
For Lanka would surely perish, along with all its heroic Rākṣasas, if Rāma’s beloved wife were not surrendered by you yourself. Out of our kinship, I entreat you; do as I say.
"I tell you what is beneficial and wholesome: let Maithilī be given to him.
Before long, the prince will [discharge] arrows that resemble the rays of the autumnal sun, possessing fresh nocks and being exceedingly firm."
He discharges unerring arrows for your destruction;
let Maithilī be restored to the son of Daśaratha. Abandon this anger, which destroys both happiness and righteousness.
Devote yourself to the Dharma, which increases both pleasure and fame.
Be gracious so that we may live with our sons and kinsmen;
let Maithilī be restored to the son of Daśaratha.
To Vibhīṣaṇa, who had spoken words that were well-founded and beneficial,
Rāvaṇa, impelled by fate, spoke harsh words:
"One might dwell even with an enemy or with an enraged venomous serpent."

6.010.002c But one should not dwell with one who serves the enemy merely out of the reputation of being a friend. 6.010.003a O Rākṣasa, I know the character of kinsmen in all the worlds: these relatives always rejoice in the misfortunes of their kin.

"O Rākṣasa, kinsmen despise one who is preeminent, successful, learned, and virtuous; they indeed treat a hero with contempt. Always delighted by one another's misfortunes, they act as assassins when calamities strike."
"6.010.005c Relatives with hidden hearts are terrible and bring fear. 6.010.006a Verses sung by elephants in a certain lotus grove are heard;
having seen men with nooses in their hands, listen as I recite them."

Neither fire, nor other weapons, nor our snares bring us fear; rather, our own kinsmen, incited by their selfish interests, are the ones who bring us terrible fear. They will undoubtedly suggest means for our capture.
6.010.008c We know that among all fears, the fear of kinsmen is the most grievous.
6.010.009a Abundance is found in cattle; self-restraint is found in a Brahmin;
6.010.009c fickleness is found in women; and fear is found from kinsmen.
"Therefore, O gentle one, this is not desirable for me— that I, honored by the world, born into sovereignty, and standing at the head of my enemies,
should speak such words as another might say, O night-stalker."
"If you do not [act] at this very moment, then shame on you, defiler of your lineage!
Having been addressed with these harsh words, Vibhīṣaṇa, who speaks according to justice,
sprang up with mace in hand, accompanied by four Rākṣasas.
Then the glorious Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with wrath, spoke these words from the sky to his brother, the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"O King, you are my brother; tell me whatever you wish."

"But I cannot endure these harsh and false words of yours. O Ten-necked One, well-spoken advice given by one who desires your welfare is not accepted by those of undisciplined soul who have fallen under the power of Time."
"O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to such words, are both rare to encounter.
Bound by the noose of Time, which carries away all living beings,"
I shall not neglect you as you perish, like a burning shelter. With sharp arrows adorned with gold that resemble blazing fire, I do not wish to see you slain by Rāma.
6.010.019 Even those who are brave, powerful, and skilled in weapons on the field of battle perish when overtaken by Time, like bridges made of sand.
6.010.020 Protect yourself by all means, as well as this city together with its rākṣasas.
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Be happy without me.
O night-stalker, though I, seeking your welfare, am trying to dissuade you, your words do not please you.
"For men whose time has come and whose life-span is spent do not accept the beneficial advice offered by friends.
Having spoken these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa—

In a mere moment, he arrived at the place where Rāma was with Lakṣmaṇa. Those lords of the monkeys, standing upon the earth, beheld him stationed in the sky, resembling a peak of Mount Meru and glowing like a flash of lightning.
Seeing him as the fifth among them, the wise and invincible Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, reflected along with the other monkeys.
Having reflected for a moment, he spoke to those monkeys.
To all those led by Hanumān, he spoke these excellent words:
"Behold! This Rākṣasa, equipped with every weapon and accompanied by four other Rākṣasas, approaches; there is no doubt that he comes to slay us."
6.011.006 Having heard the words of Sugrīva, all those best of monkeys raised up *sāla* trees and rocks and spoke these words:
6.011.007 "O King, quickly command us for the slaughter of these evil-minded ones!"
"Let these short-lived ones fall slain upon the earth!
While they were thus conversing with one another, Vibhīṣaṇa reached the northern shore and remained stationed there while still in the air.
And the great and highly wise Vibhīṣaṇa, while still stationed in the sky, looked toward Sugrīva and the others and spoke with a mighty voice:
"There is a wicked Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas."
"I am his younger brother, known by the name Vibhīṣaṇa.
By him, having slain Jaṭāyu, Sītā was seized from Janasthāna;
she is now held captive, helpless and distressed, closely guarded by Rākṣasa women."
6.011.012a I demonstrated this to him with various reasons and arguments, saying again and again: "Let Sītā be properly restored to Rāma.
6.011.013a But Rāvaṇa, impelled by fate, did not accept it.
Though spoken to with beneficial words, he was like one who rejects medicine;
thus insulted by him and treated with contempt like a slave,
I have abandoned my sons and wife and sought refuge with Rāghava.
"Quickly announce to the high-souled Rāghava, the refuge of all the world, that Vibhīṣaṇa has arrived. Having heard these words, Sugrīva, who is swift in action, [acted accordingly].
In front of Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke these words to the agitated Rāma:
"The younger brother of Rāvaṇa, known as Vibhīṣaṇa,
has come to you for refuge along with four other rākṣasas."
"Know that this Vibhīṣaṇa has been sent by Rāvaṇa;
O best among the forgiving, I consider his restraint appropriate.
This Rākṣasa has arrived, dispatched with a deceitful intent."
"O Rāghava, while you were trusting him, he struck you, concealed by his illusory power.
Let this Vibhīṣaṇa— indeed the brother of the cruel Rāvaṇa— be executed along with his ministers by means of severe punishment."

Having spoken thus to Rāma, the commander of the army, who was skilled in speech, became agitated and then fell silent before him who was likewise skilled in speech. But having heard those words of Sugrīva, the exceedingly powerful Rāma—
6.011.022c He spoke these words to the monkeys standing nearby, headed by Hanūmat:
6.011.023a "The speech that was uttered by the king of the monkeys concerning the younger brother of Rāvaṇa— 6.011.023c that highly reasoned statement has also been heard by you."
"For a wise and virtuous friend,
even when capable, ought to offer counsel during times of financial distress for one who desires eternal prosperity.
Having been thus questioned, they each, without weariness, set forth their respective opinions.
Then, desiring his welfare, they spoke with courtesy to Rāma:
"O Rāghava, there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to you. Honoring yourself, O Rāma, you ask us out of friendship."

"For you are one whose vows are true, a hero, righteous, and firm in prowess; you are circumspect in action, possessed of memory, and have entrusted yourself to your friends. Therefore, let your ministers speak to you one by one."
"Endowed with intelligence by reason and capable again and again"—
when this had been said to Rāghava, the wise monkey Aṅgada then spoke these words before him for the purpose of testing Vibhīṣaṇa.
6.011.030a For one who has come from the presence of an enemy must indeed be suspected in every way;
6.011.030c Vibhīṣaṇa should not be hastily made worthy of trust.
6.011.031a For those of deceitful intellect move about concealing their true nature.
And they strike at one's vulnerabilities; that would result in a very great calamity.

Having carefully determined what is beneficial and what is harmful, one should indeed apply oneself with resolve. One should adopt [actions] based on their merits and abandon them based on their defects.
"If there is a great fault in him, let him be abandoned without hesitation;
or, O King, having recognized many virtues, let him be accepted.
Then Śarabha, having reached a decision, spoke these words to the caravan leader:
6.011.034c O tiger among men, let a spy be quickly dispatched against him. 6.011.035a For, having employed a spy of subtle intellect to act accordingly,
6.011.035c and having investigated [the matter], one should then proceed with the undertaking according to what is right.
Then Jāmbavat, discerning through his knowledge of the scriptures,
addressed these words, which were virtuous and free from fault:
"Vibhīṣaṇa is afraid of the lord of the Rākṣasas, who is both wicked and harbors enmity."
"Since he has arrived at an improper place and time, he must be suspected in every way.
Then Mainda, who was skilled in discerning right from wrong conduct and endowed with eloquence, looked [at him] and spoke these highly reasoned words.

"O lord of the best of men, this speech of Rāvaṇa is indeed terrifying; let him be questioned gently and with sweet words. Having ascertained his true intention, you may then act according to the facts."
"O bull among men, if he was seen, yet not harmed intentionally;
then Hanumān, the best of ministers, endowed with refined conduct,
spoke words that were gentle, meaningful, sweet, and concise."

6.011.042a Even Bṛhaspati himself, though speaking, would not be able to surpass you— the best of the wise, the most capable, and the foremost among those who speak. 6.011.043a Not through debates, nor through contests, nor through superiority, nor out of desire [could he do so].

"O King, out of respect for Rāma, I shall speak words that are true to the facts. Regarding what was said by your ministers concerning the cause of gain and loss, I perceive a flaw therein; for such an action is not appropriate."
"Without an assignment, it is impossible to understand one's capability;
indeed, an impulsive appointment appears to me to be fraught with danger.
What your ministers have said regarding the dispatching of a spy is appropriate."
6.011.046c Because the matter is impossible, no reason for it is plausible there.
6.011.047a That Vibhīṣaṇa has arrived at an improper place and time— 6.011.047c I have a desire to speak on this matter; listen to it according to my understanding.
In this world, just as this place and time are what they are,
so too do faults and virtues follow from one person to another;
having observed the wickedness in Rāvaṇa and likewise your own valor.
"His arrival is fitting and consistent with his intelligence;
O King, let him be questioned by men in disguise.
Regarding what was said here, I have some considered insight."

6.011.051a When questioned, a wise man should not hastily speak; 6.011.051c for there, a friend might become alienated by words asked improperly or out of place. 6.011.052a Indeed, O King, it is impossible to suddenly discern the true disposition of another.

6.011.052c Beholding his great skill in those songs sung with such inner naturalness, 6.011.053a no sign of malice is ever perceived in him as he speaks; 6.011.053c and his face is serene; therefore, I have no doubt.
One whose mind is free from suspicion remains composed and does not approach with deceit;
nor is his speech wicked—therefore, there is no doubt in this matter.
Even when one's outward appearance is being concealed, it is impossible to hide it entirely.
For indeed, by force one reveals the inner disposition of men. O best among those who know what must be done, an action performed at the proper place and time,
when intended for application, quickly bears fruit.
Having observed your exertion and Rāvaṇa’s deceitful conduct,
and having heard of the slaying of Vālin and the consecration of Sugrīva,
he has come here intentionally, seeking the kingdom.
6.011.058c Taking this much into account, however, his reconciliation is appropriate; 6.011.059a I have spoken thus regarding the Rakshasa's straightforwardness according to my ability,
6.011.059c but you, O best among the wise, are the authority for what remains after hearing this.

6.012.001 Then Rāma, whose soul was serene, having heard the son of the Wind-god, replied— being invincible and learned in the scriptures— with his mind fixed upon himself: 6.012.002 "I too have a certain desire to speak concerning Vibhīṣaṇa."
"I wish to hear all that from you who are established in the highest good.
Having approached me with the spirit of friendship, I would not abandon it under any circumstances, even if there were a fault in him; for this is not censured among the virtuous."
6.012.004 Having heard Rāma’s words, Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys,
replied to the descendant of Kakutstha, impelled by his friendly affection.
6.012.005 O knower of dharma, crest-jewel of the lords of the world, what is surprising in this?
Since you, O courageous one, standing firm upon the path of truth, have spoken what is noble,
my inner self also knows Vibhīṣaṇa to be pure;
he has been thoroughly examined from every perspective through his intentions and his disposition.
"Therefore, O Rāghava, let the highly wise Vibhīṣaṇa quickly become our equal; let him enter into friendship with us.
Having heard those words of Sugrīva and having reflected upon them, Rāma—
Then he spoke these even more auspicious words to the bull among monkeys:
"Whether this night-stalker is very wicked or not wicked,
he is in no way capable of doing me even the slightest harm."

O Lord of the monkey hosts, if I so desired, I could slay with the tip of my finger the piśācas, dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas upon this earth. For it is heard that even a pigeon took refuge with an enemy who had come to him for protection.
6.012.011c Honored according to custom and invited with his own flesh,
6.012.012a he indeed welcomed that one who had come as the abductor of his wife.
O best of monkeys, how much more so would a person like me?
Listen to this righteous verse, spoken of old by the supreme seer Kaṇḍu, the son of the ṛṣi Kaṇva, who was a speaker of truth:
"To one who has come for refuge, wretched and with palms joined in supplication, begging for protection..."
6.012.014c One should not strike even an enemy for the sake of compassion, O best of men.
6.012.015a Whether he be distressed or arrogant, once an enemy has gone to the protection of others, he must be protected by one of self-restrained soul, even at the cost of his own life.
If, out of fear, delusion, or even desire, one does not protect [the seeker] according to their own ability and in accordance with the truth, that sin is condemned by the world;
for the one who has sought refuge perishes while the protector looks on.
Taking all of his merit, he would depart unguarded;
thus there is a great fault in failing to protect those who have sought refuge—
it leads away from heaven, brings dishonor, and destroys strength and valor.
"I shall indeed act according to the sublime words of Kaṇḍu; they are most righteous, conducive to fame, and lead to heaven when their fruit is realized—
for he has sought refuge in me once and entreated me, saying, 'I am yours.'"
"I grant fearlessness to all beings; this is my vow. Bring him here, O best of monkeys, for I have granted him safety—whether he be Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, or even Rāvaṇa himself."
Then, having heard those words of Sugrīva spoken by the lord of monkeys,
the lord of men quickly entered into an alliance with Vibhīṣaṇa.
When Rāghava granted him safety, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa bowed down like Purandara before the king of birds;
joyful, he descended from the sky to the earth together with his devoted followers.
Then the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, seeking refuge, fell at the feet of Rāma along with four other rākṣasas. And there,
Vibhīṣaṇa spoke these words to Rāma:
"It is righteous, appropriate, timely, and heartening.
"I am the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, and I have been insulted by him;
I have come to you for refuge, for you are the protector of all beings."
6.013.005a Lankā has been abandoned by me, along with my friends and my wealth; 6.013.005c my kingdom, my life, and my pleasures are now centered upon you.
6.013.006a [I shall provide] assistance in the slaughter of the Rākṣasas and in the assault upon Lankā.
"I shall do my utmost and enter the army.
To Vibhīṣaṇa, who was speaking thus, Rāma embraced him and,
being pleased, said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Bring water from the ocean."
"Therefore, O bestower of honor, since I am pleased with you, quickly consecrate this highly wise Vibhīṣaṇa as the king of the Rākṣasas.
Having been addressed thus, the son of Sumitrā consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa.
By the command of Rāma, he was placed in the midst of the monkey leaders as their king.
Seeing that favor from Rāma, the monkeys immediately raised great shouts and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
And Hanumān and Sugrīva said to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"How shall we cross the unshakeable ocean, the abode of Varuṇa? By what means may we approach that lord of rivers and streams?"
"Let us all, together with our armies, cross swiftly to the abode of Varuṇa.
Thus addressed, Vibhīṣaṇa, the knower of dharma, replied:
"King Rāghava ought to seek refuge with the ocean."
6.013.014a This immeasurable great ocean was dug by Sagara;
6.013.014c this great ocean ought to perform a service for Rāma, his kinsman.
6.013.015a When the wise Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa had spoken thus,

This was pleasing even to Rāghava, who by nature is devoted to righteousness. Then that one of great splendor, skilled in action, spoke with a smile to Lakṣmaṇa and Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, for the sake of performing the rites of hospitality.
"Lakṣmaṇa, this counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa appeals to me;
speak it also to Sugrīva, if it appeals to you as well.
Sugrīva is always wise, and you are an expert in counsel."
"Having deliberated together on both [options], let that which is pleasing to the noble one be spoken.
When they had been addressed thus, those two heroes, Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa,
spoke these words consistent with proper decorum.

"O tiger among men, O Raghava, why does what was spoken by Vibhīṣaṇa— which is conducive to happiness at this time— not please us? For without having bound a bridge across this terrible ocean, the abode of Varuṇa..."
6.013.021c Laṅkā cannot be reached even by the gods and asuras, including Indra himself.
6.013.022a Let the word of the heroic Vibhīṣaṇa be acted upon according to its true meaning. 6.013.022c Enough of wasting time; let this ocean be harnessed for our purpose.

Thus addressed, Rāma then lay down upon the bank of the lord of rivers and streams, which was strewn with *kuśa* grass, like the sacrificial fire upon an altar. As Rāma slept upon the surface of the earth covered with *kuśa* grass—
6.014.001c By virtue of his vigilance, three nights passed for him who was free from negligence. 6.014.002a Yet, at that time, the ocean did not reveal itself to Rāma,
even though it had been duly honored by the striving Rāma.
Then Rāma, his eyes red at the corners with rage,
spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks who was standing nearby:
"Behold, O Lakṣmaṇa, this ignoble man being honored."
That he himself does not display pride toward the ocean—
tranquility, forbearance, straightforwardness, and kind speech:
these virtues of the virtuous bear fruit even among those who lack merit.

The world honors that man who praises himself, who is wicked, audacious, and a reviler, and who wields his rod of punishment everywhere. Fame cannot be achieved through conciliation; glory cannot be achieved through conciliation.

"O Lakṣmaṇa, victory in this world or on the front lines of battle can only be attained [by such means]. Today, O son of Sumitrā, behold the ocean of Makaras with its waters obstructed on all sides by sea-monsters pierced by my arrows as they float about."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, behold here the massive coils of the fish and the trunks of the elephants; see also the coils of the serpents, all pierced by me with my arrows,
along with their nets of conch shells and mother-of-pearl, and their schools of fish and crocodiles."
6.014.010c Today, by means of a great battle, I shall dry up the ocean.
6.014.011a For this abode of sea-monsters regards me, though endowed with forbearance, as incapable; fie on such forbearance toward a person like this!
"O Saumitri, bring my bow and arrows that resemble venomous serpents!
Today, even though he is unshakeable, I shall, when enraged, agitate the ocean—
its boundaries fixed by the shore and its surface turbulent with a thousand waves."
"I shall make the abode of Varuṇa shoreless with my arrows.
Having spoken thus, Rāma, bow in hand and eyes wide with rage,
became invincible like the blazing fire at the end of an eon.
Having strung his formidable bow and made the world tremble with his arrows,
he released fierce shafts like Śatakratu discharging thunderbolts.
Blazing with great speed and brilliance, those excellent arrows—

They entered the waters of the ocean, which was filled with terrified serpents. Then a great and most terrible surge arose in the ocean, along with its crocodiles and sharks, accompanied by the roar of the wind.
6.014.018a Spread with garlands of great waves and filled with conch shells and mother-of-pearl,
6.014.018c the great ocean suddenly became one whose surging billows were wreathed in smoke.
6.014.019a And the serpents were distressed, their mouths flaming and their eyes blazing.
And then the Dānavas of great prowess, who dwell in the depths of Pātāla,
and the waves of the king of oceans, along with crocodiles and sea-monsters resembling the Vindhya and Mandara mountains, surged upward by the thousands.

With its mass of waves violently surging, its serpents and rākṣasas bewildered, and its great crocodiles tossed about, that ocean became agitated. Then, from the midst of the sea, Sāgara himself rose up.
For as the sun rises over the great mountains of Meru,
so did the ocean appear with its blazing-mouthed serpents;
it resembled smooth lapis lazuli and was adorned with gold.

Wearing red garlands and garments, with eyes resembling lotus petals, the valiant Sāgara approached, paid his respects, and, bowing with palms joined, addressed these words to Rāghava, who held an arrow in his hand: 6.015.002c Wearing red garlands and garments, with eyes resembling lotus petals; 6.015.003a Having first approached and offered salutations, the valiant Sāgara, 6.015.003c With palms joined, spoke these words to Rāghava, who held an arrow in his hand.
"O Raghava, earth, wind, space, water,
and light abide in their own nature, O gentle one, having taken recourse to the eternal path.
This very same nature belongs to me as well, such that I am unfathomable and without a raft."

"O Rādhā, I shall tell you this: there would indeed be a transformation [in me]. O son of a king, neither out of desire, nor out of greed, nor out of fear would I ever cause the waters, teeming with crocodiles and sharks, to solidify."
"O Rāma, I shall employ such means by which I may endure [the task],
so that the crocodiles will not strike until the army has crossed.
O gentle one, this is Nala by name, the son of Viśvakarman."
"Having been granted this boon by his father, this glorious monkey, who is equal to Viśvakarman,
shall build the bridge with great energy;
I will support him, for he is just like his father."
Having spoken thus, the Ocean vanished; then the mighty Nala, the best of monkeys, rose up and addressed these words to Rāma:
"I shall build a bridge across the vast abode of Varuṇa."
Relying on his father’s power, the Great Ocean spoke the truth:
"On Mount Mandara, a boon was granted to my mother by Viśvakarman;
I am his legitimate son, equal to Viśvakarman himself."
"Nor indeed would I speak of my own merits without being asked.
Let the foremost of monkeys build the bridge this very day, if they so desire.
Then, with Rāma having given his permission, the leaders of the monkey troops [proceeded] from all sides.
6.015.014c They entered the great forest joyfully by the hundreds of thousands.
6.015.015a Those monkeys, resembling mountains and being the leaders of the hosts of forest-dwellers,
6.015.015c broke down trees there and dragged the ocean along.
Those monkeys [fought] with *sāla*, *aśvakarṇa*, *dhava*, and *vaṃśa* trees,
as well as with *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, *tāla*, *tikta*, and *timiśa* trees,
and with flowering *bilvaka*, *saptaparṇa*, and *karṇikāra* trees.
With mango trees and *aśoka* trees, they filled the ocean;
lifting up trees— both those with roots and those without— the best of monkeys,
like the banners of Indra, hurled the trees [into the sea].
As the mountains were being cast in, the water suddenly surged upward;
it rose into the sky and then receded in every direction for ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.
Nala constructed a great bridge across the middle of the lord of rivers and streams. As stones were being cast and rocks were being dropped there,
a tumultuous sound arose then upon that great ocean.
6.015.022a That bridge built by Nala over the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
shone forth, auspicious and glorious, like the path of the constellation Svātī in the sky.
6.015.023a Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis, [gathered there].
Leaping, bounding, and roaring,
all living beings beheld that inconceivable, irresistible, wonderful, and hair-raising construction of a bridge across the ocean by the monkeys.
Those thousands of millions of monkeys of great prowess went forth, binding a bridge across the ocean to the far shore of the great sea;
it was vast, well-constructed, glorious, with excellent foundations and perfectly laid out.
The great bridge shone like a parting line upon the ocean.
Then, on the far side of the sea, Vibhīṣaṇa stood with mace in hand together with his ministers, intent on attacking the enemy.
At the head of that army went the illustrious Rāma, righteous-souled and armed with his bow, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and joined by Sugrīva;
other monkeys marched through the center, while others proceeded along the flanks.
Some fell into the water, while others could not find the path;
some, having gone into the air, leaped like Garuḍas. With their great clamor, they drowned out the rising roar of the ocean.
The formidable army of monkeys, crossing over, vanished from sight as they moved through the terrifying expanse.
Indeed, that host of monkeys had crossed by means of the bridge built by Nala;
they settled upon the shore, which abounded in roots, fruits, and water, under the command of the king.
6.015.032a Having observed that wondrous and difficult feat, O Rāghava, the gods together with the Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
6.015.032c approached Rāma along with the great seers (maharṣis) in unison.
They consecrated him individually with most auspicious waters:
"Be victorious over your enemies, O god among men! Protect the earth, together with its oceans, for eternal years."
Thus, with various auspicious words, they honored Rāma, who was revered by the lords of men.
When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, had crossed the ocean together with his army, [the people rejoiced].
The illustrious Rāvaṇa spoke to his two ministers, Śuka and Sāraṇa:
"The monkey army has crossed the entire ocean, which is otherwise so difficult to cross;
furthermore, Rāma has performed the unprecedented feat of building a bridge across the sea."
"I could not, under any circumstances, believe that a bridge could be built across the ocean;
nevertheless, I must certainly ascertain the number of that monkey army. Therefore, you two should enter the monkey host unobserved."
The extent [of the army], their prowess, and those who are the foremost monkeys;
those who are the ministers of Rāma and those esteemed by Sugrīva;
those who have already set out, and those heroic monkeys.
And how that bridge was constructed across the ocean, the vast expanse of water;
and how those high-souled monkeys were stationed there;
and [how] Rāma’s resolve, his prowess, and his weapons [were described].
"You ought to learn in truth about the heroic Lakṣmaṇa as well.
Who is the commander-in-chief of those mighty monkeys? Having learned this according to the facts, you ought to return quickly."
Thus commanded, the two heroic Rākṣasas, Śuka and Sāraṇa, assuming the forms of monkeys, entered the monkey army. Then that inconceivable and hair-raising host of monkeys—
At that time, Śuka and Sāraṇa were unable to count them;
they were stationed upon mountain peaks, in caves and ravines,
on the shores of the ocean, and in forests and groves.

The one of great splendor, Vibhīṣaṇa, saw them all— those of terrible roar and great strength— who were crossing, those who had already crossed, and those desiring to cross; as well as those who were encamped and those who were still setting up camp, all remaining concealed.
Then, having captured Śuka and Sāraṇa, he reported to Rāma that those two spies,
conquerors of enemy cities, had arrived at Laṅkā. Seeing them, Rāma was then distressed and despaired for his own life.
With palms joined in reverence and filled with fear, they spoke these words:
"O gentle one, O delighter of the Raghus, we two have come here sent by Rāvaṇa to ascertain the full extent of this entire army of yours."
Having heard those words of theirs, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, spoke these words with a smile:
"If you have seen our entire army, or if we have been well scrutinized..."
"Or, let the task as described be performed according to your own will.
Having entered the city of Laṅkā, you two must speak these words of mine, exactly as spoken, to the King of the Rākṣasas, the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth."
"Show that strength by which you carried off my Sītā, together with your army and your kinsmen, according to your desire;
tomorrow at the hour of day, [show it] to the city of Laṅkā, with its walls and its gateways."
"Behold the Rākṣasa army destroyed by my arrows!
O Rāvaṇa, restrain your strength as I unleash a terrible wrath,
like Vāsava wielding the thunderbolt against the Dānavas at the break of dawn."
Thus commanded, the two Rākṣasas, Śuka and Sāraṇa,
returned to the city of Laṅkā and spoke to the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"O Lord of Rākṣasas, we have been captured by Vibhīṣaṇa and are worthy of death."
6.016.023c Having seen that they were liberated by the righteous Rāma of immeasurable splendor, [the people rejoiced].
6.016.024a There, those four bulls among men, who resembled the guardians of the world, were gathered in one place— heroes skilled in weapons and firm in their prowess.
The illustrious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, Lakṣmaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa,
and Sugrīva, who possesses great splendor and valor equal to that of Mahendra—
these are capable of [overcoming] the city of Laṅkā, together with its walls and its gateways.
"Let all the monkeys stand aside to uproot and transport it;
let those three remain, for they alone shall slay that Rāma— such as he is in form and weaponry— and destroy the city of Laṅkā."
Protected by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva,
that army became more invincible than ever, even to all the gods and asuras;
the host of forest-dwellers appeared truly exultant.
Now that these great-souled ones desire to fight, enough with hostility; let peace be established,
and let Maithilī be restored to the son of Daśaratha.
6.017.001 Having heard those wholesome and resolute words spoken by Sāraṇa, King Rāvaṇa replied to Sāraṇa: 6.017.002 "Even if the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas should attack me..."
6.017.002c I will not give up Sītā, even out of fear of all the worlds.
6.017.003a But you, gentle one, are utterly terrified and have been thoroughly defeated by the monkeys;
6.017.003c therefore, you now consider it right to restore Sītā this very day.
"Who indeed among my enemies is worthy of defeating me in battle?
Having spoken these harsh words, the glorious Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas,
then ascended his palace, white as snow.
Then Rāvaṇa, desiring to see [them], rose to a height of many palm trees;
accompanied by those two spies, Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage,
gazed upon the ocean, the mountains, and the forests.
6.017.005e He beheld the region of the earth completely filled with monkeys. 6.017.006a Seeing that vast army of monkeys, boundless and innumerable, King Rāvaṇa questioned Sāraṇa.
Among these monkey chiefs, who are the heroes and who possess great strength?
Who are those of great energy who advance from all sides first?
Whom does Sugrīva listen to, and who are the leaders of the troop-leaders?
6.017.008c "Sāraṇa, tell me everything: which monkeys are the leaders?
6.017.009a Sāraṇa, knowing who the chiefs were, then related those forest-dwellers who were the leaders to the Lord of the Rākṣasas as he questioned him.
6.017.010a This monkey who stands facing Laṅkā, roaring aloud,
6.017.010c is surrounded by a hundred thousand troop-leaders.
6.017.011a By his great clamor, the city with its walls and its archways—
6.017.011c All of Laṅkā trembles, together with its mountains, forests, and groves.
6.017.012a This hero named Nīla, the leader of a troop, stands at the vanguard of the army of the high-souled Sugrīva, the lord of all the monkeys.
6.017.013a The heroic one, stretching out his arms, strides upon the earth with his feet;
6.017.013c facing toward Laṅkā, he yawns repeatedly out of anger.
6.017.014a Resembling a mountain peak, he has the hue of the filaments of a lotus.
Furious, he lashes his tail again and again,
so that by the sound of his tail the ten directions seem to resound;
he has been consecrated by Sugrīva, the king of the monkeys.
6.017.015e "Aṅgada by name, the crown prince, challenges you to battle.
6.017.016a "Those bull-like monkeys, having stiffened their limbs, roar and shout; 6.017.016c rising up, they stretch themselves with fury."
"These eight hundred thousand and ten billion fierce ones, difficult to withstand, violent, and of terrible prowess—
these heroes dwelling in Cāndana follow him."
6.017.018c He hopes to crush Laṅkā with his own army.
6.017.019a White, resembling silver, accompanied by his forces, and of terrible prowess—
this wise and heroic monkey is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having quickly approached Sugrīva, the monkey returns once more,
distributing the monkey army and gladdening the ranks.
He is the one who formerly used to roam the lovely mountain on the banks of the Gomatī.
6.017.021c There is a mountain named Saṃkocana, filled with various trees;
6.017.022a there this leader of the herd named Kumuda rules the kingdom,
6.017.022c he who leads a thousand times a hundred thousand [elephants].

The long tail of that one of terrible deeds supports hair that extends for many fathoms; copper-colored, yellow, white, and bright-white, it is scattered about. Undepressed, irascible, and fierce, he longs for battle.
6.017.024c This very one hopes to crush Laṅkā with his own army.
6.017.025a But this one who resembles a lion, tawny and with a long mane,
6.017.025c gazes intently at Laṅkā as if wishing to consume it with his eye.
O King, this troop-leader named Rambha constantly dwells upon the Vindhya, the Kṛṣṇagiri, the Sahya, and the Sudarśana mountain;
he has one hundred times one hundred thousand and thirty leaders of monkey-troops.
Surrounding Laṅkā, they pursue it to crush it with their might.
But he who keeps his ears open and yawns again and again,
who does not tremble at death and does not run away from the herd— [he is one of us].

O King, a leader of the herd named Śarabha— possessing great strength and free from fear— constantly dwells upon the beautiful Sālveya mountain. All the leaders of the herds belonging to this powerful one are known as the Vihāras.
O King, there were likewise four million of them.
He who stands there like a cloud covering the sky,
a great being in the midst of the monkey heroes, like Vāsava among the gods—
This great and terrible clamor, like the sounding of kettledrums,
is heard from the lords of the monkeys who long for battle;
he sits upon the unsurpassed Pāriyātra mountain.

In battle, he is ever difficult to withstand; his name is Panasa, a leader of the host (yūthapa). Fifty thousand [monkeys] attend upon him, the best of leaders, whose own troops are divided into groups.
But he who stands beautifying the formidable, surging army as it halts upon the shore of the ocean like a second sea—
this is the troop-leader named Vinata, who resembles Mount Dardara.
Drinking from the Parṇāśā, the supreme river among rivers, he roams about. His army consists of sixty hundred thousand monkeys;
a troop-leader named Krathana is challenging you to battle.
But that monkey who possesses a body with the hue of red chalk—
the spirited one named Gavaya— is advancing against you in anger;
seventy hundred thousand [monkeys] attend upon him.

6.017.039c He hopes to crush Laṅkā with his own army. 6.017.040a These are the formidable, powerful leaders of the hosts who can assume any form at will; they are the best among troop-leaders, and their number is unknown.
I shall describe those leaders of the troops to you as you observe them—
those who, for the sake of Rāghava, exerted their prowess and did not spare their own lives.
He whose glossy, dark-tawny young calves cling to his tail—
Copper-colored, yellow, reddish, and white, scattered about, the followers of this performer of terrible deeds shine like the rays of the sun when held aloft;
they are drawn across the earth by him who is named Hara, the leader of the herd.
6.018.004a Those who follow behind him by the hundreds and thousands, 6.018.004c lifting up trees together, intent on ascending Laṅkā;
6.018.005a this one [is followed] by ten billion monkeys of great prowess.
O conqueror of enemy cities, he desires to defeat you in battle.
As for those dark ones whom you see standing there like great blue clouds— men who resemble the color of black antimony and possess true prowess in combat— [they too seek victory].
6.018.007a Heroes who have claws and fangs as their weapons, fierce in anger and terrifying;
6.018.007c Innumerable and indescribable, like the further shore of the ocean;
6.018.008a And those who dwell upon the mountains and in whatever rugged places or rivers there may be.
"O King, these most dreadful ṛkṣas are advancing toward you.
Standing in their midst, O King, is one with terrifying eyes and a fearsome appearance,
surrounded on all sides like Parjanya by clouds."
6.018.010a He dwells upon Ṛkṣavān, the best of mountains, drinking from the Narmadā. 6.018.010c This leader of the herd, named Dhūmra, is the sovereign lord of all the bears.
6.018.011a Behold his younger brother, who resembles a mountain.
Equal to his brother in appearance, yet superior in prowess,
he is this one named Jāmbavān, the leader of great troop-leaders;
he is tranquil, obedient to his elders, and indomitable in battles.
By that wise Jāmbavān, a very great assistance was rendered to Śakra during the war between the gods and the asuras, and many boons were obtained;
having climbed to the mountain peaks, he brought down rocks as vast as massive clouds.
They release themselves in various forms and do not tremble before death;
some resemble Rākṣasas, while others are hairy like Piśācas—
many such beings, possessing the brilliance of fire, roam within his army.

6.018.016a All the monkeys behold him, the leader of leaders, standing there like one who has leaped up in agitation; 6.018.016c [they behold] him standing there, intensely excited, as if poised for flight.
6.018.017a O King, this lord of monkeys is attending upon the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra).
6.018.017c This troop-leader named Rambha is endowed with great strength;
6.018.018a as he moves, he brushes his side against a mountain standing a yojana away, 6.018.018c and likewise, when he travels upward, he reaches a height of one yojana with his body.
Because no superior form exists among those with four legs,
there was heard the name of the grandfather of the monkeys, known as Saṃnādana,
by whom that battle against Śakra was then waged in the field of combat, O wise one.

And yet he has not suffered defeat; this very one is the leader of leaders, whose prowess as he displays his valor is like that of Śakra himself. He was born of a Gandharva maiden by the Fire-god (Kṛṣṇavartman).
In ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, for the sake of assisting the inhabitants of heaven,
King Vaiśravaṇa took refuge upon that Jambū tree.
He is the king of the lords of mountains, who is served by many kinnaras.

"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, this glorious and powerful bull among monkeys, a leader of the host named Krathana who never boasts in battles, dwells there constantly providing his brother with the comfort of a residence."
Surrounded by a thousand crores of monkeys, he has arrived;
with his own army, he hopes to crush Laṅkā.
He who wanders along the Gaṅgā, terrifying the leaders of elephant herds.
Remembering the former enmity between the elephants and the monkeys,
this leader and guide of the herd, dwelling in mountain caves and foremost among the army of monkeys, proceeded along the Haimavatī river.
Residing upon Mount Uśīrabīja, which resembles Mount Mandara,
that best of monkeys rejoices like Śakra himself in heaven;
a thousand times a hundred thousand [monkeys] attend upon him.
"O King, this is the leader of the herd named Pramāthin, who is difficult to withstand.
This one whom you see before you, like a cloud driven up by the wind, is he who,
as he turns about repeatedly, raises this thick dust."
"These fierce and mighty black-faced golāṅgūlas,
numbering hundreds of hundreds of thousands, having seen the construction of the bridge,
[approached] the golāṅgūla leader named Gavākṣa, who possesses great speed."
Surrounding Laṅkā, they advance with might to crush it—
[the city] where trees that yield all desires are frequented by bees,
and which encircles that mountain whose luster is equal to the sun.
33. By whose light the beasts and birds always shine with that same color;
34. Whose plateau great-souled maharṣis never abandon—there, O King, this one delights on that beautiful golden mountain.

6.018.034c The leader of the monkey chiefs, a troop-leader named Kesari, [ruled]. 6.018.035a There were sixty thousand beautiful golden mountains; O sinless one, among them you are like the preeminent mountain for the Rākṣasas.
There, these tawny, white, copper-faced, and honey-brown monkeys dwell on the highest mountain, with sharp fangs and claws as their weapons;
like lions they have four tusks, and like tigers they are difficult to approach.
All were equal to Vaiśvānara in brilliance, resembling blazing venomous serpents;
with their long, curved tails, they resembled rutting elephants,
like great mountains, and possessed the roar of massive thunderclouds.
And this powerful one stands in their midst as their leader;
O King, he is renowned on earth by the name Śatabali. He alone hopes to crush Laṅkā with his own army.
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Nala, and the monkey Nīla—
