each one was surrounded by ten crores of troops.
Likewise, there were other foremost monkeys dwelling on the Vindhya mountains.
6.018.041c Because of their great number, those of swift prowess cannot be counted.
6.018.042a O Great King, all of them possess immense power;
all of them have bodies resembling massive mountains.
6.018.042c All of them were capable, in an instant, of making the earth one where the mountains were shattered and scattered;
6.019.001a Having heard the words of Sāraṇa, [they addressed] Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas.
Surveying the entire force, Śuka then spoke these words:
"Do you see those who stand here like maddened great elephants—
like banyan trees from the Ganges region, or like *sāla* trees from the Himalayas?"
6.019.003a O King, these are difficult to withstand, powerful, and able to assume any form at will; 6.019.003c they resemble Daityas and Dānavas, possessing the prowess of gods in battle.
6.019.004a Of them, there are nine thousand crores, as well as five and seven [crores].
Likewise, there were thousands of Śaṅkhas and hundreds of Vṛndas;
these ministers of Sugrīva always dwell in Kiṣkindhā. These monkeys, capable of assuming any form at will, were born from gods and Gandharvas.
Those two youths of divine form whom you see standing there,
Mainda and Dvivida— there is no one equal to them in battle.
Both have been consecrated by Brahmā and have partaken of the nectar of immortality.
These two hope to crush Laṅkā by their might through battle;
these two standing at their sides, resembling mountains,
are Sumukha and Vimukha, the sons of Death, equal to their father.
But that monkey whom you see standing there like an elephant in rut—
he who, when enraged, could by his might agitate even the ocean— is the one,
O Lord, who will come to Laṅkā for the sake of Vaidehī and yourself.
"Look at this monkey who has returned, whom you have seen before!
He is the eldest son of Kesarin, known as the son of the Wind;
he is celebrated as Hanumān, by whom the ocean was leaped across."
6.019.012a Capable of assuming any form at will, the best of monkeys was endowed with strength and beauty; 6.019.012c his movement was irresistible, like that of the Lord who is ever-moving.
6.019.013a Seeing the rising sun, the young one, it is said, became thirsty.
"Having descended for a journey of three thousand yojanas, I shall seize the sun; hunger shall not overcome me.
Thinking thus in his mind, he was formerly arrogant in his strength.
6.019.015a Even by gods, celestial sages, and dānavas, he was most invincible;
6.019.015c yet, without even reaching [his goal], he fell upon the mountain at the rising of the sun.
6.019.016a Of this monkey who has fallen, one jaw lies upon the surface of a rock.
"By his firm jaw, this one is indeed Hanumān, slightly different from him.
Truly, through the application of traditional knowledge (*āgama-yoga*), I have recognized this monkey;
it is impossible to describe his strength, form, or power."
6.019.018a This one alone hopes to crush Laṅkā by his might; 6.019.018c and this hero who follows him, dark-complexioned with eyes like lotuses,
6.019.019a is an Atiratha among the Ikṣvākus, whose prowess is renowned in the world.
He in whom dharma never wavers, who does not transgress dharma;
he who is the best among the knowers of the Vedas, knowing both the Brahma-weapon and the Vedas;
he who could pierce the sky with his arrows and even split mountains asunder.
"O King, this is that very Rāma who approaches you to fight, his wrath like that of Death and his prowess like that of Śakra.
And he who is on the right side, with the luster of pure gold— "
Broad-chested, with copper-hued eyes and dark, curly hair—
this is his brother named Lakṣmaṇa, as dear to him as his own life. He is skilled in both statesmanship and warfare, and is learned in all the scriptures.
Impatient, invincible, a conqueror, courageous, wise, and powerful,
he is Rāma’s right arm and his very life-breath moving outside his body;
for he does not spare his own life for the sake of Rāghava.

6.019.025c This very one hopes to slay all the Rākṣasas in battle. 6.019.026a But he who stands there, having taken his place on Rāma’s left flank, 6.019.026c surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas, is indeed King Vibhīṣaṇa.
He has been consecrated in Laṅkā by the illustrious Rājarāja;
provoked against you alone, he now advances for battle.
As for the one whom you see standing like an immovable mountain in the midst [of the army]—
The unconquered lord of all the monkeys of the branches,
who surpassed other monkeys in brilliance, fame, intellect, knowledge, and noble lineage,
just as the Himalaya mountain surpasses all other mountains.
He who dwells in Kiṣkindhā, a cave-city filled with dense trees,
difficult of access and situated in a mountain fastness, together with his principal troop-leaders;
he upon whom this golden garland, adorned with a hundred lotuses, shines resplendent.

6.019.031c She is beloved by gods and men, in whom prosperity is firmly established. 6.019.032a Having slain Vālin, Sugrīva was restored by Rāma to this very garland, to Tārā, and to the eternal kingdom of the monkeys.
"Thus, with ten billion and one hundred thousand stakes,
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, advances against you for the sake of battle.
Behold this army, O Great King!"
She stands present, like a blazing planet;
therefore, let the utmost effort be exerted so that there may be victory and no defeat by our enemies.
Having seen those leaders of the monkey hosts described by Śuka,
as well as his own brother Vibhīṣaṇa standing near Rāma,
and the highly heroic Lakṣmaṇa— who was like Rāma’s right arm— [he rejoiced].

With a somewhat agitated heart and filled with wrath, Rāvaṇa rebuked those two heroes, Śuka and Sāraṇa, at the conclusion of their conversation, [mentioning] Sugrīva, the king of all monkeys, who possesses terrifying prowess.
To Śuka and Sāraṇa, who stood bowed with their faces cast down, he,
agitated and speaking in a voice faltering with rage, addressed these harsh words:
"It is truly not fitting for ministers who subsist upon their master..."
To speak what is unpleasant to the lord regarding his restraint or favor, or toward hostile enemies advancing for the sake of battle—
to utter praise of both in an inappropriate context is indeed a contradiction.
6.020.007 Your teachers, elders, and preceptors have been served in vain, for you have not grasped that which is the essence of the treatises on statecraft—that which is to be lived by.
6.020.008 Or, even if it was grasped, it was not understood; this is called the burden of knowledge upon you.
"Endowed with such foolish ministers as these, by good fortune I still draw breath.
Is there no fear of death for me that you speak such harsh words to me— one whose tongue, while I rule, bestows both good and evil?"
Even after touching a fire, trees remain standing in the forest; yet those who have committed offenses do not remain when they have been touched by the king’s wrath.
I would slay these two wicked men who praise the side of the enemy.
6.020.011c If, despite my former services, my anger does not turn to gentleness,
6.020.012a Depart, go away from my presence! 6.020.012c For I do not wish to kill you two, remembering the favors you have done for me.
"Those two are indeed destroyers and ungrateful, having turned their backs on their affection for me.
When they were addressed in this way, both Śuka and Sāraṇa, filled with shame,
greeted Rāvaṇa with cries of victory and departed.
6.020.014a That ten-necked one spoke to Mahodara, who was standing nearby:
6.020.014c "Quickly bring me spies who are experts in statecraft. 6.020.015a Then, by the king's command, the spies arrived in great haste.
Having approached with palms joined in reverence and having offered him blessings of victory,
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, then addressed these words to those trustworthy,
heroic, devoted, and fearless spies:
"Go from here and examine Rāma’s resolve—
those who are his intimate counselors and who have joined him out of affection.
Observe how he sleeps, how he wakes, and what else he intends to do."
Having understood everything skillfully, one should act without omission; for when an enemy is known through spies by wise lords of the earth,
he is encountered and cast out with very little effort in battle.
Having said "So be it" to the Lord of the Rākṣasas, those spies, filled with joy,
circumambulated him and departed for where Rāma was with Lakṣmaṇa.
They [found] Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa near Mount Suvela.
Having gone there in disguise, they saw him together with Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa. Those Rākṣasas were seen by the righteous-souled lord of the Rākṣasas,
and while staying there, they were seized at will by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Harassed by those monkeys of great prowess and swift stride,
they returned once more to Laṅkā, panting and deprived of their senses;
then they approached the Ten-necked One.
The spies, who constantly roamed outside and traveled even at night, being possessed of great strength, reported that he of fearsome power was residing near Mount Suvela.

Then, spies reported to the lord of Laṅkā that Rāghava, whose strength was unshakeable, had encamped upon Mount Suvela. Upon hearing from the spies that the mighty Rāma had arrived, Rāvaṇa [was informed].
Slightly agitated, he spoke these words to Śārdūla:
"O night-stalker, your complexion is unnatural and you appear dejected;
have you perhaps fallen under the power of your enraged enemies?"
Thus instructed by him, that tiger among monkeys, overwhelmed by fear, then uttered these words softly to the tiger among rākṣasas:
"O King, those bulls among monkeys cannot be driven away."
6.021.005c Valiant and powerful, they are protected by Rāghava.
6.021.006a They cannot even be spoken to; no inquiry can be obtained here.
6.021.006c The path is guarded on all sides by monkeys who resemble mountains.
As soon as I had entered, I was recognized by that Bala even before he had acted;
seized by force by many, I was torn apart in many ways. I was struck violently with knees, fists, teeth, and palms.
"I have been carried away by powerful and impatient monkeys;
having been carried off, I was led everywhere until I reached the assembly of Rāma,
my entire body smeared with blood, overwhelmed, and my senses agitated."
6.021.010a While being struck by the monkeys and supplicating with palms joined in reverence,
6.021.010c I have been rescued by Rāghava and live on by sheer chance.
6.021.011a Here he is, having filled the great ocean with mountains and boulders.
Rāma stands at the gate of Laṅkā, armed with weapons;
having assumed the Garuḍa formation and being surrounded on all sides by monkeys,
that one of great splendor has sent me away and is advancing toward Laṅkā itself.
"Before he reaches the rampart, quickly prepare one [of the two options]:
either give Sītā to him immediately, or offer him a fair fight.
Upon hearing this, the lord of the Rākṣasas was deeply distressed in his mind.
Then Rāvaṇa spoke these great words to Śārdūla:
"Even if the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas were to fight against me,
I would not give up Sītā, even out of fear of all the worlds."
Having spoken thus, the immensely radiant Rāvaṇa spoke again:
"Your army has been traversed by you; who among those monkeys are heroes?
What are those monkeys like, and what is their power, that they are so difficult to approach?"
"Whose sons and whose grandsons are they? Tell me the truth, O Rākṣasa.
Having learned their relative strength and weakness, I shall decide my course of action there. One who desires war must certainly calculate the number of forces."
6.021.019a Then, having been thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, that excellent spy Śārdūla began to speak these words in the presence of Rāvaṇa.
6.021.020a Now, O King, the son of Ṛkṣarajas was exceedingly difficult to defeat in battle.
6.021.020c Now, Gadgada’s son here was renowned as Jāmbavat.
6.021.021a Another son of Gadgada was Guruputra, [the son] of Śatakratu,
6.021.021c by whose single son the slaughter of the rākṣasas was accomplished.
And Suṣeṇa, the virtuous and powerful son of Dharma;
and here, O King, is the gentle monkey Dadhimukha, the son of Soma;
and also Sumukha, Durmukha, and the monkey Vegadarśin.
"Surely Death himself was created by the Self-Existent One in the form of a monkey; furthermore,
Nīla is himself the son of Agni and the commander of the army,
and here is Hanumān, renowned as the son of Anila."

The youthful Aṅgada, the grandson of Śakra, is invincible and powerful; both Mainda and Dvivida are mighty, born of the Aśvins. Here also are the sons of Vaivasvata, who resemble the five Ages and Antaka (Death) himself.
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana;
and here also Śveta and Jyotirmukha, who were born from the self of Bhāskara;
furthermore, Hemakūṭa, the son of Varuṇa, was a leaper.

The heroic Nala, son of Viśvakarman and best among the monkeys, is courageous, swift, and difficult to restrain; he is here, a son of the Vasus. And there are ten crores of heroic monkeys who long for battle.
"I do not venture to describe the rest of the illustrious sons of the gods.
This youth, with the powerful build of a lion, is the son of Daśaratha;
by him Dūṣaṇa was slain, as well as Khara and Triśiras."
6.021.031a There is no one on earth equal to Rāma in prowess,
6.021.031c by whom Virādha was slain, as well as Kabandha, who resembled Death itself.
6.021.032a No man on this earth is able to fully describe the virtues of Rāma.
By him, while in Janasthāna, so many Rākṣasas were slain;
and here is the righteous Lakṣmaṇa, like a bull among elephants,
in whose path of arrows even Vāsava could not live.
"And your brother Vibhīṣaṇa, the most excellent of the Rākṣasas,
having taken possession of the city of Laṅkā, is devoted to the welfare of Rāghava.
Thus has all this regarding your monkey army been related to you.
"Established upon Mount Suvela, you are the refuge for the remaining task.
Then, the king's spy reported to him that Rāghava, whose strength is unshakeable, had taken up his position on Mount Suvela in Laṅkā.
6.022.002a Upon hearing from his spies that the mighty Rāma had arrived, 6.022.002c Rāvaṇa became somewhat anxious and spoke thus to his ministers:
6.022.003a "O counselors, let all of you come quickly, with your minds fully composed."
"O Rākṣasas, this time for counsel has indeed arrived for us.
Having heard that command of his, the ministers quickly approached;
then he held a consultation together with those Rākṣasa counselors.
Having consulted with them, that invincible one,
having immediately dismissed his ministers, entered his own abode.
Then, he summoned the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva.
The master of great illusions entered the abode of the master of illusions where the princess of Mithilā was.
Then the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke to Vidyujjihva, who was skilled in magic:
"We shall delude Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, by means of illusion."
"O night-stalker, take Raghava’s illusory head and present yourself before me with that great bow and arrow.
Thus addressed, the night-stalker Vidyujjihva replied, "So be it."
The king was pleased with him and bestowed ornaments upon him.
Then the mighty one entered the Aśoka grove;
there, the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) beheld her, who was dejected though she deserved not to be so.
Seated upon the ground with her face cast downward, overcome by grief,
she had gone to the Ashoka grove and was meditating only upon her husband,
attended nearby by terrible Rakshasa women.
Then, approaching Sītā and proclaiming his name with great joy,
he spoke these bold words to the daughter of Janaka:
"O blessed lady, whom you rely upon and for whom you exult while being comforted by me?"
"O Sītā, that Rāghava, the slayer of Khara, has been killed by you in battle;
the very root of your existence has been severed from all sides, and your pride has been destroyed by me.
Through your own misfortune, O Sītā, you shall become my wife."

"O Sītā, listen to the terrible slaying of your husband, which was like the slaying of Vṛtra, concerning that one of little merit, whose purpose has failed, who is deluded, and who fancies himself wise. Rāghava has indeed arrived at the edge of the ocean to kill me."
Surrounded by a vast army led by the lord of monkeys,
Rāma, having reached the southern shore of the ocean, encamped there as the sun was setting with his great host.
Then, having encountered my army— which was exhausted from the journey, stationed at midnight,
and sleeping soundly— the first watch was patrolled by scouts.
That [army] was then attacked by my great force led by Prahasta.
His strength was destroyed at night where Rāma and the noble Lakṣmaṇa were;
[he saw] pattas, iron clubs, swords, discs, great iron staffs,
nets of arrows, spears, radiant mallets, and spiked hammers.
6.022.021a Staves, javelins, spears, discuses, and clubs—
6.022.021c having been raised again and again, they were hurled by the *rakṣasas* upon the monkeys.
6.022.022a Then, while Rāma was asleep, by Prahasta the destroyer...
With unhesitating hand, his head was severed by a great sword;
then Vibhīṣaṇa, leaping up, seized him by chance,
and Lakṣmaṇa was driven away in all directions along with all the monkeys.
6.022.024a Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, lies with his neck broken;
6.022.024c Hanumān, struck down by the Rākṣasas, lies with his jaw dislocated.
6.022.025a Then Jāmbavān, rising up on his knees, was slain in battle.
Cut by many strips of cloth, like a tree lopped off at the base,
both Mainda and Dvivida, those two bulls among monkeys, were slain;
sighing and weeping, they lay drenched in blood.
Struck and cut in the middle with a sword by the destroyer of enemies,
Panasa thunders upon the earth like a ripe jackfruit.
Cut down by many iron shafts, Darīmukha lies in a mountain cave.
But the highly energetic Kumuda, having been struck by arrows while crying out, was slain;
and Aṅgada, having been assailed by many Rākṣasas with numerous shafts, was cut to pieces,
vomiting blood, and fell prostrate upon the earth.
6.022.030a Some monkeys were crushed by elephants, while others were likewise struck down by masses of chariots;
6.022.030c they lay there, trampled, like clouds scattered by the force of the wind.
6.022.031a Others, terrified and being slain from behind, fled away.
Chased by the rākṣasas like great elephants by lions,
some fell into the ocean, while others took refuge in the sky;
the bears, mingled with the monkeys, climbed up into the trees.
On the shores of the ocean, on the mountains, and in the forests,
those many tawny-eyed ones were slain by many deformed-eyed ones.
Thus has your husband, along with his army, been killed by my forces.
"This head of hers, wet with blood and covered in dust, has been brought here.
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, who was exceedingly difficult to overcome,
spoke these words to a rākṣasī while Sītā was listening.
"Bring here the Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva, who performs cruel deeds,
by whom that head of Rāghava was personally brought back from the battle.
Then Vidyujjihva took that head along with the bow.
Having prostrated with his head, he stood before Rāvaṇa. Then King Rāvaṇa spoke to that Rākṣasa, Vidyujjihva of the great tongue, who was standing nearby.
"O son of Daśaratha, quickly place the head of Sītā before you,
so that the wretched woman may properly behold the final state of her husband.
When he had spoken thus, that Rakṣasa presented the head, which was pleasant to behold.
Having placed it near Sītā, he quickly vanished;
and Rāvaṇa also cast down a great, radiant bow,
famous throughout the three worlds, and spoke thus to Sītā.
"This is that very bow of yours, Rāma, still equipped with its string,
which was brought here by Prahasta after he had slain that human being in the night.
It was brought along with that head [of Mārīca] by Vidyutjihva."
Having cast his bow upon the ground, Rāvaṇa then spoke to the illustrious daughter of the King of Videha: "Become subject to my will."

6.023.001 Seeing that head and that excellent bow, as well as the account of Sītā’s reunion with Sugrīva related by Hanumān, 6.023.002 and seeing eyes and the complexion of the face— his face being just like her husband’s— Sītā [was filled with hope].
Recognizing his hair, the parting of his hair, and that auspicious crest-jewel by all these identifying marks, she,
being deeply distressed,
lamented Kaikeyī, crying out like a female osprey.
"6.023.004a Your desire is fulfilled, Kaikeyī; this delight of the lineage has been slain.
6.023.004c The entire family has been destroyed by you, who are fond of strife. 6.023.005a What unpleasant thing indeed was done to Rāma by the noble Kaikeyī?"
"Because she, clad in bark garments, was sent from the house to the forest by him.
Having spoken thus, the ascetic Vaidehī, trembling,
the young woman went to the ground like a severed plantain tree.
After a moment, having regained her composure and recovered her consciousness, that large-eyed woman smelled his head and lamented:
"Alas! I am destroyed, O mighty-armed one, I who was devoted to the vow of a hero."

"6.023.008c I have reached this final state of yours and have been made a widow. 6.023.009a For a woman, the first death is said to be the failure of her husband; yet you, who were of excellent conduct, have passed away before me, you who were ever virtuous."
6.023.010a For you, who were prepared to rescue me as I have fallen from sorrow to sorrow and am submerged in an ocean of grief— 6.023.011a even you,
O Raghava, have been struck down by me, your mother Kausalyā, who is my mother-in-law.

Just as a cow, though fond of her calf, is made to feel abandoned when deprived of her calf; O you of inconceivable prowess, those by whom a long life was predicted for you have spoken a falsehood, for you are short-lived, O Rāghava.

"Or rather, even though you are wise, your wisdom has perished; for time cooks all beings, as it is indeed the source of all creatures. Having encountered death—which is unseen—why do you, who are a knower of the treatises on policy, remain [unmoved]?"

6.023.014c For you are indeed skilled and knowledgeable in the means of avoiding calamities; 6.023.015a yet, having been closely embraced by me— that fierce and most cruel Night of Doom— you, the lotus-eyed one, were snatched away and taken from me.
"O mighty-armed one, O bull among men, you have abandoned me, a poor ascetic woman, and lie upon the earth as if it were a beautiful and beloved wife.
This bed of yours, which has been constantly honored by me with great effort with perfumes and garlands— "
"O hero, this bow adorned with gold is dear to me;
O sinless one, you have surely met in heaven with my father Daśaratha, your father-in-law, and your ancestors."
"O you who have become a constellation in the heavens, you have performed a great and pleasing deed;
yet you utterly neglect your own lineage of royal seers.
Why do you not look at me, O King? Why do you not answer me?"
I am a young girl who has come to you as a child, your wife and companion.
Remember that which was promised by you when you took my hand, saying, "I shall walk [this path] with you," O descendant of Kakutstha; take me too, for I am suffering.
"O best among those who possess a goal, why have you departed from this world to that other world, leaving me here in sorrow,
after having been embraced by me alone— that which is worthy of the virtuous?"
"Your body is surely being torn apart now by flesh-eating creatures.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees,
why will you not receive the consecration through the Agnihotra?"
Of the three who have entered the life of renunciation, one has arrived;
Kausalyā, overwhelmed with grief, will question Lakṣmaṇa regarding the slaughter of your friend’s army as she interrogates him.
He shall tell her, as she questions him, of that destruction of your ally’s forces.
"Surely they will tell you of your slaughter by the rākṣasas during the night.
Hearing that you were killed while asleep and that I have gone to the abode of the rākṣasa,
O Rāghava, she will cease to exist with her heart torn asunder."
"O Rāvaṇa, quickly cast me down upon Rāma!
Unite husband with wife; perform this supreme act of merit. Join his head with my head, and his body with my body."
"O Rāvaṇa, I shall follow the path of my high-souled husband;
I do not wish to live for even a moment with one who lives such a sinful life.
I heard this from the Veda-knowing brahmins in my father's house."
6.023.030c For those women whose husband is dear, their worlds are of great prosperity.
6.023.031a In whom there is forgiveness, self-control, renunciation, truth, righteousness, gratitude,
6.023.031c and non-violence toward all beings— without him, what refuge is there for me?
6.023.032a Thus, tormented by grief, that large-eyed daughter of Janaka lamented; 6.023.032c for she beheld there her husband’s head and his bow.
6.023.033a While Sītā was thus wailing there, the Rākṣasa—
Standing in his chariot and with palms joined in reverence, he approached his master;
having saluted him and sought his favor by saying, "May you be victorious, O noble son," he announced that Prahasta, the commander of the army, had arrived.
"Accompanied by all his ministers, Prahasta has arrived;
there is some urgent matter for them, so please grant them an audience.
Having heard this report from the Rākṣasa, the Ten-necked One [responded].
Leaving the Aśoka grove, he went to see his ministers.
Having deliberated with his ministers on all that was to be done for himself,
and having recognized Rāma’s prowess, he entered the assembly hall and took action.
That head and that supreme bow vanished immediately after Rāvaṇa’s departure.
But the lord of the Rākṣasas, together with those ministers of fearsome prowess—

Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, who resembled Time itself, confirmed his resolve regarding Rāma’s task and spoke to all the well-wishing army commanders standing nearby: 6.023.039c He then confirmed his determination for Rāma’s destruction. 6.023.040a To all the well-wishing commanders of the forces standing not far away, 6.023.040c Rāvaṇa, the sovereign of the rākṣasas, who was like Time itself, spoke.
"Quickly, with the sound of kettledrums struck by resonant sticks, assemble my troops, and no reason need be given. Then,
accepting those words with "So be it," they departed.
Those commanders of forces, having assembled their own great armies and gathered them together,
reported this to their lord who was longing for battle.
6.024.001a Seeing Sītā thus bewildered, a Rākṣasī named Saramā,
a dear and affectionate friend, quickly approached the princess of Videha. 6.024.002a For she had been made a friend there by Sītā while she was being guarded.
Protecting herself from Rāvaṇa, beloved, compassionate, and firm in her vows,
she saw her friend Sītā, who had lost consciousness,
as Saramā saw a mare that had risen after rolling in the dust.

6.024.004a Her virtuous friend consoled her with affection, [saying]: "O timid one, everything that was said to you by Rāvaṇa and everything that you yourself replied has been promised by me out of friendship for my friend. 6.024.005a O timid one, out of love for my friend, all of that has been undertaken by me.
6.024.005c Having hidden in the hollow of the mountain, casting aside fear of Rāvaṇa,
6.024.005e for your sake, O large-eyed one, my life is indeed not dear to me.
6.024.006a It was for your sake that the lord of the Rākṣasas emerged in such agitation.
6.024.006c And all that is known to me, O Maithilī, after my departure from home.
6.024.007a It is not possible to carry out a night-attack upon Rāma, who is self-knowing; 6.024.007c and his slaughter would only be appropriate against that tiger among men [Rāvaṇa].
Moreover, those monkeys who fight with trees cannot be slain,
for they are well protected by Rāma, just as the gods are protected by the Bull among the Gods.
He is long-armed, handsome, broad-chested, and full of majesty.
A bowman endowed with a firm physique, righteous in soul, and renowned throughout the earth;
valiant, he is a constant protector of both himself and others;
together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he is well-being personified and learned in the treatises on statecraft.
"O Sītā, the glorious Rāghava, the slayer of enemy hosts, possessed of inconceivable strength and prowess, and the destroyer of his foes,
has not been killed by one who acts with unwise intent and opposes all living beings."
6.024.012c This illusion was employed against you by the fierce one, who is skilled in illusions. 6.024.013a All your sorrow has vanished; prosperity has come to you.
6.024.013c Fortune will surely attend you; listen to what is pleasing and delightful.
6.024.014a Having crossed the ocean with the army of monkeys, Rāma,
6.024.014c having reached the southern shore of the sea, has encamped there.
6.024.015a "I have seen that descendant of Kakutstha, together with Lakṣmaṇa, his purpose fully accomplished."
He remains protected by forces stationed as far as the edge of the ocean;
and those rākṣasas of swift prowess sent by him have brought back this report here: "Rāghava has crossed over."
"O large-eyed lady, having heard that news, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, is consulting with all his ministers. Speaking thus, the rākṣasī Saramā remained with Sītā.
With all his effort, he heard the terrifying roar of the armies;
hearing the great sound of the kettledrum sounding like the stroke of a staff,
Saramā, speaking sweetly, said this to Sītā:
For this terrifying kettledrum, O timid one, is the progenitor of battle array;
hear the deep resonance of the drum, sounding like the roar of clouds. The rutting elephants are being prepared, and the chariot horses are being yoked.
Here and there, armored foot-soldiers rushed together;
the royal highways were filled with armies of wondrous appearance,
like the ocean by its surging, roaring torrents of water.
Behold the various colors of light arising from the bright weapons, from shields and armor, and from the chariots, horses, elephants, and the adorned Rākṣasas as they discharge their radiance.
Just as is the nature of fire when it consumes a forest,
hear the resonance of the bells, hear the sound of the chariots,
and hear the neighing of the horses and the sound of the musical instruments.
This tumultuous and hair-raising agitation of the rākṣasas, whose hands hold upraised weapons as they follow the lord of the rākṣasas, has arisen;
may Fortune, who destroys sorrow, attend you, for fear has come upon the rākṣasas.

O lotus-petal-eyed one, having conquered Rāvaṇa in battle— whose prowess is inconceivable and who has mastered his anger— he will come to you as your husband, just as Vāsava came forth from among the Daityas.
Your husband, together with Lakṣmaṇa, will display his prowess against the Rākṣasas,
just as Śatrughna does among his enemies when accompanied by Viṣṇu and Vāsava; for when Rāma has arrived, you shall quickly be placed upon his lap in your virtuous state.
"I shall see you successful when the enemy has been struck down; O beautiful one,
you shall shed tears born of joy upon meeting and embracing the chest of that broad-chested man."
"O Goddess Sītā, before long the mighty Rāma will loosen this braid of yours, which has been held upon your hips for many months. O Queen,
having beheld his face like the risen full moon— "
6.024.033c You shall shed the water born of grief, like a female serpent casting off its skin.
6.024.034a Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle before long, O Maithilī,
he who deserves happiness shall obtain it in its entirety with you as his beloved.
"Having united with the high-souled Rāma, you shall rejoice,
just as the earth rejoices when joined with a bountiful rain and its crops.
[He] follows along the slopes of the great mountain."
O Goddess, seek refuge here with him who swiftly traces a circle like a horse;
for he is the maker of day and the source of light for all creatures.
6.025.001 Then Saramā gladdened her, who was tormented by grief and bewildered by those words, just as the sky refreshes the earth with rain.
6.025.002 Then, desiring to do what was beneficial for her friend, the friend spoke these words.

6.025.002c At the proper time, she who knew the right moment spoke with a smile: 6.025.003a "O dark-eyed one, I am able to go and deliver your message; 6.025.003c after reporting my welfare to Rāma, I shall return in disguise."
"Indeed, as I move through the supportless sky, neither the wind nor even Garuḍa is capable of following my course. To Saramā,
who was speaking thus, Sītā replied once more:
With sweet and gentle words, though overcome by prior grief, you said:
"Though you are capable of traveling through the sky or even to the subterranean realm,
I understand that what you have done for my sake was something that ought not to have been done."
6.025.007a If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, and if your resolve is firm,
6.025.007c I desire to go and learn for myself what that Rāvaṇa is doing.
6.025.008a For that cruel Rāvaṇa, who makes his enemies cry out, possesses the power of illusion.
This evil-minded one deludes me, like *vāruṇī* liquor as soon as it is drunk. He constantly threatens me and repeatedly reviles me,
even though he is guarded at all times by most terrible *rākṣasa* women.
I am anxious and apprehensive, and my mind is not at ease;
it is out of fear of that [news] that I have come to this Ashoka grove. Whether it be mere talk or something certain regarding him—whatever it may be—[it troubles me].
"6.025.011c You should report all of that; it would be a supreme favor to me.
6.025.012a To Sītā, who was speaking thus, Saramā, the sweet-voiced one, spoke these words while touching her, who was overwhelmed with tears."
"O Jānakī, if this is your intention, then I shall go;
having ascertained the enemy's purpose, you shall see me returned.
Having spoken thus, he then went into the presence of that Rākṣasa.
She heard it recounted by him, Rāvaṇa, together with his ministers.
Having heard the resolve of that evil-minded one,
she who was skilled in discerning intentions then returned quickly once more to the Aśoka grove.
6.025.016a Having entered there once more, she saw the daughter of Janaka,
6.025.016c waiting for her very self, like the goddess Śrī fallen from her lotus.
6.025.017a Sītā, however, [beheld] Saramā, who had arrived again and spoke so sweetly.
Having embraced her very affectionately, he himself offered her a seat:
"Sit here comfortably and tell me everything in truth regarding the cruel resolve of that evil-minded Rāvaṇa."
Thus addressed by the trembling Sītā, Saramā related everything that had been said to Rāvaṇa and his ministers: "Indeed,
the Lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these great words to his mother for the sake of your liberation."
And, O Vaidehī, having been enlightened by the uncorrupted elder minister, [he said]:
"Let Maithilī be given with due honor to the lord of men.
Your own example in Janasthāna is sufficient proof of that wonder."
"Who on earth could leap across the ocean, behold Hanumān,
and slay the rākṣasas in battle?
Thus was he addressed extensively by his aged ministers and his mother."

"O Maithilī, he does not dare to release you, just as one intent on his own welfare cannot bear to release a victim in distress; for it is his firm resolve that even an immortal would not dare to release you from battle,
along with his ministers and his cruel nature."
Therefore, this firm resolve has arisen in him out of greed for death; yet,
out of fear, he is unable to abandon you in battle,
for he fears the slaughter of all the Rākṣasas as well as his own.
"O dark-eyed one, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle by all means with sharpened arrows,
Rāma will lead you back to Ayodhyā.
In that interval, there arose a sound tumultuous with kettledrums and conchs.
Having been heard by all the armies, it made the surface of the earth tremble.
But having heard that sound of the monkey army,
the servants of the Rākṣasa king who were in Laṅkā [were alarmed].
Deprived of their vigor, their movements overwhelmed by dejection,
they saw no good fortune due to the king's faults.
Then, Rāghava [heard] that sound of kettledrums mingled with the sound of conchs.
6.026.001c As the mighty-armed Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, approached,
6.026.002a Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, having heard that roar,
6.026.002c remained in meditation for a moment and then looked toward his ministers.
Then Rāvaṇa, the one of great strength, having addressed all those ministers there, spoke thus, making the entire assembly resound:
"The crossing of the ocean, as well as valor and the accumulation of forces— "
"What you have said regarding Rāma has been heard by me;
and I also know you both to be of true prowess in battle.
Then, however, a very wise rākṣasa named Mālyavat spoke.

6.026.005c Having heard Rāvaṇa’s words, the grandfather of his mother spoke: 6.026.006a “O King, that monarch who is thoroughly trained in the sciences and follows the path of policy 6.026.006c rules over sovereignty for a long time and brings his enemies under his control.”
For by making peace at the proper time and waging war against his enemies,
while increasing his own side, he enjoys great sovereignty. A king who is declining, as well as one who is equal [to his foe], should make peace.
"One should not despise an enemy; one who is superior should avoid conflict.
Therefore, O Rāvaṇa, an alliance with Rāma appeals to me.
Let Sītā, for whose sake we have been attacked, be restored to him."
"All the celestial rishis and the gandharvas, desiring victory for you, say:
'Do not enter into conflict with him; let an alliance with him be pleasing to you.
For the Blessed Grandfather indeed created only two sides."
6.026.011c Righteousness and unrighteousness depend upon those two [sides] for both the gods and the asuras.
6.026.012a For righteousness is heard to be the side of the high-souled gods,
6.026.012c while unrighteousness is the side of the Rākṣasas and the asuras, O Rāvaṇa.
"Righteousness indeed swallows unrighteousness; from that, the Kṛta age arises. Unrighteousness swallows righteousness; from that, the Tiṣya age proceeds.
But while you were wandering through the worlds, that great righteousness was destroyed by you."
"6.026.014c Unrighteousness has been embraced by him, and because of that, our enemies have become stronger than we are.
6.026.015a That unrighteousness, having increased through his negligence, is indeed swallowing us like a serpent; 6.026.015c and he, the benefactor of the gods, increases the faction of the gods."
"By you, who were attached to sensual objects and acted recklessly, a great agitation has been caused among the seers who are like fires;
their power is invincible, like a blazing fire."
6.026.017 With their selves purified by austerity and devoted to the favoring of dharma,
these twice-born ones constantly perform various principal sacrifices. 6.026.018 They offer oblations into the fires according to the rules and recite the Vedas aloud.
Having overwhelmed the *rakṣasas*, they raised the sound of Vedic chanting;
all the *rakṣasas* fled in every direction like thunder at the end of the hot season.
[The sound] arose from the *agnihotra* sacrifices of the seers who were like fires themselves.
The smoke, pervading the ten directions, takes away the splendor of the *rākṣasas*.
And in those various holy places,
the intense austerity being practiced by those of firm vows causes the *rākṣasas* to burn with heat.
Having seen various portents and likewise many kinds of terrible omens,
I foresee the destruction of all the rākṣasas. The clouds, emitting harsh and dreadful peals of thunder, are most terrifying.
They rain down hot blood everywhere upon Laṅkā;
and from the weeping mounts, drops of tears fall.
The banners are shattered and discolored, no longer shining as they did before.
6.026.024a Beasts of prey, jackals, and vultures howl most terrifyingly;
6.026.024c having entered Laṅkā incessantly, they gather in great numbers.
6.026.025a Dark-skinned women stand before them, laughing with their white teeth bared.
In dreams, women, having spoken [ominously], plunder houses;
dogs consume the sacrificial offerings of the dwellings;
donkeys are born from cows, and mice with mongooses.
Cats joined with leopards, pigs with dogs,
and even kinnaras with rākṣasas and humans;
white birds with red feet, impelled by Time, [flew about].
Doves wander about for the destruction of the Rākṣasas; female mainas, perched within the houses, warble "cīkī kūcī"; and even sparrows, seeking quarrels, fall down entangled as if defeated.
Terrible, hideous, shaven-headed, and dark-brown in hue—
a personification of Time— surveys the houses of all at every appointed hour.
These and other such evil omens are arising.
6.026.031a We consider Rāma to be Viṣṇu, who has assumed a human body.
6.026.031c For this Rāghava of firm prowess is by no means merely human.
6.026.032a By him was that most wonderful bridge built across the ocean.
"O Rāvaṇa, make peace with Rāma, the king of men. Having spoken these words there, Mālyavat again examined the mind of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
6.026.033c Among those who were unsurpassed, the powerful one of supreme prowess remained silent, having gazed at Rāvaṇa.
6.027.001a But as for those beneficial words spoken by Mālyavat, the Ten-faced One—
6.027.001c The evil-minded one, having fallen under the sway of Time, could not endure it.
6.027.002a Having come under the power of anger, he knit his brows upon his face;
6.027.002c with eyes rolling in indignation, he then spoke to Mālyavat.
6.027.003a When harsh words, though intended for one's benefit, are spoken,
6.027.003c having entered the camp of the enemy, they do not even reach my ears. 6.027.004a [He speaks of] the wretched human Rāma, alone and dependent on the monkeys.

"By what means do you consider me capable [of harm], who have been abandoned by my father and dwell in the forest? (6.027.004c) And why do you consider me, the lord of the *rākṣasas* and a source of terror to the gods, to be deficient, when I am not lacking in any heroic prowess? (6.027.005ab–c)

I suspect that I have been addressed with such harsh words by you either out of hatred for a hero, or out of partiality for an enemy, or perhaps because you were incited by another. For who would speak harshly to one who is powerful and established in his position?
"A wise man who knows the true nature of the scriptures, even without encouragement from an enemy,
having brought Sītā back from the forest like the goddess Śrī deprived of her lotus—
why should I return her out of fear of Rāghava?"
"Surrounded by millions of monkeys, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa—
behold Rāghava slain by me within a few days,
he against whom even the gods cannot stand in single combat."
"Why then would Rāvaṇa entertain fear in battle? Even if I were to break in two, I would never bow down to anyone.
This is my innate flaw; my nature is difficult to overcome."
6.027.012 If a bridge were built across the ocean by Rama merely by chance, what cause for wonder would there be in that, such that fear has come upon you?
6.027.013 For Rama, together with the army of monkeys, has already crossed the great ocean.
"I promise you this truly: he shall not return alive.
Perceiving Rāvaṇa speaking thus, agitated and enraged, Mālyavān was ashamed and did not offer any further reply.
Having honored the king with appropriate blessings of victory,
Mālyavat, having received permission, departed for his own residence.
But Rāvaṇa, together with his ministers, having deliberated and reflected, [proceeded].
The Rākṣasa caused incomparable defenses to be constructed in Laṅkā. He stationed the Rākṣasa Prahasta at the eastern gate,
and the two of great prowess, Mahāpārśva and Mahodara, at the southern gate.
Then, at the western gate, he likewise commanded his son Indrajit,
who possessed great illusory powers and was surrounded by many rākṣasas;
and having assigned Śuka and Sāraṇa to the northern city gate, [he gave orders].
"I myself shall be there," he said to those ministers.
Then he stationed the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa, who possessed great heroism and prowess,
in the central division along with many other Rākṣasas.
Having made such arrangements in Laṅkā, that bull among Rākṣasas,
having fallen under the power of Death, considered himself to have achieved his purpose;
he then dismissed his ministers.
Having ordered the extensive preparations for the city and being honored with a multitude of mantras and blessings of victory,
he entered his magnificent inner apartments.
The king of men and the king of monkeys, that monkey son of the Wind, Jāmbavān the king of bears, the Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa,
Aṅgada the son of Vālin, the son of Sumitrā, and the monkey Śarabha— [all these were there].
Suṣeṇa with his kinsmen, Mainda, and Dvivida;
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Kumuda, Nala, and likewise Panasa—
having reached the territory of the enemy, they gathered together and took counsel.
6.028.004a This is that city of Laṅkā seen before us, protected by Rāvaṇa;
6.028.004c it is difficult to conquer even for the Asuras, Uragas, Gandharvas, and the immortals.
6.028.005a Keeping the accomplishment of our purpose foremost, deliberate upon the final decision.
"For Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, is always present here.
While they were speaking thus, Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, spoke words that were refined in their phrasing and rich in meaning.
6.028.007 My ministers Anala, Śarabha, Saṃpāti, and Praghasa went to my city, Laṅkā, and have now returned here again.
6.028.008 Having all become birds, they entered the enemy's army.
Having seen that which was ordained as the plan, they have assembled here.
O Rāma, listen to me as I relate everything exactly as it happened, concerning the arrangements made by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
6.028.010a Previously, Prahasta stood having reached the eastern gate with his forces; 6.028.010c and at the southern gate were the two of great heroism, Mahāpārśva and Mahodara.
6.028.011a Indrajit, surrounded by many Rākṣasas, occupied the western gate.

Surrounded by thousands of Rākṣasas with weapons in their hands— heroes bearing swords, bows, and shields, and holding spears and mallets in their grasp— the son of Rāvaṇa was encircled by many warriors equipped with various implements of war.
6.028.013a Prepared and deeply agitated, surrounded by many rākṣasas,
6.028.013c Rāvaṇa himself took his station at the northern city gate. 6.028.014a Virūpākṣa, however, [stood] with a great force equipped with spears, swords, and bows.
6.028.014c With his forces, together with the Rākṣasas, he took his position in the central division.
6.028.015a Having observed such divisions as these in Laṅkā,
all my ministers have quickly returned here once again.
In that city there were a thousand elephants, ten thousand chariots,
twenty thousand horses, and more than ten million Rākṣasas—
valiant, powerful, and intent on striking down their enemies in battle.
6.028.017c These night-rangers are always beloved by the king of the rākṣasas.
6.028.018a O lord of the people, for each individual rākṣasa here who is set upon battle, 6.028.018c an entourage of a thousand times a thousand [soldiers] attends upon him.
6.028.019a Having heard this report from Laṅkā as told by the ministers,
Vibhīṣaṇa spoke these words in reply to Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals: 6.028.020a "O Rāma, when Rāvaṇa fought against Kubera..."
Then sixty hundred thousand rākṣasas marched forth, equal in prowess, valor, splendor,
and weight of character to the evil-minded Rāvaṇa himself in their arrogance.
"In this matter, you should not feel anger; I do not seek to provoke you nor to frighten you.
For you are indeed capable by your own prowess of subduing even the gods. Therefore, may you proceed surrounded by a great fourfold army."
"Having arrayed this army of monkeys, you shall crush Rāvaṇa. When the younger brother of Rāvaṇa had spoken these words, Rāghava spoke these words for the purpose of repelling the enemies.
At the eastern gate of Laṅkā, Nīla, the bull among monkeys,
surrounded by many monkeys, shall be the opponent of Prahasta. Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, however, shall be surrounded by a great force.
Let Mahāpārśva and Mahodara guard the southern gate;
let Hanumān, the son of the Wind, whose soul is immeasurable, enter the western gate after pressing down upon it,
surrounded by many monkeys.
He is a base man who delights in harming the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas as well as the high-souled sages; endowed with the power of a boon,
he wanders through all the worlds, afflicting all living beings.
I myself am resolved to slay that lord of the rākṣasas. Together with the son of Sumitrā, I shall press against the northern city gate and enter where Rāvaṇa is, accompanied by my forces.
Let the powerful lord of monkeys and Jāmbavān, the king of the bears,
as well as the younger brother of the lord of the Rākṣasas, be stationed in the central division.
Furthermore, the monkeys must not assume human forms in the battle.

"Let this be our designation in this battle against the monkey force: let the monkeys themselves be the mark for those among our own people. As for us, we seven shall fight the enemies as mere mortals."

"I myself, along with my brother Lakṣmaṇa of great prowess, and this friend of mine, Vibhīṣaṇa, as the fifth— [these shall go] for the sake of accomplishing the task. Having spoken thus to Vibhīṣaṇa, that Rāma—
The wise one then set his mind upon ascending Mount Suvela.
Thereupon, the high-souled Rāma, having covered the entire earth with his great army, [proceeded].
With a joyful appearance, that high-souled one set out for Laṅkā, having resolved upon the slaughter of his enemy;
he then made up his mind to ascend Mount Suvela.
6.029.001c Followed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma spoke these words to Sugrīva,
6.029.002a And to Vibhīṣaṇa, the night-stalker who knows dharma, is devoted, 6.029.002c And who is skilled in counsel and ritual procedure, with gentle and supreme speech.
"Let us all ascend this excellent Suvela, the king of mountains, adorned with hundreds of minerals; we shall spend this night here and survey Laṅkā, the abode of that Rākṣasa."
"By that evil-minded one, my wife has been carried off to the very brink of death;
by him who knows neither dharma, nor proper conduct, nor his own lineage,
and who, with the base intellect of a Rākṣasa, has committed such a despicable act."
6.029.006a My wrath increases when that lowest of Rākṣasas is mentioned; 6.029.006c because of the offense of that base wretch, I shall witness the slaughter of the Rākṣasas.
6.029.007a For it is only one person who commits evil, having fallen under the power of the noose of Time.
"By his own base misconduct, that family is being destroyed.
While thus deliberating with anger toward Rāvaṇa,
Rāma ascended Mount Suvela, with its variegated peaks, to take up residence there.
Behind him, Lakṣmaṇa followed with a concentrated mind,
raising his great bow with an arrow fixed to it, intent upon valor.
Sugrīva, along with his ministers and Vibhīṣaṇa, ascended after him.
Hanumān, Aṅgada, Nīla, Mainda, and Dvivida;
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana; Panasa, Kumuda, Hara, and Rambha the troop-leader.
These and many other swift-moving monkeys,
who range the mountains and possess the speed of the wind,
ascended by the hundreds onto Mount Suvela, where Rāghava was.
6.029.013a But in no long time, having ascended the mountain from all sides,
they beheld upon its peak a city as if suspended in the sky. 6.029.014a It was beautiful, with excellent gates and adorned by a magnificent wall.

6.029.014c The leaders of the monkey hosts beheld Laṅkā, filled with rākṣasas. 6.029.015a And they saw those dark night-stalkers stationed upon the massed ramparts; 6.029.015c those best of monkeys also beheld another wall that had been constructed.
Seeing those Rākṣasas eager for battle, all the monkeys let out loud roars while Rāma looked on. Then the sun, colored by the twilight, went to its setting.
And the night, with the full moon as its lamp, was drawing to a close.
Then Rāma, the lord of the monkey host,
was greeted and honored by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and surrounded by a multitude of troop-leaders,
he dwelt at his ease upon the ridge of Suvela.
Having spent that night there on Suvela, those bulls among monkeys remained.
In Laṅkā, the heroes beheld forests and groves— level, gentle, delightful, vast, and extensive;
seeing those sights pleasing to the eye, they were filled with wonder.
It was filled with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *sāla*, and *tāla* trees;
it was covered by groves of *tamāla* and surrounded by rows of *nāga* trees. It abounded with flowering *hintāla*, *arjuna*, *nīpa*, and *saptaparṇa* trees.
With *tilaka*, *karṇikāra*, and *paṭala* trees on all sides,
their tops in full bloom and entwined with creepers, Laṅkā shone with various divine trees like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Adorned with various flowers and tender red shoots, with dark-green meadows and variegated forest ranges,
the blossoms and fruits were fragrant and delightful.
There the sacred scriptures abide, like ornaments upon men.
That forest, resembling Caitraratha and comparable to Nandana, was beautiful, delightful,
filled with bees, and possessed of the splendors of every season.

The sound of *natyūha* and *koyaṣṭika* birds, as well as dancing peacocks and the warbling of cuckoos, was heard by the mountain stream; likewise, there were birds that were perpetually intoxicated and the humming of bees.
6.030.010c There were groves crowded with cuckoos and filled with the songs of various birds;
6.030.011a they were celebrated by *bhṛṅgarāja* birds and frequented by bees; 6.030.011c they resounded with the cries of *koṇālaka* birds and the calls of cranes.
Then those heroes, the monkeys who could assume any form at will, entered those forests and groves, joyful and exceedingly delighted.
As those monkeys of great prowess were entering there, [the following occurred].

A breeze, fragrant from contact with flowers and pleasing to the sense of smell, blew pleasantly. Meanwhile, other troop-leaders among the monkey heroes, having emerged from their respective divisions and being authorized by Sugrīva, marched toward Laṅkā, which was adorned with banners.
Terrifying the birds and frightening the deer and elephants,
those best of roarers made Laṅkā tremble with their own shouts;
possessing great speed, they caused the earth to be oppressed by their movement.
6.030.016c And the dust, kicked up by his feet, rose suddenly into the air.
6.030.017a Bears, lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and deer—
terrified by that sound, they fled in fear toward the ten directions.
But the single peak of Trikūṭa was lofty and touched the heavens;
it was covered on all sides with flowers, resembled great silver,
was a hundred yojanas in extent, stainless, and beautiful to behold.
Smooth, glorious, and vast, it is difficult to reach even for birds;
it is hard to ascend even in thought, let alone by people through physical action.
There, upon that peak, stands Laṅkā, protected by Rāvaṇa.
That city, adorned with high gate-towers resembling white clouds,
and beautified by enclosures of gold and silver,
was exceedingly magnificent with its palaces and celestial mansions; such was Laṅkā.
Like the middle station of Viṣṇu when the heat has subsided, thick with clouds;
upon it a palace was adorned with a thousand pillars,
resembling the peak of Kailāsa, appearing as if it were scraping the sky.

That monument of the lord of the rākṣasas became an ornament of the city, which was constantly guarded by a full hundred rākṣasas. To that prosperous city, the fortunate elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, who had achieved all his goals, [proceeded].
6.030.025c Rāma, together with the monkeys, beheld the city of Rāvaṇa. 6.030.026a It was filled with jewels, possessed many arrangements,
and was adorned with rows of palaces.
6.030.026c Rāma, with his great army, beheld the city whose principal gates were fitted with massive mechanical engines;
6.031.001a Then, having observed certain omens in that place, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa—
He spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with splendor:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, taking possession of cool water and fruit-bearing forests, let us remain here after dividing this flood of troops and arranging them in battle formation."
"I behold a terrifying danger at hand that will bring about the destruction of the world—
a slaughter of the foremost heroes among the bears, monkeys, and rākṣasas.
The winds blow harshly, and the earth trembles."
The mountain peaks tremble and the earth-supporting mountains fall. Clouds resembling carnivorous beasts, harsh and emitting harsh sounds, rain cruelly, pouring down a mixture of drops of blood.
Resembling red sandalwood, the twilight is most dreadful;
this blazing orb of fire falls from the sun,
and as it howls toward the sun, it generates great terror.
The beasts and birds are wretched, uttering piteous cries, and are ominous and ill-omened;
moreover, the moon, lacking its usual brilliance during the night,
causes distress like the sun at the end of an eon, its rays appearing dark and reddish at the edges.

6.031.009a The halo around the sun is short, rough, and inauspicious, and it is deep red; O Lakṣmaṇa, a blue mark is seen upon the solar disc. 6.031.010a The constellations are not visible as they should be, and they appear to be moving astray.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, behold this which foretells the end of the world as it were;
crows, hawks, and vultures are swooping down from on high,
and jackals are uttering inauspicious cries with great sound."
"Surrounded on all sides by the monkeys, let us today swiftly attack with speed that invincible city protected by Rāvaṇa.
Speaking thus to Lakṣmaṇa, the heroic elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa—

6.031.013c Therefore, the mighty one quickly descended from the mountain peak. 6.031.014a Having descended from that mountain, the righteous Rāghava beheld his own army, which was exceedingly difficult for enemies to overcome.
6.031.015 Having equipped the great army of the king of monkeys along with Sugrīva,
Rāghava, who knew the proper time, urged them toward battle at the opportune moment.
6.031.016 Then, at that time, the mighty-armed one, surrounded by a vast force, set forth.
Having set out toward the city of Laṅkā with his bow in hand,
Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Nala,
the king of the bears, as well as Nīla and Lakṣmaṇa, then followed behind him.
Thereafter, a vast army of bears and forest-dwellers followed behind Rāghava, covering the great expanse of the earth;
they carried hundreds of mountain peaks and massive trees.
The monkeys, who resembled elephants and were capable of resisting enemy forces, seized [the fruit].
Then, in no long time, those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
the subduers of their enemies, reached Laṅkā, the city of Rāvaṇa.
Adorned with garlands of banners, delightful, and beautified by gardens and groves;
possessing variegated ramparts, difficult to approach, and featuring high walls and gateways— that city,
unassailable even by the gods, was [entered] by those urged by the words of Rāma.
6.031.022c Having pressed together according to their instructions, the forest-dwellers took up their positions.
6.031.023a At the northern gate of Laṅkā, which was as lofty as a mountain peak,
Rāma, the archer, along with his younger brother, both guarded and besieged it.
6.031.024a And Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having arrived at Laṅkā,
6.031.024c the hero followed by Lakṣmaṇa, reached the city ruled by Rāvaṇa.
6.031.025a Having reached the northern gate, he stood where Rāvaṇa was stationed.
"Indeed, no one other than Rāma is capable of guarding that gate,
which is occupied by the fearsome Rāvaṇa like the ocean by Varuṇa,
and is protected on all sides by Rakṣasas bearing weapons."
It was like the netherworld (pātāla) filled with dānavas, causing terror to the small-hearted;
and he beheld many various collections of weapons and likewise armor laid out by the warriors.

6.031.028a But first, having reached the eastern gate, the powerful Nīla, the commander of the monkey army, 6.031.028c stood there together with Mainda and Dvivida. 6.031.029a The exceedingly mighty Aṅgada seized the southern gate.
The powerful monkey Hanumān guarded the western gate together with Ṛṣabha, Gavākṣa, Gaja, and Gavaya, joined by Pramāthin, Praghasa,
and other heroes.
And Sugrīva himself took his position at the central division,
together with all the foremost of monkeys who were like Garuḍa and the wind.
There were thirty-six crores of monkeys, each a renowned troop-leader.
And Sugrīva, the monkey, was stationed there, pressing closely against them;
by the command of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, together with Vibhīṣaṇa,
stationed ten million monkeys at every gate.
To the west of Rāma, Sugrīva, together with Jāmbavat and followed by a great force, took his position in the central division not far away. Those tigers among monkeys were like fanged tigers.
Seizing trees and mountain peaks, they stood ready for battle with joy;
all had deformed tails, all were armed with fangs and claws,
all had strangely variegated limbs, and all had distorted faces.
Some possessed the strength of ten elephants, while others were ten times greater still;
some became equal in prowess to a thousand elephants. Some possessed the strength of a flood, while others were a hundred times greater than that.
And there were other leaders of the monkey hosts there, possessed of immeasurable strength;
their gathering was both wonderful and diverse,
like the emergence of a swarm of locusts from the monkey armies.
The sky seemed completely filled and the earth covered by the monkeys who had settled upon and were descending toward Laṅkā;
there were hundreds of hundreds of thousands of separate groups of bears and forest-dwellers.
6.031.041c Others approached the gates of Laṅkā from all sides to do battle.
6.031.042a That mountain was completely covered on every side by all those monkeys;
6.031.042c and ten million of them surrounded that city.
Surrounded on all sides by powerful monkeys with trees in their hands, Laṅkā became impenetrable even to the wind;
the Rākṣasas, suddenly overwhelmed, were filled with amazement.
With monkeys resembling clouds and possessing prowess equal to that of Śakra,
a great roar arose there from the surging flood of the army,
like the sound of the waters of the ocean when it is broken apart.
By that great sound, all of Laṅkā, including its walls and gate-towers, as well as its mountains, forests, and groves, was shaken;
so too was the army protected by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva.

She became more difficult to overcome than ever by all the gods and asuras alike. Having thus stationed his own army for the slaughter of the Rākṣasas, Rāghava consulted with his ministers and deliberated again and again.
Desiring to achieve the immediate [success], he who knew the truth of the sequential application of means,
with the consent of Vibhīṣaṇa and recollecting the duty of kings,
summoned Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, and spoke as follows.
"O gentle monkey, having gone to the Ten-necked one, speak my words to him—
having leaped across the city of Laṅkā, casting off fear and being free from distress—
to him whose fortune has fallen, whose sovereignty is gone, who is about to die, and whose mind is lost."

O night-stalker, whatever sin has been committed through delusion by one who is arrogant— whether toward the seers, the deities, the gandharvas and apsarases, the nāgas, the yakṣas, or kings— that [is known] by you, O Rākṣasa.
Surely today the pride born from the boon granted by the Self-Existent One has vanished,
since I, the wielder of the rod of punishment, have been humbled by the abduction of your wife and stand stationed at the gate of Lanka holding that very rod.
"O Rākṣasa, slain by me, you shall go the path of the gods, the great ṛṣis, and all the royal seers. By that very power and through which illusion you [abducted] Sītā, O lowest of Rākṣasas!"
"Having bypassed me, you have carried her away; show yourself!
I shall rid this world of Rākṣasas with my sharpened arrows, unless you come to me for refuge, taking Maithilī with you."
6.031.057a This Vibhīṣaṇa, the best of the Rākṣasas, who is righteous in soul, has arrived.

6.031.057c This illustrious one shall surely obtain the sovereignty of Laṅkā, free from all thorns. 6.031.058a For it is not possible for you to enjoy the kingdom even for a moment through unrighteousness.
"It is possible for one who has evil companions, who is foolish, and whose self is unsubdued;
but fight, O Rākṣasa, summoning your resolve and relying on your heroism! Once you have been laid to rest in battle by my arrows, you will then become purified."
"Even if you enter the three worlds as a bird, swift as thought, once you have come within the range of my vision, you shall not return alive.
I speak these words for your benefit: let the funeral rites be performed."
"Take a final look at Laṅkā; your life depends upon me.
Thus addressed by Rāma of unwearied deeds, Tārā’s son entered the sky and departed like the embodied sacrificial fire.
In a mere moment, the illustrious one, having leapt across to Rāvaṇa’s palace,
beheld Rāvaṇa seated calmly with his ministers.
Then, that bull among monkeys alighted not far from him.

Aṅgada, adorned with golden armlets, stood there like a blazing fire. Having introduced himself by his own hand, he caused all those excellent words of Rāma— neither deficient nor redundant— to be heard by him along with his ministers.
"I am a messenger of Rāma, the lord of Kosala, whose deeds are untiring. You have likely heard of Aṅgada, the son of Vālin.
Rāghava Rāma, the increaser of Kausalyā’s joy, speaks to you."
"Come out and fight me, you cruel one, lowest of men!
I shall slay you along with your ministers, sons, kinsmen, and relatives.
When you are killed, the three worlds will be free from anxiety."

"Today I shall uproot this enemy of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as this thorn in the side of the sages. And when you have been slain, sovereignty shall belong to Vibhīṣaṇa."
"If you do not respectfully bow down and restore Vaidehī,"—
while that bull among monkeys was speaking these harsh words,
the lord of the hosts of night-stalkers fell under the sway of indignation.
Then, his eyes copper-red with rage, he commanded his ministers repeatedly:
"Let this evil-minded one be seized; let him be put to death! Hearing these words of Rāvaṇa, whose splendor was like a blazing fire, [the ministers acted].
Then four terrible night-rangers seized him; at that time,
the hero, son of Tārā, himself by his own power caused himself to be captured in order to demonstrate his strength to the host of Yātudhānas.
Seizing those who clung to his two arms like birds, Aṅgada then leapt up from the palace, which resembled a mountain;
shaken by his speed, those Rākṣasas were cast out from the sky.

6.031.076c They all fell to the ground while the lord of the Rākṣasas looked on. 6.031.077a Then that palace pinnacle, as lofty as a mountain peak, 6.031.077c shattered when he stepped upon it, even as Daśagrīva watched.
Having shattered the pinnacle of the palace and proclaimed his own name,
he let out a tremendous roar and leapt into the sky.
Rāvaṇa, however, was filled with supreme rage because of the assault upon his palace.
Perceiving his own destruction, he became lost in deep sighs.
But Rāma, surrounded by many joyful, shouting monkeys,
advanced for battle, desiring the slaughter of his enemy.
But the monkey Suṣeṇa, of great prowess and resembling a mountain peak,
was there surrounded by many monkeys who could assume any form at will;
and by the command of Sugrīva, that monkey [secured] all the four gates.
The invincible one advanced like the moon among the stars.
Having observed those forest-dwellers— numbering a hundred akṣauhiṇīs—
who had encamped at Laṅkā and were crossing over the ocean.
6.031.084 Some Rākṣasas were filled with amazement, while others were seized with terror; yet others, out of their martial exultation, became even more defiant.
6.031.085 For the entire space between the ramparts and the moats was completely covered by the monkeys.
The dejected rākṣasas beheld the rampart turned into monkeys. While that most terrifying clamor was raging in the capital of the rākṣasas, [the city was thrown into chaos].
Seizing their great weapons,
the *rākṣasa*s rushed about like the winds at the end of an eon. Then those *rākṣasa*s went there to Rāvaṇa’s palace.
They reported that the city was besieged by Rāma along with the monkeys.
Hearing that the city was besieged, the night-stalker was filled with rage;
hearing that the defenses were doubled, he ascended the palace.
He beheld Laṅkā, with its mountains, groves, and forests,
covered on all sides by innumerable hosts of monkeys eager for battle;
seeing the entire earth thus swallowed up by the vanaras.
"How might they be destroyed?"— thus he became absorbed in thought.
Having reflected for a very long time and summoning his fortitude, the large-eyed Rāvaṇa gazed upon Rāghava and the leaders of the monkey hosts.
While the lord of the rākṣasas looked on, those divisions of the army,
desiring to do what was pleasing to Rāghava, then ascended toward Laṅkā.
Having copper-colored faces and golden luster, they were ready to sacrifice their lives for the sake of Rāma.
6.032.007c They turned back toward Laṅkā itself, armed with *sāla* trees, *tāla* trees,
and rocks. 6.032.008a With trees, mountain peaks, and their fists, those monkeys crushed the high tops of palaces and the arched gateways.
The monkeys filled the moats, which were filled with clear water, with earth, mountain peaks, grass, and wood. Then,
leaders of thousands of troops and leaders of ten-million-strong troops [arrived].
Then another hundred million yoked together ascended Laṅkā;
the monkeys crushed the golden archways and demolished the gate-towers that resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.
Leaping, bounding, and roaring, those monkeys, resembling great elephants, rushed toward Laṅkā.
"Victorious is the exceedingly powerful Rāma, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa! they cried.
"King Sugrīva, protected by Rāghava, is victorious!"—
shouting and roaring thus, the monkeys,
who could assume any form at will, rushed toward the rampart of Laṅkā.
Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, and Nala, who roams the forest—
these leaders of the monkey troops settled down after pressing against the rampart.
In the meantime, they established their military camp.

6.032.017a But Kumuda, surrounded by ten *koṭis*, stood at the eastern gate, 6.032.017c the powerful one, having taken his position with his monkeys who looked like victors. 6.032.018a Having approached the southern gate, the heroic monkey Śatabali—

The powerful Suṣeṇa, the father of Tārā, went to the western gate; surrounded by twenty crores, that mighty monkey stood there, having blocked the way. Surrounded by sixty crores, that powerful one stood there, having blocked the way.
Having reached the northern gate with the son of Sumitrā, the mighty Rāma stood there, as did Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys;
and Golāṅgūla, who was of massive body, Gavākṣa, of fearsome appearance.

Surrounded by ten million [monkeys], the highly heroic Dhūmra, the destroyer of enemies, stood at Rāma’s side with a host of monkeys of terrible speed. Surrounded by ten million [monkeys], the highly heroic one stood at Rāma’s side.
But the immensely powerful Vibhīṣaṇa, of great heroism, stood there clad in armor with mace in hand,
surrounded by those ministers:
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana.
6.032.024c Running about on all sides, they protected the army of monkeys.
6.032.025a Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, his soul overcome with anger,
6.032.025c immediately ordered the departure of his entire army.
Then, urged by Rāvaṇa, the troops rushed forth joyfully,
like the surging currents of the great ocean when it is filled at the proper time.
In that interval, a terrible battle ensued.
Like the battle between the gods and the asuras in ancient times, there was a conflict between the rākṣasas and the vānaras.
With blazing maces, spears, tridents,
and axes, those terrible rākṣasas struck down the vānaras while proclaiming their own prowess.
Likewise, with trees and mountain peaks, the monkeys— those great-bodied ones—
along with the *rākṣasas*, impetuously attacked those *rākṣasas* with their claws and teeth.
But other terrifying *rākṣasas*, stationed upon the ramparts, [attacked] those on the ground.
With slings, swords, and spears, they tore [the enemy] apart;
and the monkeys, filled with rage, whether stationed on the ramparts or standing upon the ground,
leaped forward and struck down the Rākṣasas.
That tumultuous battle between the *rākṣasas* and the monkeys, a mire of flesh and blood, became like a marvel. Then,
as those high-souled monkeys continued to fight...
Then, a most terrible fury of power arose among the *rakṣasas*.
They [advanced] with horses adorned with golden crests, with banners resembling tongues of fire,
with chariots brilliant as the sun, and with beautiful armor.
The tiger-like rākṣasas went forth, making the ten directions resound—
rākṣasas of fearsome deeds who desired victory for Rāvaṇa. And the great army of the monkeys also set out, longing for victory.
He rushed toward that army of Rākṣasas, who could assume any form at will. In the meantime, as they were charging at one another,
a duel broke out between the Rākṣasas and the monkeys.
The immensely powerful Rākṣasa Indrajit fought with Aṅgada, the son of Vāli, just as Andhaka once fought with Tryambaka; and Saṃpāti,
ever intolerant in battle, fought with Prajaṅgha.
The monkey Hanumān also set out against Jambūmālin; meanwhile,
the Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, joined the fray with great fury against the friend-slayer Mitraghna, who possessed fierce speed in battle.
The immensely powerful and highly energetic Nīla fought with the Rākṣasa Tapanas, while along with Nikumbha;
and Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, encountered Praghasa.
The illustrious Lakṣmaṇa encountered Virūpākṣa in battle;
and the invincible Agniketu, the Rākṣasa Raśmiketu,
Suptaghna, and Yajñakopa were all engaged with Rāma.
Vajramuṣṭi, shining like a thunderbolt, encountered Mainda; and Aśaniprabha met Dvivida—those two foremost of monkeys came face to face with two most terrible Rākṣasas.
The heroic Pratapana was a fierce Rākṣasa, difficult to withstand in battle.
In the battle, he fought with Nala of fierce speed;
the powerful son of Dharma, renowned as Suṣeṇa,
that great monkey, fought together with Vidyunmālin.
Other fearsome monkeys, together with other rākṣasas,
encountered one another in various duels for battle against many foes.
There occurred a truly great battle, tumultuous and hair-raising.

6.033.016c From the bodies of the heroic Rākṣasas and Vanaras who desired victory, 6.033.017a rivers of blood flowed forth from the corpses of monkeys and demons, with hair for their grassy meadows and carrying away heaps of carcasses.
Enraged, Indrajit struck the heroic Aṅgada— the tearer of enemy armies— with his mace, just as Śatakratu struck with his thunderbolt;
he destroyed his chariot, which was adorned with gold, along with its horses and charioteer.
In that battle, the glorious and impetuous monkey Aṅgada struck him down.
Sampāti, however, having been struck by Prajaṅgha with three arrows,
slew Prajaṅgha at the forefront of the fray with an *aśvakarṇa* tree.
But Jambumali, the mighty one standing upon his chariot,
being enraged in battle, pierced Hanuman between the breasts with a chariot-spear.
Hanuman, the son of the Wind, mounting that very chariot of his, [proceeded].
Then, together with that very *rākṣasa*, he quickly struck him with his palm. With his limbs pierced by the sharp arrows of the swift-handed *rākṣasa*,
he struck Tapana with a mountain peak, as an elephant strikes with its trunk.
Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, pierced and struck Praghasa— who was devouring the armies as it were— with a *saptaparṇa* tree,
after having oppressed that Rākṣasa of fearsome appearance with a shower of arrows.
With a single arrow, Lakṣmaṇa struck down Virūpākṣa. Then the invincible Agniketu, the Rākṣasa Raśmiketu,
Suptighna, and Yajñakopa pierced Rāma with their arrows.
In that battle, the enraged Rāma severed the heads of those four with four terrible arrows resembling tongues of fire.
But Vajramuṣṭi was struck down in the fray by Mainda’s fist.
6.033.028c Together with his chariot and horses, he fell to the ground like a city tower.
6.033.029a Dvivida, whose touch was like a thunderbolt, struck Aśaniprabha with a mountain peak while all the rākṣasas looked on.
But he, who possessed the brilliance of a thunderbolt, pierced Dvivida, the lord of monkeys who fights with trees in battle, with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
With his limbs deeply pierced by those arrows, Dvivida was overcome with rage.

With a *sāla* tree, he struck down [the demon] who possessed the brilliance of a thunderbolt, along with his chariot and horses. But Nikumbha, in that battle, pierced Nīla— who had the luster of a mass of black collyrium—
with sharp arrows, just as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.
Then, with a hundred more arrows, the swift-handed night-stalker Nikumbha pierced Nīla in battle and laughed aloud; meanwhile,
Nīla [struck him] with his chariot wheel in the fray, like Viṣṇu.
In that battle, he severed the head of Nikumbha’s charioteer;
then Vidyunmālin, standing upon his chariot, struck Suṣeṇa with arrows adorned with gold and roared again and again.
Then, seeing him standing upon the chariot, Suṣeṇa, the best of monkeys,
swiftly struck down the chariot with a great mountain peak. However,
the night-stalker Vidyunmālī was endowed with such agility.
Quickly leaping down from his chariot, mace in hand, he stood upon the ground.
Then Suṣeṇa, that bull among monkeys, overcome with rage,
seized a massive boulder and rushed toward the night-stalker.
As he was rushing forward, the night-stalker Vidyunmālin swiftly struck Suseṇa, the best of monkeys, on the chest with his mace.
That foremost of monkeys disregarded that terrible blow from the mace.
In that great battle, he caused that rock to fall upon his chest.
Struck by the blow of the rock, the night-stalker Vidyunmālin fell to the ground, lifeless, his heart crushed to pieces.
Thus, by those heroic monkeys, those heroic night-rangers were crushed in single combat there, like the Daityas by the gods,
with broad-headed arrows, swords, maces, spears, javelins, and pattisas.
Scattered and broken were the war chariots and horses; likewise,
there were slain rutting elephants, as well as monkeys and Rākṣasas, along with wheels, axles, yokes, and poles, all shattered and lying upon the earth.
The battlefield became terrible, frequented by packs of jackals; headless trunks of monkeys and rākṣasas sprang up in all directions during that tumultuous clash,
which was like the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then, being torn apart by the bulls among monkeys,
the night-stalkers, their limbs smeared with blood,
once again resorted to fierce combat with great vigor.
While those monkeys and rakshasas were still fighting, longing for the setting of the sun,
the sun went down and a life-taking night began.
