6.034.002a Among those fierce beings who harbored mutual enmity and desired victory, 6.034.002c a night-battle between the elephants and the *rākṣasas* then commenced.
6.034.003a "He is a *rākṣasa*! cried the monkeys; "And he is a monkey! cried the *rākṣasas*.
In that terrible darkness, they struck one another in battle. "Kill! "Tear asunder! "Why do you flee?"—such was the tumultuous clamor heard in that darkness.
In that darkness, the Rākṣasas, clad in golden armor,
appeared like great mountains with forests of glowing medicinal herbs. In that impenetrable darkness, the Rākṣasas were frantic with rage.
They rushed forward with great speed, devouring the monkeys;
those beasts of terrible wrath, leaping up, tore apart the horses adorned with golden crests and the banners resembling tongues of fire with their sharp teeth.
6.034.008a Elephants and elephant-riders, as well as chariots adorned with banners and standards,
6.034.008c were dragged and bitten by their tusks by those who were frantic with rage.
6.034.009a And Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma [struck them] with arrows resembling venomous serpents.

They struck down the foremost *rākṣasas*, both those visible and invisible. The dust of the earth, raised by the rims of chariot wheels and kicked up by the hooves of horses, obstructed the ears and eyes of those fighting.
6.034.011 While that terrible, hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
rivers of blood with great velocity flowed there. 6.034.012 Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, clay drums, and small drums.
6.034.012c Mixed with the sounds of conchs and flutes, it became a wondrous spectacle.
6.034.013a And the roar of the slain and the groaning Rākṣasas, along with the sound of weapons and the cries of the monkeys, became exceedingly terrible.
And that battlefield there was strewn with offerings of weapons and flowers;
it was difficult to discern, hard to traverse, and mired in the mud of flowing blood.
That night became terrible, carrying away both monkeys and rākṣasas.
Like the Night of Doom for all living beings, she was difficult to overcome.
Then those Rākṣasas, in that terrible darkness,
rushed joyfully toward Rāma with showers of arrows.
The sound of those [demons] as they rushed forward, roaring in their fury,
was like the roar of the seven oceans when they overflow.
With six arrows, Rāma struck down six of those night-stalkers.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, with sharp arrows resembling flames of fire,
the invincible Yajñaśatru struck Mahāpārśva, Mahodara,
Vajradaṃṣṭra, and those two of massive body, Śuka and Sāraṇa.
Struck by Rāma with a flood of arrows in all their vital organs,
they retreated from the battle, their lives remaining only partially spent.
Then, with arrows whose shafts were variegated with gold and which resembled the flames of fire—
The one of great strength made the cardinal directions and the intermediate points clear.
But those other heroic rākṣasas who stood facing Rāma also perished upon encountering him, like moths in a fire.
With thousands of gold-feathered arrows falling,
the night became as variegated as an autumnal sky filled with fireflies;
it was further filled with the roars of the Rākṣasas and the shouts of the monkeys.
That night became terrible, and at that time it became even more terrifying.
Because of that great sound swelling on all sides,
the mountain Trikūṭa, filled with caves, seemed to roar aloud.
6.034.026a Great-bodied golangulas, possessing a luster equal to darkness,
6.034.026c embraced the night-stalkers with their arms and devoured them; 6.034.027a Aṅgada,
however, stood ready in battle to slay the enemy.
Rāvaṇa’s son swiftly struck down both the charioteer and the horses.
But Indrajit, his horses slain and his charioteer killed, abandoned the chariot; that master of great illusion vanished right there before Aṅgada.
That wicked son of Rāvaṇa, fierce in battle, vanished from sight; that hero, the son of Rāvaṇa, who had received a boon from Brahmā, was overcome with rage and,
remaining invisible, loosed sharpened arrows possessing the brilliance of thunderbolts.
Enraged in battle, that Rākṣasa pierced both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in all their limbs with terrible arrows made of serpent-venom. Seeking his path, the powerful prince—
The exceedingly powerful Rāma commanded ten leaders of the vanara hosts:
the two heirs of Suṣeṇa, Nīla the bull among monkeys, Aṅgada the son of Vālin, and the swift Śarabha.
The scorcher of enemies commanded Vinata, Jāmbavān, the mighty Sānuprastha, Ṛṣabha, and Carṣabhaskaṇḍha.
Those monkeys, greatly delighted, uprooted formidable trees.
They all entered the sky, searching through the ten directions; the son of Rāvaṇa, skilled in weapons, checked the speed of those swift ones with even swifter arrows using his supreme weapon.
6.035.006a The monkeys, though wounded and mangled by iron shafts, could not see him because of his terrifying speed, just as one cannot see the sun obscured by clouds in the darkness.
6.035.007a [He discharged] arrows that pierced every vital organ of both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
The son of Rāvaṇa, victorious in battle, violently overwhelmed them both.
The two heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, their bodies covered without interval by the arrows that had become serpents, were tormented by the enraged Indrajit.
From the wounds of those two, much blood flowed;
both of them shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Then, with his eyes reddened at the corners and resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, [he appeared].

6.035.010c Having become invisible, the son of Rāvaṇa spoke these words to his two brothers: 6.035.011a "Even Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods, would not be able to see or approach you while you are fighting and remain unseen; how much less so could you two?"
"During the rainy season, with a net of arrows feathered with heron plumes, I shall send these two Raghavas— whose souls are overcome by rage— to the abode of Yama.
Having spoken thus to the two brothers, Rama and Lakshmana, who were both knowers of dharma, [he departed].
He pierced him with sharp arrows, rejoiced, and let out a roar;
dark as a mass of crushed collyrium, he drew his massive bow and repeatedly discharged terrible shafts in that great battle.

Then that hero, who knew the vital spots, plunging sharpened arrows into the vital organs of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, roared again and again. But both of them were bound by the bond of arrows at the forefront of the battle.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, they were unable to look upon one another. Then, with all their limbs pierced and covered with arrow-heads,
both of them trembled like the banners of great Indra when their ropes have been released.
6.035.018a Those two heroes, having been severely shaken and tormented by the piercing of their vital organs, 6.035.018c those two great archers, lords of the earth, fell upon the ground.
6.035.019a Those two heroes, drenched in blood, lay there upon the bed of heroes.
With all their limbs enveloped by arrows, they were both pained and utterly tormented; for there was not even a space of a single finger’s breadth on their bodies that was not pierced,
nor anything unbored or unparalyzed by those straight-flying shafts reaching down to the tips of their hands.
Slain by that cruel Rākṣasa who could assume any form at will, the two of them bled profusely like two mountain springs discharging water.
First, Rāma, pierced in his vital organs by the arrows, fell down.

6.035.022c By that Indrajit, out of anger, Śakra was formerly defeated; 6.035.023a He pierced him with iron arrows, half-iron arrows, bhallas, and añjalikas, as well as with vatsadantas, simhadashtas, and kshuras.
He lay upon the hero’s bed, having taken up his strung bow—
its grip and circumference broken, yet triple-curved and adorned with gold.
Within the distance of an arrow’s flight, Rāma, that bull among men, had fallen.
6.035.025c Seeing him there, Lakṣmaṇa lost all hope for his life.
6.035.026a But when the two heroes were seen bound and lying fallen, the monkeys stood surrounding them on all sides.
6.035.026c Having assembled, those led by the son of the Wind,
being distressed, fell into a state of supreme despondency.
6.036.001a Then the forest-dwellers, looking toward both heaven and earth, [beheld...]
The two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, saw themselves covered by a continuous stream of arrows,
like when the rain has ceased after the deity has finished his work, once the Rākṣasa had performed his deed.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, together with Sugrīva, arrived at that place.
6.036.003 Nīla, Dvivida, Mainda, Suṣeṇa, Sumukha, and Aṅgada,
together with Hanumān, quickly began to mourn for the two descendants of Raghu. 6.036.004 They were motionless, breathing faintly, and drenched in a flood of blood.
Covered with a web of arrows and rendered motionless, they lay upon their beds of shafts,
hissing like two serpents, devoid of movement and with their vigor spent;
their limbs smeared with flowing blood, they resembled two golden banners.
Those two heroes, lying upon the bed of heroes with but faint movements,
were surrounded by those leaders of the monkey troops whose eyes were clouded with tears;
seeing the two Raghavas fallen and covered by a net of arrows.
All the monkeys, including Vibhīṣaṇa, became distressed;
looking toward the sky and all the directions,
the monkeys could not see the son of Rāvaṇa in battle, for he was concealed by his illusory power.
But Vibhīṣaṇa, beholding that [illusion] which was cut away by illusion itself,
then saw his brother’s son standing there,
a man of incomparable deeds and without rival in battle.
6.036.010c Vibhīṣaṇa beheld the hero vanished by virtue of the boon he had received.
6.036.011a But Indrajit, seeing those two lying there and observing his own deed,

With trembling hearts, they all descended from the rampart;
with dejected faces, all those night-rangers approached the lord of the Rākṣasas,
reporting that unpleasant news to Rāvaṇa.
Those experts in speech reported everything exactly as it had happened:
how those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who had been bound in battle by Indrajit with a net of arrows, were rendered motionless in their arms.
"Released from their bonds of arrows, those two are seen on the field of battle like two lordly elephants who have snapped their snares, possessing prowess equal to that of the king of elephants.
Hearing those words, the immensely powerful lord of the rākṣasas—
Overcome by anxiety and grief, with a dejected countenance, he said:
"In battle, Indrajit has overwhelmed us with terrible, unerring arrows that resemble the sun— arrows granted as boons, bound with cords, and as venomous as serpents."
"If my two enemies have escaped that bond of weapons, I perceive this entire army of mine to be in a state of peril. Indeed,
the arrows empowered by Vāsuki’s splendor have become utterly fruitless."
"By whom my life was seized from my enemies in battle"—
having spoken thus, enraged and hissing like a serpent,
he addressed the rākṣasa named Dhūmrākṣa in the midst of the rākṣasas.
"Endowed with a great force of Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds,
go forth for the sake of slaying Rāma along with the monkeys.
Thus was Dhūmrākṣa addressed by the wise lord of the Rākṣasas.
Having offered his salutations, he departed from the king’s palace in high spirits. Having emerged through that gate, he spoke to the commander of the forces:
"Hurry the army quickly; why delay for one who desires to fight?"
6.041.022 Having heard the words of Dhūmrākṣa, the commander of the forces, who was followed by his troops,
swiftly mobilized the army at the command of Rāvaṇa.
6.041.023 Those powerful night-stalkers were of terrible appearance and had bells fastened to them.
Roaring and filled with joy, they surrounded Dhūmrākṣa;
with various weapons in their hands, spears and mallets in their grasp,
and with clubs, sharp-edged spears, staffs, iron bars, and pestles, they assailed him violently.
With iron clubs, slings, broad-headed arrows, spears, and battle-axes,
the terrible Rākṣasas went forth, roaring like rain-clouds;
others, clad in armor, advanced on chariots adorned with banners.
With mules adorned with golden nets and possessing various faces,
with horses of extreme speed, and with lordly elephants intoxicated with rut,
those tigers among Rākṣasas went forth like unassailable tigers.
Dhūmrākṣa, whose voice was harsh, mounted a divine chariot yoked with mules that had the faces of wolves and lions and were adorned with gold;
that immensely powerful Dhūmrākṣa then set forth, surrounded by Rākṣasas.
Laughing, Hanumān went to the western gate where the troop-leader was;
as that most terrible and fearsome-looking Rākṣasa was advancing,
cruel birds situated in the sky flew against him to ward him off.

On the front of the chariot, a terrifying vulture alighted; and from the tip of the banner, carrion-eaters fell, entangled together. A great, white, blood-drenched headless trunk (kabandha) fell upon the earth.
Emitting a discordant cry in the presence of Dhūmrākṣa,
the god rained down blood and the earth trembled;
a wind blew contrary to its course with a sound like a thunderclap.
6.041.033e There, the quarters of the sky, shrouded by a mass of darkness, did not shine.
6.041.034a Having then seen those portents, which brought fear to the Rākṣasas, 6.041.034c and which had appeared most terrible, Dhūmrākṣa became distressed.
Then the exceedingly formidable and powerful one, surrounded by many night-stalkers,
emerged eager for battle and beheld that city protected by the arm of Rāghava.
Beholding the rakshasa Dhumraksha, who possessed a roar as terrifying as the ocean and commanded an army of many monkeys,
all the monkeys, eager for battle, roared with great joy.
A tumultuous battle then broke out between those monkeys and the rākṣasas;
they struck one another with terrible trees, spears, and mallets.
The formidable monkeys were hacked on all sides by the rākṣasas.
The monkeys and the rākṣasas likewise leveled the ground with trees.
Then the enraged rākṣasas pierced the monkeys with sharp,
straight-flying arrows, terrible to behold and fletched with heron feathers.
Being torn apart by those rākṣasas with terrifying maces, sharp-edged spears, spiked hammers,
formidable and variegated iron clubs, and sharpened tridents,
those exceedingly powerful monkeys—
6.042.006c Their spirits emboldened by indignation, they acted fearlessly. 6.042.007a With their limbs pierced by arrows and their bodies transfixed by spears,
those leaders of the monkey troops seized trees and rocks there.
Those monkeys of terrifying speed, roaring here and there,
crushed the fearsome rākṣasas and called out their names.
Then, a wondrous and terrible battle took place between the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Some *rākṣasas* were crushed by the monkeys, who appeared radiant in their victory, using various kinds of rocks and trees with many branches;
some blood-drinking *rākṣasas* vomited blood from their mouths.
Some were torn along their flanks, some were crushed by trees piled together,
some were ground to powder by rocks, and some were split open by tusks;
with banners mangled and broken, and donkeys struck down.
With chariots shattered and night-rangers fallen,
the Rākṣasas were mangled in their faces by the sharp claws of the monkeys, who possessed terrifying prowess and leaped forward again and again with great speed.
With pale faces and disheveled hair,
bewildered by the stench of blood, they fell to the surface of the earth;
yet the Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess remained supremely enraged at this course of events.

They rushed at the monkeys with palms as hard as the touch of a thunderbolt; those attacking monkeys were violently crushed by the even more powerful forest-dwellers with fists, feet, teeth, and trees.
But seeing Sāṃya fleeing, Dhūmrākṣa, the bull among rākṣasas,
wrought a slaughter with fury upon the monkeys who were eager for battle.
Some monkeys, mangled by his spears, flowed with streams of blood.
Some, struck by mallets, fell upon the surface of the earth;
some were crushed by iron clubs and torn apart by javelins;
others, struck by spears, lay gasping, their lives departed.
6.042.020a Some forest-dwellers were struck down on the ground, drenched in blood;
6.042.020c others were routed and fled from the battle by the enraged Rākṣasas. 6.042.021a Some, their hearts pierced, lay on one side.
Some were torn apart by missiles and spears, while others had their entrails spilling out.
That great and most terrifying battle, crowded with monkeys and rākṣasas,
abounding in weapons and thick with rocks and trees, shone forth with splendor.

The music of war resounded, sweet with the string of the bow as its lute-string, accompanied by the rhythm of gasping sighs, and featuring the deep thundering of roars. But Dhūmrākṣa, bow in hand, stood at the forefront of the battle against the monkeys.
Laughing, he put them to flight in all directions with showers of arrows.
Seeing the army afflicted by Dhūmrākṣa and distressed, Māruti,
seizing a massive rock, rushed forward in a great rage.
With eyes twice as red from rage and possessing prowess equal to his father’s,
he hurled that rock toward Dhumraksha’s chariot.
Seeing the rock falling, he raised his mace in great agitation.
Leaping from the chariot with speed, she stood upon the ground;
having crushed his chariot, she fell upon the rocky earth,
together with its wheels, pole, horses, banner, and bow.
Having shattered his chariot, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
wrought a slaughter of the Rākṣasas with trees complete with trunks and branches.
With their heads split open and drenched in blood, the Rākṣasas lay fallen.
6.042.030c Others, crushed by the trees, fell upon the surface of the earth.
6.042.031a Having routed the Rākṣasa army, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
6.042.031c took up a mountain peak and rushed toward Dhūmrākṣa.
6.042.032a As he was rushing forward, the valiant Dhūmrākṣa, raising his mace,
6.042.032c rushed suddenly toward Hanumān while letting out a roar.
6.042.033a Then, filled with rage, [Hanumān] with great speed [struck] that mace which was covered in many thorns.
Dhūmrākṣa brought it down upon the head of Hanumān.
Struck there by that mace of terrifying form,
that monkey, possessing the strength of the Wind-god, disregarded the blow.
6.042.034e He struck Dhūmrākṣa’s head in the middle with a mountain peak.
6.042.035a Struck by the mountain peak, his entire body overwhelmed,
6.042.035c he suddenly fell to the ground like a shattered mountain.
Seeing Dhūmrākṣa slain, the remaining night-stalkers,
terrified and being slaughtered by the monkeys, fled into Laṅkā.
But that son of the Wind-god, having destroyed his enemy;
Having scattered the rivers flowing with blood,
the high-souled one, his fatigue born from the slaughter of the enemy relieved, attained joy while being honored by the monkeys.
6.043.001 Having heard that Dhūmrākṣa had been slain, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
spoke these words to the commander of the forces as he stood before him with palms joined in reverence:
6.043.002 "Let the invincible rākṣasas of terrible prowess march forth quickly."
Placing Akampana, who was skilled in all weapons, at their head,
the principal Rākṣasas— armed with various weapons, possessing terrifying eyes and fearsome appearances— then rushed forth, urged on by the commander of the forces.

6.043.004a Mounted upon a massive chariot, wearing earrings of refined gold, 6.043.004c Akampana then set forth, surrounded by terrible Rākṣasas. 6.043.005a For he could not be shaken, even by the gods, in a great battle.
Then Akampana, among them, was like the sun in his splendor.
As he rushed forward, enraged and eager for battle,
a sudden dejection came upon the horses drawing his chariot.
The left eye of him who rejoiced in battle throbbed;
his facial complexion turned pale and his voice became faltering.
Even on a clear day, it became as if stormy, with a harsh wind blowing.
6.043.008 All the birds and beasts uttered cruel and terrifying cries.
6.043.009 He, whose shoulders were as broad as a lion’s and whose prowess was equal to that of a tiger,
disregarded those portents and went forth to the field of battle.
Then, as that *rākṣasa* was departing along with his *rākṣasa* followers,
there arose a truly great roar, as if agitating the ocean.
By that sound, the vast army of monkeys was terrified.
Armed with trees and rocks as weapons, they stood ready to fight;
a most terrible battle then broke out between those monkeys and rakshasas,
who had utterly cast away their lives for the sake of Rama and Ravana.
For all were exceedingly powerful heroes, all resembling mountains;
both the monkeys and the rākṣasas were intent on slaying one another.
The sound of those exceedingly swift warriors as they roared in the encounter [reached the heavens].
A very great roar was heard from those shouting at one another out of rage; a most terrifying dust, with the hue of dawn,
was violently stirred up by the monkeys and the rākṣasas, and it obstructed the ten directions.

6.043.016a Covered by that silk-like dust which was stirred up and turned pale, the beings on the field of battle could not see one another. 6.043.017a Neither banner, nor standard, nor armor, nor even a horse could be discerned.
Neither weapon nor chariot could be seen through that dust;
yet the immense sound of them roaring and charging was heard in the tumultuous battle, while their forms did not shine forth.
6.043.019a In that battle, the monkeys, being greatly enraged, slaughtered only their own kin;
6.043.019c and the Rākṣasas likewise slaughtered the Rākṣasas in that darkness.
6.043.020a Thus, the monkeys and the Rākṣasas struck down both their enemies and their own people.
Then they made the earth wet with blood, smeared as if with mud. Sprinkled by that flood of blood, the dust was laid to rest,
and the earth became strewn with the corpses of bodies.
With trees, spears, rocks, and javelins, with clubs, iron maces, and lances,
the monkeys and the Rākṣasas swiftly struck one another with great vigor;
those who resembled mountains fought with arms shaped like iron bars.
6.043.023c The monkeys, performers of terrible deeds, slaughtered the rākṣasas in the battle.
6.043.024a And the rākṣasas, likewise enraged, with spears and javelins in their hands,
6.043.024c struck down the monkeys there with most dreadful weapons.
But the heroic monkeys, having approached, tore apart the rākṣasas with great trees and massive boulders, snatching away their weapons by force of valor.
In the meantime, the heroic monkeys Kumuda and Nala—
And Mainda, exceedingly enraged, exerted his unsurpassed speed.
With great velocity, those leaders of the monkey hosts wrought a truly massive slaughter among the vanguard of the Rākṣasa army, as if in mere play, using trees.
6.044.001 Having seen that very great deed performed by the best of the monkeys,
Akampana summoned a fierce rage in the battle. 6.044.002 His form overwhelmed by anger, he shook his supreme bow.
Having seen the deeds of his enemies, he spoke these words to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, drive the chariot quickly right there!
These many [enemies] here are slaying a great number of rākṣasas in battle."
"For these monkeys here are indeed powerful and possess formidable bodies;
armed with trees and mountains as weapons, they stand before me. I desire to slay them, for they boast of their prowess in battle."

6.044.005c By these, the entire Rākṣasa army was seen being crushed. 6.044.006a Then, with his horses galloping swiftly, Akampana, the best of chariot-warriors, out of anger struck the monkeys with nets of arrows.
The monkeys were unable even to stand their ground, much less fight in the battle;
shattered by Akampana’s arrows, they all fled away.
Seeing them fallen under the power of death and brought under the control of Akampana—
6.044.008c Having observed his kinsmen, the mighty Hanumān approached them.
6.044.009a Seeing that great leaper, all the leaders of the monkey troops,
those heroes, gathered together in the battle and surrounded him.
6.044.010a Seeing Hanumān stationed there, those leaders of the monkey troops—
6.044.010c being themselves powerful— became truly strong, for they had taken refuge in one who was powerful.
6.044.011a But Akampana [beheld] Hanumān standing there, resembling a mountain.
Like Mahendra raining down torrents, he showered him with arrows; yet,
disregarding the masses of sharp shafts falling upon his body,
the one of great strength set his mind upon slaying Akampana.
Laughing, the immensely radiant Hanumān, son of the Wind-god,
rushed toward that Rākṣasa as if making the earth tremble;
he was roaring and blazing with splendor.
His form became invincible, like that of a blazing fire. But perceiving himself to be unarmed, the bull among monkeys, filled with rage,
uprooted a mountain with great force.
Seizing that great mountain with a single hand, the heroic son of the Wind-god let out a tremendous roar and whirled it around.
Then he rushed toward Akampana, the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Just as Purandara [Indra] with his thunderbolt in battle [slew] Namuci,
so too Akampana, seeing that mountain peak raised up,
tore it apart from afar with great crescent-headed arrows.
Seeing that mountain peak, torn apart by the Rākṣasa’s arrows in the sky,
scattered and fallen, Hanumān was overcome with rage. That monkey, filled with fury and pride, approached an Aśvakarṇa tree.
He swiftly uprooted it, which was as lofty as a great mountain.
Taking that horse-ear tree (aśvakarṇa) with its massive trunk,
he of great splendor laughed and, with supreme joy, whirled it about in the battle.
6.044.022a Running with great speed and violently shattering trees by his force,
6.044.022c Hanumān, supremely enraged, tore up the earth with his feet. 6.044.023a He likewise destroyed elephants along with their riders, as well as chariots and chariot-warriors.
The wise Hanumān struck down the rākṣasa foot-soldiers. Beholding Hanumān in battle, like the enraged God of Death who takes away life, the rākṣasas fled in all directions.
6.044.025a Seeing him rushing forward, enraged and bringing terror to the rākṣasas, 6.044.025c the hero Akampana became furious and let out a roar.
6.044.026a He [struck him] with fourteen sharp arrows that tear the body asunder.
6.044.026c Akampana pierced Hanumān, who possessed great heroism.
6.044.027a Thus pierced by many showers of arrows,
the heroic Hanumān appeared like a mountain with its peaks overgrown.
Then, uprooting another tree and exerting unsurpassed force,
he swiftly struck Akampana, the lord of the Rākṣasas, on the head. Struck by that tree by the great-souled one in his wrath, [he fell].
Struck by the lord of monkeys, the Rākṣasa fell down and died.
Seeing Akampana, the lord of the Rākṣasas, slain upon the ground,
all the Rākṣasas were shaken like trees during an earthquake.
6.044.031ab All those Rākṣasas, having cast away their weapons and being defeated,
6.044.031cd fled toward Laṅkā in terror, pursued by those monkeys.
6.044.032a With disheveled hair, agitated, their pride shattered, they were utterly vanquished.
With limbs dripping with sweat from exhaustion and gasping for breath, they fled away;
terrified, they trampled one another and entered the city, looking back again and again, utterly bewildered.
When those immensely powerful Rākṣasas had entered Laṅkā,
all the monkeys gathered together and honored Hanumān.
He too, being delighted, in turn paid honor to all those monkeys.
Hanumān, endowed with courage, acted appropriately and favorably; and the monkeys, appearing victorious, roared as loudly as their strength allowed,
while they once again dragged the Rākṣasas there even while they were still alive.
Having encountered and slain the Rākṣasas, that great monkey, the son of the Wind, attained the splendor of a hero;
he was a fearsome great Asura, the destroyer of enemies.
Just as the hosts of gods then honored Viṣṇu at the head of the army against Bālin, so too did Rāma himself and the exceedingly powerful Lakṣmaṇa honor the monkey.
In the same way, the monkeys headed by Sugrīva and the mighty Vibhīṣaṇa were there;
and upon hearing of the slaughter of Akampana, the lord of the Rākṣasas was indeed filled with rage.
With a somewhat dejected face, he looked toward those ministers;
having reflected for a moment and consulted with his counselors,
he traversed the city of Laṅkā to inspect all the military outposts.
He beheld that city of Laṅkā, guarded by hosts of Rākṣasas, surrounded by many military outposts, and adorned with garlands of banners and flags.
But seeing the city thus besieged, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [was filled with concern].
6.045.004c At that time, provoked to anger, he spoke to Prahasta, who was skilled in battle:
6.045.005a "O you who are expert in war, for this city that has been besieged and suddenly oppressed, 6.045.005c I see no means of liberation other than through combat."
"Either I, or Kumbhakarṇa, or you as my commander-in-chief, or Indrajit, or Nikumbha— any of us could bear such a burden. Therefore,
take and gather your forces from here with all speed."
"Set out for victory where all the forest-dwellers reside. As soon as you depart, your fickle monkey army will surely flee upon hearing the roar of the shouting lords of the rākṣasas."
For monkeys are fickle, undisciplined, and of restless mind;
they will not endure your roar, just as elephants cannot endure the roar of a lion. And when that army has fled, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, [will act].
6.045.010c Cursed and without support, he will fall under the power of Prahasta.
6.045.011a A perilous situation is better than one that has been rendered certain; 6.045.011c Whether it be contrary or favorable, whatever you deem to be for our benefit.
6.045.012a Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Prahasta, the commander of the army,
6.045.012c spoke these words to the lord of the rākṣasas, just as Uśanas spoke to the lord of the asuras:
6.045.013a "O King, this was previously deliberated by us together with our skilled ministers."
6.045.013c Furthermore, a dispute has arisen between us as we look at one another;
6.045.014a however, by giving Sītā [in marriage], I have determined what is best. 6.045.014c On the other hand, if she is not given, war is clearly seen to be the inevitable outcome for us.

6.045.015a Since I have been constantly honored by you with gifts, honors, and various kinds of conciliatory words at the proper time, what dear service would I not perform for you? 6.045.016a For neither my life, nor my sons, wife, or wealth is to be protected [at the cost of your welfare].
"Behold me, who am about to sacrifice my life for your sake in battle.
Having spoken thus to her husband Rāvaṇa, the commander of the army said,
"Quickly assemble for me the great force of the rākṣasas."
"Let the forest-dwelling birds today feast upon the flesh of those slain on the field of battle by the thunderbolt-like force of my arrows.
Having been thus addressed by Prahasta, the army commanders made haste.

6.045.019c They mobilized their forces within that palace of the Rākṣasa. 6.045.020a In a mere moment, Laṅkā became crowded with those fierce Rākṣasa heroes armed with various sharp weapons, like it were filled with elephants.
As they offered oblations to the fire and paid homage to the brahmins,
a fragrant breeze blew, carrying the scent of clarified butter;
and they took up various kinds of garlands that had been consecrated with mantras.
Then the Rākṣasas, joyful and ready for battle, took up their positions;
equipped with bows and clad in armor, those Rākṣasas leaped forward with speed and,
beholding King Rāvaṇa, surrounded Prahasta.
Then, having addressed the king and struck a terrifying kettledrum,
Prahasta ascended a divine chariot that had been fully prepared,
yoked with horses of great speed and properly managed by a skilled charioteer.
It had the roar of a great rain-cloud, was as radiant as the sun and moon themselves,
was unassailable with its serpent-banner, possessed an excellent fender and fine equipment,
was adorned with golden lattices, and seemed to laugh with its splendor.
Then, having mounted that chariot and bearing the command bestowed by Rāvaṇa,
he quickly set out from Laṅkā, surrounded by a vast army.
Thereupon, there arose a roar like the sound of kettledrums, resembling the thundering of rain clouds.
And as the commander of the army set forth, the sound of conch shells was heard;
uttering terrible cries, the Rākṣasas went before him—
those of fearsome form and massive body who marched as the precursors of Prahasta.
Surrounded by that vast and most formidable army, which resembled a herd of elephants and was like a surging ocean, he marched forth from the eastern gate.
Surrounded by that force, he appeared like the ocean itself.
6.045.031c Prahasta went forth swiftly, enraged like Time at the end of an aeon.
6.045.032a At the sound of his departure and the roaring of the rākṣasas,
6.045.032c all beings in Laṅkā shrieked with discordant voices.
Entering a cloudless sky, birds that feed on flesh and blood performed counter-clockwise circles around the chariot; meanwhile,
fierce jackals, vomiting flames of fire, howled dreadfully.
From the atmosphere a meteor fell and a harsh wind blew;
the planets, clashing against one another, did not shine.
They rained down blood upon him and drenched his attendants.
On the top of his banner, a vulture, facing south, became motionless;
and as he plunged repeatedly into the battle,
the goad fell from the hand of his charioteer, the driver of the horses.
The glorious and radiant splendor of her departure, so difficult to attain,
vanished in an instant, and the horses stumbled on level ground.
But as Prahasta, renowned for his strength and prowess, was setting forth—
Armed with various weapons, the monkey army advanced in battle. Then a most tumultuous roar arose from the monkeys as they broke down trees and seized massive boulders.
6.045.041a Both armies— those of the hosts of Rākṣasas and the forest-dwellers— were greatly delighted;
6.045.041c a great roar was heard from those who were rushing forward, capable, desiring to slay one another, 6.045.041e and challenging each other.
Then the evil-minded Prahasta set out for victory against the army of the king of monkeys,
and he entered that host whose momentum was swelling.
Just as a moth about to die flies into a fire, so [he saw] Prahasta emerging— terrible, of fearsome prowess,
roaring, possessed of a massive body, and surrounded by Rākṣasas.
He beheld a vast army of powerful monkeys,
their fury fully aroused, roaring toward Prahasta; they bore swords,
spears, javelins, arrows, pikes, and maces.
Maces, iron clubs, spears, and various battle-axes,
as well as diverse bows belonging to the Rākṣasas who desired victory,
shone brightly as they were brandished by those charging toward the monkeys.
The bull-like monkeys seized flowering trees as well as massive,
long boulders,
eager for battle; and having encountered one another, a truly great conflict ensued between them.
While many were raining down showers of stones and showers of arrows,
numerous Rākṣasas in the battle struck many leaders of the monkey hosts; likewise,
many monkeys also slew many Rākṣasas.
Some were crushed by spears, others by supreme weapons;
some were struck by iron clubs, and others were cut down by battle-axes.
Furthermore, some fell upon the surface of the earth, breathless.
Some, their hearts pierced and bound by volleys of arrows, fell to the earth; others, split in two by swords, lay quivering on the ground;
and some monkeys were torn at the flanks with spears by the rākṣasas.
And by the enraged monkeys, the throngs of rākṣasas were crushed all around upon the surface of the earth with trees and mountain peaks;
they were also struck violently with hands whose palms had the touch of thunderbolts and with fists.
With their teeth and eyes shattered, they vomited blood from their mouths; as they uttered cries of distress and roared like lions,
a tumultuous sound arose in that battle between the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
6.046.014a The monkeys and the Rākṣasas, enraged and devoted to the path of heroes,
6.046.014c with cruel, rolling eyes, performed their deeds fearlessly.
6.046.015a Narāntaka, Kumbhahanu, Mahānāda, and Samunnata—
6.046.015c These [monkeys], together with Prahasta’s ministers, all slew the forest-dwellers. 6.046.016a As they were swiftly attacking and striking down the monkeys,
6.046.016c Dvivida struck one of them, Narāntaka, with a mountain peak.
6.046.017a Again, the monkey Durmukha, having uprooted a massive tree,
6.046.017c being swift of hand, crushed the towering Rākṣasa.
6.046.018a Jāmbavat, however, filled with great rage, seized a large rock.
The radiant one struck Mahānāda on the chest;
then the valiant Kumbhahanu, having encountered Tāra there,
was struck on the head with a tree by him, and that Rākṣasa gave up his life.
Unable to endure that deed, Prahasta mounted his chariot and,
bow in hand, wrought a terrible slaughter among the forest-dwellers.
Then, a whirlpool as it were arose between the two armies.
The sound was like that of an immeasurable, agitated ocean.
For Prahasta, skilled in battle, being enraged, tormented the monkeys with a great shower of arrows in that supreme combat.
The earth, strewn with the bodies of monkeys and rākṣasas,
became a terrifying sight, as if covered by fallen mountains.
Overspread by a flood of blood, that ground appeared as if veiled in darkness.
In the month of Mādhava, it was covered as if with flowering *palāśa* trees; its embankments were the multitudes of slain heroes, its great trees were shattered weapons,
and its vast waters were streams of blood, flowing toward the ocean of Yama.
[He saw the river] with its liver and spleen as its great mud, its scattered entrails as its moss,
its severed trunks and heads as its fish, and its limbs and members as its grassy weeds; it was crowded with flocks of vultures and swans, and frequented by *kaṅka* and *sārasa* cranes.
Filled with the foam of brains and echoing with the sounds of piteous groans—
that river consisting of the battlefield, difficult for cowards to cross—
was like a river frequented by swans and cranes at the end of the rainy season.
The Rākṣasas and the leaders of the monkeys crossed that difficult river,
just as the leaders of elephant herds cross a lotus pond covered with the pollen of lotuses. Then [they encountered] Prahasta, standing in his chariot and discharging a flood of arrows.
6.046.030c Nīla saw him swiftly slaughtering the monkeys.
6.046.031a As that most invincible one was charging forward, the heroic great monkey 6.046.031c uprooted a tree and struck Prahasta.
Struck by him, that bull among rākṣasas, roaring in anger,
rained down showers of arrows upon the commander of the monkey host.
Unable to ward them off, he received them with his eyes closed.
Just as a bull withstands the sudden onset of the autumnal rain,
even so Nīla, with eyes closed, suddenly endured that most terrible and unassailable shower of arrows from Prahasta.
Enraged by that great shower of arrows from Sāla,
the mighty Nīla struck Prahasta’s horses, which were as swift as thought.
Deprived of his bow by him, Prahasta, the commander of the army, [fell].
Seizing his terrible mace, he leaped down from his chariot. Both of those swift leaders of the army, filled with rage,
stood there with their limbs smeared with blood like two elephants in rut.
Scratching one another with their exceedingly sharp fangs,
resembling lions and tigers and possessing the prowess of lions and tigers,
those two heroes were valiant victors who never retreated in battles.
Desiring to attain the fame of Vṛtra and Vāsava, which were equal [in his eyes], Prahasta, exerting himself to the utmost,
then struck Nīla on the forehead with a mace;
blood flowed from him.
Then, his limbs smeared with blood, the great monkey, seizing a massive tree,
furiously hurled it at Prahasta’s chest.
Grasping a great mace, he [Prahasta] disregarded that inconceivable blow.
The powerful one rushed toward the powerful monkey Nīla. Then,
beholding him approaching with fierce speed and fury, the great monkey of immense velocity seized a massive rock.
As that Prahasta, who fought with clubs, was eager for battle in the fray,
Nīla swiftly brought down a boulder upon his head.
That great boulder, released by that leader of the monkeys, [fell].
Then that terrible [missile] split Prahasta’s head into many pieces. Deprived of life, deprived of fortune, deprived of vitality, and deprived of his senses,
he suddenly fell to the ground like a tree cut at its roots.
From his severed head, much blood flowed forth;
it also streamed from his body like a spring from a mountain. When Prahasta was slain by Nīla, that great and unshakable army trembled.
The Rakshasas, being disheartened, retreated toward Lanka;
they were unable to maintain their position once their army commander had been slain,
like water breaking apart upon reaching a breached dam.
When that leader of the army was slain, those rākṣasas became despondent;
having returned to the palace of the lord of the rākṣasas, they fell into a state of silent brooding.
Then the victorious Nīla, endowed with great strength—
Praised for his own deed,
the leader of the troop met with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and became filled with joy.
When that protector of the Rākṣasa army had been slain in battle by the bull among monkeys,
[he who possessed] terrible weapons and a speed equal to the ocean—
The army of the king of the Rākṣasas fled;
having returned, they reported to the lord of the Rākṣasas that the general had been slain by the son of Agni.
Having heard those words of theirs as well,
the lord of the rākṣasas fell under the sway of anger,
having learned that Prahasta had been slain in battle.
Afflicted by grief and his mind overwhelmed with anger,
he spoke to those chief commanders of the Nairṛtas,
just as Indra speaks to the chief commanders of the immortals' hosts.

"One should not show contempt for enemies by whom my commander-in-chief, the destroyer of Indra’s strength, was slain along with his followers and his elephants. Therefore, I shall act without hesitation for the destruction of the enemy and for victory."
I myself shall go to that wonderful front of the battle. Today, with floods of arrows, I will consume that army of monkeys along with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, just as blazing fires burn down a forest.
Having spoken thus, he [mounted] that chariot which was as radiant as fire, yoked with a row of the finest horses,
shining and blazing with its own form.
The enemy of the king of the immortals ascended it amidst the blaring of conchs, kettledrums,
and tabors, and the sounds of slapping arms, shouts of defiance, and lion-roars.
Being honored with meritorious hymns of praise,
that chief of the Rākṣasa kings then departed,
his forms resembling mountains and clouds.
Surrounded by the foremost leaders of the Rākṣasas, who were meat-eaters with eyes blazing like fire,
he shone like Rudra, the lord of the immortals, surrounded by spirits.
Then, having suddenly emerged from the city, he of great power beheld that fierce army of monkeys,
which roared like the great ocean or a thundercloud.
Beholding that exceedingly fierce army of Rākṣasas with trees and mountains raised as weapons, Rāma, whose arms were like those of the lord of serpents, [prepared for battle].
6.047.011c Accompanied by his army, the one of vast glory spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, the best among those who bear weapons;
6.047.012a [He spoke to him] who was equipped with various banners, standards, and weapons.
Whose is this army, filled with spears, swords, pikes, and discuses, inhabited by elephants like the lords of mountains,
unshakeable, and frequented by the fearless?
Then, having heard Rāma’s words,
Vibhīṣaṇa, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra,
described to Rāma the excellence of his army.
That great-souled one, mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant, was a bull among the high-minded Rākṣasas,
his copper-hued face resembling the newly risen sun.
"O King, know that he who stands upon his chariot with the lion-banner— who approaches shaking the heads of the elephants— is indeed Akampana."
Shaking his bow, which shines like Indra’s rainbow, he—
named Indrajit, the foremost recipient of boons— appears like an elephant with its fierce tusks bared.
And this man, who resembles the Vindhya and Mahendra mountains, a bowman standing in his chariot, an *atiratha* of exceeding prowess,
is stretching his incomparable bow.
Named Atikāya, his body was exceedingly large;
he had eyes like the copper-colored orb of the newly risen sun,
and having mounted [the chariot], it resounded with the ringing of bells.
The high-souled one who roars like an elephant or a donkey is indeed that hero named Mahodara;
he is the one who [seizes] the horse with its variegated golden trappings.
Having mounted [his chariot], which shone like a mountain of twilight clouds,
this Piśāca, possessing a speed equal to a thunderbolt, raised his spear entwined with rays of light.
And he who, grasping a sharpened trident as radiant as lightning and possessing the speed of a servant’s thunderbolt,
mounts a bull-king that resembles a mountain;
There comes that illustrious Triśiras,
and he who has a form resembling a cloud,
and Kumbha, whose broad chest is well-developed and handsome.
6.047.020c Samāhita, whose banner bears the king of serpents, shines as he draws and brandishes his bow; 6.047.021a and this [man] who wields a bow adorned with gold and diamonds...
Brandishing a flaming, smoke-enshrouded iron club,
he approaches as the very banner of the Rākṣasa host—
that Nikumbha of wondrous and terrible deeds.
And he who, having mounted a chariot equipped with a multitude of bows, swords, and arrows, adorned with banners and possessing a form blazing like fire, shines forth exultant;
This is Narāntaka, who fights with mountain peaks;
and he who possesses various kinds of terrible forms with the faces of tigers, camels, lordly elephants, and lions.
Surrounded by spirits with rolling eyes, he shines forth; he is that very one who destroys the pride even of the gods,
where this [city] gleams like the moon.
Here, this high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas, surrounded by spirits, shines like Rudra with his white umbrella of exquisite ribs.
There he is, wearing a diadem, his face adorned with swinging earrings,
his terrifying body like that of the king of serpents or the Vindhya mountains—
the destroyer of the pride of Mahendra and Vaivasvata.
The lord of the Rākṣasas shone like the sun. Then Rāma replied to Vibhīṣaṇa, the subduer of enemies:
"Aho! How radiant is Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, possessed of such great splendor!"
Like the sun, Rāvaṇa shines with his rays, difficult to behold;
for I clearly perceive his form enveloped in splendor.
Such a body could not belong to any of the heroes among the gods or the Dānavas.
Just as this body of the lord of the *rākṣasas* shines forth,
so too do all his warriors appear like mountains; all are mountain-fighters,
all bear blazing weapons, and they possess great majesty.

"That king of the Rākṣasas shines forth, surrounded by fierce beings of terrible prowess who are like Death incarnate; he blazes with his flaming attendants. Having spoken thus, the valiant Rāma then took up his bow.
6.047.031c Having extracted that excellent arrow, Lakṣmaṇa’s follower stood firm.
6.047.032a Then that high-souled lord of the rākṣasas spoke to those mighty rākṣasas:
"Remain at ease and without fear at the gates, the assembly halls, and the city portals; having suddenly dismissed them from there," 6.047.033a he then sent them away.
When the Rākṣasas had departed according to their orders,
he tore through the flood of the monkey-ocean,
just as a great fish rends the mass of the ocean's waters.
Seeing that lord of the rākṣasas suddenly attacking in battle with his blazing bow and arrows,
he uprooted a great mountain peak.
The lord of monkeys rushed toward the ruler of the rākṣasas;
seizing that mountain peak with its many trees and ridges, he hurled it at the night-stalker.
Seeing him suddenly rushing toward him,
he pierced him with arrows having golden feathers;
at that time, [he was like] a mountain with its excellent peaks and trees fully grown.
When his horn was shattered and fell to the earth,
the lord of the world of rakshasas took up a great arrow, resembling the Destroyer at the end of an eon.
Having seized that arrow, which possessed a speed equal to the wind,
which shone like a blazing fire with sparks,
and which had a velocity like the thunderbolt of great Indra;
Enraged, he hurled that arrow for the sake of slaying Sugrīva;
released from Rāvaṇa’s arm,
it possessed a form like Indra’s thunderbolt and had a sharp point.
Having reached Sugrīva, he pierced him with force,
like a fierce spear hurled by a hidden archer at a heron; afflicted by that arrow, his mind became deranged.
Uttering cries, the hero fell to the earth.
Seeing him fallen on the ground, unconscious,
the Yātudhānas shouted with joy in the battle.
Then Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Sudaṃṣṭra, as well as Ṛṣabha, Jyotimukha, and Nala,
their bodies swelling with strength, uprooted mountains.
They rushed toward that lord of the Rākṣasas;
the sovereign of the Rākṣasas countered their blows with multitudes of sharp-pointed arrows.
He pierced those lords of monkeys as well with nets of arrows whose feathers were variegated with gold.
Those lords of monkeys [were struck] by the arrows of the enemies of the thirty gods.
Torn apart, they fell to the earth in terrifying forms;
then that fierce army of monkeys was completely covered by his nets of arrows.
Being slaughtered, those foremost heroes fell,
crying out in various ways, pierced by the arrows of fear and afflicted by the shafts of Rāvaṇa; they were like monkeys struck by the arrows of Rāvaṇa.
They went for refuge to Rāma, the protector.
Then that great-souled Rāma, the wielder of the bow, took up his bow and departed together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Approaching him with palms joined in reverence, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words consistent with the highest truth:
"Noble brother, you are certainly capable of slaying this evil-minded one."
"I shall destroy that base wretch; give me your leave, O Lord.
To him, the immensely radiant Rāma, whose prowess is truth, replied:
"Go, and remain intent on effort in this battle, Lakṣmaṇa."
For Rāvaṇa is of great heroism and possesses wonderful prowess in battle;
when enraged, he would be difficult to withstand even by the three worlds, there is no doubt.
Therefore, seek out his vulnerabilities and guard your own.
"With eyes as his bow, remain composed and protect yourself with effort.
Having heard the words of Raghava, having embraced and honored him,
and having saluted Rama, Saumitri then departed for the battle.
He, whose arms were like the trunks of elephants, beheld Rāvaṇa, who held aloft his blazing and formidable bow,
covering [the sky] with masses of showers of arrows.
Seeing those monkeys with their bodies pierced and scattered, the highly energetic Hanumān, son of the Wind-god,
warded off the nets of arrows and rushed toward Rāvaṇa.
Approaching his chariot and raising his right arm,
the wise Hanumān, terrifying Rāvaṇa, spoke these words:
"The gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas together— "
"Because you were invulnerable, you were spared by him; however, you shall have cause for fear from the monkeys.
Here is my right arm, five-fingered and uplifted;
it shall drive the soul of the elements, long resident within your body, out from your frame."
Having heard Hanumān’s words, Rāvaṇa, of terrifying prowess, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke these words:
"Strike quickly and without hesitation; attain enduring fame!"
"Therefore, O monkey, I shall destroy you, whose prowess is so great toward your kinsmen.
Having heard Rāvaṇa's words, the son of Vāyu spoke these words:
"Remember Akṣa, your son, whom I struck down long ago."
Thus addressed, the highly energetic Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas,
the valiant one, struck the son of the Wind-god on the chest with his palm.
Struck by that palm, he trembled again and again.
Highly incensed, he struck the enemy of the gods with his very palm.
Then, struck by the palm of the high-souled monkey,
the Ten-necked one shook like a mountain during an earthquake.
6.047.061a Seeing Rāvaṇa thus struck by the palm of the hand in battle,
the ṛṣis, monkeys, siddhas, and gods along with the asuras raised a shout. 6.047.062a Then, having recovered his composure, the highly energetic Rāvaṇa spoke these words:
"Excellent! By virtue of your monkey-like prowess, you are a praiseworthy enemy in my eyes.
When Rāvaṇa had spoken thus, Māruti replied with these words:
"Fie upon my own prowess, since you, O Rāvaṇa, still live!"
"O evil-minded one, strike me now! Why do you boast?
Then my fist shall send you to your destruction. At these words of the son of the Wind-god, his anger then blazed up.
With bloodshot eyes, the valiant one exerted himself, raised his right fist,
and brought it down with force upon the chest of the monkey;
struck on his broad breast, Hanumān staggered and was momentarily overcome.
Seeing the mighty Hanumān thus distressed,
that great car-warrior quickly approached Nīla in his chariot with terrifying arrows resembling serpents, which pierce the vital organs of the enemy.
With his arrows, he set ablaze Nīla,
the commander of the monkey host. Oppressed by that torrent of arrows, Nīla,
the leader of the monkey army, hurled a mountain peak with one hand at the lord of the rākṣasas.
The radiant and high-minded Hanumān, having recovered his composure and desiring battle, looked about and spoke these words with wrath,
[addressing] Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, as he was engaged in combat with Nīla.
"It is not proper to charge while one is fighting with another.
Then the immensely powerful Rāvaṇa struck that horn with seven exceedingly sharp-pointed arrows,
and it fell down shattered.
Seeing that mountain peak shattered, the commander of the monkey army,
the slayer of enemy heroes, blazed with wrath like the fire of universal destruction at the end of time.
He [saw] aśvakarṇas, dhavas, sālas, and mango trees in full bloom.
In that battle, Nīla hurled various other kinds of trees;
having reached those trees, Rāvaṇa cut them down and showered the son of Agni with a most terrible rain of arrows.
Drenched by that shower of arrows like a great mountain by a cloud,
he then made his form small and alighted upon the tip of the banner.
Beholding the son of Agni stationed there at the top of the banner, [the king was amazed].

Rāvaṇa blazed with rage, and then Nīla let out a roar. Seeing that monkey upon the tip of the banner, the tip of the bow, and the tip of the crown, Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān, and Rāma were all struck with wonder.
The highly energetic Rāvaṇa, too, amazed by the monkey’s agility, summoned a brilliant and wondrous fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*). Then those monkeys, having found their mark, cried out in joy.
Seeing Rāvaṇa bewildered by Nīla’s swiftness in the battle,
and further agitated by the roar of the monkeys, Rāvaṇa then became frantic;
with his heart overcome by confusion, he did not know what to do.
Then Rāvaṇa, the night-stalker, having taken up an arrow charged with the power of Agni,
looked up at the dark-blue [Hanumān] stationed atop the tip of his banner.
Thereupon, the immensely radiant Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, spoke.
"O monkey, you are endowed with agility through this supreme illusion.
O vanara, protect your life if indeed you are able,
for you create those various forms of yourself many times over."
"Nevertheless, this arrow released by me, empowered by a divine weapon,
shall deprive you of your life as you strive to protect it.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, [discharged the shaft].
Having aimed an arrow with a divine weapon, he struck the commander of the army.
Struck in the chest by that arrow charged with the weapon, Nīla,
being consumed by fire, suddenly fell to the surface of the earth.
Due to the power of his father’s majesty and by his own splendor,
he fell to the ground on his knees but was not deprived of life. Seeing the monkey unconscious, the ten-necked one, eager for battle, [proceeded].
With a chariot that roared like a cloud, he rushed toward the son of Sumitrā. To him,
as he was stretching his immeasurable bow, the son of Sumitrā, undaunted in spirit, spoke:
"Follow me alone, O lord of the night-rangers;
you ought not to fight against the monkeys.
He [Rāvaṇa] [heard] his words, which were uttered with a full resonance.
Hearing that fierce sound of the bowstring, the king approached the son of Sumitrā as he stood there and,
filled with anger, spoke these words to the Rākṣasa.
"By good fortune, O Rāghava, you who were destined for destruction and possessed of perverted intellect have come within the range of my sight;
at this very moment, you shall go to the realm of death."
As he was being overwhelmed by my nets of arrows,
the son of Sumitrā, remaining unperturbed, spoke to that roaring one whose white-tipped fangs were bared.
"O King, those of great power do not boast;
you brag, O foremost among evildoers! I know your prowess, O Lord of Rākṣasas."
Standing here with bow and arrows in hand, possessing strength, majesty, and prowess,
come— what is the use of this vain boasting?
Thus addressed, the enraged lord of the rākṣasas discharged seven well-feathered arrows;
Lakṣmaṇa [countered] them with arrows adorned with variegated golden feathers.
He cut them down with arrows possessing sharp, keen edges,
watching as they were suddenly severed like great serpents whose coils have been lopped off.
The Lord of Laṅkā fell under the sway of anger;
he discharged other sharpened arrows. He rained down that intense shower of shafts.
Rāmānuja cut down the arrows discharged from the bow— those excellent kṣuras, ardhacandras, karṇis,
and bhallas— and yet he did not waver.
Then Lakṣmaṇa quickly fixed upon his bow sharp-pointed arrows,
blazing like fire and possessing a velocity equal to the thunderbolt of great Indra.
He discharged them for the sake of slaying the lord of the rākṣasas; the king of the rākṣasas indeed cut them down,
and having cut them down, he struck Lakṣmaṇa.
Struck in the forehead by that arrow given by Svayambhū, which possessed a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction,
Lakṣmaṇa was afflicted by Rāvaṇa’s shaft.
Grasping his bow loosely, he trembled; then, regaining consciousness with great difficulty,
he cut the bow of the enemy of the lord of the thirty gods.
Then the son of Daśaratha struck him, whose bow had been severed, with three sharp-pointed arrows;
pained by those shafts, the king trembled.
With great difficulty he regained consciousness;
his bow was severed, he was struck by arrows,
his limbs were wet with sweat, and he was drenched in blood.
6.047.101c He of the exalted power, the enemy of the gods, seized the spear given by Svayambhū in battle;
6.047.102a it resembled a smokeless fire.
The lord of the Rākṣasa kingdom swiftly hurled a blazing spear, which struck terror into the monkey host, at the son of Sumitrā.
As it was falling upon him, the younger brother of Bharata struck it with missiles and arrows resembling blazing fires;
nevertheless, that spear entered his body.
Struck in the middle of his chest by the spear of Brahmā, the son of Sumitrā, whose broad chest belonged to the son of Daśaratha,
recalled himself as the inconceivable portion of Viṣṇu.
Then the thorn of the gods, having oppressed with his two arms Saumitri— the destroyer of the pride of the Dānavas— became unable to leap over him,
even as Himavat, Mandara, Meru, or the three worlds together with the immortals might be.

6.047.106c The younger brother of Bharata cannot be lifted up by [mere] arms in battle. 6.047.107a Then, seeing Lakṣmaṇa— who was a portion of Viṣṇu yet had assumed a human body— unconscious, Rāvaṇa was struck with amazement.
Then the son of the Wind-god, enraged, rushed toward Rāvaṇa;
in his fury, he struck him on the chest with a fist that was like a thunderbolt.
By that blow of the fist, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
He fell to the ground on his knees, reeled, and collapsed.
Seeing Rāvaṇa, who possessed terrifying prowess, unconscious in the battle,
the seers, the monkeys, and the gods led by Indra raised a great shout.
The radiant Hanumān, too, having taken Lakṣmaṇa— who was being tormented by Rāvaṇa—
into his arms, brought him into the presence of the two descendants of Raghu;
this he did out of friendship for the son of the Wind-god and with supreme devotion.

6.047.112c Though unshakable by his enemies, he attained lightness for the sake of the monkey. 6.047.113a Having released it against that Saumitri, who was difficult to conquer in battle, that spear returned once more to its place on Rāvaṇa’s chariot.
6.047.114a Rāvaṇa too, possessed of great splendor, having regained consciousness in that great battle,
6.047.114c took up sharpened arrows and seized his mighty bow. 6.047.115a And Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemies, was comforted and freed from his wounds.
6.047.115c Recalling himself to be the inconceivable portion of Viṣṇu,
6.047.116a seeing the great army of monkeys with its mighty heroes struck down in battle, 6.047.116c Rāghava, however, rushed toward Rāvaṇa in the fray.
Then, having approached him, Hanumān spoke these words:
"Mounting my back, you ought to subdue the Rākṣasa.
Having heard those words spoken by the son of the Wind-god, Rāghava—
6.047.118c The hero suddenly mounted the great monkey Hanumān;
6.047.118e the lord of men beheld Rāvaṇa standing upon his chariot in the battle. 6.047.119a Upon seeing him, that Rāghava of great splendor rushed forward.
Like the enraged Vairocana, Viṣṇu with his weapon raised,
Rāma let out a sharp sound from his bowstring that resonated like the crash of a thunderbolt;
then, with a deep voice, he spoke to the lord of the rākṣasas.
"Stay! Stay! For you have done such a grievous wrong to me.
O tiger among rākṣasas, where can you go to find escape? Even if you were to seek refuge with Indra, Yama, or the Sun;"
Whether you go to Svayambhū, Vaiśvānara, or Śaṅkara, or even to the ten directions,
nevertheless, having gone from me today, you shall not be released.
And he who was struck by you with a spear today,
who, though wishing for it, suddenly fell into despair—
he, O king of the hosts of Rākṣasas, is Death himself.

Having heard the words of Rāghava, "Today in battle [I shall slay] you along with your sons and wife," the Lord of the Rākṣasas struck the great monkey with sharp arrows resembling the crests of the fire of cosmic destruction.
6.047.125a Even though he had been struck by the arrows of that Rākṣasa in battle, 6.047.125c the energy of him who was endowed with innate splendor increased all the more.
6.047.126a Then the highly energetic Rāma [beheld] the wound inflicted by Rāvaṇa.
Seeing that tiger among monkeys, he fell under the sway of anger;
having approached his chariot, complete with its wheels,
horses, banner, umbrella, and great pennants.
Rāma, with well-feathered arrows, cut down [the chariot] along with its charioteer, thunderbolt, spear, and sword;
then he swiftly struck the enemy of Indra.
With an arrow resembling a thunderbolt,
he struck him in the broad and well-formed chest,
just as the blessed Indra struck Mount Meru with his vajra.
The king, who had not been agitated nor shaken even by the falling of thunderbolts or the crashing of lightning,
was now violently afflicted, struck by Rāma’s arrow.
The hero trembled and released his bow;
seeing him thus overwhelmed, Rāma then took up a blazing crescent-headed arrow.
With that [arrow], the high-souled one suddenly severed the sun-colored crown of the lord of the Rākṣasas,
which resembled a venomless serpent. It was like a venomless serpent.
To the lord of the rākṣasas, who was like a sun with extinguished rays, devoid of luster, his crest-jewel shattered, Rāma spoke in the midst of battle.
"You have performed a great and most terrifying deed;
you have left me with my foremost heroes slain. Therefore, considering yourself exhausted—"
"I will not bring you under the power of death with my arrows. Thus addressed, his pride and joy destroyed, his bow cut asunder, and his horses and charioteer slain, he remained there.
Afflicted by arrows and with his great crown shattered,
the king suddenly entered Laṅkā; when that lord of the night-rangers had thus entered, [the city was filled with joy].
In the presence of that great warrior, the enemy of the Dānavas and gods,
Rāma rendered the monkeys free from their wounds along with Lakṣmaṇa at the front of the supreme battle.
When that enemy of the lord of the thirty gods was thus broken, the gods,
asuras, hosts of spirits, the quarters of space along with the oceans, the sages, and the great serpents—
Likewise, those who move on land and in water were filled with joy;
yet, having entered the city of Laṅkā, the king— afflicted by the fear of Rāma’s arrows, his pride shattered— then became distressed in his senses.
Like a Mātaṅga elephant by a lion, or a serpent by Garuḍa,
the king was utterly overwhelmed by the high-souled Rāghava—
by those [arrows] which resembled the staff of Brahmā and possessed a brilliance like lightning.
Recalling the arrows of Rāghava, the lord of the rākṣasas was deeply distressed.
Taking his place upon a divine, golden, supreme throne,
Rāvaṇa looked about at the rākṣasas and spoke these words.
"All that supreme austerity which I have practiced has indeed been in vain,
since I, though equal to Mahendra, have been defeated by a mere mortal.
This terrible word of Brahmā has now come upon me."
"Understand that your fear is of humans; it is even so.
"I have obtained invulnerability from gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, but I did not ask for it from humans."
"Having accepted this very [plan], you ought to exert yourselves here;
let the Rākṣasas also remain upon the tops of the watchtowers and gateways.
And he is incomparably profound, the destroyer of the pride of gods and Dānavas."

But let Kumbhakarṇa, who is overwhelmed by the curse of a Brahmin, be awakened. Having learned that he himself was defeated and that Prahasta had been slain, the immensely powerful one commanded his formidable army of Rākṣasas.
"Let effort be made at the gates and let the ramparts be ascended;
let Kumbhakarṇa, who is overcome by the power of sleep, be awakened.
This Rākṣasa sleeps for nine, six, seven, and eight months."
"Quickly awaken that mighty Kumbhakarṇa;
for he, the long-armed one, is the preeminent leader among all the Rākṣasas in battle,
and he will swiftly slay the monkeys and the two princes."
Kumbhakarṇa always sleeps, a fool devoted to vulgar pleasures;
there will be no grief for me if Kumbhakarṇa is awakened when this most terrible battle with Rāma has begun.
"What shall I do with him, for he possesses strength equal to Śakra? When such a calamity has arrived, he is not capable of providing assistance.
Having heard those words of the lord of the rākṣasas, the rākṣasas...
Greatly agitated, they went to the residence of Kumbhakarṇa. Commanded by Rāvaṇa, those who feed on flesh and blood quickly departed, taking with them perfumes, garlands, and various foods.
Having entered that great gateway, which extended for a yojana in every direction, they—
with great effort and difficulty— entered the delightful cave of Kumbhakarṇa, which wafted all manner of fragrances.
Having entered that delightful and auspicious cave with its golden floor,
they beheld the tiger among the Nairṛtas lying there, of terrifying appearance. They saw him, deformed and sleeping, like a mountain strewn about.
Together they awakened Kumbhakarṇa from his great sleep—
he whose body was covered with bristling hair, who was hissing like a serpent,
and who lay there of fearsome aspect, terrifying all with his heavy breaths.

They beheld that immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa, a tiger among the Nairṛtas, whose nostrils were terrifying and whose mouth was as vast as the underworld. Then those great-souled ones stood before Kumbhakarṇa.

Those tigers among the Nairṛtas made a heap of flesh resembling Mount Meru, providing supreme satisfaction; they gathered piles of deer, buffaloes, and boars, and created a marvelous mountain of food.
Then the enemies of the gods placed jars of blood and various kinds of liquor before Kumbhakarṇa,
and they anointed that scorcher of foes with the most excellent sandalwood.
They covered him with divine garlands and fragrant perfumes;
they released sweet-smelling incense and praised the scorcher of foes.
And thousands of Yātudhānas roared like clouds.
They blew conchs that possessed a luster like the moon;
simultaneously, filled with indignation, they let out a tumultuous roar. Those night-stalkers shouted, slapped their arms, and hurled [their weapons].
To awaken Kumbhakarṇa, they made a great noise—
a clamor of conchs, kettledrums, and tabors, along with the slapping of arms, war-cries, and lion-roars.
6.048.031c Running in all directions and scattering toward the third heaven,
the birds suddenly descended upon hearing those sounds; 6.048.032a when the Great-Souled One was [disturbed] by those intense cries, they fell down.
Kumbhakarṇa did not wake while he was fast asleep;
then all those hosts of rākṣasas seized maces, clubs, and bludgeons.
With mountain peaks, clubs,
maces, trees, palms, hammers, and fists,
they struck Kumbhakarna as he lay sleeping soundly upon the ground.
Then the fierce *rākṣasas* were struck down by the breath of that *rākṣasa* Kumbhakarṇa;
even though they were powerful, they were unable to stand before him.
Then, before him, ten thousand rākṣasas of terrifying prowess simultaneously sounded mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, kettledrums, conchs, and jars.
They, however, sought to awaken him—who resembled a mass of blue collyrium—striking him and shouting; yet he did not regain consciousness at all.
And when they were unable to awaken him, then...
Then they undertook a most strenuous and terrible effort;
they struck the horses, camels, donkeys, and elephants with sticks, whips,
and goads, and they sounded kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums with all their might.
And they struck his limbs with great logs and planks,
with mallets and pestles, exerting all their strength;
by that great noise, Laṅkā was completely filled.
Even though all the mountains and forests were shaken, he did not wake at all.
Then, a thousand kettledrums, struck simultaneously with polished golden drumsticks on all sides without interruption, were sounded.
Even so, when he did not wake up despite being in such deep sleep,
the night-stalkers, having fallen under the power of the curse, became enraged;
then all those beings of terrible prowess were possessed by great fury.
Desiring to awaken that Rākṣasa, others exerted their prowess:
some beat kettledrums, others made a great noise;
some disheveled their hair, and others bit their ears.
6.048.044e Kumbhakarṇa, having fallen under the power of a great sleep, did not stir.
6.048.045a And his other powerful [servants], with sledgehammers in their hands,
6.048.045c brought down those sledgehammers upon his head, chest, and limbs.
Though being struck from all sides with *śataghnīs* bound with ropes,
the huge-bodied Rākṣasa did not wake up; indeed,
a thousand elephants rushed against his body.
Then Kumbhakarṇa, having awakened, perceived a supreme sensation;
as mountain peaks and trees were being cast down upon him,
he disregarded those massive blows.
Afflicted by the exhaustion of sleep and the pain of hunger and fear,
he suddenly sprang up while yawning;
he [was like] two mountain peaks formed from the coils of a serpent.
Throwing out his arms, which were as strong as mountain peaks,
and opening his mouth like the submarine fire,
that night-stalker yawned hideously.
As he yawned, his mouth appeared like the netherworld (pātāla),
resembling the sun risen upon the peak of Mount Meru;
the exceedingly powerful night-stalker, having awakened, was yawning.
And his breath issued forth like the wind from a mountain;
as Kumbhakarna rose up,
his form shone like a rain-showering cloud accompanied by cranes at the end of the hot season.
His two great eyes, resembling blazing fires and possessing a luster like lightning, appeared like two flaming great planets. Hungry, he ate the flesh; thirsty, he drank the blood.
Then the enemy of Śakra drank a jar of fat and wine;
perceiving that he was now satiated, the night-stalkers sprang up,
bowed their heads before him, and surrounded him on all sides.
That bull among the Nairṛtas consoled all the Nairṛtas;
and, astonished by the awakening, he spoke this to the Rākṣasas:
"For what reason have I been struck and awakened by you?"
"Is all well with the king, and is there no danger whatsoever here?
Or has some certain and great danger from others arisen,
for which reason you have awakened me with such haste?"
"Today I shall uproot the fear of the king of the rākṣasas;
I shall cast down Mahendra or likewise strike down Agni.
For he will not wake me from my sleep unless for a very serious reason."
"That [dream] was the cause of my awakening through its true meaning.
To Kumbhakarṇa, the subduer of enemies, who was speaking thus with agitation,
the king’s minister Yūpākṣa spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, we have no fear whatsoever caused by the gods at any time,
nor indeed is there such fear from the Daityas or Dānavas as this human fear that has now come upon us."
This city of Laṅkā is surrounded by monkeys as large as mountains;
from Rāma, who is tormented by the abduction of Sītā, we face a tumultuous fear.
Formerly, this great city was burnt by a single monkey.
The prince Akṣa was slain along with his followers and his elephant; and even the lord of the Rākṣasas himself, the descendant of Pulastya and thorn of the gods,
was killed in battle by Rāma, who possesses the splendor of the sun.
"He who was not made king by the gods, nor by the Daityas, nor by the Dānavas—
he has been made king here by Rāma and released from the danger to his life.
Having heard these words of his brother Yūpākṣa regarding his defeat in battle, [he spoke].
6.048.067c Kumbhakarṇa, his eyes rolling, spoke these words to Yūpākṣa:
6.048.068a "O Yūpākṣa, having slain today itself the entire army of monkeys along with Lakṣmaṇa and Rāghava in battle, I shall afterwards see Rāvaṇa."
"I shall satiate the rākṣasas with the flesh and blood of the monkeys,
and I myself shall drink the blood of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard those words as he spoke them;
The chief of the Nairṛta warriors, Mahodara, filled with pride and his faults increased by rage,
spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:

Having heard Rāvaṇa’s words and having reflected upon their merits and defects, O mighty-armed one, you shall later conquer your enemies in battle. Having heard Mahodara’s speech, he was surrounded by the rākṣasas.
The immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa, endowed with great splendor, set forth.
Having raised up that one of terrifying eyes and fearsome form and prowess,
the Rākṣasas hurriedly went to the residence of the Ten-necked One.
Then, having gone there, all the night-stalkers, with their palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Ten-necked one as he sat upon his supreme throne:
"O bull among Rākṣasas, that brother of yours, Kumbhakarṇa, has awakened."
"How might he depart from that very place so that you may see him come here? Rāvaṇa, however, spoke boldly, saying, "I wish to see him here, honored according to the proper custom."
Having said, "So be it," all those rākṣasas, urged by Rāvaṇa, returned and spoke these words to Kumbhakarṇa:
"The king, the bull among all rākṣasas, desires to see you."
"Set your mind on departing and gladden your brother. Then the invincible Kumbhakarṇa, of great prowess, having received his brother’s command, said "So be it" and leapt up from his bed.
Having washed his face, joyful, bathed, and most exquisitely adorned, he,
being thirsty, hurriedly called for the drink that provides strength.
Then, by the command of King Rāvaṇa, they quickly brought it for him.
Quickly serving various kinds of liquor and foods,
he drank a thousand jars and prepared to depart,
slightly intoxicated and exhilarated, yet endowed with his usual splendor and strength.
6.048.083c Kumbhakarṇa shone, joyful, resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
6.048.084a Proceeding to his brother’s residence, accompanied by a force of Rākṣasas,
6.048.084c Kumbhakarṇa made the earth tremble with the stamping of his feet.
Illuminating the royal highway with his physical form,
as the thousand-rayed sun illuminates the earth with its beams,
he proceeded there, surrounded by a multitude of people with joined palms.
Some went to Rāma for refuge as he was their protector, like Śatakratu going to the house of Svayambhū; others, distressed, fell down.
Some fled toward the quarters of the sky in agitation,
while others, afflicted by fear, lay prostrate upon the earth; they beheld him, crowned with a diadem, resembling the peak of a mountain.
Seeing that extraordinary being grown to such a size, who seemed to touch the sun with his own radiance, the forest-dwellers,
afflicted by fear, fled here and there.

Then the valiant Rāma, endowed with great splendor, took up his bow and beheld the massive-bodied Kumbhakarṇa wearing a diadem. Having seen that foremost of Rākṣasas, who appeared like a mountain, he [stood there].
Seeing the Lord Nārāyaṇa advancing as if through the sky—
resembling a water-laden cloud and adorned with golden armlets—
the great army of monkeys fled once more.
Seeing the army in flight and the Rākṣasa growing in power,
Rāma spoke these words with wonder to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"Who is this who resembles a mountain, wearing a diadem and having tawny eyes?"
In Laṅkā, that hero appears like a rain-cloud flashing with lightning;
he is seen here as the sole great banner of the earth,
upon seeing whom all the monkeys flee in every direction.
"Tell me, who is this great being? Is he a Rākṣasa or perhaps an Asura? Never before have I seen such a creature.
Thus was he questioned by Prince Rāma, the one of unwearied deeds.
The highly wise Vibhīṣaṇa spoke thus to the descendant of Kakutstha:
"This is that very powerful Kumbhakarṇa, the son of Viśravas, by whom both Vaivasvata and Vāsava were defeated in battle."
By this [weapon], the gods, Dānavas,
Yakṣas, Bhujaṅgas, Piśitāśanas,
Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kiṃnaras were conquered in battle.
O Raghava, though they were shattered by the thousands,
the gods were unable to slay the spear-wielding Virupaksha or the mighty Kumbhakarna; bewildered, they thought, "This is Time itself."
"For by his very nature, this Kumbhakarṇa is radiant and possesses great strength;
whereas the strength of other lords of the rākṣasas is produced by the granting of boons.
By this high-souled one, as soon as he was born and afflicted by hunger—"
Thousands of beings, indeed very many, were devoured. While they were being consumed, the creatures, oppressed by fear,
went for refuge to Śakra and reported that matter to him as well.
Enraged, the wielder of the thunderbolt, Mahendra, struck Kumbhakarṇa with his sharp vajra;
that high-souled one was thus assailed by Śakra’s vajra.
And he trembled with rage and roared loudly.
As that wise Kumbhakarṇa was roaring,
the earth, already terrified upon hearing his roar, trembled once again.
