Then, out of anger toward Mahendra, the immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa tore off a tusk from Airāvata and struck Vāsava in the chest.
Afflicted by Kumbhakarṇa’s blow, that Vāsava trembled.

Then the gods, the brahmin-sages, and the dānavas were suddenly despondent; Śakra, together with the subjects, went to the abode of the Self-Existent One (Brahmā) and reported the wickedness of Kumbhakarṇa to the Lord of Creatures.
6.049.019e There is the devouring of living beings and even the assault upon the gods. 6.049.020a If he thus constantly devours these creatures,
6.049.020c in a very short time the world will become empty.
Having heard the words of Vāsava, the Grandfather of all the worlds summoned the Rākṣasas and beheld Kumbhakarṇa. Upon seeing Kumbhakarṇa, the Lord of Creatures was struck with terror.
Having seen this and sighing deeply, the Self-Existent One spoke thus:
"Surely you have been created by the Eastern One for the destruction of the world;
therefore, from this day forward, you shall lie like one who is dead."
Then, overcome by the curse of a Brahmin, he fell before the Lord.
Thereupon, Rāvaṇa, greatly agitated, spoke these words:
"A golden tree, having grown large, is being cut down at the very time it bears fruit."
"O Prajāpati, it is not right for you to curse your own grandson in this manner;
nor shall you speak falsely, for he will surely sleep—of this there is no doubt. However, let a time be set for his sleeping and likewise for his waking."
Having heard Rāvaṇa’s words, the Self-born One spoke this:
"For he shall sleep for six months and remain awake for a single day. During that one day, however, the hero, wandering the earth, will be hungry."
With his mouth wide open, he would devour the worlds like a blazing fire in its fury. Having fallen into this calamity, that very king Rāvaṇa, now terrified by your prowess, has awakened Kumbhakarṇa.
This hero of terrible prowess has emerged from the camp;
violently enraged, he runs about devouring the monkeys.
Upon merely seeing Kumbhakarṇa, the monkeys fled in all directions.
"How will the monkeys restrain him when he is enraged in battle?
Let all the monkeys be told that this machine has been raised up;
once they have learned this, the monkeys here will become fearless."
Having heard these reasoned words spoken by Vibhīṣaṇa from his pleasant countenance,
Rāghava then spoke these words to Nīla, the commander of the army:
"Go, and having drawn up all the troops in battle array, take your position at the head."
Having seized the gates of Laṅkā, as well as the pathways and the bridges,
and gathering mountain peaks, trees, and rocks,
let all the monkeys stand ready, armed and with mountains in their hands.
Commanded by Rāghava, Nīla, the commander of the monkey army and an elephant among monkeys, duly instructed the host of monkeys.
Then Gavākṣa, Śarabha, Hanumān, Aṅgada, and Nala—
6.049.036c Taking hold of mountain peaks, those who resembled mountains advanced toward the gate.
6.049.037a Then that fierce army of monkeys shone, with trees raised aloft like mountains in their hands.
Just as a vast and formidable mass of great clouds hovers near a mountain,
so too did that tiger among rākṣasas, overwhelmed by the intoxication of sleep.
He of immense prowess proceeded along the royal highway, which was graced with splendor;
surrounded by thousands of Rākṣasas, he who was exceedingly difficult to conquer then went forth while being showered with a rain of flowers from the houses.
He beheld the vast and beautiful residence of the lord of the rākṣasas, covered with a network of gold and radiant as the sun. At that time, he was like the sun breaking through a mass of clouds.
Having entered the residence of the lord of the rākṣasas,
he saw his elder brother seated at a distance,
like Śakra seeing Svayambhū seated upon his throne.
6.050.005a Having approached his brother’s house and entered the inner chamber,
6.050.005c he beheld his elder brother sitting dejectedly in the Puṣpaka chariot.
6.050.006a Then, seeing Kumbhakarṇa standing nearby, the Ten-necked One—
Rising quickly and filled with joy, he brought him close. Then,
as his brother sat upon the couch, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa paid homage at his feet and asked, "What is to be done?"
6.050.007e Springing up, Rāvaṇa joyfully embraced him.
6.050.008a Embraced by his brother and duly congratulated,
Kumbhakarṇa ascended an auspicious, divine, and excellent throne.
6.050.009a Having taken his seat upon that throne, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa,
his eyes bloodshot with rage, addressed these words to Rāvaṇa:
6.050.010a "O King, for what purpose have I been awakened by you with such great effort?"
"Tell me, from what do you have fear? Who today shall become a ghost?
Rāvaṇa, standing before his enraged brother Kumbhakarṇa, spoke these words with his eyes turned slightly askance.
"O one of great strength, a very long time has passed while you have been sleeping;
being so well-off, you do not know of the fear caused by Rāma for me.
This is the mighty Rāma, son of Daśaratha, accompanied by Sugrīva."
"Having crossed the ocean with his army, he is cutting away our very roots. Come, behold the forests and groves of Laṅkā;
having easily reached them by means of the bridge, the monkey has turned the sea into a single expanse."
"Those most eminent rākṣasas have been slain by the monkeys in battle;
I do not see any depletion of the monkeys in the fight at all. Therefore, you must assist me, whose treasury has been entirely exhausted."
"Protect this city of Laṅkā, leaving behind only the children and the elderly! O mighty-armed one, for the sake of your brother, perform a most difficult task!
Indeed, O scorcher of foes, never before have I spoken such words to anyone, my brother."
"O bull among Rākṣasas, I have affection for you and the highest regard for you, especially during the many conflicts between the gods and the asuras;
for by you, having arrayed the forces, the gods and the asuras were conquered in battle."

Indeed, among all living beings, no one is seen who is your equal in strength. O you who are dear to your friends, your enemies, and your kinsmen, perform this supreme service for my benefit and well-being, according to what is pleasing to you.
"By your own splendor, scatter the army of my rivals, as a great, rising wind disperses the autumn clouds.
Having heard these lamentations of that king of the rākṣasas, [he replied: 6.051.001a.
Then Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words and laughed aloud:
"The very fault that we previously foresaw during the deliberation of counsel has now been brought upon you by you, who were not intent on our welfare."
"Indeed, the fruit of your evil deed has swiftly come upon you,
just as the fall into the hells awaits one who has committed wicked acts.
O Great King, this was truly the first consequence of your actions, which you had not considered."
6.051.004c Out of mere pride in his own prowess, he did not consider the consequences.
6.051.005a He who, established in power, performs later what should have been done first, 6.051.005c and performs first what should be done later, does not understand right policy and wrong policy.
6.051.006a Ritual acts performed at the wrong place or time, or performed in a contrary manner,
become defective, just as sacrificial oblations do when offered by those who are unpurified.
6.051.007a He who perceives the fivefold application of these three types of ritual acts—
Having established an agreement with his ministers, he conducts himself on the path of the assembly;
and that king who desires to carry out the agreement according to the scriptures perceives the ministers with his intellect and regards his friends accordingly.

6.051.009a O Lord of the Rākṣasas, a man pursues virtue, wealth, and pleasure, or all three at the appropriate time, or again, two of these pairs at once. 6.051.010a But having heard what is most excellent among these three, he does not comprehend it.
Whether it be a king or one of royal rank, his extensive learning is useless [if he lacks these].
O best of Rākṣasas, [he must employ] bribery, conciliation, sowing dissension, and timely valor; as well as strategic application, and both policy and its opposite.
6.051.012a He who, being self-possessed, deliberates with his ministers at the proper time regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and then pursues them, shall not encounter misfortune in this world.
6.051.013a Having observed what is beneficial for himself and the consequences thereof, he discerns between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done in this world.
A king lives together with ministers who understand the true nature of affairs;
whereas men of beast-like intellect, ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures,
desire to speak out of sheer audacity once they have been admitted into the inner circle of counsel.

The advice of those who do not know the treatises should not be acted upon— those who are ignorant of the science of statecraft yet desire vast prosperity. For there are men who, out of audacity, speak what is harmful while pretending it to be beneficial.
Having observed them, those who are outside the circle of counsel should be treated as malevolent agents who corrupt the king's affairs;
for, acting in concert with wise enemies, they destroy their master by causing him to undertake contrary actions in this world.
A ruler should discover through their conduct those ministers who, though appearing as friends, are actually enemies when deliberating on counsel;
for the undertakings of one who is fickle and rushes headlong into action in this world [fail].
Others fall into the opening like birds into the hollow of a crane;
for he who, disregarding the enemy, does not protect himself,
surely encounters misfortunes and is cast down from his position.
Having heard those words spoken by Kumbhakarṇa,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa knit his brows in anger and said to him:
"Why do you instruct me as if I were a venerable elder or a teacher?"
6.051.022c Why indeed, having exhausted yourself with such speech, should you now do what is appropriate for the occasion?
6.051.023a Whether through confusion, delusion of mind, or by relying on [mere] strength and prowess,
6.051.023c that which was not seized at the time— your efforts to recover it now are in vain.
At this time, let that which is appropriate now be performed;
counteract the fault born of my misconduct with your prowess.
If indeed you have affection for me, or if you recognize our brotherhood.

6.051.025c Or if this task is considered by you to be the most important duty to be performed in your heart, [then do it]. 6.051.026a He is a true friend who assists one who is distressed and whose purpose has failed; 6.051.026c he is a kinsman who provides help when others have been led astray.
Then, perceiving that he who spoke such firm and harsh words was indeed enraged, she addressed him slowly and gently;
for she observed that her brother’s senses were exceedingly agitated.

6.051.028c Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words slowly, consoling him: 6.051.029a "Enough, O King of the Rākṣasas; do not give way to such distress. 6.051.029c Casting aside your anger, you ought to remain composed."
"O King, this should not be taken to heart while I am alive:
'I shall destroy him on whose account you suffer.
"However, I must certainly speak what is beneficial to you in every situation."
"O King, what has been spoken out of kinship and brotherly affection is indeed worthy of a loving kinsman to do at such a time;
behold the slaughter of the enemies being carried out by me in battle."

6.051.033a Today, O mighty-armed one, behold at the forefront of the battle the army of monkeys fleeing, now that Rāma has been slain along with his brother by me. 6.051.034a Today, having seen that head of Rāma brought here from the battlefield by me, you shall see it.
"Be happy, O mighty-armed one; let Sītā be sorrowful.
Today, let all the Rākṣasas in Laṅkā, whose kinsmen have been slain, behold this most great and dear death of Rāma."
Today, for those overwhelmed by grief on account of the slaughter of their own kinsmen,
I shall wipe away their tears by destroying the enemy in battle. Today, I shall [shatter] him who resembles a mountain, like a cloud accompanied by the sun.
"Behold Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, scattered in battle!
O you of incomparable prowess, no one else needs to be dispatched by you for the fight.
I myself shall destroy your enemies, O mighty one!"
Whether it be Śakra, or Yama, or Agni and Vāyu,
or even Kubera and Varuṇa— I shall fight them all,
for I possess a body as massive as a mountain and wield a sharpened trident.
Even Purandara would fear him as he roars with his sharp fangs;
or rather, when he has laid down his weapons and crushes his enemies with his own might,
no one who wishes to live is able to stand before him face to face.
Neither with a spear, nor with a mace, nor with a sword, nor with sharp arrows— rushing forward with my bare hands alone, I shall slay even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself,
if that Rāghava can endure the force of my fist today.
"Then those floods of arrows shall drink the blood of that Raghava. Why do you distress yourself with anxiety, O King, while I am here?
I am prepared to set forth for the destruction of your enemy."
"O King, cast away your fear of Rāma; I shall slay here in battle both Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as the mighty Sugrīva. I desire to bestow upon you great and extraordinary glory."
"By slaying that son of Daśaratha,
I shall go forth to secure for you a happiness that brings true joy, having struck down Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa."
I shall devour all the leaders of the monkey troops.
Enjoy yourself as you wish, drink the finest wine of Varuṇa,
perform your duties, and let your fever be dispelled.
"Once Rāma has been sent today to the abode of Yama by me,
Sītā will come under my control for a long time.
These words were spoken to the mighty Atikāya, who was possessed of powerful arms.
6.052.001c Having heard Kumbhakarṇa’s words, Mahodara said:
6.052.002a “Born in the family of Kumbhakarṇa, yet arrogant and of vulgar vision,
6.052.002c you are so conceited that you are unable to discern what ought to be done in every situation.”
"Indeed, the king does not fail to know right and wrong, O Kumbhakarṇa;
but you, being arrogant due to your youth, merely wish to speak.
He who understands the distinctions of place and time knows the proper station, as well as growth and decline."

O bull among Rākṣasas, he understands both his own [intentions] and those of others. What wise man would do that which can be accomplished by one who is powerful yet possesses an ordinary intellect and has not served his elders?

6.052.006ab Those things you call dharma, artha, and kāma, which you describe as having distinct bases— 6.052.006cd in their true nature, they possess no defining characteristic by which they may be individually understood.
6.052.007a For indeed, action alone is the purpose of all these causes.
6.052.007c Furthermore, even among the most wicked deeds, there exists here a superior fruit.
6.052.008a Dharma and artha both have the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) as their fruit; the other two likewise [have this fruit].
6.052.008c Adharma and anartha result in the attainment of misfortune, and their fruit is one of transgression.
6.052.009 Men perform actions for the sake of this world and the next; however, one who is established in desire obtains actions that must be fashioned.
6.052.010 In this regard, this has been ordained by the King; it should be held in the heart, and it is our opinion as well.
6.052.010c For what is there to be removed from the violence that might be directed against an enemy?
6.052.011a As for the reason you have proposed for attacking alone,
6.052.011c even in that regard, I shall tell you what is improper and unjust.
"How will you alone conquer that Raghava, by whom many exceedingly powerful rakshasas were previously slain in Janasthana?
Those of great prowess who were formerly defeated by him in Janasthana— "
Even now you see all those Rākṣasas in the city terrified; you wish to awaken that son of Daśaratha, Rāma— who is like an enraged lion—
out of ignorance, as if awakening a sleeping serpent.
6.052.015a Who is capable of approaching him, who is constantly blazing with splendor and difficult to withstand because of his wrath,
as unbearable as Death itself? 6.052.016a All this is placed in jeopardy when one encounters the enemy.
6.052.016c Your going there alone does not please me at all. 6.052.017a For who, being destitute himself, would wish to bring a prosperous enemy under his control like a common person,
6.052.017c unless he were certain to sacrifice his own life?
"O best of Rākṣasas, there is no one among men who is your equal;
how then can you hope to fight with one who is the equal of Indra and Vivasvat?
Having spoken thus to the enraged Kumbhakarṇa, Mahodara—
In the midst of the *rākṣasas*, Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out, said:
"Having recovered Vaidehī once again, for what purpose do you prattle on?
Whenever you wish, Sītā shall come under your control."
"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, I have perceived a certain means for the service of Sītā; if it pleases you by your own judgment, listen to it.
I am Dvijihva, Saṃhrādin, Kumbhakarṇa, and Vitardana."
"Proclaim this: 'These two are setting out to slay the five Rāmas.
Then, having gone there, we shall diligently give battle to him;
if we conquer your enemies, there will be no need for us to employ further stratagems."
"If our enemy still lives and we have engaged in battle,
then we shall achieve that which we have envisioned in our minds.
We shall return here from the fight, drenched in blood."
"Having torn our own bodies apart with sharp arrows inscribed with Rāma’s name,
we shall say, 'Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa have been devoured by us,' and we shall seize your feet; O you who grant desires, fulfill our wish!"
Then, O King, having mounted the back of an elephant, you should have it proclaimed everywhere throughout the city:
"Rāma has been killed along with his brother and his army.
Then, O subduer of enemies, you must appear joyful toward your servants.
"Grant them enjoyments, retinues, and all objects of desire.
Then provide garlands, garments, and ointments for the heroes, and abundant drink for the warriors; you yourself, being joyful, should drink as well."
6.052.030a Then, when this rumor has become widespread and has spread everywhere, 6.052.030c enter, comfort her, and console Sītā in private;
6.052.030e entice her with wealth, grain, objects of desire, and jewels.
"O King, through this stratagem which is followed by fear and grief,
Sītā— though against her will and now deprived of her protector— will fall under your power,
for she will perceive that her charming husband has perished."

6.052.032c Out of despair and because of her womanly frailty, she will submit to your power. 6.052.033a Having been raised in comfort and deserving of happiness, though now emaciated by suffering, she will approach you in every way, knowing that her well-being depends on you.
This is well-guided by my insight:
for upon merely seeing Rāma, disaster would surely follow. Your purpose will be accomplished right here; do not be anxious.
O lord of men, there is a great gain of happiness through avoiding battle; for one who conquers enemies without fighting does not lose his army and incurs no risk.
6.052.035c And he enjoys great fame, merit, prosperity, and renown for a long time, O lord of the earth.
6.053.001a Having been addressed in this manner, Kumbhakarṇa rebuked Mahodara.
Then he spoke to his brother Rāvaṇa, the best of the rākṣasas:
"I shall today wipe away that terrible fear of yours arising from the slaughter of that evil-minded Rāma; you shall be free from enmity and at peace."
O hero, the brave do not roar in vain like waterless clouds;
behold rather their roaring being realized through action in battle. He does not tolerate [the enemy], nor does he hold himself in high esteem.
"O Mahodara, heroes perform difficult deeds without showing [their prowess] to those kings who are cowardly, lacking in wisdom, and merely imagining themselves to be learned—
such as you, who have been listening from the very beginning."
"O cowards, you who always speak pleasant words yet follow the king in battle—this task has been ruined by you.
Laṅkā has been reduced to the state of having only its king remaining; the treasury is exhausted and the army is slain."
"Having encountered this king, who bears the marks of a friend yet acts as an enemy,
I now go forth to battle, prepared for the conquest of my foes,
in order to rectify your misconduct today in this great conflict."
When the wise Kumbhakarṇa had thus spoken these words,
the lord of the rākṣasas then replied with a laugh:
"This Mahodara is undoubtedly terrified of Rāma."
"O dear one, you who are skilled in battle, I do not relish war;
for there is no one equal to you in friendship and in strength. Go, therefore, for the slaying of the enemy and for the victory of Kumbhakarṇa."
6.053.012a The destroyer of enemies swiftly took up a sharpened spear,
6.053.012c made entirely of iron, blazing, adorned with refined gold,
6.053.013a as terrible as Indra’s thunderbolt and as heavy as a diamond.
6.053.013c The destroyer of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kiṃnaras;
6.053.014a Bearing a great garland of red flowers and naturally emitting fire,
he took up a sharpened trident stained with the blood of his enemies.

6.053.014e The immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words to Rāvaṇa: 6.053.015a "I shall go alone; let this great army remain here. 6.053.015c Hungry and enraged today, I will devour those monkeys."
6.053.016 Having heard Kumbhakarṇa’s words, Rāvaṇa spoke these words:
"Go, surrounded by troops who carry pikes and mallets in their hands.
For the high-souled monkeys are swift and resolute."
They might bring about the destruction of one who is alone or heedless with their fangs.
Therefore, proceed surrounded by an army that is exceedingly difficult to overcome;
destroy the entire hostile faction, which is detrimental to the rākṣasas.
Then, rising from his seat, the immensely radiant Rāvaṇa fastened upon Kumbhakarṇa a garland interspersed with jewels,
as well as armlets, finger-rings, and excellent ornaments.
And he fastened upon the high-souled one a necklace resembling the moon;
Rāvaṇa also placed divine, fragrant garlands and two glorious earrings upon his ears.
Adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, and decorated with ornaments of gold coins,
Kumbhakarna, whose ears were large, shone like a well-fed sacrificial fire;
he was resplendent with a great dark-blue girdle around his hips.
Like Mount Mandara bound by the serpent during the churning for the nectar of immortality, he was clad in golden armor capable of bearing great weight, wind-tight,
and radiant with its own luster like a flash of lightning.
As he put on his armor,
he shone like the king of mountains enveloped in evening clouds;
that Rākṣasa, with all his limbs adorned with ornaments, held a trident in his hand.
Resolute in his undertaking of the three strides, he shone like Nārāyaṇa;
having embraced his brother and performed a circumambulation,
the mighty Bali bowed his head to him and set forth.
6.053.026e Rāvaṇa sent him forth with auspicious blessings.
6.053.027a Amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and with armies bearing excellent weapons, 6.053.027c he was accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots that roared like clouds.
Charioteers followed that high-souled one, the best among charioteers;
and they followed the formidable and mighty Kumbhakarṇa with serpents, camels, donkeys, horses, lions, elephants, wild beasts, and birds.
Scattered with flowers of many colors,
with a parasol held over him and a sharp spear in his hand,
he was fierce with intoxication and maddened by the scent of blood.
The enemy of the gods and the Dānavas marched forth; many foot-soldiers of great roar and immense strength followed him—
terrible Rākṣasas with fearsome eyes, weapons in hand.
With bloodshot eyes and massive bodies resembling heaps of black collyrium,
they brandished their swords and sharpened battle-axes;
they also carried many vast and formidable projectiles, several fathoms in length, that were difficult to withstand.
He hurled massive palm trunks that were difficult to withstand;
then, assuming another body that was fierce and hair-raising,
the immensely powerful and highly energetic Kumbhakarṇa rushed forth.
Three hundred *dhanus* in circumference and six hundred in height,
fierce, with eyes like the wheels of a cart, resembling a massive mountain, that great being,
having gathered the *rakṣasas* together, was like a scorched mountain.
6.053.035c Kumbhakarṇa, of the massive mouth, spoke these words while laughing:
6.053.036a "Today, filled with rage, I shall consume those hosts of monkey leaders, division by division, 6.053.036c like a fire consuming moths."
"Granted, the forest-dwelling monkeys do not offend me;
for that species is the very ornament of the city gardens of those like us.
But Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, is the root cause of the siege of the city."
"When he is slain, all will be slain; therefore, I shall slay him in battle.
As Kumbhakarna was speaking thus, the Rākṣasas let out a most terrible roar, as if making the ocean tremble.
As the wise Kumbhakarṇa rushed forth swiftly,
portents of terrible form appeared on all sides;
clouds accompanied by meteors and thunderbolts roared most dreadfully.
The earth, together with its oceans and forests, trembled;
jackals of terrible form howled with mouths full of flaming embers,
and birds circled in counter-clockwise mandalas.
As he was traveling along the road, a vulture flew out from his shoulder-pike;
his eye throbbed and his left arm trembled. Then, a blazing, terrifyingly roaring voice spoke forth.
The sun became lusterless, and the pleasant breeze ceased to blow.
Disregarding these great portents that had arisen, causing the hair to stand on end,
Kumbhakarṇa nevertheless went forth, impelled by the force of Death.

Having leaped over the wall on foot, he who resembled a mountain beheld that wondrous army of monkeys, which looked like a dense mass of clouds. Upon seeing that best of Rākṣasas, who was like a mountain, those monkeys—
Then, like clouds driven by the wind, that entire army went in all directions;
that exceedingly fierce host of monkeys fled in every direction like a scattered mass of clouds.
6.053.048c Beholding him with joy, that Kumbhakarṇa, who resembled a dark cloud, roared again like a thundercloud. 6.053.049a They, hearing his terrible roar, [were struck with fear].
Like the roar of a rain-cloud in the sky,
many monkeys fell upon the earth like *sāla* trees with their roots severed.
That great-souled Kumbhakarṇa, possessing massive iron bars for arms, went forth to destroy his enemies,
inspiring a most terrifying fear in the hosts of monkeys.
Like a lord wielding the staff of his servants at the end of an eon,
he let out a great roar that made the ocean resound,
as if generating thunderclaps and shattering the mountains.
6.054.002a Seeing him approaching with terrifying eyes— one who was incapable of being slain by Maghavan, Yama, or Varuṇa— the monkeys fled in all directions.
6.054.003a But seeing them fleeing, Vālin’s son Aṅgada said:
"Nala, Nīla, Gavākṣa, Kumuda, and Mahābala—
having forgotten yourselves here, as well as your own heroic deeds and noble lineage,
where are you going, terrified by fear like common monkeys?"
"Excellent, gentle ones! Turn back; why do you seek to protect your lives?
This demon is not capable of battle; this is but a great intimidation.
This vast display of terror has been raised by the rākṣasas."
"By our prowess we shall scatter him; turn back, O monkeys!
Having thus consoled one another with great difficulty and having gathered from here and there, the monkeys, with trees and rocks in their hands, set out for the field of battle.
6.054.008a But those forest-dwellers, turning back in a fury, struck Kumbhakarṇa, 6.054.008c being exceedingly enraged like elephants in rut;
6.054.008e those of great strength assailed him with lofty mountain peaks and boulders.
Though struck by trees with flowering tops, he did not tremble;
the rocks that fell upon his limbs shattered into hundreds of pieces,
and the flowering-topped trees, broken, fell to the surface of the earth.
Enraged, he too, exerting his supreme effort, crushed the armies of the mighty monkeys like a fire that has arisen and consumes the forests.
Many of those bull-like monkeys lay there, drenched in blood.
Cast down, they fell upon the ground like trees with copper-colored blossoms;
leaping and rushing, the monkeys did not look back—
some fell into the ocean, while others took refuge in the sky.
Being struck by that more powerful rākṣasa, those heroes fled by the very same path by which they had crossed the ocean;
with dejected faces due to fear, they fled over both dry land and low-lying ground.
Some bears climbed up trees, while others took refuge on mountains;
some plunged into the ocean, and others sought shelter in caves. Some monkeys sat down, while others did not remain at all.
6.054.016a Beholding those broken monkeys, Aṅgada spoke this to them: 6.054.016c "Stand firm! We shall fight! Turn back, O monkeys!
6.054.017a "I see no way for you who are broken, even after traversing this entire earth."
"Stay where you are! All of you, turn back! Why do you seek to preserve your lives?
O you whose prowess lies in unimpeded movement, why flee while disarmed? For your wives will mock you; indeed, that would be a death worse than living."
6.054.019a We were all born into families that are extensive and great;
6.054.019c yet you, being ignoble, have fled in fear, abandoning your valor.
6.054.020a As for those boasts of yours in the assembly of people, when [the time comes]...
Where have those sharp and great weapons of yours gone? The cries of cowards are heard; fie upon him who lives!
Let the path frequented by the virtuous be followed, and let fear be abandoned.
Either we shall lie slain upon the earth with our lives nearly spent, or,
being killed in battle, we shall attain the world of Brahmā which is so difficult to reach;
or else, having struck down the enemy in combat, we shall obtain fame.
"O Kumbhakarṇa, having seen the descendant of Kakutstha, you shall not escape alive,
just as a moth that has approached a blazing fire. We have resolved to save our lives by fleeing."

"By one alone, many have been broken; our fame shall go to ruin. To the heroic Aṅgada, adorned with golden armlets, as he was speaking thus, they fled and uttered words that were contemptible for a hero.
"A terrible slaughter has been wrought upon us by the Rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa. This is no time to remain; let us depart, for our dear lives are at stake.
Having spoken these words, they all fled in every direction.

Seeing Bhīma approaching with his terrifying eyes, those leaders of the monkey troops began to flee; but then all those heroic monkeys were turned back by Aṅgada through conciliatory words and great honors.
Ṛṣabha, Śarabha, Mainda, Dhūmra, Nīla;
Kumuda, Suṣeṇa, Gavākṣa, Rambha, Tāra;
Dvivida, Panasa, and the son of Vāyu as their leaders;
Having heard the words of Aṅgada, those great-bodied warriors then turned back; adopting a resolute resolve, they all desired battle and marched swiftly toward the fray.
6.055.002a Their vigor having been roused and their prowess instilled,
6.055.002c those monkeys were rallied by the words of Aṅgada.
6.055.003a Having set out, they attained joy, though they were resolved upon death.
6.055.003c The monkeys, having renounced their lives, waged a most tumultuous battle.
6.055.004a Then the massive-bodied monkeys, swiftly uprooting trees and very large mountain peaks, rushed toward Kumbhakarṇa.

6.055.005a That valiant Kumbhakarṇa, filled with rage and possessing a truly massive body, raised his mace and struck the enemies on all sides. 6.055.006a Seven hundred and eight thousand monkeys [were slain].
6.055.006c Scattered about, they lie upon the ground, crushed by Kumbhakarṇa.
6.055.007a Sixteen, eight, ten, twenty, and likewise thirty—
6.055.007c Enveloping them with his arms, he runs about devouring them.
Like Garuḍa, intensely enraged, devouring serpents,
Hanumān, stationed in the sky, rained down many various mountain peaks and trees upon Kumbhakarṇa’s head.
With his spear, he indeed shattered those mountain peaks;
the immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa also broke apart the rain of trees.
Then that fierce army of monkeys—
Grasping a sharp spear, he rushed forward;
then Hanumān stood before him as he was charging, seizing the peak of a mountain.
Enraged, he struck Kumbhakarṇa,
whose body was as formidable as a great mountain, with such force that he was then overwhelmed and shaken by it.
With his limbs drenched in fat and sprinkled with blood,
he brandished a trident as radiant as lightning,
like a mountain with its peaks ablaze.
He struck the son of the Maruts in the chest with a fierce spear,
just as Guha once struck Mount Krauñca;
his great chest was thus pierced by the trident.
Reeling and vomiting blood from his mouth,
Hanumān let out a terrible roar in that great battle,
sounding like the thundering of clouds at the end of an eon.
Then, seeing him distressed, the hosts of Rākṣasas suddenly rejoiced and let out a roar;
but the monkeys were distressed and afflicted by fear.
They fled from Kumbhakarṇa in the battle.
Nīla hurled a mountain peak at the wise Kumbhakarṇa;
seeing it falling toward him, he struck it down with his fist.
Struck by the blow of his fist, that mountain peak shattered;
emitting sparks and flames, it fell to the surface of the earth.
Then Ṛṣabha, Śarabha, Nīla, Gavākṣa, and Gandhamādana—
6.055.017c Five tiger-like monkeys rushed toward Kumbhakarṇa.
6.055.018a With rocks, trees, palms, feet, and fists, those of great strength 6.055.018c struck the massive-bodied Kumbhakarṇa from every side.
Feeling those blows like mere touches, he did not waver;
yet the bull among monkeys embraced the bull of great speed with his two arms,
while being pressed by Kumbhakarna’s own arms.
6.055.020c The formidable bull, with blood flowing from his mouth, fell down.
6.055.021a Having struck Śarabha with his fist and Nīla with his knee in the battle,
the enemy of Indra then struck Gavākṣa with his palm.
Pained by the blows they had received and drenched in blood,
they fainted and fell upon the earth like *kiṃśuka* trees cut down.
When those high-souled leaders of the monkeys had thus fallen, [the battle continued].
Thousands of monkeys rushed toward Kumbhakarna;
all those bulls among the monkeys, resembling mountains themselves, climbed upon him— who was like a mountain—
and leaping up, those of great strength bit him.
With their claws, teeth, fists, and likewise their knees,
those bulls among monkeys struck the massive-bodied Kumbhakarṇa;
covered by those thousands of monkeys, he resembled a mountain.
That tiger among rākṣasas shone like a mountain with trees growing upon it;
seizing all the monkeys with his two arms, that one of great strength,
filled with rage, devoured them as Garuḍa devours serpents.
6.055.028a Cast into his mouth, which resembled the netherworld (pātāla),
the monkeys emerged from his nostrils and ears. 6.055.029a Enraged and resembling a mountain, he devoured the monkeys with great ferocity.
Enraged, that best of Rākṣasas shattered all the monkeys;
making the ground a mire of flesh and blood,
that Rākṣasa moved through the monkey armies like the intensified fire of cosmic destruction.
In that place, the mighty Kumbhakarna shone with a spear in his hand, like Śakra with the thunderbolt in his hand, or like Antaka with the noose in his hand;
he burned the dry forests as fire consumes them in the summer heat.
Thus Kumbhakarṇa scorched the monkey armies;
then, being slaughtered and deprived of their leaders,
those monkeys, agitated by fear, shrieked discordantly and intensely.
Being struck down many times by Kumbhakarṇa, the monkeys,
distressed and dejected in heart, sought refuge with Rāghava.
Beholding that mighty Kumbhakarṇa rushing toward them—
Then the heroic Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, leapt up;
that great monkey, having lifted and whirled a mountain peak,
rushed with speed toward the mighty Kumbhakarṇa.
Beholding that monkey rushing toward him, Kumbhakarṇa stood facing the lord of monkeys with all his limbs exposed,
devouring the great apes whose bodies were smeared with the blood of monkeys.
Seeing Kumbhakarṇa standing there, Sugrīva spoke these words:
"The heroes have been struck down by you; a most difficult task has been accomplished. The armies have been devoured, and supreme glory has been attained by you."
"Abandon that army of monkeys; what will you do with commoners?
O Rākṣasa, endure this single fall of my mountain!
These were the words of the king of the monkeys, endowed with courage and fortitude.
6.055.041c Having heard this, Kumbhakarṇa, that tiger among rākṣasas, spoke these words:
6.055.042a "You are the grandson of Prajāpati and likewise the son of Ṛkṣarajas; 6.055.042c endowed as you are with learning and prowess, therefore you roar, O monkey!"
Having heard Kumbhakarṇa’s words,
he brandished a mountain and suddenly hurled it;
with that, he struck Kumbhakarṇa in the chest.
That mountain peak, resembling a thunderbolt of adamant,
was suddenly shattered against his broad chest.
Then the monkeys suddenly despaired,
while the hosts of Rākṣasas roared with joy;
struck by the mountain peak, he grew enraged.
And opening his mouth in rage, he roared; brandishing a trident that flashed like lightning,
he hurled it for the sake of slaying the lord of the monkeys and bears.
That sharp spear, adorned with golden bands, which had been hurled by Kumbhakarṇa’s arm,
he quickly leapt up and seized with both his arms.
The son of Anila,
that bull among monkeys, joyfully placed his foot upon the great iron spear— which weighed a thousand bhāras— and broke it with force.
Seeing that trident shattered at that moment, the high-souled lord of the rākṣasas grew furious;
uprooting a mountain peak from the Malaya mountain of Laṅkā, he—
Approaching Sugrīva, he struck him with that [weapon];
thus struck by the mountain peak, the lord of monkeys fell unconscious to the ground in the battle.
Seeing him fallen on the ground unconscious,
the Yātudhānas rejoiced and shouted in the battle.
Approaching him of wondrous and terrible prowess, they...
In battle, that Kumbhakarṇa seized Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, and carried him off,
just as a most violent wind carries away a cloud.
Tearing up that tree which resembled a great cloud as he advanced in battle, Kumbhakarṇa shone with a form like Mount Meru.
Like Mount Meru with its exceedingly lofty and formidable peaks,
the hero then uprooted it and departed,
being praised by the lords of the rākṣasas in battle.
Hearing the clamor of the dwellers of the triple heaven,
who were astonished by the seizing of the king of the monkeys,
he then took him and thought:
"He is the lord of monkeys, equal to Indra, possessing the prowess of Indra.
If he is slain, all this—
including the army with Rāghava— will be lost," thought the enemy of Indra.
Seeing the army of monkeys fleeing here and there,
and seeing that Sugrīva had been seized by Kumbhakarṇa,
the wise Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, reflected.
"Once Sugrīva has been captured in this way, what should I do?
Whatever is right for me to do, that I shall certainly perform. Becoming like a mountain, I will destroy the Rākṣasa."
When Kumbhakarṇa of great strength had been slain by me in battle, his body shattered by my fist,
and when the king of the monkeys had been liberated;
"May all the monkeys be joyful;
or else this king himself shall attain liberation,
even if he were seized by the gods together with the asuras and the serpents."
"I think that the lord of monkeys,
struck by Kumbhakarna with a mountain-blow in the encounter, has not yet regained consciousness of himself; in this great battle, Sugriva will regain his senses only after a short while."
"He will do what is beneficial for himself and for the monkeys.
But if I were to release this high-souled Sugrīva, he would become displeased; it would be a painful situation and lead to the eternal destruction of my reputation."
"Therefore, I shall wait for a moment to observe the prowess of our king;
meanwhile, I will reassure this broken army of monkeys.
Having reflected thus, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, [proceeded].
6.055.063c He once again rallied the great army of monkeys.
6.055.064a Then that Kumbhakarṇa entered Laṅkā, carrying that great monkey who was still quivering.
Being showered with rains of the finest flowers by those stationed upon celestial chariots, moving through the air, and atop houses and gate-towers,
he then regained consciousness with great difficulty.
Standing between the arms of that powerful one and gazing at the royal highway of the city,
the high-souled one reflected again and again.
"How indeed can this be accomplished by me now that he has been captured?
I shall act in such a way that for the monkeys— "
Then, having quickly gathered together with the tips of his trunk, the king [tried to seize] the enemy of the lord of the monkeys for the sake of what was desirable, beneficial, and necessary.
With his claws he bit Kumbhakarna’s ears, with his teeth his nose, and he tore at his sides.
With his ears and nose thus torn away, Kumbhakarna—
Torn apart and crushed by him,
overcome with rage and his limbs drenched in blood,
he seized Sugrīva and dashed him against the ground.
Crushed upon the earth by those enemies of the gods with their terrible strength and being struck down by them,
he rose up with great speed and went into the sky.
And again, the mighty Kumbhakarna, deprived of his ears and nose, encountered Rama;
drenched in blood, he shone like a mountain with its waterfalls.
Then that great-souled Rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa, having suddenly emerged from the city, devoured that fierce army of monkeys in battle.
Like the blazing fire at the end of an eon,
hungry and greedy for blood and flesh,
he entered that fierce army of monkeys.
Out of delusion, Kumbhakarṇa devoured the Rākṣasas, monkeys, Piśācas, and bears in battle—
whether one, two, three, or many— along with the enraged monkeys and Rākṣasas.
Taking it with one hand, he quickly hurled it into his mouth;
then, that immensely powerful one, streaming with fat and blood,
was being struck by the tips of the lords of mountains as he devoured the monkeys.
While being devoured, those monkeys then went to Rāma for refuge.
At that time, Sumitrā’s son Lakṣmaṇa— the crusher of enemy forces and conqueror of hostile cities— fought in a rage.
The valiant Lakṣmaṇa drove seven arrows into Kumbhakarṇa’s body; he took up others and discharged them as well. Then the immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa bypassed the son of Sumitrā.
He rushed toward Rāma alone, as if tearing asunder the earth.
Then Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, employing the Raudra weapon,
loosed sharpened arrows into the heart of Kumbhakarṇa.
As he rushed forward suddenly, pierced by Rāma,
flames mixed with glowing coals issued from the mouth of the enraged one.
And those arrows with peacock-feathered shafts sank deep into his chest.
And that great mace, slipping from his hand, fell upon the earth. When that one of great strength perceived himself to be disarmed,
he wrought a great slaughter with his fists and his feet.
With his limbs pierced by arrows and drenched in blood, he flowed with gore like a mountain with its springs. Overwhelmed by intense rage and fainting from the blood, he—
Devouring monkeys, rākṣasas, and bears, he ran about in all directions.
At that time, the righteous Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma,
intent upon the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa and reflecting upon many strategic means.
"O King, this one does not distinguish between monkeys and Rākṣasas;
intoxicated by the smell of blood, he devours both his own kind and others.
Let the bulls among monkeys climb all over him."
"Let the troop-leaders, each according to their rank, stand around him on all sides.
Perhaps this evil-minded Rākṣasa, when crushed by the heavy burden at the critical moment and falling to the ground, will not kill the other monkeys."
Having heard those words of the wise prince,
the monkeys joyfully climbed upon Kumbhakarna.
But Kumbhakarna, having been mounted by the monkeys, became enraged.
He shook them off with great force, like a rogue elephant shaking off its mahouts.
Seeing them shaken off, the Rākṣasa thought, "This Rāma is enraged," and he sprang up with speed and took up his excellent bow.
Taking up his formidable bow, which was like a serpent, possessed a firm string, and was adorned with gold,
he comforted the monkeys and leapt upward.
Rāma, with his excellent quiver and arrows fastened on,
surrounded by those hosts of monkeys and followed by Lakṣmaṇa, set forth, he of great strength and supreme invincibility.
He beheld the high-souled Kumbhakarṇa, the subduer of enemies and wearer of the diadem, his entire body drenched in blood and possessed of great strength,
charging toward everyone like a furious elephant of the quarters.
Surrounded by Rākṣasas, he was angrily searching for the monkeys;
resembling the Vindhya or Mandara mountains, adorned with golden armlets,
blood flowed from his mouth like a rain-cloud that has arisen.
Licking with his tongue the blood that drenched him,
crushing the monkey host like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time,
they beheld that best of Rākṣasas, possessing the splendor of a blazing fire.
Then that bull among men drew his bow. At the thunderous sound of his bow, the bull of the Nairṛtas was provoked;
unable to endure that noise, he rushed toward Rāghava.
Then, as he approached— resembling a cloud driven by the wind, with arms like the coils of the best of serpent-kings, and possessing the splendor of a mountain—
Rāma said to Kumbhakarṇa in battle: "O Lord of Rākṣasas, do not fall into despair;
I stand here with my bow grasped."
"Know me, O enemy of Śakra, to be Rāma; in a moment he shall be deprived of his senses.
Recognizing that "this is Rāma," he laughed with a distorted sound.
As if striking the hearts of all the forest-dwellers,
the immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa laughed a distorted, terrifying laugh resembling the roar of a thundercloud, and addressed these words to Rāghava.
"I am not to be known as Virādha, nor Kabandha, nor Khara;
I am neither Vālī nor Mārīca—I have come as Kumbhakarṇa. Behold my terrible mallet, made entirely of great iron."

"By him the gods were conquered; formerly, the Dānavas were conquered by me. You ought not to despise me on account of my missing ears and nose, for even the slightest pain was not caused to me by the destruction of my ears and nose."
"O tiger among the Ikṣvākus, quickly display your prowess upon my limbs;
then, having witnessed your manly valor, I shall devour you.
Having heard these words of Kumbhakarṇa, [he...]
Rāma discharged arrows with beautiful feathers; struck by those shafts, which possessed a force equal to the thunderbolt,
the enemy of the gods neither trembled nor suffered pain.
Those very arrows by which the excellent *sāla* trees were cut down and Vālin,
the bull among monkeys, was slain—
those now struck the body of Kumbhakarṇa.
Those arrows, though like thunderbolts, caused him no pain; the enemy of Mahendra drank them in with his body as if they were streams of water.
Brandishing that mallet of fierce velocity, he struck away the force of Rāma’s arrow;
then the Rākṣasa was smeared with blood.
Brandishing that mallet of fierce velocity, which struck terror into the great armies of the gods,
he put the host of monkeys to flight.
Then, taking up that supreme Vāyavya weapon,
Rāma hurled it at the night-stalker; with it, he struck off the arm along with the mace.
With his arm severed, he let out a tumultuous roar;
that arm, resembling a mountain peak,
was cut off by Rāghava’s arrow along with the mallet.
6.055.112c He fell upon that army of the king of monkeys and struck down that host of vanaras.
6.055.113a Those vanaras who remained after being broken and slain—
Then, reaching the limit [of their endurance], despondent and with trembling limbs,
they beheld that most terrible encounter between the lord of men and the king of the rākṣasas.
With his arm severed by the weapon, that great Kumbhakarṇa, like a lordly mountain with its peak cut away,
uprooted a tree with his hand.
Then he rushed in battle toward that king,
his arm raised together with the *sāla* tree,
resembling the coiled body of a serpent.
Rāma struck off Kumbhakarṇa’s arm with an arrow adorned with gold, joined with Indra’s weapon. That arm was severed.
Resembling a mountain, he fell to the ground;
writhing, he struck down trees,
rocks, monkeys, and rākṣasas.
Seeing him with his arm severed,
rushing forward suddenly while roaring,
Rāma took up two sharp crescent-shaped arrows.
In battle, he severed the feet of the Rākṣasa;
with his arms cut off and his feet lopped away,
the demon tore open his mouth, which resembled the submarine fire of Vaḍavāmukha.
Roaring loudly, he suddenly rushed at Rāma,
just as Rāhu rushes toward the moon in the sky;
he filled his mouth with sharp-pointed [arrows].
With his mouth filled by Rāma’s arrows whose feathers were bound with gold, he was unable to speak;
he uttered a cry with great difficulty and even fainted.
Then he took up the unerring Aindra weapon, sharp and well-feathered, which resembled the rays of the sun and was like the staff of Brahmā, the Destroyer, and Death itself.
Rāma [took] that arrow, equal in speed to the wind,
with a beautiful shaft of diamond and Jāmbūnada gold,
shining like the blazing sun and fire.
Rāma hurled at the night-stalker that arrow, whose velocity was equal to the thunderbolt of great Indra;
impelled by the arm of Rāghava, that shaft—
Illuminating the ten directions with his own radiance,
appearing as brilliant as a smokeless fire,
he proceeded with a stride equal to the thunderbolt of Śakra.
Then he severed that head of the lord of the Rākṣasas, which resembled the peak of a great mountain, with its bared fangs and its swinging, beautiful earrings.
Just as in ancient times Purandara [struck] Vṛtra, so did that head of the Rākṣasa, resembling a mountain, fall when struck by Rāma’s arrow.
He shattered the walkways, inner chambers, and gate-towers,
and he brought down that high rampart;
and that massive body, radiant as the Himalayas—
Then that *rakṣas* fell into the ocean; it crushed the crocodiles, the multitudes of great fish, and the serpents,
and likewise entered the earth.
When that enemy of the Brahmins and gods,
the mighty Kumbhakarṇa, was slain in battle,
the earth and all the mountains trembled.
And out of joy, the gods raised a tumultuous roar.
Then the celestial sages, the great sages, the serpents, the gods, the spirits, the Suparṇas, and the Guhyakas [rejoiced].
6.055.127c The hosts of yakṣas and gandharvas dwelling in the sky were delighted by Rāma’s prowess;
6.055.128a many monkeys, moreover, attained great joy.
With faces resembling blossomed lotuses,
they honored Rāghava, the recipient of their desired reward,
now that the enemy of terrible strength and invincible power had been slain.
Having slain Kumbhakarṇa—
the crusher of the celestial armies, whose fatigue was never known in great battles— the elder brother of Bharata rejoiced in the fray.
Seeing the great asura Kumbhakarna slain by the high-souled Raghava— just as the lord of the immortals slew Vritra—
the rakshasas reported it to Ravana, the lord of the rakshasas.
6.056.002 Having heard that the mighty Kumbhakarṇa had been slain in battle,
Rāvaṇa, tormented by grief, fainted and fell to the ground.
6.056.003 Upon hearing that his paternal uncle had been killed, Devāntaka and Narāntaka [were likewise overcome].
Triśiras and Atikāya wept, oppressed by grief,
having heard that their brother had been slain by Rāma of unwearied deeds;
Mahodara and Mahāpārśva likewise became overwhelmed with sorrow.
Then, having regained consciousness with great difficulty, that bull among Rākṣasas,
Rāvaṇa, dejected by the slaughter of Kumbhakarṇa, lamented:
"Alas, O hero, destroyer of the pride of enemies, Kumbhakarṇa of mighty strength!"
"Having scorched the enemy host alone, where are you going now, abandoning me? Indeed,
I am no more now that my right arm has fallen— that arm relying upon which I had no fear of gods or asuras."
How could such a hero, the destroyer of the pride of gods and dānavas,
who was indeed like the fire of cosmic destruction, have been slain today by Rāghava in battle— you,
whom even the strike of a thunderbolt could never cause to suffer?
"How is it that you, afflicted by Rāma’s arrow, lie fast asleep upon the earth?
These hosts of gods, together with the sages, stand in the sky;
seeing you slain in battle, they roar with great joy."
"6.056.011a Surely this very day the monkeys, joyful and having found their mark, 6.056.011c will scale the difficult fortifications and the gates of Laṅkā from every side.
6.056.012a I have no need for the kingdom; what shall I do with Sītā?"
6.056.012c Without Kumbhakarṇa, I have no delight in living.
6.056.013a If I do not slay Rāghava, the killer of my brother, in battle,
6.056.013c then death is surely better for me than this useless life.
"This very day I shall go to that place where my younger brother is;
for I cannot bear to live even for a moment having abandoned my brothers.
Indeed, the gods will mock me upon seeing one who has previously committed such an offense."
"6.056.015c How shall I conquer Indra now that you, Kumbhakarṇa, have been slain?
6.056.016a Thus has this auspicious word of Vibhīṣaṇa come upon me, 6.056.016c which, out of ignorance, was not accepted by me from that high-souled one."
6.056.017a As long as Vibhīṣaṇa’s words remain unheeded, this destruction of Kumbhakarṇa and Prahasta has arisen; 6.056.017c this terrible event causes me deep shame.
6.056.018a This is the fruit of that deed now reaped by me, bringing only sorrow.
"Because I rejected that righteous and illustrious Vibhīṣaṇa," thus lamenting most piteously in many ways with a deeply agitated inner soul, he spoke to Kumbhakarṇa.
Then the ten-faced one, deeply afflicted, fell down;
for he had learned that his younger brother, the enemy of Indra, was slain.
As the evil-minded Rāvaṇa was thus lamenting, [the earth shook].
6.057.001c Having heard the words of him who was tormented by grief, Triśiras spoke: 6.057.002a "O dear one, it is exactly so; our middle brother, possessed of great heroism, has been slain.
6.057.002c But virtuous men, O King, do not lament as you do."
"O Lord, surely you are sufficient even for the three worlds;
why then, like an ordinary man, do you thus subject yourself to grief?
You possess the power bestowed by Brahmā, as well as armor, arrows, and a bow."
A chariot yoked with a thousand donkeys and possessing a sound like a thundercloud—
by you, though unarmed, the gods and dānavas have been repeatedly slaughtered.
Equipped with all weapons, it is right for you to subdue Rāghava.
"Stay as you wish, O Great King; I shall go forth to battle.
I will uproot your enemies here, just as Garuḍa [uproots] serpents, or as Śambara was by the King of the Gods, or Naraka by Viṣṇu."
"Thus today Rāma, struck down by me in battle, shall lie prostrate.
Hearing these words of Triśiras, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
impelled by Time, considered himself as if born anew.
Having heard the words of Triśiras, Devāntaka, Narāntaka, and the radiant Atikāya became filled with the joy of battle.
Then those bulls among the Nairṛtas roared, each crying out, "Me first! Me first!"
The heroic sons of Rāvaṇa possess prowess equal to that of Śakra;
they all range through the atmosphere, and all are experts in the arts of illusion. They have all crushed the pride of the gods, and all are intoxicated with the fury of battle.

6.057.012 All were endowed with the power of weapons, all possessed far-reaching fame; 6.057.012c it was never heard that any of them, having encountered battle, were ever defeated. 6.057.013 All these heroes were learned in the use of weapons, and all were experts in combat.
6.057.013c All possessed the highest knowledge, and all had likewise obtained boons.
6.057.014a He was thus surrounded by those sons, who were equal to the sun in splendor and were the crushers of enemy forces.
He shone like King Maghavan surrounded by the immortals, who destroy the pride of the great Dānavas. Having embraced his sons and adorned them with ornaments, he—
And with auspicious blessings,
Rāvaṇa dispatched Mahodara and Mahāpārśva, his two brothers,
into the battle for the protection of the princes.
Having saluted the high-souled Rāvaṇa, the terrifier of his enemies,
and having circumambulated him clockwise, those great-bodied ones of immense strength set forth,
having anointed themselves with all kinds of medicinal herbs and fragrances.
These six foremost of the Nairṛtas, desiring battle, went forth. Then Mahodara mounted the elephant named Sudarśana, who resembled a dark blue cloud and was born in the lineage of Airāvata.
Equipped with all kinds of weapons and well-adorned with quivers,
he shone as he sat upon his elephant like the sun atop the western mountain;
[he was] yoked to excellent horses and filled with every sort of weapon.
6.057.021c Triśiras, the son of Rāvaṇa, ascended that best of chariots.
6.057.022a Standing upon the chariot, the bow-wielding Triśiras shone resplendent,
6.057.022c like a cloud accompanied by lightning and meteors, blazing with fire and bearing Indra’s bow.
With three diadems, that three-headed one shone upon his excellent chariot,
like Himavat, the lord of mountains, with its three golden peaks;
so too did the radiant Atikāya, the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas, appear at that time.
The best of all archers ascended that preeminent chariot, which had excellent wheels and axles, was well-yoked, equipped with a chassis and a pole, and was radiant with quivers and bows,
and filled with spears, swords, and clubs.
Resplendent with his shining crown variegated with gold and with his ornaments, he shone like Mount Meru radiant with its own splendors. That mighty prince gleamed upon that chariot.
Surrounded by tigers among the Nairṛtas like Indra with the thunderbolt in hand surrounded by the immortals,
Narāntaka mounted a white horse adorned with gold, resembling Uccaiḥśravas, swift as thought, and of massive body.
Grasping a spear as bright as fire, Narāntaka shone resplendent;
the radiant Guha, taking up his javelin, appeared like [Śiva] in battle against his enemies.
Devāntaka, having seized a mace adorned with diamonds, [shone forth].
Encompassing the mountain with his two arms and mimicking the form of Viṣṇu,
the immensely powerful and highly energetic Mahāpārśva took up his mace;
with mace in hand, he shone in the battle like Kubera.
Those high-souled ones set forth, surrounded by incomparable forces,
like the gods in Amarāvatī surrounded by incomparable forces.
They [proceeded] with elephants, horses, and chariots that rumbled like clouds.
The high-souled Rākṣasas, armed with excellent weapons, followed them.
Those great-souled youths, possessing the splendor of the sun, shone resplendently;
adorned with diadems and endowed with beauty, they were like blazing planets in the sky.
The white row of parasols held aloft by them shone like a flight of swans in the sky resembling autumnal clouds—
[those who had resolved] either upon their own death or the defeat of their enemies.
Having thus resolved their minds, those heroes went forth seeking battle;
they roared, shouted aloud, and discharged their arrows.
As they marched out, those high-souled warriors, intoxicated by the frenzy of war, were filled with joy.
With the sounds of their roars and the slapping of their arms, the earth seemed to tremble;
and with the lion-like shouts of the Rākṣasas, the sky seemed to burst asunder. Then those mighty lords of the Rākṣasas emerged, filled with joy.
The monkey host saw the army of the Nairṛtas with its rocks and mountains raised high;
the great-souled monkeys also beheld that Nairṛta force,
crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells.
Resembling dark blue clouds, with great weapons raised aloft,
and surrounded on all sides by Nairṛtas who resembled blazing fire and the sun—
seeing that army approaching, the monkeys regained their composure.
With great mountains raised aloft, they roared again and again.
Then, hearing that clamorous sound of the monkey leaders, the hosts of rākṣasas—
Unable to endure that fierce and terrible joy of the enemy,
those of great strength roared most fearfully.
Having entered that formidable army of the Rākṣasas, those leaders of the monkey hosts—
6.057.044c With upraised crags, they moved about like peaked mountains.
6.057.045a Some monkeys entered the sky, while others moved upon the earth;
6.057.045c enraged and armed with trees and rocks, they roamed among the armies of the rākṣasas.
With trees, stones, and crags, they unleashed an unsurpassed rain;
though being warded off by floods of arrows,
the monkeys of terrifying prowess let out lion-like roars in the battle, as did the rākṣasas.
The monkeys crushed the Yātudhānas with rocks;
enraged in the conflict, they struck down those covered in armor and ornaments—
some heroes mounted on chariots, and others even on elephants and horses.

Leaping forward with sudden force, the monkeys struck down the Yātudhānas; with the falling of mountain peaks and blows from their fists, those bull-like Rākṣasas lost their sight, reeled, fell, and shrieked there.
Then, by the mountains and swords hurled by the monkeys and the Rākṣasas,
the earth was covered in a moment and became drenched in blood,
strewn with those Rākṣasas, the crushers of enemies, who resembled mountains.
Thrust forward, being hurled, and with their spears broken by the monkeys,
those night-stalkers struck the monkeys with their very own monkeys;
and those monkeys likewise struck the rākṣasas with their very own rākṣasas.
Having hurled rocks at them, the rākṣasas struck the monkeys;
and having snatched away their weapons, the monkeys struck the rākṣasas.
They struck one another with mountain peaks, spears, and missiles, and tore each other apart.
And the monkeys and rākṣasas let out lion-like roars in the battle. Struck by the monkeys, the rākṣasas— whose armor and body-protectors were shattered—
streamed blood there like trees exuding their sap.
In that battle, some monkeys struck chariot against chariot, elephant against elephant, and horse against horse;
they did so with razor-edged arrows, crescent-shaped shafts, broad-headed missiles, and sharpened arrows.
The Rākṣasas cut down trees and rocks upon the lords of the monkeys. With mountain peaks scattered, trees severed in the fray,
and monkeys and Rākṣasas slain, the earth became impassable.
When that tumultuous conflict had begun,
while the faces of the monkeys were filled with joy,
and as the Rākṣasas were being struck down;
The great seers and the hosts of gods raised a cry.
Then, mounting a horse with speed equal to the wind and grasping a sharpened spear, [he set forth].
Like a fish entering the great ocean, Narāntaka plunged into the army of the monkey king;
that hero [then slew] seven hundred monkeys.
In a single moment, that great-souled enemy of Indra pierced [the foe] with a flaming spear and struck down the army of the foremost among the monkeys.
And the Vidyādharas and great ṛṣis beheld that high-souled one stationed upon the back of a horse, moving among the monkey armies;
his path was seen to be a mire of flesh and blood.
Surrounded by monkeys who had fallen like mountains,
as soon as those bulls among the monkeys resolved to display their prowess,
Narāntaka bypassed them and pierced through them.
Raising his flaming spear at the edge of the battle, Narāntaka consumed the monkey armies like the fire consumes forests. Meanwhile,
the forest-dwellers continued to uproot trees and mountains.
6.057.066c So many fell, struck down by force, like mountains shattered by the thunderbolt.
6.057.067a The powerful Narāntaka roamed through all directions,
6.057.067c crushing everything on every side in battle, like the wind during the rainy season.
The heroes were unable to run, nor could they stand still, much less move;
whether he was leaping up, standing, or walking, the valiant one pierced them all with a single spear that resembled the God of Death and possessed the brilliance of the sun.

The monkey armies, shattered, fell to the surface of the earth. The monkeys were unable to endure the falling of the spear, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt; they cried out with a great roar.
6.057.071a As the heroic monkeys were falling, their forms shone forth,
6.057.071c like mountains with their peaks shattered by thunderbolts as they fall.
6.057.072a But those great-souled ones who had previously been struck down by Kumbhakarṇa—
Those best of monkeys, being unwell, approached Sugrīva.
Looking about, Sugrīva beheld the monkey army fleeing here and there,
terrified by the fear of Narāntaka.
Seeing his army in flight, he beheld Narāntaka approaching on the back of a horse, brandishing a spear. Then the immensely radiant Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, spoke.
"Go, O hero, against that Rākṣasa mounted upon a horse— against the heroic prince Aṅgada, whose prowess is equal to Śakra's—
and swiftly deprive him of his life as he agitates the monkey army."
Having heard his master’s words,
Angada then leapt forth from the ranks that resembled masses of clouds, like the sun emerging from a bank of clouds;
Angada, the foremost of monkeys, was like a vast mountain peak.
Adorned with armlets, he shone like a mountain rich in minerals;
though divested of weapons and possessing only his claws and fangs, the immensely energetic son of Vālin approached Narāntaka and spoke these words.
"Stay! What will you do with these ordinary monkeys? Cast this spear, whose touch is like a thunderbolt, at my chest!
Hearing Aṅgada's words, Narāntaka became enraged.
Biting his lip with his teeth and hissing like a serpent,
he then brandished a flaming spear and suddenly hurled it at Aṅgada.
That spear, like a thunderbolt, struck the chest of Vāli’s son;
shattered, it fell to the ground. Seeing that lance thus broken, he then—
Raising his palm, which resembled the expanded coils of a serpent with beautiful wings, that son of Vālin struck the head of the horse.
With his feet sunk deep, his eyes wide open and staring,
his tongue lolling out, and resembling a mountain,
that horse of his fell to the ground.
With his head shattered by that blow,
Narāntaka fell under the sway of rage upon seeing his horse slain and fallen.
Raising his fist, he of great power struck the son of Vālin on the head in battle;
then Aṅgada’s head was split by that fist.
Hot and very warm blood flowed profusely;
he repeatedly flared up and fainted,
and upon regaining consciousness, he was filled with wonder.
Then the high-souled Aṅgada, having clenched his fist— which possessed a force like a thunderbolt and was like a mountain peak— struck down [the enemy] at that time.
On the chest of Narāntaka, the son of Vālin—
his breast crushed and split by that fist,
vomiting flames and his limbs smeared with blood— [fell].
Narāntaka fell upon the surface of the earth like a mountain shattered by the strike of a thunderbolt; then,
in the sky, [the sound] of the foremost of the thirty gods [resounded].
And when that foremost hero Narāntaka had been slain in battle by the son of Vālin, there arose a great roar from the forest-dwellers.
Then Aṅgada, who possessed exceeding heroism and prowess, was filled with wonder that he had performed such a most difficult feat which gladdened Rāma’s heart.
And once again he became joyful in the battle.
Seeing Narāntaka slain, the foremost of the Nairṛtas—
Devāntaka, Trimūrdhan, and Mahodara, the son of Pulastya— cried out.
6.058.002 Ascending a lordly elephant resembling a cloud,
the powerful Mahodara charged toward the son of Vālin, who possessed great heroism.
6.058.003 Then the mighty Devāntaka, tormented by the calamity that had befallen his brother, [advanced].
Taking up a blazing iron club, Aṅgada rushed forward. Then the hero Triśiras, mounting a chariot resembling the sun and yoked with excellent horses, advanced against the son of Vālin.
6.058.005a Attacked by those three lords of the Nairṛtas, who destroy the pride of the gods, 6.058.005c Aṅgada uprooted a tree with massive branches.
6.058.006a That hero, Aṅgada, suddenly hurled it at Devāntaka.
Śakra [aimed] at that great tree with its massive branches, which was like a blazing thunderbolt; Triśiras cut it down with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Seeing the tree severed, Aṅgada then leapt up from there.
Then that elephant among monkeys rained down trees and rocks;
enraged, Triśiras cut them apart with sharpened arrows,
and Surāntaka shattered those trees with the tip of his iron club.
Triśiras rushed at the heroic Aṅgada with arrows;
then Mahodara, charging on his elephant toward the son of Vālin,
furiously struck him in the chest with javelins resembling thunderbolts.
Then Devāntaka, filled with rage, approached Aṅgada and,
having struck him swiftly with an iron club, departed with great speed.
He was then simultaneously assailed by those three foremost of the Nairṛtas.
The son of Vālin, possessed of great energy and prowess, was not shaken;
leaping up violently, he struck that great elephant with his palm. Both its eyes fell out, and that elephant let out a roar.
6.058.014a Having extracted his tusk, the mighty son of Vālin 6.058.014c rushed toward Devāntaka and struck him in the combat.
6.058.015a With all his limbs reeling, he was like a tree uprooted by the wind.
And blood, the color of liquid lac, flowed from his mouth. Then,
having recovered with difficulty, the powerful and highly resplendent Devāntaka whirled his terrible iron club and struck Aṅgada.

Then, though struck by the iron bar, the son of the lord of monkeys fell to the ground on his knees and sprang up once more. As he was leaping upward, Triśiras [struck him] with three arrows resembling venomous serpents.
With fierce blows, he struck the son of the Lord of Monkeys on the forehead. Then, seeing Aṅgada surrounded by those three foremost of the Nairṛtas,
Hanumān and Nīla also set forth.
Then Nīla hurled the mountain peak at Triśiras;
the wise son of Rāvaṇa shattered it with sharpened arrows.
Pierced by hundreds of those shafts, its surface of rock was rent asunder.
6.058.021c With sparks and flames, the peak of the mountain fell down.
6.058.022a Then, beholding that yawning, Devāntaka, out of joy,
6.058.022c rushed at the son of the Wind-god in the battle with his iron club.
As he was rushing forward, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
leaped up and then struck him on the head with a fist possessing the force of a thunderbolt.
With his head crushed and shattered by that fist, he—
With his teeth, eyes, and tongue protruding,
Devāntaka, the son of the Rākṣasa king,
fell lifeless upon the earth in an instant.
When that mighty leader of the Rākṣasa warriors, the enemy of the gods, had been slain in battle,
the enraged Trishiras drew his fierce, sharp-pointed [spear].
He rained a shower of arrows upon Nīla’s chest;
being rained upon by those floods of shafts,
the protector of the monkey army had his limbs pierced.
Then Nīla’s limbs were released,
for he had been paralyzed by that one of great strength;
thereafter, Nīla regained consciousness.
Then, having uprooted a mountain together with its groves of trees and leaping up with extremely fierce speed,
he struck Mahodara on the head with it.
Then Mahodara, crushed by the falling mountain and trampled along with his elephant,
lay lifeless upon the surface of the earth.
Struck by the thunderbolt, he fell like a mountain;
seeing his uncle slain, Triśiras took up his bow and,
filled with rage, pierced Hanumān with sharpened arrows.
Then Hanumān, springing up in fury, tore at the horses of Triśiras with his claws, like a lion attacking a lordly elephant. Then, seizing a spear like Death himself grasping the Night of Doom, he—
Triśiras, the son of Rāvaṇa, hurled that spear at the son of the Wind;
but seizing that unattached spear as it was cast through the sky like a falling meteor,
the tiger among monkeys broke it and let out a roar.
Seeing that spear of terrible appearance shattered by Hanumān,
the hosts of monkeys rejoiced and roared like clouds. Then Triśiras, the best of the Rākṣasas, raised his sword.
Then, out of rage, he struck the chest of the lord of monkeys;
struck by that sword-blow, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
the valiant one, struck the three-headed Rāvaṇa on the breast with his palm.

Struck by him on the sole of his foot, the immensely powerful Triśiras fell to the ground, unconscious, with his hands and garments slipping away. As he was falling, the great monkey severed his sword.
Resembling a mountain, he roared, terrifying all the Nairṛtas. Unable to endure that sound, the night-stalker leapt up;
having leapt up, he struck Hanumān with his fist.
By that blow of the fist, the great monkey was provoked to anger;
and being enraged, he seized the bull among Rākṣasas by the crest. With a sharp sword, he [severed] his heads.
Enraged, the son of Anila severed those heads adorned with crowns and earrings, just as Śakra severed the heads of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
Those heads of the enemy of Indra— long-eyed, resembling mountains, and possessing eyes like blazing fires— fell upon the earth.
When that three-headed enemy of the gods was slain by Hanumān, who possessed the prowess of Śakra, the luminous bodies were released from the path of the sun.
The monkeys roared and the earth trembled,
while the rākṣasas fled in every direction upon seeing Triśiras and Mahodara likewise slain.
Seeing that the invincible Devāntaka and Narāntaka had been slain,
the immensely powerful Mahāpārśva, filled with supreme indignation, grew furious;
he then seized a splendid mace made entirely of iron, which blazed with fiery luster.
Encircled by bands of gold, smeared with flesh and blood,
shining with a magnificent form and stained with the blood of enemies,
its tip blazing with splendor and adorned with red garlands.
Seizing his mace, which was as terrifying as Airāvata, Mahāpadma, and Sārvabhauma, the mighty Mahāpārśva, filled with rage,
rushed toward the monkeys like the blazing fire at the end of an eon.
Then the ṛṣis, having risen up, approached Mahāpārśva, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa; the powerful monkey stood before him like a mountain.
Seeing that monkey standing before him, resembling a mountain, [he spoke].
Enraged, he struck him on the chest with a mace that was like a thunderbolt.
Struck by that mace from him, the bull among monkeys had his chest shattered; shaken violently, he bled profusely.
6.058.051a Having regained consciousness after a long time, Ṛṣabha, that bull among monkeys,
6.058.051c looked up at Mahāpārśva with his lips quivering in rage. 6.058.052a Seizing that formidable mace and brandishing it again and again, he—
He struck down Mattānīka and Mahāpārśva at the forefront of the battle.
Split by his own mace, with his teeth and eyes shattered,
Mahāpārśva fell like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When that brother of Rāvaṇa was slain,
that army of the Nairṛtas, which resembled the ocean,
cast aside their weapons and sought only to save their lives.
Seeing his own army distressed, resembling a shattered ocean, and witnessing that tumultuous, hair-raising carnage,
as well as seeing his brothers— whose prowess was equal to that of Indra— slain, he fled.
Beholding his two paternal uncles,
those two brothers Mahodara and Mahāpārśva— bulls among the Rākṣasas—
slaughtered in battle, the one of great splendor, who had received a boon from Brahmā, grew enraged in the fray.
6.059.003c Atikāya, who resembled a mountain and humbled the pride of gods and dānavas,
6.059.004a mounting a chariot as radiant as the massed brilliance of a thousand suns, 6.059.004c the enemy of Śakra, rushed toward the monkeys.
Stretching his great bow, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, adorned with polished earrings,
proclaimed his name and let out a mighty roar. By that lion-like roar and by the proclamation of his name, [the enemy was struck with fear].
And with the terrifying sound of his bowstring, he struck fear into the monkeys.
Beholding his form, which was like that of Viṣṇu during the Trivikrama incarnation,
all the monkeys, afflicted by fear, fled in the ten directions.
6.059.008a Having encountered Atikāya, those monkeys, their minds bewildered,
6.059.008c sought refuge in the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa as their protector in the battle.
6.059.009a Then the descendant of Kakutstha [beheld] Atikāya, who stood upon his chariot like a mountain.
From afar, he saw an archer roaring like a dark rain-cloud.
Upon seeing that high-souled one, Rāghava was greatly amazed;
having comforted the monkeys, he then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa.
Who is this man, resembling a mountain, armed with a bow and having tawny eyes,
standing upon a vast chariot yoked to a thousand horses;
he who [is surrounded] by sharpened spears, very keen lances, and *tomaras*?
Surrounded by these radiant beings, he shines like Maheśvara surrounded by his attendants;
he who blazes forth with splendor like the tongues of Time is encompassed by chariot-spears as a rain-cloud is by flashes of lightning.
And his strung bows, with their golden backs, adorn this best of chariots on all sides, like the thunderbolt of Śakra adorning the sky.
Who is this tiger among Rākṣasas, illuminating the field of battle?
The best of chariot-warriors approaches on a chariot possessing the splendor of the sun;
it shines brilliantly with a banner fixed upon its pole like Rāhu,
illuminating the ten directions with arrows radiant as the rays of the sun.
His bow, curved in three places, with the roar of a cloud, adorned with a golden back,
and resembling the rainbow of Indra, shone brilliantly; likewise,
the great chariot was equipped with a banner, a pennant, and a chassis.
Equipped with four chariot-steeds and possessing a roar like the thundering of clouds,
twenty-eight quivers were mounted upon the chariot;
there were also formidable bows and bowstrings the color of gold.
And two swords, mounted upon the chariot, stood at its sides, beautifying the flanks; they were four cubits long with well-fashioned hilts, clearly ten spans in length,
possessing red throat-strings, steadfast, and resembling great mountains.
6.059.021c Time itself, with its great mouth of time, like the sun situated within a cloud;
6.059.022a He shines with his two arms bound by golden bracelets,
6.059.022c like Himavat, the best of mountains, with its two lofty peaks.
"O mighty-armed one, tell me who this best of Rākṣasas is, whose auspicious-eyed face shines with these two earrings like the full orb of the moon situated between the two stars of Punarvasu."
Seeing him, all the monkeys, afflicted by fear, fled in every direction.
Questioned by the prince Rāma of immeasurable splendor,
the highly resplendent Vibhīṣaṇa explained it to the descendant of Raghu.
The ten-necked one, of great splendor, King Vaiśravaṇa’s younger brother,
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas— fearsome in his deeds and possessed of great energy—
