had a heroic son who was his equal in battle.
He was a servant of the elders, a retainer of sacred learning, and the best among all those skilled in weapons;

he was highly esteemed for his skill on horseback, in chariots, and on elephants, as well as in the use of the sword and bow, in drawing [the bowstring], in sowing dissension, in conciliation, in giving gifts, in policy, and in counsel.
Relying upon whose arm Laṅkā is free from fear— know him to be this Atikāya, the son of Dhānyamālinī. By him,
whose soul was purified through asceticism, Brahmā was propitiated.
He has acquired celestial weapons and his enemies have been defeated; furthermore, he has been granted by the Self-born Creator immunity from being slain by gods or asuras.
This is his divine armor, and this is his chariot, radiant as the sun.
By him, the gods and the Dānavas have been defeated by the hundreds;
I have protected those who were to be guarded, and even the Yakṣas have been destroyed. By him, the thunderbolt of the wise Indra was paralyzed with his arrows.
In that battle, the noose of the King of Waters was likewise repelled.
This is Atikāya, the powerful bull among the Rākṣasas,
the wise son of Rāvaṇa who destroys the pride of gods and Dānavas.
Therefore, O bull among men, exert yourself quickly in this matter before he destroys the monkey armies with his arrows. Then the powerful Atikāya entered the host of monkeys.
He drew his bow and roared again and again.
Seeing him of formidable form standing upon his chariot, the best of car-warriors,
those high-souled and preeminent monkeys rushed toward him.
Kumuda, Dvivida, Mainda, Nīla,
and Śarabha rushed forward simultaneously with trees and mountain peaks.
With arrows adorned with gold, they struck down those trees and mountains.

Atikāya, possessed of great majesty and the best among those skilled in weapons, severed them; and that powerful night-stalker of terrifying form, facing his enemies in battle, pierced all those monkeys with arrows made entirely of iron.
Afflicted by that shower of arrows, their limbs mangled,
those monkeys were unable to retaliate against Atikāya in the great battle.
That Rākṣasa struck terror into that army of monkey heroes.
Like an enraged lion attacking a herd of deer, that lord of the Rākṣasas, established in his youth,
did not strike anyone among the monkey army who was not fighting.
Approaching Rāma with his bow and quiver,
he spoke these words with pride:
"Standing upon my chariot, bow and arrow in hand, I— "
I do not fight with just anyone who is ordinary;
let whoever possesses the strength joined with resolve give me battle here today quickly.
Having heard those words as he spoke them, the son of Sumitrā, the slayer of enemies, grew enraged;
unable to endure it, he sprang up.
Then, smiling,
the enraged son of Sumitrā leapt up, drew an arrow from his quiver,
and pulled back his great bow before Atikāya.
Filling the earth, the mountains, the sky, the ocean,
and the quarters with the fierce sound of his bowstring, which terrified the night-stalkers,
the terrifying roar of Saumitri’s bow was then heard.
The mighty son of the lord of the Rākṣasas, possessed of great splendor, was struck with amazement.
Then Atikāya, enraged upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa standing there,
took up a sharpened arrow and spoke these words.
"O Saumitri, you are but a child, unskilled in displays of prowess. Go away! Why do you wish to fight me, who am like Time itself?
For even the Himavat mountain cannot withstand the weapons released from my arms."
Neither the atmosphere nor the earth can endure his impetus;
you wish to awaken the Fire of Time while he sleeps in peace.
Lay down your bow and turn back; do not destroy the life-breaths that have come into my power.
Or rather, since you are obstructed and do not wish to turn back, stay; having abandoned your life-breaths, you shall go to the abode of Yama.
Behold my sharpened arrows, which destroy the pride of enemies.
Resembling the weapons of the Lord and adorned with ornaments of refined gold—
this arrow, resembling a serpent, shall drink your blood,
just as an enraged king of beasts drinks the blood of a king of elephants.
Having heard the words of Atikāya, which were full of wrath and pride in battle, that prince of immense strength and great glory grew enraged.
Then he spoke these words of great significance:
"One does not become preeminent by mere speech,
nor do virtuous men become so through self-praise."
"While I stand here as an archer with arrows in hand, O evil-minded one, display your own strength! Reveal yourself through action; you ought not to engage in mere boasting."
But he who is endowed with manly prowess is remembered as a hero.
You, however, are equipped with all weapons, armed with a bow, and mounted upon a chariot;
display your valor now, whether with arrows or with celestial missiles.
Then, with sharpened arrows, I shall strike down your head,
just as the wind fells a palm fruit from its stalk when it has ripened in due season.
Today my arrows, adorned with refined gold, [shall fall upon you].
They shall drink blood rising from their limbs, issuing from the points of arrow-heads;
knowing that "this one is a child," you ought not to treat me with contempt.
Whether he be a child or an old man, know that death awaits him in battle.
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, which were reasoned and full of ultimate truth, Atikāya became enraged and took up an excellent arrow.
Then the Vidyādharas, spirits, gods, Daityas, and great sages [were struck with fear].
Then the high-souled Guhyakas witnessed that battle.
Thereupon, the enraged Atikāya, having strung his bow,
loosed an arrow at Lakṣmaṇa as if contracting the very sky.
6.059.066a As that sharpened arrow, resembling a venomous serpent, was falling toward him,
6.059.066c Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, cut it down with a crescent-shaped shaft.
6.059.067a Seeing that arrow severed, like a snake with its coils cut through, [he was struck with wonder].
6.059.067c Atikāya, violently enraged, took up five arrows;
6.059.068a that night-stalker discharged those shafts at Lakṣmaṇa. 6.059.068c Before they could reach him, the younger brother of Bharata cut them down with his own sharp arrows.
Having severed those [arrows] with his own sharp shafts, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
took up a whetted arrow that blazed as if with splendor.
Taking it, Lakṣmaṇa fixed it upon his excellent bow.
He drew the bow with great force and released the arrow;
with that straight-knotted shaft discharged from a fully drawn bow,
the valiant one struck the foremost of the Rākṣasas in the forehead.
That arrow, smeared with blood, was seen sunk into the forehead of that fearsome Rākṣasa Bhīma, like the lord of serpents in battle;
and the Rākṣasa trembled, shaken by Lakṣmaṇa’s shafts.
Like the terrifying gateway of Tripura struck by the arrow of Rudra, the immensely powerful one reflected and, having regained his composure, deliberated:
"Excellent! By the fall of this arrow, you are a foe worthy of my praise."
Having reflected thus, he lowered his face and bent both his arms;
then, taking his place upon the seat of the chariot, he moved forward on the chariot.
That bull among Rākṣasas discharged one, three, five, and seven arrows.

He took up his arrows, fixed them to the bow, drew it back, and released them. Those arrows, resembling Death itself, discharged from the bow of the lord of the Rākṣasas, were gold-feathered and radiant as the sun; they made the sky appear ablaze.

Then the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, remaining unperturbed, cut down those showers of arrows released by the rākṣasas with many sharp shafts of his own. Observing those arrows severed in battle, the son of Rāvaṇa—
The enemy of the lord of the thirty gods became enraged and seized a sharpened arrow.
Having fixed that arrow, he of great splendor suddenly released it;
then, it struck the son of Sumitrā as he approached between the breasts.
Struck in the chest by Atikāya in battle, the son of Sumitrā shed copious blood, like an elephant in rut. Then the powerful lord suddenly made himself free of the arrow-heads.
He seized a sharp arrow and charged it with a mantra;
he then joined that shaft with the Āgneya weapon.
Thereupon, the arrow and the bow of that high-souled one blazed forth.
Atikāya, possessed of exceeding brilliance, took up the Saura weapon;
with it, he fixed an arrow resembling a serpent and adorned with golden feathers.
Then Lakṣmaṇa [beheld] that blazing and terrible shaft aimed [at him].
Like Antaka wielding the staff of Time, he hurled it at Atikāya.
Seeing that arrow charged with the fiery weapon (āgneya),
the night-stalker then released a blazing shaft joined with the solar weapon (sūryāstra).
Those two arrows struck one another in the sky,
their tips blazing with splendor like two enraged serpents;
having scorched each other, they both fell to the surface of the earth.
Deprived of their flames and reduced to ashes, those two excellent arrows did not shine.
Then Atikāya, filled with rage, discharged the *aiṣīka* weapon;
the valiant son of Sumitrā cut that weapon down with an *aindra* weapon.
Seeing the Aiṣīka weapon destroyed, the prince, Rāvaṇa’s son,
became enraged and charged an arrow with the Yāmya weapon.
Then that night-stalker discharged that missile at Lakṣmaṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa struck down that weapon with the Vāyavya missile; then,
filled with rage, Lakṣmaṇa showered the son of Rāvaṇa with streams of arrows, just as a rain-cloud pours down torrents of water.
Having reached Atikāya, whose armor was adorned with diamonds,
those arrows suddenly fell to the surface of the earth with their tips shattered. Seeing them rendered futile, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, [acted].
The highly illustrious one showered him with a thousand arrows. Though being rained upon by those floods of shafts, the immensely powerful Atikāya,
that Rākṣasa whose armor was impenetrable in battle, did not waver at all.
That best of men was unable to inflict any wound upon him in battle;
then Vāyu, approaching him, spoke these words:
"For he has received a boon from Brahmā; covered by his armor, he is invincible."
"Destroy him with the Brahma-weapon, for he must be slain in no other way.
Then, having heard the words of Vāyu,
the son of Sumitrā, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra, [acted accordingly].
He took up an arrow of unerring velocity and suddenly employed that Brahma-weapon;
as that supreme weapon was being discharged, [the earth trembled].
At that excellent, sharp-pointed arrow released by the son of Sumitrā,
the quarters of the sky along with the moon, sun, and great planets trembled,
and the heavens roared while the earth quaked.
Having fixed that well-feathered arrow, which resembled a messenger of Yama, upon his bow with the Brahmā-weapon,
the son of Sumitrā [aimed it] at that son of Indra’s enemy.
He discharged an arrow in battle that was like a thunderbolt;
that arrow, released by Lakṣmaṇa, possessed unfailing velocity and fell upon him with the brilliance of fire.
Then Atikāya beheld in battle that arrow, variegated with a shaft adorned with gold and the finest diamonds;
as he gazed upon it, Atikāya suddenly—
He struck him with many sharpened arrows;
that arrow, possessing the speed of Garuḍa,
then flew to his side with extreme velocity.
Then, seeing that Bāṇa had arrived— resembling the blazing God of Death at the end of time—
atikāya struck him with spears, double-edged swords, maces, and axes.
With his movements unimpaired by spears and plows,
that arrow, blazing like fire, rendered those weapons of wondrous form futile.
Then, by force, he severed the very head of Atikāya, which was adorned with a diadem;
that head, along with its helmet, was struck down, tormented by Lakṣmaṇa’s arrow.
He fell suddenly upon the ground like a peak of the Himalayas. At that time, many monkeys, their faces resembling blooming lotuses, were filled with great joy.
When the enemy of terrible strength and difficult to overcome had been slain, they honored Lakṣmaṇa, who was entitled to the desired share. Then, those foremost of Rākṣasas were killed.
The remaining hosts of Rākṣasas there who had survived the slaughter of Devāntaka, Triśiras, Atikāya,
and the others, quickly reported this to Rāvaṇa.
Then, suddenly hearing that they had been slain,
the king fainted, his eyes overflowing with tears at the terrible destruction of his sons and the slaughter of his brothers.
Having reflected thus, the king fell into deep meditation.
Then, beholding the king dejected and completely submerged in an ocean of grief, [the sage spoke].
Then Ṛṣabha, the son of the Rākṣasa king,
spoke these words to Indrajit:
"O father, you ought not to succumb to delusion."
Where Indrajit, the lord of the Rākṣasas, lives,
no one struck by the arrows of Indra’s enemy is able to maintain his life-breaths in battle.
Behold today Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
their bodies pierced and mangled by my arrows,
their life departed, lying upon the surface of the earth.
With his entire body covered by sharp arrows—
listen to this firm vow of the enemy of Śakra,
which is joined with both human prowess and destiny.
This very day, with my unerring arrows, I shall torment Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa;
today, [I shall overcome] Indra, Yama, Viṣṇu, and Mitra.
Sādhya, Aśvin, Vaiśvānara, Candra, and Sūrya shall behold my immeasurable prowess,
as fierce as that of Viṣṇu at the sacrificial ground of Bali.
Having spoken thus, that enemy of the lord of the thirty gods,
undaunted in spirit, took leave of the king and mounted [the chariot] whose speed was equal to the wind.
Mounting his chariot, which was yoked with the finest of mules and resembled the chariot of Indra, the one of great splendor,
the subduer of enemies, went swiftly to the place where the battle was taking place.
As that high-souled one set forth, many of great strength followed him, exulting and with excellent bows in their hands;
some were mounted on the shoulders of elephants, and others on the finest horses.
Bearing spears, mallets, swords, axes,
and clubs, the enemy of the lord of the thirty gods departed while being praised by the night-stalkers amidst the terrifying blasts of conchs and the great sounds of kettledrums.
With that parasol, white as a conch shell or the moon, the subduer of enemies shone like the sky with the full moon. Then the hero was fanned with fans made of gold and adorned with gold.
And with his excellent, beautiful whisks, he who was the foremost of all archers shone; then Laṅkā, by Indrajit— who possessed splendor equal to the sun and irresistible valor—
shone like the sky with the radiant sun.
But seeing him departing, surrounded by a great force, the glorious Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, spoke to his son:
"O son, you are an unrivaled chariot-warrior; even Vāsava has been conquered by you in battle."
"How much more so, then, will you not dare to slay Rāghava, a mere mortal?
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Rākṣasas, the hero accepted those great blessings and,
mounting a chariot yoked with horses, went quickly to Nikumbhilā.
6.060.019a Having reached the field of battle, that subduer of enemies, possessed of great splendor,
6.060.019c stationed the *rakṣas* on all sides around the chariot.
6.060.020a Then, he whose radiance was like that of the consumer of oblations (*hutabhuj*) [stationed] the eater of oblations (*hutabhoktṛ*).

Then that best of Rākṣasas offered oblations according to the rules and with the recitation of mantras. There, the powerful lord of the Rākṣasas made offerings into the fire, accompanied by the preparation of sacrificial nets and preceded by garlands and perfumes.
6.060.022a Weapons, arrow-leaves, sacrificial fuel, and then the *vibhītaka* tree;
6.060.022c Red garments, as well as a ladle made of black iron;
6.060.023a Having spread out a fire there with those arrow-leaves together with the tomara-spears, [he performed the rite].
He seized the throat of a living goat that was entirely black;
as it was offered once into the kindled fire, which was smokeless and possessed great flames,
there appeared those signs that portended victory.
With his crest curling to the right and resembling molten gold, the Fire-god himself arose and accepted that oblation. Then he,
the best among those skilled in weapons, invoked the Brahma-weapon.

6.060.026c He consecrated his bow and his chariot, as well as everything else there, with mantras. 6.060.027a While that weapon was being invoked and the fire was being offered oblations, the vault of heaven, along with the sun, planets, moon, and stars, trembled with fear.
He, whose radiant splendor was like that of fire,
having offered oblations into the fire, possessed power equal to that of Mahendra;
equipped with his bow, arrows, sword, chariot, horses, and charioteer, he set forth.
Having abandoned his army and quickly approached the monkey hosts in that great battle, he of inconceivable form vanished from sight in the sky.
Remaining invisible, he rained down a fierce net of arrows like a dark rain-cloud pouring forth water;
their bodies shattered by the arrows of Śakra’s Conqueror, they—
Struck by Māyā, the monkeys, who were like mountains, fell in battle crying out discordantly,
like the lords of mountains struck by Indra’s thunderbolt.
They saw only sharp-pointed arrows falling upon the monkey hosts in battle,
and the enemy of the lord of the gods hidden by his illusory power.
And they did not see that Rākṣasa there;
then that high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas [covered] all directions with multitudes of sharp-pointed arrows.
He shrouded [the sky] with the brilliance of the sun and caused the leaders of the monkeys to despair;
he [discharged] spears, swords, and battle-axes.
Brandishing weapons that resembled blazing fires and were radiant with sparks,
he rained them down fiercely upon the army of the lord of monkeys.
Then, struck by the sharp arrows of Śakrajit, which resembled blazing fire, the leaders of the monkey hosts appeared like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees;
they crawled over one another and uttered discordant cries.
Pierced by the weapons of the lord of the *rākṣasas*, those bulls among monkeys fell;
some, struck in the eyes, gazed upward at the sky,
while others entered one another with their arrows and fell upon the surface of the earth.
And Hanumān, Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Gandhamādana,
Jāmbavān, Suṣeṇa, and Vegadarśin; as well as Mainda, Dvivida, Nīla, Gavākṣa, Gaja, and Gomukha.
Keśarī, Hariloman, and the monkey Vidyuddaṃṣṭra;
Sūryānana, Jyotirmukha, and the monkey Dadhimukha; Pāvakākṣa, Nala, and the monkey Kumuda.
With spears, pikes, and sharp arrows charged with mantras by Indrajit,
that best of Rākṣasas pierced all those tigers among the monkeys.
Indeed, he struck the leaders of the monkey hosts with maces.
Having pierced through with gold-feathered arrows,
he rained down upon Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa a multitude of arrow-showers resembling the rays of the sun.
Being showered with those volleys of arrows,
he regarded them as if they were falling torrents of rain;
observing this, his supreme splendor was most wonderful.
Then Rāma spoke thus to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, that lord of the rākṣasas, the enemy of the lord of the gods, has once again resorted to the Brahmāstra."
Having struck down the fierce monkey army,
that high-souled one, who has received boons from the Self-Existent, incessantly afflicts us with his arrows.
Having entered the earth with his terrifying body vanished,
how indeed can Indrajit— now with his body lost and his weapons raised— be slain in battle today?

"I consider the Blessed Self-Existent One to be inconceivable— he from whom this weapon originates and who is its source— since you, O wise one, have today here [neutralized] the falls of his arrows."
Endure with an undistracted mind alongside me;
for this lord of the rākṣasas is indeed shrouding all directions with nets of showers of arrows.
And this entire army of the king of monkeys, with its foremost heroes fallen, no longer shines;
but seeing us two fallen and unconscious, [it will surely rally].
Having ceased from battle and having cast off both anger and joy, he will surely enter the abode of the enemies of the gods,
taking with him the fortune of the forefront of war.
Then, by means of nets of missiles, Indrajit pierced them both there; and he,
having caused them to despair there—
The lord of the rākṣasas roared with joy in battle;
he [then] [assailed] that army of the monkey king,
and Rāma in the conflict along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Having suddenly caused [them] to despair, he entered the city protected by the arms of the Ten-necked One;
at that time, those two were overcome at the front of the battle.
The army of the monkey leaders was bewildered; Sugrīva, Nīla, Aṅgada, and Jāmbavān did not perceive anything at all.
Then, observing the army despondent,
Vibhīṣaṇa, the foremost among the wise,
spoke to the heroic leaders of the monkeys.
Comforting them with incomparable words, he said:
"Do not fear; this is no time for despondency, even though my two noble sons are helpless and dejected."
Then, while they were carrying out the words of Svayambhū,
which had been thwarted by the nets of Indrajit’s weapons,
that supreme weapon was bestowed upon him.
If these two princes, honoring that Brahma-weapon of unerring speed created by the Self-Existent One, have been struck down, what occasion for despair is there here?
Then the wise son of the Wind-god, having honored that Brahma-weapon and having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa,
spoke to him:
"Now that this army of the swift monkeys has been destroyed..."
"Whosoever still holds onto their life-breaths, those very ones we shall reassure.
Then, both those heroes— the best of monkeys, Hanumān, and the best of Rākṣasas—
roamed together at night upon the front lines of the battlefield with torches in their hands.
It was crowded with monkeys who had fallen like mountains, their tails, hands, thighs, feet, and fingers severed, and whose limbs were dripping with blood flowing from all sides.
And with fallen, blazing weapons, they beheld the earth strewn with Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Nīla, Śarabha, Gandhamādana,
Jāmbavān, Suṣeṇa, Vegadarśana, and Āhuka.
6.061.011a Mainda, Nala, Jyotimukha, Dvivida, and Panasa,
as well as Vibhīṣaṇa and Hanumān, beheld them slain in battle.
6.061.012a Sixty-seven crores of the swift monkeys had been killed.
With five-sixteenths of the day remaining,
accompanied by his beloved [brother] Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanumān beheld the army— terrifying like the surge of the ocean and afflicted by arrows— and sought out Jāmbavān.
Seeing that heroic son of Prajāpati, who was joined with the decay of old age, covered by hundreds of arrows, and appearing like a fire being extinguished,
the descendant of Pulastya approached him and spoke these words.
"I hope that your life has not been destroyed by those sharp, noble arrows?
Having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa, Jāmbavān, the bull among bears,
spoke these words, uttering them with great difficulty.
"O Nairṛta of great prowess, I recognize you by your voice;
though I am being tormented by sharp arrows, I cannot see you with my eyes—
by whom Añjanā was blessed with noble offspring and by whom Mātariśvan [was begotten], O Nairṛta."
"Does Hanumān, the best of monkeys, still cling to life anywhere?
Having heard Jāmbavān’s words, Vibhīṣaṇa said this:
"Why do you ask about the son of the Wind-god, bypassing my two noble brothers?"

"O noble one, neither toward King Sugrīva, nor toward Aṅgada, nor even toward Rāghava was such supreme affection displayed as that shown toward the son of the Wind-god. Having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa, Jāmbavān spoke these words:
6.061.021c Listen, O tiger among the Nairṛtas, why I question the son of the Wind-god:
6.061.022a As long as that hero lives, even if slain, the army is not truly defeated;
6.061.022c But when Hanumān has surrendered his life, though we live, we are as good as dead.

"O dear one, if the son of the Maruts remains alive— being equal to the Maruts themselves and like Vaiśvānara in prowess— then there may still be hope for life. Then, approaching the elder, she saluted him according to the prescribed rule.
6.061.024c Grasping the feet of Jāmbavat, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
6.061.025a having heard the words of Hanumān, though his senses were still distressed,
6.061.025c that bull among bears considered himself as if born again.
Then the highly resplendent Jāmbavān said to Hanumān:
"Come, O tiger among monkeys; you ought to save the vanaras.
No one else possesses sufficient prowess; you are their supreme friend."
"This is the time for your prowess; I see no one else who can do it.
Gladden the ranks of the bear and monkey heroes, and heal these two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who have been struck down and pierced by arrows."
6.061.029a Having traveled the supreme path higher and higher above the ocean,
6.061.029c you must go, O Hanumān, to Himavat, the best of mountains. 6.061.030a Beyond that is the exceedingly formidable golden mountain, Ṛṣabha, the highest of peaks.
And you shall also see the peak of Kailāsa, O slayer of enemies;
between those two peaks,
O hero, you will behold the mountain of medicinal herbs, blazing with incomparable radiance and endowed with every kind of herb.
O tiger among monkeys, you shall see four blazing medicinal herbs growing upon his head, illuminating the ten directions:
the Mṛtasañjīvanī and the Viśalyakaraṇī as well.
"O Hanumān, you must take all of these— the Sauvarṇakaraṇī and the great medicinal herb Saṃdhānī— and return quickly. O son of the Wind, restore the monkeys to life and give them heart."
Having heard the words of Jāmbavān, Hanumān, the bull among monkeys,
was filled with surges of strength, like the ocean by the force of its waters.
Standing upon the edge of a mountain slope, he pressed down upon that foremost of mountains.
The heroic Hanumān appeared like a second mountain;
struck by the feet of the monkey, that mountain sat down,
unable to support itself, being so violently oppressed.

6.061.038a His trees fell to the ground, and from the force of the monkey, they burst into flames; 6.061.038c and the peaks were shattered as he was crushed by Hanūmat. 6.061.039a While he was being thus tormented, the surfaces of the trees and rocks were broken.
The monkeys were unable to stand firm as that best of mountains reeled.
With its great gates whirling and its houses and gate-towers shattered,
Lankā, agitated by terror, seemed then at night to be dancing.
Resembling a mountain,
the son of the Wind-god pressed down upon that upholder of the earth and caused the earth, together with its oceans, to tremble;
pressing his feet against the mountain, his mouth was like the submarine fire of the Mare’s Head.
Opening his mouth wide, he roared fiercely and loudly, as if terrifying the rākṣasas.
Hearing that extraordinary roar of his as he was shouting,
all the rākṣasas dwelling in Laṅkā were unable to move for fear.
Then, having paid homage to Rāma, the son of the Wind-god,
possessed of terrible prowess and a scorcher of foes, resolved upon a supreme task for the sake of the descendant of Raghu.
Raising his tail, which resembled a serpent, he—
Bending his back, contracting his ears,
and opening his mouth which resembled the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha),
he, with fierce speed, leapt into the sky.
He swiftly swept away groves of trees,
mountain crags, and ordinary monkeys,
driven and hurled forth by the force of his arms and thighs.
Their momentum exhausted, they fell into the water;
he, whose valor was like that of the enemy of serpents, stretched out his two arms which resembled the coils of a snake.
The son of the Wind went toward Meru, the foremost king of mountains, as if dragging the very quarters of the sky along with him;
he reached the ocean, garlanded with rolling waves.
Then, beholding all beings utterly bewildered, he suddenly departed like the discus released from the tip of Viṣṇu’s hand.
He beheld mountains, groves of trees, lakes, rivers, ponds, and excellent cities, as well as those populous regions of people.
He went with speed, possessing a velocity equal to his father's;
taking to the path of the sun, he proceeded free from fatigue.
That best of monkeys beheld Himavat, the foremost of mountains.
Endowed with various springs, many caves, and waterfalls,
and possessing beautiful peaks resembling masses of white clouds—
he reached that great king of mountains.
He beheld sacred great hermitages frequented by the most eminent hosts of celestial rishis, where the highest and most formidable peaks rose exceedingly high.
He [beheld] the treasury of Brahmā and the silver abode;
the abode of Śakra and the discharge of Rudra’s arrows; the horse-headed [weapon], the blazing head of Brahmā; and—
And he saw the servants of Vaivasvata,
as well as the abode of Vajra and the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
the radiance of the sun, and the bond of the sun.
He beheld the seat of Brahmā and the bow of Śaṅkara, as well as the navel of the earth,
the preeminent Kailāsa, and the rock of Himavat.
Likewise, he beheld the preeminent golden mountain Ṛṣabha, the lord of all medicinal mountains, blazing with every kind of luminous herb.
Beholding him blazing with rays like fire,
the son of Vāsava’s messenger was struck with wonder;
and having leaped up, he reached that king of mountains, the mountain of medicinal herbs.
There,
the great monkey, the son of the Wind-god, having traversed many thousands of yojanas, searched through the mountains that bore divine medicinal herbs.
All those great medicinal herbs on that best of mountains,
perceiving that a seeker had arrived, then vanished from sight. The high-souled Hanumān, however, did not see them.
Enraged, he roared loudly; unable to endure it, his eyes like fire,
he addressed these words to that lord of mountains.
"Is this so firmly resolved by you—
that you have shown no compassion toward Rāghava? Behold today, overcome by the strength of my arms!"
Then, O lord of mountains, he scattered himself upon his peak, which was filled with mountains and serpents, adorned with gold, and graced by thousands of mineral ores.
Seizing it with force, he suddenly uprooted that mountain, its peaks scattered and its ridges trembling at the tips;
having torn it out, he leapt into the sky.
Having terrified the worlds, including the gods and the lords of the gods,
he of fierce prowess like Garuḍa departed with speed while being praised by many sky-dwellers.
Having set out upon the path of the sun and grasping that peak which shone like the sun,
he then gleamed with a splendor resembling the sun itself.
Near the sun,
he shone intensely like a second sun;
yet the son of the Wind-god, though resembling a mountain, was surpassed by that mountain.
With his thousand-spoked,
flaming wheel raised aloft in the sky like Viṣṇu,
the monkeys, beholding him, then let out a great roar.
Seeing them as well, he roared with joy;
hearing their loud shouting,
the inhabitants of Laṅkā let out an even more terrifying cry.
Then the high-souled one descended upon that best of mountains, in the midst of the monkey army;
having saluted the foremost of the monkeys with his head;
And there he embraced Vibhīṣaṇa,
as well as both those sons of the human king; they too,
having smelled that fragrance of great medicinal herbs.
At that time, those two became free from their arrows there,
and the other foremost heroes among the monkeys rose up.
Then the monkey, the son of the Wind-god, spoke.
That hero of exalted prowess swiftly carried him to the Himavat, the mountain of medicinal herbs,
and then returned once more to Rāma.
Then the highly effulgent Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, spoke to the mighty Hanumān, making him understand the matter that was at hand:
"From where Kumbhakarṇa was slain and the princes were destroyed..."
6.062.002c Rāvaṇa will not be able to provide a defense now.
6.062.003a Those monkeys who possess great strength and are swift,
those bulls among monkeys, should quickly leap toward Laṅkā, seizing torches.
Then, when the sun had set and at that fierce onset of night,
those bulls among monkeys advanced toward Laṅkā carrying torches;
pursued from all sides by the hosts of monkeys with torches in their hands, they proceeded forward.
The hideous-eyed guardians stationed there suddenly fled in all directions;
in the gate-towers, the watchtowers, the main streets, and various pathways,
as well as in the palaces, they joyfully set fire to everything.
Then the fire consumed thousands of their houses,
as well as the dwellings of all those Rākṣasa householders who wore golden-decorated armor and were clad in garments adorned with garlands.
With their senses unsteady from drinking *sīdhu* liquor, their gait faltering with intoxication, with their garments clutched by their beloveds, filled with rage toward the enemy,
and with maces, spears, and swords in hand, they were even devouring and drinking.
As they fled in haste from all sides, taking their sons with them, those who were sleeping with their loved ones upon costly couches became terrified;
at that time, there were thousands of houses belonging to the inhabitants of Laṅkā.
There the fire consumed them and blazed up again and again—
those objects which were substantial, highly precious, and possessed of profound qualities,
adorned with golden moons and crescents, and elevated with moon-chambers.
6.062.013a With jeweled windows and excellent foundations on all sides,
6.062.013c variegated with gems and coral, they seem to touch the sun;
6.062.014a with the sounds of cranes, peacocks, lutes, and ornaments, [they resound].
That fire consumed the houses, which were as solid as mountains and filled with cries;
the archways, enveloped by the flames,
shone like masses of clouds wreathed in lightning during the summer heat.
And beautiful women, fast asleep in their celestial palaces, were consumed by fire;
casting off their ornaments, they cried out loudly, "Alas!
Alas! And there, the very mansions themselves fell, enveloped in flames.
Like the peaks of a great mountain struck by the thunderbolt of Indra,
those [trees], being consumed by fire, shone from afar like the peaks of the Himalayas with their forests of glowing medicinal herbs.
With the tops of its palaces burning and ablaze with flames,
that city of Laṅkā was seen at night as if covered in blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees; likewise,
with elephants released by their keepers and horses also set free.
Lanka became like the ocean with its swirling crocodiles at the edge of the world. In one place, seeing the horse released, a frightened elephant retreated;
in another, seeing the frightened elephant, a horse turned back.
In an instant, that city was set ablaze by the monkeys;
it appeared like the earth burning at the terrible destruction of this world. The women of the people, enveloped in smoke, wailed aloud.
The roar of those bodies heated by the flames was heard for ten *yojanas*. Then, as other *rākṣasas* emerged outside with their bodies ablaze,
the monkeys, eager for battle, suddenly leaped up toward them.
The clamor of the monkeys and the roar of the Rākṣasas resounded,
making the ten directions, the ocean, and the earth vibrate.
Both those great-souled ones, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were now free from their arrows.
Without any agitation, they both took up their excellent bows.
Then, as Rāma drew back his supreme bow,
there arose a tumultuous sound that struck terror into the Rākṣasas.
Then Rāma shone as he drew his great bow,
like the enraged Lord Bhava wielding his bow composed of the Vedas;
there was the roar raised by the monkeys and the clamor of the rākṣasas.
And the sound of Rāma’s bowstring also pervaded the ten directions. And by the arrows released from his bow, that city’s gateway—
resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa— was shattered and fell to the earth.
Then, seeing Rāma’s arrows upon the palaces and in the houses,
a tumultuous preparation by the lords of the rākṣasas ensued. As they were arming themselves, they let out lion-like roars.
The night became as terrible for the lords of the rākṣasas as it was for them. Commanded by the high-souled Sugrīva,
those leaders of the monkeys approached the gate and said, "O bulls among the monkeys, fight!"
"Whoever among you, established in his respective place, should act falsely—
he who violates the king's command— must be attacked and slain.
While those monkey leaders stood there with blazing torches held in their hands, [the king spoke].
When they had halted and reached the gate, fury took possession of Rāvaṇa. From the expansion of his yawning, the ten directions became truly intermingled;
like the form of Rudra, his fury was visible upon his limbs.
Enraged, he dispatched both Nikumbha and Kumbha, the two sons of Kumbhakarṇa, along with many Rākṣasas;
and the lord of the Rākṣasas issued these commands to all those Rākṣasas.
"O Rākṣasas, go right there and let out lion-roars! Then,
urged by him, those heroic Rākṣasas with flaming weapons marched forth from Laṅkā, roaring again and again.

That formidable army of Rākṣasas, possessing terrifying prowess and heroism, was filled with fearsome horses, chariots, and elephants, crowded with various foot soldiers, and equipped with blazing spears, maces, swords, javelins, lances, and bows.
He was seen with a flaming spear, resounding with hundreds of tiny bells;
his arms were encased in golden netting, and he brandished a battle-axe. He whirled great weapons about and held a bow to which arrows were fixed.
6.062.043a The great wind was made fragrant by perfumes, garlands, and the sprinkling of honey;
6.062.043c it was formidable, crowded with brave men, and possessed the roar of a massive rain-cloud.
6.062.044a Seeing that most dreadful army of the Rākṣasas approaching, [he...]
The army of the monkeys surged forward and roared loudly;
then, leaping again with great speed toward that vast host of Rākṣasas,
they rushed against the enemy force like moths into a fire.
The preeminent strength of those foremost rākṣasas shone even more brightly as their iron clubs were struck and rubbed by the grasp of their arms;
likewise, others among them [struck] those monkeys with sharp swords.
The night-stalkers of terrible form struck down the heroes on all sides;
one struck another who was striking, one brought down another who was bringing down,
others reviled one who was reviling, and others bit one who was biting.
"Give! said some; "I give," said another; yet another said, "I am giving.
"Why do you trouble yourself? Stay! they spoke thus to one another.
[The scene was] crowded with raised great spears, fists, tridents, and swords.
A most fierce battle then unfolded between the monkeys and the rākṣasas.
Ten or seven at a time, the rākṣasas struck down the monkeys;
likewise, ten or seven at a time, the monkeys slew the rākṣasas in the fray.
Seizing the Rākṣasa army— its hair and girdles disheveled, its armor and banners cast aside— the monkeys surrounded it.
While that tumultuous and terrible battle, which caused the destruction of heroic men, was raging on, [the monkeys continued their assault].
6.063.001c Aṅgada, eager for battle, encountered the heroic Kampana.
6.063.002a Summoning Aṅgada, Kampana, impelled by anger, swiftly struck him with his mace; 6.063.002c having been struck violently, he reeled at first.
Having regained consciousness, the radiant one hurled a mountain peak;
and Kampana, afflicted by that blow, fell to the ground. Then the army of the lord of the rākṣasas was distressed, its foremost heroes having been slain.
She went toward where the son of Kumbhakarṇa was; and as she rushed forward with speed, Kumbha tried to appease that army. That best of archers, being well-composed, took up his bow.
He released arrows resembling venomous serpents that tore through the body; that supreme bow of his, with its arrow fixed, shone even more brilliantly,
like a second rainbow of Indra, radiant with lightning and the splendor of Airāvata.
Then, with an arrow drawn back to his ear and released, he struck Dvivida;
with that feathered shaft, gold-tufted and adorned with plumage,
he was suddenly struck and, quivering, his footing slipped away.
Resembling a mountain peak, that best of monkeys fell down, overwhelmed.
But Mainda, seeing his brother broken there in that great battle,
rushed forward with speed, seizing a massive rock.
The one of great strength hurled that rock at the Rākṣasa;
Kumbha shattered that rock with five smooth, well-aimed arrows.
Then, having fixed another well-pointed arrow, resembling a venomous serpent, he released it.
6.063.011c The one of great splendor struck the elder brother of Dvivida on the chest.
6.063.012a But by that blow, Mainda, the leader of the monkey hosts,
6.063.012c being struck in his vital organs by him, fell to the ground unconscious.
6.063.013a Seeing his two maternal uncles fallen, those two of great strength, Aṅgada rushed with speed toward Kumbha, who stood with his bow raised.
6.063.014a As he was charging, Kumbha pierced him with five iron arrows.
And with three other sharp arrows, as if striking an elephant with iron pikes,
the heroic Kumbha pierced Aṅgada with various shafts— whetted, keen, sharp, and adorned with gold, their edges unblunted.
Though his limbs were pierced, Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, did not tremble;
yet [Indrajit] rained down showers of rocks and trees upon his head.
He cut all of them to pieces and shattered the rocks as well.
6.063.017c The illustrious son of Kumbhakarṇa [pierced] those discharged by the son of Vālin; 6.063.018a And beholding the leader of the monkey hosts rushing toward him,
Kumbha 6.063.018c pierced him between the eyebrows with two arrows, as one might strike an elephant with two flaming torches.
6.063.019a Angada, covering his blood-smeared eyes with one hand, grasped a nearby *sāla* tree with the other.
6.063.020a That tree, resembling the banner of Indra and like Mount Mandara—
As he was discharging [the weapon] with speed before the eyes of all the rākṣasas,
Aṅgada cut it down with seven sharp, body-piercing arrows;
he was repeatedly pained, sank down, and fainted.
Seeing Aṅgada distressed, as if sinking in the ocean,
those foremost of monkeys reported him— though he was difficult to overcome— to Rāghava.
And Rāma, having heard that the son of Vālin was distressed in the great battle, [acted accordingly].
6.063.023c Then he commanded the foremost of monkeys, headed by Jāmbavān.
6.063.024a But those tigers among monkeys, having heard Rāma’s command, 6.063.024c rushed forward, highly enraged, toward Kumbha who stood with his bow raised.
Then those bulls among monkeys, with trees and rocks in their hands and eyes bloodshot with rage, rushed forward, desiring to protect Aṅgada.
Jāmbavān, Suṣeṇa, and the monkey Vegadarśin also joined them.
Enraged, they rushed together toward the heroic son of Kumbhakarṇa.
But seeing those immensely powerful lords of monkeys advancing against him,
he blocked them with a torrent of arrows, as a mountain obstructs a body of water.
Having encountered his mass of arrows, those high-souled lords of monkeys were unable to overcome their grief, just as the great ocean cannot overstep its shore.
But seeing those hosts of monkeys afflicted by the showers of arrows, [he...]
Placing his brother’s son Aṅgada behind him,
Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, rushed with speed toward Kumbha in the battle,
like a swift lion toward an elephant roaming on a mountain ridge.
Uprooting massive boulders, many *aśvakarṇa* and *dhava* trees,
and various other kinds of trees, the one of great strength hurled them;
that unassailable rain of trees covered the sky.
The illustrious son of Kumbhakarṇa cut [them] down with sharpened arrows;
covered by those sharp arrows from the fierce and well-aimed Kumbha,
those trees shone like terrible *śataghnī* weapons.
Seeing that shower of trees cut down by Kumbha, the valiant,
glorious, and great-souled lord of the monkeys was not distressed;
though suddenly pierced, he endured those arrows.
Having seized Kumbha’s bow, which shone like Indra’s rainbow, he broke it. Then,
having quickly leaped down after performing that most difficult feat,
he spoke in anger to Kumbha, who was like an elephant with its tusks shattered.
O elder brother of Nikumbha, your heroism, that wondrous speed of Bāṇa, your humility, and your power— whether yours or Rāvaṇa’s—
are equal to those of Prahrāda, Bali, Vṛtrahan, Kubera, and Varuṇa.
"You alone have been born as the equal of your father, yet you are even more powerful.
O mighty-armed subduer of enemies, the gods cannot overcome you alone when you stand with spear in hand, just as mental afflictions cannot overcome one who has conquered his senses."
"By virtue of a boon, your paternal uncle [Vibhīṣaṇa] overcomes gods and dānavas;
Kumbhakarṇa, however, by his prowess, overcomes both gods and asuras. Indrajit is equal to Dhanuṣi, and Rāvaṇa is equal in majesty."

"Today you are the foremost in the world of Rākṣasas by virtue of your strength and heroism. Let all beings today behold this wonderful and great conflict between us in battle, like that between Śakra and Śambara."

An incomparable deed has been performed and your skill with weapons has been displayed; these heroic monkeys of terrible prowess have been struck down by you. Yet, O hero, out of fear of reproach, you were not slain by me.
"Having completed my task and being weary, I have now rested; behold my strength!
By those words of Sugrīva, which were both insulting and yet honored him, his splendor increased like that of a fire into which clarified butter has been poured.

Then Kumbha, springing up and reaching Sugrīva, struck him in the chest with his fist, which possessed the force of a thunderbolt, being filled with rage. His hide split open and blood began to flow from him.
And that fist, possessing great momentum, struck against the framework of his bones; then,
by that force, a brilliance was repeatedly ignited there,
like the flames produced by the impact of a thunderbolt upon Mount Meru.
Struck there by him, that mighty Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, clenched his fist, which was like a thunderbolt,
blazing with a thousand rays and possessing the splendor of the solar disc.
The valiant one brought down his fist upon Kumbha’s chest;
struck by that fist, the Rākṣasa fell instantly,
like the red-bodied planet Mars falling from the sky with its rays ablaze by chance.
The form of Kumbha as he fell, his chest shattered by the fist, shone like that of the Lord of Bulls when struck by Rudra. When he was slain by him of terrifying prowess;
When the bull among monkeys fought in battle,
the earth with its mountains and forests trembled,
and a great fear entered the hearts of the rākṣasas.
6.064.001a Seeing his brother struck down by Sugrīva, Nikumbha, as if burning with rage, glared at the lord of monkeys.
6.064.002a Then [he saw] that auspicious [bow], adorned with garlands and flower-strings, marked with the five-fingered hand-sign.
The hero took up a spiked mace that resembled the peak of a king of mountains;
it was encircled with bands of gold, adorned with diamonds and coral,
as formidable as the staff of Yama, and the destroyer of the fear of the rākṣasas.
Brandishing that [mace], which was like the banner of Śakra, in battle, the immensely powerful Nikumbha,
of terrifying prowess, let out a roar with his mouth wide open;
he was adorned with a golden breastplate upon his chest and armlets upon his arms.
With his two polished earrings, his variegated garland,
those ornaments, and that iron club, Nikumbha shone like a cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder, adorned with a rainbow.
The wind-tumor on the great-souled one’s shoulder burst open at the tip of the iron bar;
it blazed up with a roar like a smokeless fire.
[It did so] in the city of Viṭapāvatī, amidst the finest abodes of the Gandharvas.
Together with Amarāvatī and all its palaces, along with the hosts of stars and constellations, the moon, and the great planets,
the surface of the sky seemed to whirl, as if tossed by Nikumbha’s iron club.
He became difficult to approach, radiant with his iron club as his ornament;
fueled by anger, Nikumbha was like the fire at the end of an eon rising up.
Even the Rākṣasas and the Vānaras were unable to move for fear of him.
But the powerful Hanumān, having opened wide his chest, stood directly in front of him;
then the strong one, whose arms were like iron clubs, hurled an iron club as radiant as the sun onto the chest of that powerful foe.
6.064.013a Upon his firm and broad chest, the iron club was shattered into a hundred pieces;
6.064.013c it fell apart suddenly like a hundred meteors in the sky.
6.064.014a Yet, by that blow, the great monkey merely trembled.
Like a mountain shaken by an iron club during an earthquake,
Hanumān, the best of monkeys and possessed of exceeding great strength, was thus struck by him; nevertheless,
he clenched his fist with all his might.
Raising it up, the valiant Nikumbha, possessed of great splendor,
speed, and the prowess of the wind, hurled it with force at the chest of Vāyu.
Thereupon, his shield burst asunder and blood flowed forth.
From that fist, a flame was produced, rising up like lightning.
By that blow, Nikumbha indeed wavered;
yet, regaining his composure, he seized the mighty Hanumān.
Then, seeing the mighty Hanumān being carried off by Nikumbha, the inhabitants of Laṅkā cried out in terror in the midst of the fray.
Even as he was being thus carried away by the son of Kumbhakarṇa, he—
The son of the Wind struck him with a fist possessing the force of a thunderbolt; then, having freed himself, he fell to the ground. Hanumān, the son of the Wind, swiftly crushed Nikumbha.
Having cast him down with great effort, he crushed Nikumbha; then, springing up with speed, the valiant one fell upon his chest.
Seizing him with both arms, he twisted his neck.
He tore off the head of the one who was roaring most terribly. Then,
when Nikumbha had been struck down by the son of the Wind-god while screaming in battle, the combat continued.
The battle between the army of the son of Daśaratha and that of the lord of the Rākṣasas became exceedingly terrifying as both sides were filled with intense rage; meanwhile,
hearing that Nikumbha had been slain and Kumbha struck down, [the enemy forces were demoralized].
6.065.001c Rāvaṇa, filled with supreme indignation, blazed up like a fire. 6.065.002a The Nairṛta, overwhelmed by both anger and grief,
6.065.002c urged on his large-eyed son Makarākṣa, the son of Khara.
"Go, my son, commanded by me and endowed with strength;
slay Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, along with those forest-dwellers.
Having heard Rāvaṇa's words, the heroic and proud son of Khara [prepared to depart].
"So be it," replied the bold night-stalker Makarākṣa.
Having saluted the Ten-necked one and performed a circumambulation,
the powerful one departed from Rāvaṇa’s bright palace by his command.
Standing nearby, the son of Khara spoke these words to the commander of the forces:
"Let the chariot be brought quickly, and let the army be brought with haste. Hearing those words of his, the night-stalker commander of the forces—
He brought both the chariot and his army close at hand;
having circumambulated the chariot clockwise, the night-stalker ascended it and urged the charioteer,
"Drive my chariot swiftly!"
Then Makarākṣa spoke these words to all those rākṣasas:
"O rākṣasas, all of you fight in front of me! I [shall follow] the high-souled Rāvaṇa, the king of the rākṣasas."
Commanded to slay both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in battle,
[he said: "Today, O night-stalkers, I shall kill Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
as well as Sugrīva the monkey and the other vanaras, with my finest arrows."
"Today, with the falling of my spears, I shall consume the great army of the monkeys that has arrived, just as fire consumes dry fuel.
Having heard those words of Makarākṣa, those night-stalkers...
6.065.013c All were equipped with various weapons, powerful, and composed; 6.065.014a those heroes, capable of assuming any form at will, possessed fangs and tawny eyes;
6.065.014c like trumpeting elephants, they were terrifying with their disheveled hair.
Surrounding the massive-bodied son of Khara, those of great stature then approached him joyfully, making the earth tremble; meanwhile,
thousands of conchs and kettledrums were being struck on all sides.
Then a great sound arose from their shouting and the slapping of arms;
then the goad fell from the hand of that charioteer,
and the banner of that Rākṣasa suddenly fell as well.
6.065.018a His horses, yoked to the chariot, deprived of their prowess, 6.065.018c went with faltering steps; dejected, with tearful faces, they departed.
6.065.019a A harsh and dreadful wind blew upon him, carrying dust.
6.065.019c At the departure of that fierce and evil-minded Makarākṣa,
6.065.020a seeing those omens, all the most heroic Rākṣasas 6.065.020c went forth with inconceivable speed to where Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were.
With complexions like the bodies of massive elephants and buffaloes,
repeatedly pierced by clubs and swords at the front lines of battle, they were masters of combat, each crying out, "I first! I first!"
The night-stalkers roared as they wandered about;
seeing that Makarākṣa had emerged, those bulls among monkeys all leaped forward suddenly and stood ready, desiring to fight.
Then that great battle, which caused the hair to stand on end,
commenced between the night-rangers and the monkeys, like the conflict between the gods and the dānavas—
by means of the hurling of trees and spears, and the throwing of rocks and iron clubs.
Then the monkeys and the night-stalkers crushed one another;
with spears, tridents, clubs, swords, and javelins, as well as with pattisas, bhindipālas, and volleys of arrows from every side, the night-stalkers [attacked].
With nooses, mallets, and clubs, as well as other destructive weapons,
those night-stalkers wrought carnage among the lions of the monkeys. Furthermore, the monkeys were afflicted by the floods of arrows from the son of Khara.
With their minds utterly bewildered and oppressed by fear, they all fled. Seeing those forest-dwellers running away, all the Rākṣasas— bold and appearing victorious— roared like lions.
6.066.008 While those monkeys were fleeing in every direction,
Rāma held back the Rākṣasas with a shower of arrows. 6.066.009 Seeing the Rākṣasas thus repelled, the night-stalker Makarākṣa [advanced].
Overcome by rage and indolence, he spoke these words:
"Stay, Rāma! I shall give you a duel.
I will deprive you of your life with sharp arrows released from my bow."

When I remember how he killed my father in the Daṇḍaka forest while I stood before him, established in his own duty, my rage increases. O Rāghava, my limbs burn intensely because of that evil-souled one.
"Since you were not seen by me at that time in the great forest,
it is by good fortune, O Rāma, that you have come into my sight here;
you are as longed for as another deer is by a hungry lion."
"Today, by the force of my arrows, the King of the Dead has gone to his own realm;
you shall be reunited with those heroes who were slain by you.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen, Rāma, to my words."
"Let all the worlds behold both you and me on the field of battle,
O Rāma— whether by means of missiles, or with a mace, or even with bare arms; let the combat proceed according to whichever method has been practiced."
Having heard the words of Makarākṣa, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
spoke these words with a smile to him who was speaking in reply:
"There were fourteen thousand Rākṣasas, as well as your father."
"Triśiras and Dūṣaṇa have also been slain by me in Daṇḍaka. Today, O wicked one, vultures, jackals, and crows— with their sharp beaks and goad-like claws— shall indeed be satiated with your flesh."
Thus addressed by Rāma, the night-stalker, the son of Khara,
loosed a flood of arrows at that descendant of Raghu on the field of battle. Rāma, with a shower of his own arrows, cut those shafts into many pieces.
6.066.021c Those gold-feathered arrows, severed by the thousands, fell upon the earth.
6.066.022a Then that battle took place there between the two, as they encountered one another with their full might—
the son of the Rākṣasa Khara and the son of Daśaratha.
Then, like the sound of two clouds in the sky,
the loud twang of the bowstring released from the bow was heard upon the field of battle;
and the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and great serpents [listened].
6.066.024c All those situated in the intermediate space desired to behold that wonder.
6.066.025a Pierced in their mutual limbs, their strength doubled;
6.066.025c On the field of battle, the two of them performed counter-attacks against one another.

But the Rākṣasa cut down the floods of arrows discharged at Rāma in battle; however, Rāma indeed shattered those arrows released by the Rākṣasa into many pieces with his own shafts. Thus, all the cardinal and intermediate directions were overspread with floods of arrows.
The earth was completely covered and did not shine forth on any side. Then the mighty-armed Rāghava, filled with rage, cut the bow of the Rākṣasa and pierced his charioteer with eight iron shafts.
Having shattered the chariot with his arrows, Rāma struck down the horses of the chariot. Standing on the ground without a chariot, the night-stalker Makarākṣa,
that Rākṣasa, took up a spear in his hand and stood upon the earth.
6.066.029e Terrifying all beings, with a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon, 6.066.030a the night-stalker, having whirled his great, blazing spear,
6.066.030c hurled it in anger at that Raghava in the great battle.
As that flaming spear, released from the hand of Khara’s son, was falling toward him,
Rāghava severed it in mid-air with three arrows. That trident, adorned with divine gold, was cut into many pieces.

Struck by Rāma’s arrow, it shattered upon the earth like a great clod of earth. Seeing that spear destroyed by Rāma of wondrous deeds, the beings dwelling in the sky cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Seeing that spear destroyed, the night-stalker Makarākṣa raised his fist and cried out to the descendant of Kakutstha, "Stay! Stay!
Seeing him falling upon him, the joy of the Raghus laughed.
Then Rāma fixed the Pāvaka weapon upon his bow.
By that weapon, the Rākṣasa was struck by Kākutstha in battle;
with his heart shattered, he fell there and died.
Having witnessed the fall of Makarākṣa, all those rākṣasas,
then tormented by the arrows of Rāma’s son, fled toward Laṅkā itself with the force of the shafts of Daśaratha’s royal son.
Then the gods beheld that night-stalker, the son of Khara, slain and shattered like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, and they were filled with joy.
6.067.001 Having heard that Makarākṣa had been slain, Rāvaṇa, the victor in assemblies, then,
filled with rage, commanded his son Indrajit for battle.
6.067.002 "O hero, slay the two brothers of great prowess, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa!"
Whether invisible or visible, you are in every way superior in strength. You conquer Indra, whose deeds are incomparable, in battle;
how much more so, seeing two mere mortals, will you not slay them in combat?

Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, Indrajit accepted his father’s words and duly offered oblations into the fire upon the sacrificial ground. And as he was offering the oblations there into the fire, women wearing red turbans [stood nearby].
6.067.005c Agitated, the rākṣasīs arrived there where the son of Rāvaṇa was.
6.067.006a Weapons, arrows with feathered shafts, sacrificial fuel of *vibhītaka* wood,
red garments, and likewise a ladle made of black iron.
Having strewn firewood made of arrow-reeds all around on every side,
he seized the throat of a living goat that was entirely black,
as it stood before the great-flamed, smokeless fire kindled by the offering of *caru* oblations.
Those signs appeared, indicating victory.
With its flame turning clockwise and resembling molten gold,
the Fire-god himself arose and accepted that oblation.
Having offered oblations into the fire and gratified the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas,
he ascended that excellent, auspicious chariot which possessed the power of invisibility.
It was equipped with four horses and sharp arrows.
With his great bow fixed upon it, he shone resplendent on that excellent chariot;
blazing with his own physical form and adorned with golden trappings,
that chariot was further embellished with arrows shaped like full moons and crescent moons.
The great conch of Jāmbūnada gold, resembling a blazing fire and adorned with lapis lazuli, became the banner of Indrajit;
and he was protected by that Brahmā-weapon, which was like the sun itself.
6.067.014c That son of Rāvaṇa became invincible and possessed of immense strength. 6.067.015a Having emerged from the city, Indrajit, the victor in assembly,
6.067.015c having offered oblations into the fire with Rākṣasa mantras, vanished and spoke.
"Today, having slain those two who falsely claimed to have renounced the world in the forest in battle,
I shall grant victory to my father Rāvaṇa, who is preeminent in combat. Having made the earth devoid of monkeys by killing Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa,"
"Having said, 'I shall bring you supreme joy,' he vanished. Then,
urged by the Ten-necked one, the sharp Indrajit descended in battle, enraged,
with sharp bows and iron arrows."
He saw those two heroes of great prowess standing in the midst of the monkeys like two three-headed serpents, discharging nets of arrows; thinking,
"These are they," he strung his bow.
Like Parjanya pouring down rain, he [showered] continuous streams of arrows;
having reached them in the air along with his chariot, he stood beyond the range of sight and pierced Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with sharpened shafts.
Enveloped by the force of his arrows, those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
took up their bows along with their shafts and discharged divine weapons;
those two of great strength covered the sky with nets of arrows.
Those two, who resembled gods, could not even touch him with their missiles or arrows. For he, the illustrious one, created a darkness of smoke while shrouding the sky;
enveloped in the gloom of mist, he made the quarters of the world vanish from sight.
As he moved about, neither the twang of his bowstring nor the sound of his chariot wheels and hooves was heard, nor did his form appear;
in the blinding, dense darkness, it was like a wondrous rain of arrows.

The mighty-armed one showered him with rains of iron arrows (nārāca). Enraged in battle, the son of Rāvaṇa— having received boons— pierced Rāma violently in all his limbs with arrows radiant as the sun.
Being struck by iron shafts like two mountains by torrents of rain,
those two tigers among men released sharp arrows feathered with gold. Reaching the sky, those arrows with heron-feathers [struck] the son of Rāvaṇa.

Having been mangled, those birds fell to the ground drenched in blood. Being excessively afflicted by that flood of arrows, those two best of men cut down those falling shafts with numerous broad-headed arrows (bhallas).
For whenever those two saw sharp arrows falling here and there,
the two sons of Daśaratha discharged supreme weapons from those very spots.
Meanwhile, the son of Rāvaṇa, that great car-warrior, moved through all the directions on his chariot.
6.067.032c Skilled in weapons, he pierced those two sons of Daśaratha with sharpened arrows.
6.067.033a Deeply pierced by him with those well-aimed, gold-feathered shafts, those two heroic sons of Daśaratha became like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.

No one knew his course, nor his form, his bow, or his arrows; nothing else was perceived of him, like the sun when it is shrouded by a mass of clouds. And by him were the monkeys pierced, struck down, and deprived of life.
Hundreds fell there upon the surface of the earth.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, filled with great rage, spoke these words to his brother:
"I shall employ the Brahma-weapon for the sake of slaying all the Rākṣasas."
Then Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who is endowed with auspicious marks:
"You ought not to slay the Rākṣasas on this earth for the sake of a single person—
especially one who is not fighting, who is hidden, who stands with palms joined in reverence, and who has come for refuge."
"You ought not to kill one who is fleeing or distracted here;
rather, O mighty one, we two shall strive for his slaughter alone.
We shall discharge weapons of great velocity that are like venomous serpents."
The leaders of the monkey hosts, having seen this deceitful and vile Rākṣasa who has forcibly hidden his chariot, will slay him;
whether he enters the earth or the heavens.
Whether in the subterranean realm of Rasātala or in the expanse of the sky,
even if thus concealed, he shall fall lifeless upon the surface of the earth, consumed by my weapon.
Having spoken these words,
the high-souled hero of the Raghus, surrounded by the foremost of the monkeys, set out for the slaughter of that fierce one of cruel deeds.
Then the high-souled one looked about in haste;
having understood the mind of that great-souled Rāghava,
he withdrew from that battle and entered the city.
6.068.002 Remembering the slaughter of those powerful Rākṣasas,
the hero of great splendor, his eyes copper-red with rage, went forth.
6.068.003 Surrounded by Rākṣasas, he emerged through the western gate.
6.068.003c Indrajit, the son of Pulastya, possessed great heroism and was a thorn to the gods.
6.068.004a Then Indrajit, seeing his two heroic brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa prepared for battle, manifested his illusory power (māyā) at that time.

Then Indrajit, having placed a phantom Sītā upon his chariot and surrounded by a great force, resolved to slay her. Having formed this intent for the purpose of deluding everyone, that evil-minded one acted.
Resolved to kill Sītā, he set out toward the monkeys. Seeing him emerging from the city, the forest-dwellers,
enraged and eager for battle, sprang up with rocks in their hands.
Hanumān, that elephant among monkeys, went at their head,
grasping a massive and formidable mountain peak.
He beheld Sītā, her joy destroyed, in the chariot of Indrajit.
Wearing a single braid, miserable, her face emaciated by fasting, wearing a single soiled garment, lacking cleanliness— the beloved of Rāghava,
that excellent woman, with all her limbs smeared with dust and dirt.
Having gazed upon that Maithilī for a moment and having identified her,
Hanumān, his face overwhelmed with tears, became deeply distressed.
He then spoke to her, who was afflicted by grief, joyless, and a woman of ascetic suffering.
Seeing Sītā standing upon the chariot, supported by the daughter of the Rākṣasa king,
that great monkey reflected, "What is her intention?
and together with those foremost of monkeys, he rushed toward the son of Rāvaṇa.
6.068.014a Seeing that army of monkeys, the son of Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage, 6.068.014c drew his sword Viśoka and seized Sītā by the head.
6.068.015a While they were looking on at the woman, the son of Rāvaṇa struck her.
Seeing her crying out "Rāma! Rāma! while joined to the chariot by means of illusion, her hair seized, Hanumān was overcome with dejection;
the son of the Wind-god shed tears born of sorrow from his eyes.

6.068.016e He spoke these harsh words in anger to the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas: 6.068.017a "O evil-souled one, you have seized me by the hair for your own destruction! 6.068.017c Born in a lineage of Brahmanical sages, you have entered the womb of a Rākṣasa."
"Fie on you, whose conduct is wicked and whose mind is such as this!
O cruel, ignoble, ill-behaved, base one of sinful prowess! Such is the deed of an ignoble man; you have no compassion, O pitiless one!"
Maithilī has already been deprived of her home, her kingdom, and the protection of Rāma’s hand.
What offense has she committed against you that you wish to kill her?
Moreover, having killed Sītā, you shall not live for long under any circumstances.
"By this act deserving of death, you have indeed fallen into my hands.
Those worlds reserved for the slayers of women, which are despised even by those condemned by the world—
having cast off your life here, you shall attain them after death."
Speaking thus, Hanumān, surrounded by monkeys bearing weapons,
rushed in great anger toward the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
That army of forest-dwellers, possessed of great heroism, came charging forward.
He warded off the army of *rakṣasas* of terrifying speed;
having agitated that host of monkeys with a thousand arrows,
Indrajit spoke to Hanumān, the best of monkeys.
"O Sugrīva, you, and Rāma— for whose sake you have come here—
I shall kill that Vaidehī this very day while you look on. Having killed her, O monkey, I will then [kill] Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and you."
"I shall slay Sugrīva and that ignoble Vibhīṣaṇa as well.
O monkey, as for what you say— that women must not be killed—
whatever causes suffering to one's enemies is precisely what ought to be done."
Having spoken thus to the weeping Sītā, who was an illusory creation,
Indrajit himself then struck her with a sharp-edged sword. Along the path of his sacred thread, that ascetic woman was cut down by him.
6.068.029c That woman of broad hips and lovely appearance fell upon the earth.
6.068.030a Having slain that woman, Indrajit said to Hanumān:
6.068.030c "Behold this [woman] of Rāma’s, destroyed by me in my wrath."
Then, having himself slain her with a great sword, Indrajit,
filled with joy, mounted his chariot and let out a mighty roar.
The monkeys, stationed nearby, heard that sound.
As he stood there with his mouth wide open, roaring and taking refuge in that fortress,
the evil-minded son of Rāvaṇa, having thus struck down Sītā, became exceedingly joyful in heart.
Seeing him so joyful in appearance, the monkeys,
themselves dejected in spirit, fled away.
Hearing that terrifying roar, which sounded like the thunderbolt of Śakra, they ran off.
Looking in all directions, those bulls among monkeys fled.
Then Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, spoke to them all as they were fleeing away in various directions, dejected in face, miserable, and terrified.
"O monkeys, why do you flee with dejected faces, having abandoned your enthusiasm for battle? Where indeed has your heroism gone?
Follow behind me as I go forward into the fray."
"It is indeed improper for heroes of noble lineage to turn back.
Thus addressed by the wise son of Vāyu, they became greatly incensed and,
with joyful hearts, seized mountain peaks and trees.
Roaring, the bull-like monkeys fell upon the rākṣasas and,
surrounding Hanumān, followed him in that great battle. Surrounded on all sides by those leaders of the monkeys, Hanumān—
Like a blazing fire with its flames, he consumed the enemy host;
that great monkey, resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time, surrounded by the army of monkeys, wrought a slaughter among the Rākṣasas.
6.069.009a But that great monkey Hanumān, possessed by both grief and anger, 6.069.009c hurled a massive boulder at Rāvaṇa’s chariot.
6.069.010a Seeing it falling toward him, the charioteer then [acted] with the chariot.
Yoked with obedient horses, it was driven a very great distance;
yet, failing to reach Indrajit along with his chariot and charioteer,
that stone which had been raised in vain pierced the earth and entered it.
When the rock had fallen, the army of the *rākṣasas* was distressed; shouting, the forest-dwellers rushed toward him by the hundreds. Those huge-bodied ones raised up trees and mountain peaks.
The monkeys of terrible prowess hurled [the trees] into the midst of their enemies.
Struck by those monkeys of great heroism with trees, the night-stalkers of fearsome form writhed upon the field of battle.
Then, beholding his own army afflicted by the monkeys, Indrajit,
seizing his weapons, advanced in a rage toward the enemy. Surrounded by his own troops, he discharged a torrent of arrows.
Having witnessed his prowess, he struck down many tigers among monkeys with spears,
thunderbolts, swords, javelins, and mallets;
and those monkeys also slew his followers in the battle.
With *sāla* trees possessing trunks and branches, and with boulders of great weight,
Hanumān wrought a slaughter of the Rākṣasas of terrible deeds.
Having repelled the enemy host, he spoke to those forest-dwellers.
"O Hanumān, turn back! This army cannot achieve our goal, even though we exert ourselves and risk our lives out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Rāma;
for she for whose sake we fight—that daughter of Janaka—is already slain."
"Having informed Rāma and Sugrīva of this matter,
we shall do whatever those two determine to undertake.
Having spoken thus, the best of monkeys restrained all the other monkeys.
Slowly and without fear, that powerful one turned back. But seeing Hanumān proceeding toward where Rāghava was,
Indrajit took his stand at Nikumbhilā and offered oblations into the fire.
On the sacrificial ground, the fire, being offered oblations by that Rākṣasa according to the prescribed rites,
then blazed up, feeding upon the blood of the sacrifice. Satiated with the blood of the oblation, it was seen enveloped in flames.
Like the sun at twilight, that fierce fire blazed up. Then Indrajit, for the prosperity of the Rākṣasas,
offered oblations according to the prescribed ritual.
Having seen [this], those Rākṣasas,
who were experts in both right and wrong policy, took their positions within the great multitudes.
And Rāghava also beheld that vast army of the Rākṣasas and forest-dwellers.
Hearing the roar of the battle, he spoke to Jāmbavān:
"O gentle one, surely Hanumān has performed a most difficult deed;
for the sound of his great and terrible weapons is heard."

"Therefore, O Lord of Bears, go quickly surrounded by your own forces and provide assistance to that best of monkeys as he fights. Having said, "So be it," the King of Bears set out, surrounded by his own army.
6.070.004c Hanumān, the monkey, arrived at the western gate where [the others] were. 6.070.005a Then the lord of the bears saw Hanumān approaching on the path,
surrounded by monkeys who had fought in battle and were gasping for breath.
6.070.006a Having seen on the path that formidable host of Ṛkṣas rising up, resembling a dark blue cloud, Hanumān turned back after repelling them.
6.070.007a That highly illustrious one drew near to the monkey army with him.
Having returned quickly, he spoke these words to Rāma in his distress:
"While we were fighting in battle and looking on,
Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, slew the weeping Sītā."
"O subduer of enemies, seeing her, my mind became bewildered and I was despondent.
Therefore, I have come to inform you of what occurred.
Having heard those words of his, Rāghava fainted from grief.
Then he fell to the ground like a tree severed at its roots. Seeing that Rāghava, who resembled a god, fallen upon the earth,
the best of the monkeys sprang up and rushed toward him from all sides.
They sprinkled him with water fragrant with lotuses and blue lilies—
water that was suddenly like a fierce, unbearable fire that had broken out.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, deeply distressed, embraced him with both arms.
He spoke these words, consistent with reason and purpose, to Rāma who was distressed:
"Dharma is useless; it cannot protect you—who stand upon the auspicious path and have conquered your senses through noble conduct—from calamities."
The perception of beings, both stationary and moving, exists in such a way that dharma does not exist in that same manner; therefore, it is my opinion that dharma does not exist.
Just as the stationary is manifest, so too is the moving of that same nature.
This matter is not so; one such as you does not meet with calamity. If unrighteousness were truly real, Rāvaṇa would have gone to hell;
and you, being endowed with righteousness, would never have encountered such misfortune.
Because he is free from calamity while you have fallen into calamity, he would obtain merit through righteousness and demerit through unrighteousness;
provided that people who do not delight in unrighteousness were united with righteousness.
For those who practice righteousness, righteousness shall prevail and its fruit shall likewise accrue to them; yet,
because wealth increases for those in whom unrighteousness is established, while those of virtuous character suffer, therefore these two [wealth and virtue] are rendered useless.
"O Rāghava, if those of evil deeds are slain by unrighteousness, then righteousness itself is struck down by that act of killing;
being thus destroyed, what will it slay?
Or rather, this [unrighteousness] is slain by what is ordained, or it slays another."
6.070.022c By that [means], the ritual procedure is defiled, yet he is not tainted by that sinful deed.
6.070.023a Since it is invisible, without remedy, unmanifest, non-existent though appearing as existent—
6.070.023c O crusher of enemies, how can the supreme state be attained through such a dharma?

6.070.024a O foremost of the virtuous, if existence were real, nothing non-existent would ever belong to you. 6.070.024c Since you have encountered such a fate as this, therefore existence is not tenable. 6.070.025a Or rather, the weak and the cowardly follow after strength; such is the nature of dharma.
It is my opinion that one who is weak and has violated the bounds of propriety is not to be served. If righteousness is indeed subordinate to power in the exercise of prowess,
then abandon righteousness and conduct yourself according to power as you would to righteousness.
6.070.027a If, O scorcher of the foe, truth-speaking is indeed the supreme dharma,
6.070.027c then why was your father, who spoke falsehoods to you, not bound by you as one devoid of compassion?
6.070.028a Whether it be dharma or adharma, O scorcher of the foe, let it be as it truly is.
"Even the wielder of the thunderbolt, Śatakratu, would not perform a sacrifice after killing a sage.
O Rāghava, dharma that relies upon adharma brings about destruction;
O descendant of Kakutstha, a man performs all this according to his own desire."
"O dear one, O Raghava, this was my own thought: 'This is dharma.
Yet, by renouncing the kingdom at that time, you have cut down the very root of dharma. For from wealth that has increased and flourished in every direction..."
All activities proceed from him like rivers from mountains.
For all the activities of a man who is devoid of wealth and possesses little luster are cut off, just as small streams dry up in the summer heat.
6.070.033a This very person, having abandoned wealth and desiring pleasure while raised in comfort, 6.070.033c undertakes to commit evil; thus does vice proceed.
6.070.034a He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who possesses wealth is a man in this world; he who possesses wealth is a wise scholar.
He who possesses wealth is valiant; he who possesses wealth is intelligent. He who possesses wealth is highly fortunate; he who possesses wealth is possessed of great virtues.
"O hero, these faults have been declared by me regarding the abandonment of wealth,
because of which you have resolved to renounce the kingdom. For one who possesses wealth, dharma, and pleasure, everything proceeds auspiciously."
6.070.037c By one who is without wealth and yet desires wealth, no purpose can be achieved while searching for it.
6.070.038a Joy, desire, pride, righteousness, anger, tranquility, and self-control—
6.070.038c O lord of men, all these proceed from wealth.
6.070.039a For those who practice righteousness while moving through this world, these goals vanish;
6.070.039c they are no longer seen in you, like planets obscured by cloudy days.
