6.070.040a O hero, now that you have gone forth into the religious life, remaining steadfast in the word of your preceptor—
"Your wife, dearer to you than life itself, has been carried off by a Rākṣasa.
O hero, that immense suffering caused today by Indrajit, I shall dispel through my action; therefore, arise, O Rāghava!"
"O sinless one, this [Rāvaṇa] has been incited by you for the sake of your beloved;
enraged at the sight of Janaka’s daughter’s death, he [will destroy] the earth along with its horses, elephants, chariots, and lords of the Rākṣasas."
While Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted to his brother, was consoling Rāma by saying, "I shall strike Laṅkā severely with my arrows," Vibhīṣaṇa withdrew his troops to their proper positions and arrived there.
Surrounded by four heroic ministers bearing various weapons,
he resembled a leader of a herd of elephants with the appearance of a mass of dark collyrium;
having approached the high-souled Rāghava, who was overwhelmed with grief—
With eyes clouded by tears, she beheld the monkeys as well;
and she saw the high-souled Rāghava, the joy of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
fallen into a swoon and resting upon Lakṣmaṇa’s lap.
Seeing Rāma ashamed and tormented by grief, Vibhīṣaṇa,
his soul dejected by inner sorrow, asked, "What is this?
Having looked at the face of Vibhīṣaṇa, [Rāma spoke to] Sugrīva and those monkeys.
Overwhelmed with tears, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words:
"O gentle one, as soon as Rāghava heard from Hanumān’s speech that Sītā had been killed by Indrajit here, he fell into a swoon."
But restraining the son of Sumitrā as he was speaking, Vibhīṣaṇa addressed these words of great significance to Rāma, who had lost consciousness:
"O lord of men, that which you were told by Hanumān while appearing in a state of distress— "
I consider that to be as impossible as the drying up of the ocean. However, O mighty-armed one, I know the intention of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa regarding Sītā; he will not bring about her death.
Though entreated by me many times, desiring his welfare,
with the words "Release Vaidehī," he did not follow that advice;
neither through conciliation, nor through sowing dissension, nor through bribery— how much less through war.
She could not possibly be seen by anyone else;
having bewildered the monkeys, that Rākṣasa departed for the sanctuary named Nikumbhilā, where he will perform a fire sacrifice.
For this son of Rāvaṇa has indeed sacrificed and approached even the gods together with Indra; thus he becomes unassailable in battle. Surely this illusion was employed by him while bewildering us.
"O dear one, since he seeks to obstruct the prowess of the monkeys,
let us go there with our army before he completes his task.
Let us abandon this false distress that has come upon this tiger among men."
Indeed, all our strength falters upon seeing you emaciated by grief. Remain here with a healthy heart, uplifted by your courage;
send Lakṣmaṇa along with us and the drawn-out army.
6.071.018a This tiger among men will cause that son of Rāvaṇa to abandon that deed with his sharpened arrows; 6.071.018c thereafter, he shall become vulnerable to slaughter.
6.071.019a These [arrows] of his are sharpened, keen, and possess feathers, wings, and shafts.
Like fierce birds of prey, these arrows shall drink his blood.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, command Lakṣmaṇa, who possesses auspicious marks,
for the destruction of the Rākṣasa, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt commands the vajra.
"O best of men, there is no delay in destroying the enemy that you are capable of making today. Grant your word for the slaying of the foe."
Just as Mahendra when destroying the city of the Asuras,
that lord of the Rākṣasas, having completed his task,
becomes invisible in battle to both gods and asuras.
"If he, having completed his task, should desire to fight,
even the gods would have great cause for concern.
Having heard those words of his, Rāghava was emaciated by grief.
6.072.001c He did not clearly comprehend what had been spoken by that Rākṣasa.
6.072.002a Thereupon, summoning his fortitude, Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities,
spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, who was seated nearby in the presence of the monkey.
"O Vibhīṣaṇa, lord of the Nairṛtas, I wish to hear again the words that you have spoken; speak whatever you desire to say.
Having heard the speech of Rāghava, the one skilled in speech replied with these words:

6.072.004c When Vibhīṣaṇa spoke these words once again: 6.072.005a "O mighty-armed one, the stationing of the troops as commanded by you, 6.072.005c has been carried out accordingly, O hero, immediately following your word."
All those divisions have been arrayed on every side, and the troop-leaders have been stationed according to rule and in their respective sections. Furthermore,
O highly illustrious one, listen to what I have further to report.
When you are tormented without cause, our hearts are likewise tormented. O King, abandon this grief that has come upon you as a false distress;
let this anxiety, which only increases the joy of your enemies, be cast aside.
"O hero, let effort be made; let joy be cultivated. If Sītā is to be recovered by you, then the night-stalkers must be slain.
O descendant of Raghu, I shall speak; listen to my beneficial words."
"Let this son of Sumitrā go forth auspiciously, surrounded by a great force,
so that having reached Nikumbhilā, he may slay the son of Rāvaṇa in battle with arrows released from the circle of his bow, resembling the venom of poisonous serpents."
The great archer, victorious in battle, sought to slay the son of Rāvaṇa with his arrows.
By that hero, through ascetic penance and by virtue of a boon from the Self-born One,
the Brahmāśiras weapon was obtained, as were horses capable of traveling at will.
"O enemy of Indra, that foe who slays you while you have not yet reached Nikumbhilā and have not yet offered oblations into the fire— that shall be your death.
Thus, O King, was the death of that wise one ordained.
"O Rāma, bestow that one of great strength upon Indrajit for his slaughter;
know that when he is slain, Rāvaṇa along with his circle of friends is as good as dead.
Having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāma then spoke these words.
"I know the illusion of that fierce one, O you of true prowess;
for he is wise, a master of the Brahma-weapon, a great magician, and possessed of great strength. He renders even the gods, including Varuṇa, unconscious in battle."

As he moved through the air seated upon his chariot, the course of that highly illustrious one was not perceived, like the sun when it is shrouded by a mass of clouds. But Rāghava, having recognized the power of the magic illusion of that evil-minded enemy, [acted accordingly].
He spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with fame:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, accompanied by the entire force of the lord of monkeys and by the troop-leaders headed by Hanumān..."
Accompanied by Jāmbavān, the lord of the bears, and surrounded by his army,
slay that son of a Rākṣasa, who is skilled in the power of illusion.
This high-souled night-stalker [will come] along with his ministers to meet you.
"One who is familiar with that region shall follow behind him.
Hearing these words of Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa,
endowed with formidable prowess, took up another excellent bow along with Vibhīṣaṇa.
Armed with his armor, sword, and arrows, and wielding his golden bow,
the son of Sumitrā, filled with joy, touched Rāma’s feet and said:
"Today, my arrows, released from my bow, shall pierce through the son of Rāvaṇa."
They shall descend upon Laṅkā like swans upon a lotus pond. This very day, my own arrows, released from the string of my great bow, shall shatter the body of that fierce one after slaying him.
Having spoken these words in the presence of his brother,
the radiant Lakṣmaṇa, desiring the slaying of Rāvaṇa’s son, departed in haste.
Having saluted the feet of his guru and performed a circumambulation, he went forth.
Accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa, the powerful prince went toward the Nikumbhilā shrine, which was guarded by the son of Rāvaṇa;
having had rites for his welfare performed by his brother, Lakṣmaṇa proceeded with haste.
Surrounded by many thousands of monkeys, Hanumān,
along with Vibhīṣaṇa and his ministers, then followed Lakṣmaṇa,
encompassed by the great army of monkeys moving with great speed.
And he beheld the army of the king of bears stationed upon the road.
Having traveled a long distance, Saumitri, the delighter of his friends,
saw from afar the army of the lord of the rākṣasas drawn up in battle array.
Having reached that place, O subduer of enemies, the joy of the Raghus stood with bow in hand, employing the application of *māyā* according to the ordinances of Brahmā in order to conquer.
That [place] was radiant with various stainless weapons.
He entered that vast and dense thicket of banners, most terrifying with its great chariots and of immeasurable speed— the army of his enemies, like a blinding darkness.
Then, in that situation, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa— words that were beneficial for his purpose and detrimental to his enemies:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, strive for the breaking up of this great army."
6.073.002c Even the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas will become visible here once [the mountain] is split.
6.073.003a Therefore, you, scattering arrows resembling Indra’s thunderbolt at the enemies,
6.073.003c must charge forward quickly before this task is completed.
"Kill that evil-souled hero, who is devoted to illusion and unrighteous—
Rāvaṇa’s son, a doer of cruel deeds who brings fear to all the worlds.
Having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, who bears auspicious marks, [acted].
He rained down showers of arrows upon the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas. Then the bears and monkeys, who fought from trees and excellent mountains,
rushed together toward that stationed army.
And the Rākṣasas, desiring to slay the monkey army, advanced with sharp arrows, swords, spears, and javelins raised aloft. A tumultuous clash then broke out between the monkeys and the Rākṣasas.
Making Lankā resound on all sides with a great roar,
the sky was completely covered by weapons of various forms, sharp arrows, trees, and uplifted, formidable mountain peaks.
6.073.010a Those Rākṣasas, with their deformed faces and arms, among the monkeys; 6.073.010c planting their weapons, they created a very great terror.
6.073.011a In the same way, the monkeys [attacked] with all kinds of trees and mountain peaks.
In that battle, they struck and slaughtered the leaders of the rākṣasas;
and as the rākṣasas were being slain by the great-bodied and mighty leaders of the bears and monkeys, a great fear arose among them.
6.073.013a Having heard that his own army was despondent and oppressed by the enemies, 6.073.013c the invincible one rose up even though the task had not yet been accomplished.
6.073.014a Emerging from the darkness of the trees, that son of Rāvaṇa was filled with rage.
That Rākṣasa ascended his prepared chariot, which had been yoked before;
with his formidable bow and arrows, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
his cruel face and eyes red, he shone like Death, the Ender himself.

But as soon as they saw him standing upon his chariot, that army of Rākṣasas of terrible speed, eager to fight with Lakṣmaṇa, turned back. At that moment, Hanumān raised up his most formidable [weapon].
Resembling a mountain, that subduer of enemies,
the monkey, burning that army of Rākṣasas like the fire of cosmic destruction,
rendered them unconscious in battle with many trees.
Upon seeing the son of the Wind-god destroying [the enemy] with his might,
thousands of rākṣasas showered Hanumān with spears;
those bearing sharp spears hurled their spears, and those with swords in hand flung their swords.
With spears those whose hands held spears, with swords those armed with swords,
with iron clubs, maces, and beautiful-looking lances,
and by the hundreds with *śataghnīs* and iron mallets.
The Rākṣasas,
having approached him from all sides, struck that mountain-like [Hanumān] with terrible axes, slings, fists possessing the speed of thunderbolts, and palms resembling lightning bolts.
And being enraged, he wrought a great slaughter even among them.
Indrajit beheld that best of monkeys, who resembled a mountain,
the son of the Wind-god, the slayer of enemies, as he was destroying his foes.
6.073.025a He said this to the charioteer: "Go where that monkey is;
6.073.025c for if he is neglected, he will surely bring about the destruction of us Rākṣasas.
6.073.026a Thus addressed by him, the charioteer went to where that son of the Wind was.
Seeing Indrajit, who was exceedingly difficult to overcome, standing upon his chariot,
that invincible Rākṣasa approached and rained down arrows, swords, spears, scimitars, and battle-axes upon the head of the monkey.
Having seized those terrible weapons, that son of the Wind-god,
inflamed by great rage, spoke these words:
"Fight, if you are a hero, O evil-minded son of Rāvaṇa!"
"Having encountered the son of Vāyu, you shall not return alive.
If you wish to engage in a duel with me in battle, fight with your two arms;
withstand my force, O evil-minded one, for then you shall be the foremost among the Rākṣasas."
Vibhīṣaṇa pointed out to Lakṣmaṇa the son of Rāvaṇa, who was intent on killing Hanumān with his bow raised;
he was the conqueror of Vāsava and the offspring of Rāvaṇa.
6.073.032c Having mounted his chariot, he seeks to slay Hanumān.
6.073.033a O son of Sumitrā, with arrows of incomparable form, which rend the enemy and are terrible bringers of the end of life, slay the son of Rāvaṇa.
Thus addressed then by Vibhīṣaṇa, the terror of his enemies,
the high-souled one beheld that [being] resembling a mountain.

Having thus addressed the son of Sumitrā, Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with joy, took up his bow and, standing upon his chariot, departed in haste toward that one of terrible strength who was difficult to approach.
Having gone not far from there and entered a vast forest,
Vibhīṣaṇa showed that deed to Lakṣmaṇa:
a banyan tree of terrifying appearance, resembling a dark blue cloud.
The radiant brother of Rāvaṇa announced to Lakṣmaṇa:
"The powerful son of Rāvaṇa has presented here an offering to the spirits;
having made that offering, he will thereafter advance to battle."
Then that Rākṣasa became invisible to all beings;
he slaughtered his enemies in battle and bound them with his finest arrows. While that powerful son of Rāvaṇa had not yet entered the banyan tree—
"Destroy him with your sharp arrows, together with his chariot, horses, and charioteer.
Having said, "So be it," the highly energetic son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends,
stood there brandishing his wonderful bow.

6.074.008a That powerful son of Rāvaṇa, Indrajit, appeared on a chariot the color of fire, clad in armor, bearing a sword, and accompanied by his banner. 6.074.009a The one of great splendor spoke to that unconquered descendant of Pulastya.
"6.074.009c I challenge you to battle; give me a fair fight!
6.074.010a Thus addressed, the high-spirited and immensely powerful son of Rāvaṇa, seeing Vibhīṣaṇa there, spoke these harsh words."
"O Rākṣasa, you were born and raised right here; you are the very brother of my father. How can you, as my paternal uncle, act with hostility toward your own nephew?
O evil-minded one, neither kinship, nor friendship, nor even your own birth has any effect upon you."
"Neither kinship nor righteousness is an authority for you, O defiler of dharma! You are to be pitied, O evil-minded one, and censurable by the virtuous,
since you have abandoned your own people and entered into the service of another."
With such a lax intellect, you do not perceive this great difference:
what is dwelling among one's own kin, and what is dependence upon lowly others? Whether another person be virtuous or one's own kin be devoid of merit—
One's own kinsman who is devoid of virtue is better; he who is a stranger remains a stranger indeed.
O night-stalker, such is this lack of compassion as you display toward your own kin, O younger brother of Rāvaṇa; it is possible for you, being a kinsman, to speak so harshly.
Thus addressed by his brother’s son, Vibhīṣaṇa replied:
"O Rākṣasa, why do you boast as if you were ignorant of my character?
O wicked son of the Lord of Rākṣasas, abandon such harshness out of respect for me."

"Even though I was born into a family of Rākṣasas of cruel deeds, this is the first quality of men: my character is not that of a Rākṣasa. I do not delight in cruelty, nor indeed do I delight in unrighteousness."
6.074.019c How can a brother be cast out by a brother of such wicked character?
6.074.020a Taking the property of others, violating the wives of others, and excessive suspicion toward friends— these three faults bring about one's ruin.
The slaughter of great seers, conflict with all the gods,
arrogance, wrath, enmity, and hostility—
these are the faults that will destroy my brother’s life and sovereignty.
They concealed his virtues, just as clouds shroud the mountains.
Because of these faults, I have abandoned your brother, who was like a father to you;
neither this city of Laṅkā, nor you, nor your father remain [as they once were].
"O Rākṣasa, you are arrogant, foolish, and ill-behaved;
you are bound by the noose of Time. Speak to me whatever you wish!
Today your calamity has arrived; what will you say now?"
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, you will not be able to enter the Nyagrodha tree;
having dared to attack the two descendants of Kakutstha, you shall not live.
Fight in battle with Lakṣmaṇa, the god among men!"
"Once you are slain, O deity, you shall perform your duty in the abode of Yama.
Display your own power as it is fully exerted;
exhaust all your weapons and arrows."
"Having come within the range of Lakṣmaṇa's arrows, you shall not escape today with your army alive.
Having heard Vibhīṣaṇa's words, the son of Rāvaṇa was overcome with rage.
He spoke harsh words and leapt forward with great speed;
standing upon a grand, well-adorned chariot yoked with black horses, he appeared like Death himself at the end of time, with his weapons and sword raised.
Raising his massive, vast, swift, and firm bow, and grasping his terrifying arrows that destroy enemies, he,
having begun his assault, spoke to the son of Sumitrā along with Vibhīṣaṇa.
"And behold my prowess against those tigers among monkeys!
Today in battle, you shall try to ward off the unassailable shower of arrows released from my bow, like a rain poured down from the sky."
Today my arrows, released from my great bow,
shall scatter your limbs like fire consumes a heap of cotton—
piercing you with sharp shafts, spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and lances.
"Today I shall send you all indeed to the abode of Yama. Who will stand before me in battle as I, swift-handed, discharge showers of arrows like the roaring of a cloud?"
Having heard that roar of the lord of the rākṣasas, Lakṣmaṇa,
with an undaunted face and filled with rage, then spoke these words to the son of Rāvaṇa:
"O rākṣasa, you have spoken of the difficult-to-reach limit of your undertakings."

6.075.010c He who reaches the further shore of his undertakings through action is wise. 6.075.011a But you, O evil-minded one, having failed to obtain wealth that is difficult for anyone to acquire, believe yourself to have achieved your purpose merely by uttering words.

"O Rākṣasa, that which you practiced against me in battle by resorting to invisibility was the path of a thief; it is not the way pursued by heroes. For I stood right here, O Rākṣasa, having come within the range of your arrows."
"Show that splendor of yours this very day; why do you boast with mere words?
Thus addressed, the mighty Indrajit, seeking victory in battle, grasped his formidable bow and loosed sharpened arrows.
6.075.015a Those arrows, released with great velocity and resembling the venom of serpents,
6.075.015c reached Lakṣmaṇa and fell like hissing snakes.
6.075.016a With those exceedingly swift arrows, the impetuous son of Rāvaṇa—
In battle, Indrajit pierced the auspiciously marked son of Sumitrā with arrows;
his limbs deeply pierced and drenched in blood,
the glorious Lakṣmaṇa shone like a smokeless fire.
6.075.018a But Indrajit, having reflected upon his own deed and having understood it,
let out a tremendous roar and spoke these words: 6.075.019a "Those sharp-edged arrows of yours, released from my bow, shall become feathered shafts."
"O Saumitri, today those who bring an end to life shall take away your life.
Today, O Lakṣmaṇa, let packs of jackals, flocks of hawks,
and vultures descend upon you once you have been slain by me and are deprived of life."
6.075.021a Rāma, that base kinsman of the warrior caste, ever ignoble and most evil-minded,
6.075.021c shall this very day behold you, his devoted brother, slain by me— 6.075.022a with your armor stripped away and your bow cast aside upon the ground.
"O son of Sumitrā, today I shall strike you down with your head severed!"—
to the enraged and harsh-spoken son of Rāvaṇa who was speaking thus,
Lakṣmaṇa replied with exceedingly reasoned words.
"O Rākṣasa, why do you boast here without having performed the deed? Perform that deed by which I may believe your boasting!
Without speaking harsh words and without disparaging anything at all—"

"O devourer of men, you shall see me slay you without boasting! Having spoken thus, Lakṣmaṇa drew back five iron-tipped arrows to his ear and, with great force, buried them in the chest of the Rākṣasa.
Struck by those arrows, the son of Rāvaṇa, filled with rage,
pierced Lakṣmaṇa in return with three well-aimed shafts.
That encounter between the two lions among men and Rākṣasas became truly terrifying.
A tumultuous clash occurred in the battle between those two who sought to slay one another;
for both were endowed with strength, both were possessed of prowess,
both were highly courageous, and both were experts in all weapons and missiles.
Both were exceedingly difficult to conquer, possessing incomparable strength and splendor;
those two great heroes fought like two planets that have entered the sky.
Indeed, they were as unassailable in battle as Bala and Vṛtra.
Then those two great-souled ones fought like two lions, standing their ground as they discharged vast multitudes of arrows;
those two lions among men and rākṣasas fought on with great joy.
Greatly delighted, those two best of men and rākṣasas,
seeking victory and bearing arrows and bows,
showered each other profusely.
Like two clouds with a downpour of torrents of arrows,
the son of Daśaratha, the crusher of enemies, then fixed an arrow and,
hissing like an enraged serpent, loosed it at the lord of the Rākṣasas.

Hearing the sound of his bowstring and palm-strike, the son of Rāvaṇa became pale-faced and gazed intently at Lakṣmaṇa. Seeing that Rākṣasa, the son of Rāvaṇa, with such a dejected countenance, [he spoke].
Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to the son of Sumitrā, who was engaged in battle:
"I perceive omens regarding this son of Rāvaṇa;
therefore, hasten, O mighty-armed one, for he is broken—of this there is no doubt."
Then, having aimed, the son of Sumitrā released at him sharpened arrows resembling tongues of fire— every one of them as fierce as virulent poison.
Struck by Lakṣmaṇa with those arrows, whose touch was like Indra’s thunderbolt, [he fell].
For a moment he was bewildered, his senses utterly agitated; but having regained consciousness within a moment and his senses restored,
the hero beheld the heroic son of Daśaratha standing there.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he rushed toward the son of Sumitrā;
having approached him, he spoke these harsh words once more:
"Do you not remember my prowess in that first battle?"
When you, along with your brother, were bound and struggling in battle—
you who were indeed young— both of you lay first upon the ground, unconscious, together with your followers, struck by arrows equal to Indra’s thunderbolt in that great conflict.
"I think either you have lost your memory, or it is clear that you wish to go to the abode of Yama,
since you desire to assault me. If my prowess was not witnessed by you in our first battle..."
"Today I shall show myself to you; stand now, remaining firm!
Having spoken thus, he pierced Lakṣmaṇa with seven arrows and Hanumān with ten sharp-edged, excellent shafts.
Then, with exactly one hundred well-aimed arrows, the valiant one,
doubly incensed by anger, pierced Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having witnessed that deed performed by Indrajit, Rāma’s younger brother then—
Disregarding him and laughing, saying "This is nothing," that bull among men,
Lakṣmaṇa, with an undaunted face and filled with rage, took up terrible arrows and loosed them at the son of Rāvaṇa in battle.
"O night-stalker, heroes who have entered the fray do not strike in this manner;
for these arrows of yours are light and of little power, and thus they are easy to handle.
But heroes desiring victory do not fight in battle in such a way."
Speaking thus, he covered him with showers of arrows.
His armor, adorned with gold, shattered by those shafts,
fell apart upon the seat of the chariot like a cluster of stars from the sky.
With his armor shaken off by iron arrows,
that hero Indrajit became scarred in battle, like a mountain with its peaks overgrown.
Indeed, sighing repeatedly, they fought a tumultuous battle in the fray.
With all their limbs mangled by arrows and drenched in blood on every side,
those two best among the knowers of weapons repeatedly displayed their mastery of missiles, weaving a multitude of arrows of various forms through the sky.
Discharging arrows free from fault, both light and variegated, and with great skill, both the man and the rākṣasa waged a tumultuous and terrible battle;
the terrifying sound of their palms was heard separately by each of them.
Like two most terrible clouds thundering in the sky,
those gold-feathered arrows fell upon their two bodies in battle;
smeared with blood, they flew out and entered the surface of the earth.
With other well-sharpened weapons they clashed in the sky;
their arrows, by the thousands, broke, shattered, and cut one another.
A terrible mass consisting of their arrows arose in that battle.
Like two blazing fires at a sacrificial session surrounded by a heap of *kuśa* grass,
the bodies of those two great-souled ones, marked with wounds,
shone like two *śālmali* and *kuñjaka* trees in the forest, stripped of their leaves but covered in blossoms.
Seeking victory over one another, Indrajit and Lakṣmaṇa repeatedly engaged in a tumultuous and terrible encounter;
Lakṣmaṇa fought Rāvaṇa’s son in battle, and Rāvaṇa’s son likewise fought Lakṣmaṇa.
Striking one another, those two did not experience fatigue;
with nets of arrows deeply embedded in their bodies, the two energetic and great heroes shone like two mountains overgrown with vegetation.
6.076.032a Their limbs, drenched in blood and densely covered with arrows, shone as if they were blazing fires. 6.076.033a Then, a great length of time passed while those two continued to fight.
6.076.033c Neither of them turned away from the fight nor did they succumb to fatigue.
6.076.034a Then, in order to dispel the exhaustion from battle,
[the gods approached] Lakṣmaṇa, who remained undefeated at the forefronts of combat.
Accomplishing what was dear and beneficial, the one of great power,
Vibhīṣaṇa, approached the battle and took his stand.
But seeing those two, the man and the Rākṣasa, engaged and fighting with intent, [the gods were amazed].
That heroic brother of Rāvaṇa stood at the forefront of the battle. Then, standing firm, he drew his great bow and loosed mighty arrows with sharp points upon the Rākṣasas.
Those arrows, resembling crests of fire and discharged with great concentration,
tore through the rākṣasas like thunderbolts striking mighty mountains.
The followers of Vibhīṣaṇa also [attacked] with spears, swords, and sharp-edged blades.
In that battle, those foremost of Rākṣasas slaughtered the heroic warriors.
Surrounded by those Rākṣasas, Vibhīṣaṇa then shone in their midst like an elephant among joyful young calves.
Then, urging on his two bay horses who were fond of battle with the Rākṣasas,
that best of Rākṣasas, who knew the proper time, spoke these words at the opportune moment:
"This one stands alone, like the ultimate refuge of the Lord of the Rākṣasas."

"This is the remainder of his force; why do you stand still, O lords of the monkeys? When this wicked Rākṣasa has been slain at the head of the battle, his entire army will be destroyed, with the exception of Rāvaṇa himself."
The heroic Prahasta has been slain, as well as the mighty Nikumbha;
Kumbhakarna, Kumbha, and the night-stalker Dhūmrākṣa;
and Akampana, Supārśva, and the Rākṣasa Cakramālin.
Kampana, Sattvavat, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka—
having slain these many exceedingly powerful and foremost of Rākṣasas,
cross the ocean with your two arms as easily as one would leap over a cow’s footprint.
"O monkeys, this much remains here for you to conquer:
all those Rākṣasas, arrogant in their strength, have been slain upon our meeting.
It is improper for me to bring about the death of my son, who was born from me."
6.077.013c Casting aside compassion for the sake of Rāma, I would slay my brother’s son. 6.077.014a As I desire to kill him, tears well up and my vision is obstructed.
6.077.014c But this very one, the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, will pacify that [anger].
"Let the monkeys, having gathered together, slay his servants who are nearby!
Thus urged by that highly illustrious Rākṣasa,
the monkey leaders rejoiced and lashed their tails.
Then those tigers among monkeys, roaring again and again,
let out various cries like peacocks upon seeing the clouds.
Jāmbavān, too, was surrounded by all his own troops.

He struck the Rākṣasas with stones, as well as with his claws and teeth. As the lord of the bears was thus striking them down, those immensely powerful Rākṣasas cast aside their fear and surrounded him, wielding various kinds of weapons.
With arrows, sharp axes, spears, staffs, and javelins,
they struck Jāmbavān in battle as he was slaughtering the rakṣasa army;
that tumultuous clash between the monkeys and the rakṣasas then broke out.
Like the terrifying and great roar of the enraged gods and asuras,
Hanumān, also filled with fury, uprooted a *sāla* tree from the mountain and,
having encountered them by the thousands, wrought a slaughter among the rākṣasas.
Having fought a tumultuous battle with his paternal uncle in combat,
Indrajit once again rushed toward Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes.
Then those two heroes, Lakṣmaṇa and the Rākṣasa, engaged in battle.
Raining down showers of arrows, those two struck one another;
the two mighty warriors repeatedly concealed each other with nets of shafts,
like the powerful sun and moon obscured by clouds at the end of the hot season.
For there was no taking up, no aiming, nor the grasping of the bow;
no releasing of arrows, no drawing back, nor any struggle;
no repositioning of the fist, nor the hitting of the target.

6.077.026c As those two fought there, nothing could be seen due to the swiftness of their hands; 6.077.027a and because the sky was completely shrouded on all sides by nets of arrows released with the force of their bows, no forms were visible.
Everything was shrouded in darkness, vast and most terrifying.
At that time, the wind did not blow, nor did the fire blaze;
and the great seers cried out, "May there be well-being for the worlds!"
And there, the *gandharvas* arrived together with the *cāraṇas*. Then, with four arrows, the son of Sumitrā pierced the four horses— black and adorned with gold— of that lion among *rākṣasas*.

Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the illustrious Rāghava, by means of his swiftness, severed from the body the head of the charioteer as he was moving about. Seeing his charioteer slain in battle, the son of Rāvaṇa—
He abandoned his martial exultation and became despondent. Seeing the Rākṣasa with a dejected countenance, the leaders of the monkey troops were then exceedingly thrilled and honored Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Pramāthin, Śarabha, Rabhasa, and Gandhamādana—
those four lords of monkeys, unable to endure [the situation]— made a sudden rush.
And those monkeys, quickly leaping upon his excellent horses, [attacked].
6.077.034c Those of great heroism and terrible prowess fell upon the four [quarters]. 6.077.035a As they were mounted by those monkeys who resembled mountains,
blood clearly flowed from the mouths of the horses.
Having slain his horses and crushed that great chariot,
they leaped up again with speed and stood by Lakṣmaṇa’s side.
He, having jumped down from the chariot whose horses were killed and whose charioteer was crushed, [stood there].
The son of Rāvaṇa charged at the son of Sumitrā with a shower of arrows.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, who resembled the great Indra,
[assailed] him as he stood on foot with sharp, excellent shafts.
As he was discharging sharp, excellent arrows at the outset,
[Arjuna] then warded him off violently with multitudes of shafts.
With his horses slain, that night-stalker of great splendor stood upon the ground.
6.078.001c Indrajit, supremely enraged, blazed forth with his splendor.
6.078.002a Those two archers, desiring to slay one another with their arrows,
6.078.002c set out for victory like two bull elephants in a forest.
6.078.003 Striking one another down, those Rākṣasas and forest-dwellers did not abandon their leader in battle, even as they rushed hither and thither.
6.078.004 Aiming at Lakṣmaṇa, he displayed supreme agility.

Like Purandara raining down torrents of rain, he rained down showers of arrows. But Lakṣmaṇa, the subduer of enemies, remained unperturbed and warded off that most difficult-to-withstand shower of arrows released by Indrajit.
Considering Lakṣmaṇa to be impenetrable, Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa,
being extremely enraged, quickly displayed his mastery of weapons and pierced Lakṣmaṇa in the forehead with three well-feathered arrows.

6.078.007 With those arrows fixed in his forehead, the joy of the Raghus shone at the front of the battle like a three-peaked mountain, he who delights in combat. 6.078.008 Even though he was thus afflicted by the Rākṣasa’s arrows in that great conflict, [he remained steadfast].
Lakṣmaṇa quickly pierced him in return with five arrows.
The two heroes, Lakṣmaṇa and Indrajit, both possessing great strength and formidable prowess,
struck each other with their feathered shafts from their mighty bows.
6.078.010a Those two archers, having approached one another, pierced each other in all their limbs with terrible arrows, both being intent on victory.
6.078.011a Enraged at him whose horses had been slain, Vibhīṣaṇa became even more fiercely angry toward him.
He discharged five arrows, equal to the touch of a thunderbolt, into his chest.
Piercing through his body and reaching their mark, those gold-feathered shafts became smeared with blood, like great serpents stained with vermilion.
6.078.013a Enraged at his paternal uncle, the exceedingly powerful Indrajit took up an arrow; 6.078.013c it was the supreme weapon among the Rākṣasas, which had been given by Yama.
6.078.014a Beholding that great arrow fixed upon his bow by him, the one of great splendor [Rāma]—
Lakṣmaṇa, too, of terrible prowess, took up another arrow—
one that had been given to him personally by the immeasurable-souled Kubera in a dream—
an arrow invincible and unbearable even for the gods and asuras led by Indra.
By those two, two excellent arrows were fixed upon their superior bows;
as they were drawn by the two heroes, they blazed intensely with splendor.
Those two shafts, released from the bows, illuminated the sky.
Striking face to face with great vigor, they collided;
having clashed with one another like two mighty planets,
they fell upon the earth, shattered into a hundred pieces in that battle.
Seeing those two arrows repelled at the front of the battle,
both Lakṣmaṇa and Indrajit were filled with shame and incited to rage;
then the son of Sumitrā, highly agitated, took up the Vāruṇa weapon.
Standing firm in battle, Mahendrajit discharged a fierce *raudra* weapon.
A tumultuous battle, like something marvelous, ensued between the two of them;
the beings stationed in the sky surrounded Lakṣmaṇa.
In that terrifying battle between the monkeys and the rākṣasas, filled with the fierce cries of Bhairava,
the sky appeared covered by many astonished beings.
The ṛṣis, ancestors, gods, gandharvas, garuḍas, and serpents [were there].
Placing Śatakratu at their head, they protected Lakṣmaṇa in the battle. Then the younger brother of Rāvaṇa fixed another excellent arrow,
which was as hot to the touch as fire and as fierce as the son of Rāvaṇa himself.
The hero [aimed] an arrow that had excellent feathers, smooth joints, well-knit segments, and was beautifully fashioned with gold— an arrow that brings an end to bodies,
difficult to ward off, unbearable, and terrifying to the Rākṣasas.
Resembling the venom of a poisonous serpent and worshipped by the hosts of gods—
by means of this [weapon], the powerful and highly resplendent Śakra,
whose vehicle is the green horse, conquered the Dānavas in the ancient war between the gods and the asuras.

Then the son of Sumitrā, the best among men, fixed that Indra-wielded weapon, undefeated in battles and the finest of arrows, upon his supreme bow. Having fixed it, he drew back the bowstring, which crushes the enemy.
Like Time itself, difficult to behold at the destruction of the worlds, having drawn his bow to its full extent and fixed it upon that most excellent bow, he drew it back and spoke these words,
which were conducive to his own purpose: "The illustrious Lakṣmaṇa has spoken."
"If Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is indeed righteous in soul, true to his promise,
and without rival in manly prowess, then slay this son of Rāvaṇa!
Having spoken thus, he drew that straight-flying arrow back to his ear.
6.078.032c The heroic Lakṣmaṇa discharged [the weapon] at Indrajit in battle.
6.078.032e Having joined it with the Aindra-weapon, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, [struck]. 6.078.033a That head, together with its helmet, was glorious and possessed blazing earrings.
Having been torn from the body of Indrajit,
that great head of the Rākṣasa’s son fell upon the surface of the earth; severed at the neck and drenched in blood, it was seen on the ground, shining like refined gold.

Slain, the son of Rāvaṇa quickly fell to the earth— still clad in armor and wearing his helmet, though shattered along with his bow. Then all those monkeys, together with Vibhīṣaṇa, cried out in lamentation.
6.078.036c Rejoicing at his being slain, they were like the gods after the slaying of Vṛtra.
6.078.037a Then, in the intermediate space, there arose a great clamor from living beings, from the high-souled ṛṣis, 6.078.037c and also from the gandharvas and apsarases.
Perceiving that the great army had fallen into disorder,

that host of rākṣasīs fled in all directions while being slaughtered by the monkeys, who appeared radiant with victory. Being struck down by the forest-dwellers, those rākṣasas cast away their weapons.
6.078.039c All fled toward Laṅkā, deprived of their senses;
6.078.040a the terrified Rākṣasas ran in many directions by the hundreds,
6.078.040c all abandoning their weapons— swords, scimitars, and battle-axes.
Some monkeys, terrified and tormented by Indrajit, entered Laṅkā;
some fell into the ocean, and others took refuge on the mountains.
Having seen Indrajit slain and lying upon the battlefield, they were filled with joy.
Among the thousands of *rākṣasas*, not a single one remained visible;
just as the rays do not persist once the sun has set,
so too did those *rākṣasas* flee in all directions when he had fallen.
Like the sun that has set, like a fire extinguished, he became one of great splendor whose life had departed; yet,
with his afflictions largely stilled and his enemies destroyed, he was filled with joy.
When the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas had fallen, the world then became [tranquil];
and the blessed Śakra, together with all the foremost of the gods, experienced great joy when that evil-doing Rākṣasa was slain.
The pure waters and the sky rejoiced, and the Daityas and Dānavas were filled with joy. When he had fallen— bringing fear to all the worlds—
the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas all gathered together and spoke.

"May the Brahmins wander free from feverish anxiety, their impurities stilled. Then, seeing that foremost of the Nairṛtas slain and his power rendered futile, the leaders of the monkey hosts rejoiced in the battle with great delight.
Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanumān, and Jāmbavat, the leader of the bear hosts,
congratulated Lakṣmaṇa on his victory and praised him; meanwhile,
the monkeys roared, shouted, and bellowed.
Having achieved their goal, they stood surrounding the son of Raghu;
the monkeys, lashing their tails and slapping their arms, then proclaimed these words: "Victory to Lakṣmaṇa!"
Embracing one another with joyful hearts, the monkeys engaged in conversations of various kinds concerning their reliance upon Rāghava; then,
beholding that which was so difficult to achieve, they were filled with delight.
The gods, perceiving the supreme deed of their dear friend Lakṣmaṇa in battle and hearing that the enemy of Indra had been slain, experienced great joy in their minds.
6.079.001a But Lakṣmaṇa, who possesses auspicious marks, his limbs drenched in blood,
was filled with joy at having slain the conqueror of Śakra in battle.
6.079.002a Then that valiant one [spoke] to Jāmbavān and Hanumān.
Having turned back all those forest-dwellers, the one of great splendor then quickly returned to where Sugrīva and Rāghava were;
Lakṣmaṇa followed, supporting both Vibhīṣaṇa and Hanumān.
Then, having approached Rāma and offered his salutation,
the son of Sumitrā stood near his brother like Śakra’s younger brother, Indrānuja;
at that time, the hero announced the terrible slaying of Indrajit.

Then Vibhīṣaṇa, filled with joy, reported to Rāma that the head had been severed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa. Having seated him upon his lap and embraced him as he was overwhelmed with emotion, [Rāma spoke].
Having smelled him on the head and touched him again in haste,
that bull among men comforted Lakṣmaṇa and spoke these words:
"A most auspicious deed has been performed by you, who accomplish what is difficult to do."

"Today I have been made friendless, for Rāvaṇa will surely march forth with a great military array upon hearing that his son has been struck down. [I shall encounter] that lord of the rākṣasas as he goes out, tormented by the slaughter of his son."
"Surrounding him with my great army, I shall slay that invincible one.
With you, Lakṣmaṇa, as my protector, neither Sītā nor the earth will be difficult for me to attain once the conqueror of Śakra has been slain in battle today."
6.079.010 Having comforted and embraced his brother,
Rāghava Rāma, filled with joy, addressed Suṣeṇa and spoke these words:
6.079.011 "O man of great wisdom, this son of Sumitrā, who is devoted to his friends, remains pierced by arrows."
"Act in such a way that he may become perfectly well;
let the son of Sumitrā, along with Vibhīṣaṇa, be quickly freed from his arrows.
Summon the heroic monkey troops who fight with trees."
"And those others who are fighting here, pierced by arrows and likewise wounded—
let them all also be made comfortable by you with every effort.
Thus addressed by Rāma, that high-souled leader of the monkey hosts [acted accordingly].

Suṣeṇa administered a supreme medicinal herb through the nose to Lakṣmaṇa. Having inhaled its fragrance, he became free of arrows; at that moment, his pain vanished and his wounds were completely healed.
By the command of Rāghava, he then performed medical treatment for Vibhīṣaṇa and his friends, as well as for all the leaders of the monkeys. Thereupon,
with the arrow extracted and his pain gone, he returned to his natural state.
At that moment, the son of Sumitrā was gladdened and freed from his fever;
likewise were Rāma, the lord of the monkeys,
Vibhīṣaṇa, and Jāmbavān, the lord of the bears.
Beholding the son of Sumitrā risen and free from ailment, he,
together with his army, rejoiced for a very long time with joy; he then honored the deed of Lakṣmaṇa.
The high-souled son of Daśaratha performed a most difficult feat;
the lords of the monkey hosts became overjoyed upon hearing that Śakrajit had been struck down in battle.
Then the ministers of Paulastya, having heard that Indrajit had been slain, recognized the truth and reported it with great distress to the Ten-necked One:
"O Great King, your son has been killed in battle by Lakṣmaṇa."
O one of great luster, while we were looking on and with Vibhīṣaṇa as his ally,
your heroic son Indrajit— the unconquered hero who had encountered heroes in battles—
was slain by Lakṣmaṇa.

Having heard of that terrifying and dreadful slaughter of his son Indrajit in battle, he fell into a great state of despondency. After a long time, the king, that bull among the Rākṣasas, regained his consciousness.
Afflicted by grief for his son, wretched, and with his senses distraught, he lamented:
"Alas, O chief of the Rākṣasa hosts! My child, great chariot-warrior!
Having conquered even Indra, how is it that you have now fallen under the power of Lakṣmaṇa?"
"Indeed, when enraged, you could pierce even Time and the Destroyer with your arrows;
you could shatter even the peaks of Mount Mandara—how much more so Lakṣmaṇa in battle?
Today, King Vaivasvata is held in even higher esteem by me."
"O mighty-armed one, because you have today been joined with the law of time,
this is the path of true warriors— even among all the hosts of immortals. That man who is slain for the sake of his master attains heaven."
6.080.010a Today all the hosts of gods, as well as the world-protectors and the seers,
6.080.010c seeing Indrajit slain, shall sleep happily and without fear.
6.080.011a Today the three worlds in their entirety, and the earth with its forests, [shall be at peace].
"Deprived of Indrajit alone, it appears to me as if empty.
Today, in the inner apartments, I shall hear the wailing of the daughters of the Nairṛtas,
like the roar of a herd of female elephants in a mountain cave."
O scorcher of enemies, where have you gone, abandoning the position of crown prince, Laṅkā, the rākṣasas, my mother, myself, and my wife?
O hero, now that you have gone to the abode of Yama, what will become of my name?
The funeral rites for the deceased must be performed, yet you act in a contrary manner. While Sugrīva, Rāghava, and Lakṣmaṇa are still alive,
where have you gone, abandoning us and departing without having extracted the thorn from my heart?
As Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, was thus afflicted by such lamentations,
a great fury born of the calamity that had befallen his son seized him. His form, already terrible by nature, became further intensified by the fire of his wrath.
The form of Rudra became as unassailable as that of one who is enraged.
From his two eyes, as he was angry, drops of tears fell,
like flaming drops of oil from two blazing lamps.
The sound of his teeth gnashing was heard like that of a great machine being wound by the Dānavas;
enraged like the fire of time at the end of an aeon, whichever direction he glared upon, [he consumed it].
Terrified by him, the rākṣasas hid themselves in every direction;
seeing him like the enraged God of Death, desiring to devour all moving and stationary beings as he gazed toward all quarters, the rākṣasas did not dare to advance.
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, becoming exceedingly enraged,
spoke in the midst of the rākṣasas, seeking to rally them for battle:
"By me, having performed difficult austerities for thousands of years..."
In those various places, the Self-Existent One was gratified;
by the ripening of that very asceticism and through the grace of the Self-Existent One,
I shall never have any fear of either asuras or gods.
"This armor, given by Brahmā, which possesses a radiance equal to the sun and was never pierced by thunderbolts or spears in the conflicts between gods and asuras—
armed with that today, I stand here upon my chariot in this battle."
"Who today could withstand me in battle, even if it were Purandara himself?
For that great bow,
together with its arrows, was given to me by Svayambhū when he was well-pleased during the conflicts between the gods and the asuras."
"Today, let a great and terrible bow be raised with hundreds of musical instruments for the very purpose of slaying Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the supreme battle.
Thus spoke the hero, tormented by the slaughter of his son and overcome by the power of rage.
Having reflected with his intellect, Rāvaṇa resolved to kill Sītā. Then,
having looked about, the copper-eyed and most terrible one,
distressed and speaking in a piteous voice, addressed all those night-stalkers of fearsome appearance.
"By means of an illusion, my dear son, for the purpose of deceiving the forest-dwellers,
someone was killed there and shown to them as 'this is Sītā.
This very thing I shall now make true, for it is my own pleasure."
"I shall destroy Vaidehī, who is devoted to that wretch of the kṣatriya race!
Having spoken thus to his ministers, he quickly seized his sword;
drawing it forth, which was endowed with excellent qualities and possessed the luster of a stainless sky.
Surrounded by his ministers, Rāvaṇa, his mind deeply agitated by grief for his son, rushed out from the assembly hall with great speed;
filled with rage, he seized his sword and went suddenly to where Maithilī was.
Seeing the Rākṣasa approaching, they let out lion-like roars;
and beholding him so enraged, the Rākṣasas embraced one another and said to each other:
"Today, upon seeing him, even those two brothers will be struck with terror."
"For the four world-protectors were indeed conquered by him when he was angry,
and many other enemies have been struck down by him in battles.
While they were thus conversing, [he] went to the Aśoka grove.
Overwhelmed by rage, Rāvaṇa rushed toward Vaidehī,
even as he was being restrained by well-wishing friends intent on his welfare; furiously enraged,
he charged at her like a planet in the sky rushing toward Rohiṇī.
But Maithilī, being guarded by the rākṣasīs, the blameless one,
saw a furious rākṣasa wielding an excellent sword. Seeing him with his sword drawn, the daughter of Janaka was deeply distressed.
Though repeatedly restrained by his friends, he does not turn back;
since he now rushes at me in person with such fury,
this evil-minded man will slay me— who am already like one without a protector— though I have a protector.

6.080.042a Many times he urged me, his devoted wife, saying: "Become my wife; let us take our pleasure. 6.080.042c Having been thus rejected by me, 6.080.043a it is clear that he has now fallen into despair because of my refusal to attend to him.
Overcome by anger and delusion, he has prepared himself to slay me;
or else those two tigers among men, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have been struck down today in battle by that ignoble one on my account.
"Alas! Woe is me! This destruction of the two princes was caused by me.
For that word of Hanumān was not heeded by me, a base woman.
Had I, blameless as I am, traveled upon his back at that time,"
45. "Had I been in my husband's embrace today, I would not be grieving thus;
rather, I think Kausalyā’s heart will burst when she hears that her only son has perished in battle. 46. "For she has but one son, and she shall hear that her son is lost in the fray."
For she, weeping, will remember the birth, childhood, youth, religious rites, and beauty of that great-souled one;
and when her son has been slain, she will become hopeless and senseless as she performs the *śrāddha* offering.
"He will surely ascend the funeral pyre or enter the waters. Fie on the crooked, unchaste Mantharā, whose resolve is evil,
because of whom Kausalyā shall suffer this sorrow!"
Having thus seen the ascetic Maithilī lamenting—
like Rohiṇī fallen under the power of a planet, separated from the Moon—
the wise Supārśva spoke to Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas.
Though being restrained by his ministers, he spoke these words:
"O Ten-necked One, you who are the very younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa,
how indeed can you wish to kill Vaidehī out of anger, having cast aside dharma?"

"O hero, O Lord of Rākṣasas, you who have bathed in the knowledge of the Vedas and the completion of your vows, and who are always devoted to your own duty— why do you contemplate the killing of a woman?
O King, look instead upon Maithilī, who is endowed with such beauty."
But you alone, together with us, must direct your wrath toward Rāghava.
Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; perform the preparatory rites this very day and, surrounded by your forces, set forth for victory on the new moon day.
"A hero, wise, a charioteer, and a swordsman, mounted upon an excellent chariot—
you shall obtain Maithilī after slaying Rāma, the son of Daśaratha. That evil-minded one [accepted] what was thus reported by his friend.
Having accepted those words consistent with righteousness, the valiant Rāvaṇa then went home; thereafter,
surrounded by his friends, he proceeded once more to the assembly hall.
6.081.001 Having entered the assembly hall, the king, dejected and deeply distressed,
sat upon the principal seat, hissing like an enraged lion. 6.081.002 And then that one of great strength spoke to all the leaders of the army:
6.081.002c Rāvaṇa, emaciated by the calamity of his son, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
6.081.003a "All of you, accompanied by your entire force of elephants and horses, 6.081.003c and adorned by throngs of chariots and infantry, set forth!"
Surrounding Rāma alone in battle, you ought to slay him with a shower of arrows,
as joyful clouds do during the rainy season.
Or else, let my body be pierced by sharp arrows in this great conflict.
"Tomorrow, while the world looks on, I shall slay Rāma with your assistance. Having received these words from the lord of the rākṣasas,
those rākṣasas set out swiftly, surrounded by chariots and divisions of elephants.
At sunrise, that most terrifying battle between the rākṣasas and the monkeys became a tumultuous clash.
They fought with various maces, spears, swords, and battle-axes.
Then, in that battle, the monkeys and the rākṣasas struck one another.
Rivers of blood flowed forth, carrying away heaps of bodies; they had elephants for their banks, horses for their fish, banners for their trees, and were filled with the wreckage of corpses.
Leaping again and again in the battle, the lords of the monkeys shattered standards, armor, chariots, horses, and various weapons;
the monkeys tore out hair, ears, foreheads, and noses.
With their sharp teeth and claws, they tore apart the rākṣasas;
in that battle, hundreds of bull-like monkeys rushed at each individual rākṣasa,
like birds toward a fruit-bearing tree.
Likewise, with heavy maces, spears, swords, and battle-axes,
the terrible Rākṣasas, who resembled mountains, struck down the formidable monkeys.
As the monkeys were being slaughtered by the Rākṣasas, their great army—
They sought refuge with Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who is worthy of providing protection.
Then the valiant and highly resplendent Rāma, taking up his bow,
entered the army of the Rākṣasas and rained down a shower of arrows.

Then, as Rāma entered like the sun into the sky, the clouds did not approach him, for he was most terrible, consuming everything with the fire of his arrows. The night-stalkers beheld only the most horrific deeds already wrought by Rāma.
In battle, they beheld the difficult-to-perform deeds of Rāma;
they saw him shaking the great army and scattering the mighty chariot-warriors, yet they could not truly perceive Rāma, just as one cannot perceive the wind moving through a forest.
They saw the army cut down, shattered, scorched by arrows, broken, and tormented by weapons; they saw Rāma acting with swift prowess,
but they did not see Rāvaṇa as he struck at their bodies.
Like living beings perceive the inner self abiding within the objects of the senses, [they perceive him]:
"This one slays the elephant-host; this one slays the great chariot-warriors;
this one slays the foot-soldiers along with the horses with his sharp arrows."
Thus all those rākṣasas,
enraged with one another because they resembled Rāghava, struck each other in battle, mistaking them for Rāma;
they did not see Rāma consuming the enemy host.
Deluded by the supreme Gandharva weapon of the high-souled one,
those thousands of Rākṣasas saw Rāma in the battle;
yet again, in that great conflict, they saw only the single descendant of Kakutstha.
They beheld the golden tip of the great-souled one’s bow whirling like a circle of fire, but they did not see Rāghava;
his body was the hub, his courage the radiance, his arrows the spokes, and his bow the rim.

They beheld that discus of Rāma— the very wheel of time— as it struck down the rākṣasas in battle; its sound was the twang of the bowstring and the slapping of palms, its radiance was the quality of his splendor and wisdom, and its limit was the power of his divine weapons.
An army of ten thousand chariots with the speed of the wind,
eighteen thousand swift elephants,
and fourteen thousand horses with their riders.
When two hundred thousand foot-soldier rākṣasas had been slain by Rāma alone with arrows resembling flames of fire during the eighth part of the day,
those rākṣasas were able to assume any form at will.
With their horses slain, their chariots destroyed, exhausted and with their banners crushed,
the surviving night-stalkers fled toward the city of Laṅkā.
With the elephants, foot-soldiers, and horses killed, that battlefield became a scene of carnage.
It was like the sporting ground of the enraged Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis, honored that deed of Rāma, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
And then Rāma spoke to Sugrīva, who was standing right beside him:
"This divine power of weapons belongs either to me or to Tryambaka;
having destroyed that army of Rākṣasas," he said.
Then the high-souled Rāma, equal to Śakra, having overcome fatigue in the use of missiles and weapons,
was praised by the delighted hosts of gods.
There were thousands of those thousand nāgas and horses with their riders,
and thousands of fire-colored chariots equipped with banners;
there were also thousands of rākṣasas who fought with maces and iron clubs.

By Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, those [demons] adorned with ornaments of refined gold— heroes who could assume any form at will and were distinguished by their golden banners— were slain with sharp arrows discharged by Rāvaṇa.
Having seen and heard this, the surviving night-stalkers were bewildered;
and the female rākṣasīs, having gathered together, were dejected and overwhelmed with anxiety— widows whose sons had been slain, crying out as their kinsmen had been killed.
6.082.005c Having gathered together, the rākṣasīs, afflicted with grief, lamented:
6.082.006a "How did the aged Śūrpaṇakhā, hideous and with a sunken belly,
encounter Rāma in the forest, who was like Kandarpa incarnate?"
Having seen that delicate Great Being who delights in the welfare of all creatures, she— lowly in form and desired by others, yet deserving of death by the world—
thought: "How can one so deficient in virtues [approach] him who is endowed with every virtue and possesses great majesty?"

The ugly-faced Rākṣasī desired the handsome-faced Rāma; because of the misfortune of these people, she was wrinkled and gray-haired, committing an improper act that was laughable and censured by all the world.
For the sake of destroying the Rākṣasas, Dūṣaṇa, and Khara,
that incomparable woman committed an assault against Rāghava;
it was on account of that that this great enmity was created by Rāvaṇa.
Sītā was led away for slaughter by the ten-necked Rākṣasa;
yet the ten-necked one does not obtain Sītā, the daughter of Janaka,
for he has contracted an inexhaustible enmity with the mighty Rāghava.
Having seen that Rākṣasa Virādha, who was pursuing Vaidehī,
slain by Rāma alone— this is sufficient proof—
that fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds [could likewise be overcome].
In Janasthāna, they were struck down by arrows resembling tongues of fire;
Khara was slain in battle, as were Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras. By means of arrows brilliant as the sun, that [destruction] has been fully demonstrated.

6.082.016a Kabandha, the blood-drinker whose arms were a yojana long, was slain; 6.082.016c then, roaring in the affliction of his rage, he showed that it was sufficient. 6.082.017a Rāma struck down the powerful son of the Thousand-Eyed One.
Bālin, who resembled a cloud, was sufficient proof of that;
Sugrīva, dwelling on Mount Ṛśyamūka, dejected and with his hopes shattered, was established in the kingdom— this too was sufficient proof.

The speech uttered by Vibhīṣaṇa was consistent with righteousness and purpose, and beneficial for all the Rākṣasas; yet, due to delusion, it did not please him. Had the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) acted upon the words of Vibhīṣaṇa...
This city of Laṅkā would have become a cremation ground, afflicted by sorrow, had it not been for this. Having heard that the mighty Kumbhakarṇa was slain by Rāghava,
Rāvaṇa does not even realize that his beloved son Indrajit has perished.
"My son, my brother, my husband has been slain in battle"—
such was the cry heard in every household among the Rākṣasas.
Chariots, horses, and elephants were killed by the hundreds of thousands.
In battle, the heroic Rāma [slew] the foot-soldier rākṣasas.
Whether it be Rudra, or Viṣṇu, or Mahendra the performer of a hundred sacrifices,
or even Antaka himself, he slays us in the form of Rāma.
6.082.025a With our foremost heroes slain by Rāma, we are hopeless of life;
6.082.025c Seeing no end to our fear, we lament like those who are unprotected.
6.082.026a From the hand of Rāma, the ten-necked one—who was a hero and had been granted boons in battle—[fell].
This most terrible danger has arisen, yet it is not perceived;
neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the piśācas,
nor the rākṣasas are able to protect one who is assailed by Rāma in combat.
Portents of ill omen are seen for Rāvaṇa in battle after battle;
they shall proclaim the destruction of Rāvaṇa by Rāma,
as ordained by the gratified Grandfather (Brahmā) for the sake of the gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
"6.082.029c Safety had been granted to Rāvaṇa by humans, not requested from them.
6.082.030a Therefore, I believe this danger has undoubtedly arrived from humans— 6.082.030c a terrible threat that will bring an end to the lives of the Rākṣasas and of Rāvaṇa."
Oppressed by the powerful Rākṣasa through the granting of that boon,
the gods worshipped the Grandfather with their blazing ascetic powers.
For the sake of the welfare of the deities, the high-souled Grandfather indeed [acted].
6.082.032c Being pleased, he spoke these great words to all the deities:
6.082.033a "From this day forward, all the Dānavas and Rākṣasas shall wander eternally through the three worlds, constantly enveloped by fear."
Then, having assembled with all the deities led by Indra,
Mahādeva, the destroyer of Tripura and whose banner bears the bull, was propitiated.
Being pleased, Mahādeva spoke these words to the gods:
"A woman shall be born for your benefit, bringing about the destruction of the Rākṣasas. Just as hunger was once unleashed by the gods against the Dānavas in the past,
this Sītā, the slayer of Rākṣasas, shall devour us along with Rāvaṇa."
This terrible, final wailing, overwhelmed by grief, arises from the ruin of Rāvaṇa— that ill-behaved one of wicked mind.
We do not see anyone in this world who might become our refuge.
"Like all beings assailed by Time at the end of an eon, so were they struck down by Rāghava"—
thus did all the women of the night-stalkers embrace one another with their arms.
Afflicted by intense fear and tormented by distress, they despaired and then let out a most dreadful, loud cry. Indeed,
among the families of the distressed rākṣasīs in every household of Laṅkā, there was such lamentation.
6.083.001 Rāvaṇa heard a piteous sound of lamentation. 6.083.002 Sighing deeply, he remained in meditation for a moment;
then Rāvaṇa, of fearsome appearance, became exceedingly enraged.
Biting his lip with his teeth, his eyes bloodshot with rage, and difficult even for the *rākṣasas* to behold— like the intensified fire of cosmic destruction— he,
the lord of the *rākṣasas*, spoke to the *rākṣasas* standing nearby.
There, as if burning with his very eyes those who spoke of fearful and obscure matters,
he said to the Rākṣasas Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, and Virūpākṣa:
"Quickly, by my command, tell the troops to march out!"
Having heard those words of his, those Rākṣasas, afflicted by fear,
at the king’s command, urged on those other Rākṣasas who were still unperturbed.
All those Rākṣasas of terrible appearance, however, replied, "So be it."
Having performed the rites for auspiciousness, they all set out toward Rāvaṇa.
Having honored Rāvaṇa according to custom, those great chariot-warriors all stood with palms joined in reverence, desiring victory for their lord.
Then Rāvaṇa, overcome with rage, laughed and spoke to these—
Mahodara, Mahāpārśva, and the Rākṣasa Virūpākṣa:
"Today, with arrows released from my bow that resemble the sun at the end of an eon..."
"I shall lead both Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa to the abode of Yama. Today, by slaying the enemy, I shall take my revenge for Khara, Kumbhakarṇa, Prahasta, and Indrajit."
"Neither the intermediate space, nor the quarters, nor the rivers,
nor even the ocean shall attain visibility, being shrouded by the clouds of my arrows.
Today, those divisions of the monkey hosts shall be scattered part by part."
With the wave-like arrows arising from the ocean of my bow,
I shall today crush the lake-like herds of your forces— those whose lotus-wheels are fully blossomed and whose splendor is like the filaments of a lotus— just as an elephant tramples a pond.
Today in battle, the leaders of the monkey hosts, with their faces pierced by arrows,
will adorn the earth like lotus stalks with their mud-covered roots.
Today, the monkeys, fierce in combat and fighting with trees—
With a single released arrow in battle, I shall pierce hundreds upon hundreds [of them].
For those whose husbands have been slain, whose brothers have been slain, and whose sons have been slain—
I shall today perform for them the act of wiping away their tears by the slaughter of the enemy.
Today, with monkeys pierced by my arrows, scattered about, and deprived of life,
I shall laboriously cover the surface of the earth in battle.
Today, jackals, vultures, and other flesh-eaters [shall feast].
"I shall satisfy them all with the flesh of my enemies, mangled by my arrows. Let my chariot be prepared quickly; let my bow be brought at once.
Let those night-stalkers who remain follow me into battle."
Having heard those words of his, Mahāpārśva spoke these words:
"Let the army be hurriedly mobilized from the commanders stationed there.
Then the enraged army commanders [sent for] those Rākṣasas from house after house.
Challenging [the enemy], those of swift prowess went around Laṅkā.
Then, in an instant, Rākṣasas of terrifying valor rushed forth,
roaring with fearsome faces and wielding various weapons in their arms.
With swords, spears, pikes, mallets, clubs, and plows;
with sharp-edged javelins, great mallets,
staffs, spotless discs, and whetted axes.
With *bhiṇḍipāla* slings, *śataghnī* weapons, and other excellent armaments,
the four military commanders, acting on Rāvaṇa’s command,
then swiftly brought forward a chariot yoked to eight horses and driven by a charioteer.
Rāvaṇa ascended his divine chariot, blazing with its own splendor, as if splitting the earth with the profound gravity of his being. Permitted by Rāvaṇa, Mahāpārśva and Mahodara [departed].
Then Virūpākṣa and Durdharṣa mounted their chariots. Rejoicing and roaring as if they were splitting the earth,
they went forth desiring victory, emitting a terrible roar.
Then, surrounded by the hosts of the Rākṣasa army,
that radiant one went forth for battle with his bow raised, like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time, or the Lord of Death himself.
Then, on a chariot drawn by swift horses, that great car-warrior [departed].
He went out through that gate where Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were.
Then the sun lost its luster, the quarters of the sky were shrouded in darkness,
the birds shrieked dreadfully, and the earth trembled.
The god rained down blood, and the horses stumbled;
a vulture alighted upon the tip of the banner, and jackals howled inauspiciously.
His left eye throbbed, and his left arm trembled.
His face grew pale and his voice faltered slightly.
Then, as the ten-necked Rākṣasa rushed forth for battle,
these omens appeared in the fray, foretelling his death in combat.
From the intermediate space, a meteor fell with a sound like a thunderclap;
vultures shrieked inauspiciously, followed by the cawing of crows.
Disregarding these terrible portents that had arisen, [they proceeded].
Driven by delusion and impelled by Time, Rāvaṇa set forth seeking their slaughter.
At the roar of those great-souled Rākṣasa chariots,
the army of the monkeys likewise advanced for battle.
A tumultuous battle took place between those monkeys and rakshasas,
as they challenged one another in their fury, each desiring victory.
Then the enraged Dashagriva [assailed them] with arrows adorned with gold.
He wrought great carnage among the ranks of the monkeys:
some of those long-tailed ones had their heads severed by Rāvaṇa;
some were killed and left breathless, while others were split open at the sides.
Some had their heads split apart, and some were deprived of their eyes;
wherever Daśānana approached on his chariot in battle, his eyes were wide with rage.
6.083.042c Then, from every direction, those leaders of the monkey hosts were unable to withstand the force of his arrows;
6.084.001a thus, with their bodies mangled by the shafts of the Ten-necked one, they fled.
The earth there became strewn and covered with monkeys;
they were unable to endure that blazing shower of arrows from Rāvaṇa on one side,
just as moths cannot withstand a fire.
Afflicted by those sharpened arrows, they fled away crying out,
like elephants being consumed while enveloped by the flames of a fire;
the hosts of monkeys were scattered like great clouds by the wind.
In that battle, Rāvaṇa advanced, scattering [his foes] with arrows;
having swiftly wrought a slaughter of the forest-dwellers, the lord of the rākṣasas then quickly approached Rāghava in the fight.
6.084.006a Seeing those monkeys broken and fleeing in battle, Sugrīva, having stationed Suṣeṇa in the reserve, quickly set his mind on the fight.
6.084.007a Having assigned that heroic monkey, who was his own equal, to that position, he [prepared for combat].
6.084.007c Sugrīva, armed with trees, set out facing the enemy. 6.084.008a All the leaders of the troops themselves followed him on his flanks and from behind,
6.084.008c carrying great boulders and various massive trees.
Roaring with a great voice in the battle, the mighty Sugrīva struck down various other supreme rākṣasas;
and the lord of monkeys, possessed of a massive body, crushed the rākṣasas.
At the time of the end of the eon, like a wind driving forth swollen clouds,
he rained down a shower of rocks upon the armies of the Rākṣasas,
just as a cloud rains a shower of horses upon flocks of birds in the forest.
6.084.012a By those showers of mountain peaks released by the king of monkeys, the Rākṣasas fell with their heads shattered, like mountains cut down.
6.084.013a Then, as the Rākṣasas were being destroyed on all sides,
When they had been broken by Sugrīva and were falling down, crying out in distress,
the Rākṣasa archer Virūpākṣa proclaimed his own name and,
being difficult to withstand, leaped from his chariot onto the back of an elephant.
Mounting that elephant, the great car-warrior Virūpākṣa rushed toward the monkeys, letting out a roar of terrifying sound;
at the head of the army, he loosed dreadful arrows upon Sugrīva.
He established those agitated *rākṣasas* in a state of great joy.
Deeply pierced by that *rākṣasa* with sharp arrows, the lord of monkeys,
possessed of great wrath, became enraged and set his mind upon the slaughter of him.
Then, having uprooted a tree, the heroic monkey Hari rushed forward in the battle and struck that great elephant in its front. Struck by Sugrīva’s blow, that great elephant—
He retreated the distance of a bow, sat down, and let out a roar.
Then, quickly leaping from the crushed elephant,
that valiant Rākṣasa advanced toward his enemy and confronted the monkey.
Seizing a bull's hide and a sword, he of swift prowess approached Sugrīva, who stood firm, as if to threaten him;
for he, filled with rage toward him, had grasped a massive rock.
Sugrīva hurled that mountain-like boulder at Virūpākṣa.
Seeing that rock falling toward him, that bull among Rākṣasas,
having displayed great prowess, stepped aside and then struck with his sword.
Enraged, with that sword he struck down Sugrīva’s armor at the head of the army; struck by the sword, he fell. Rising from his fall, that monkey discharged [his weapon] at him.
That palm-strike, equal to a thunderbolt and terrifying in its sound—
having skillfully evaded that palm-strike raised by Sugrīva, the rākṣasa struck him in the chest with his fist.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, became even more enraged upon seeing that he had been released from the blow dealt by that Rākṣasa;
the monkey then spotted a vulnerability in Virūpākṣa.
Then, out of anger, he struck him on the temple with his palm;
struck by that palm which was like the thunderbolt of the great Indra,
he fell upon the earth, drenched in blood and vomiting gore.
They beheld Virūpākṣa, made even more hideous than before, his eyes rolling in rage and drenched in blood mixed with foam;
he was quivering and tossing from side to side, smeared with gore.
The monkeys beheld their enemy roaring piteously. Thus did those two powerful ones, the monkey and the rākṣasa, engage with each other in battle.
The two oceans of armies roared terribly,
like two great oceans that have overstepped their shores;
they beheld Virūpanetra already destroyed.
That entire army of monkeys and rākṣasas, possessing great strength under the leadership of the monkey-king,
became like the turbulent Gaṅgā.
6.085.001 As their forces were being swiftly slaughtered by one another in that great battle, the two armies became utterly depleted,
like two lakes in the midst of a great heat. 6.085.002 This was due to the destruction of their own troops and the slaying of Virūpākṣa.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, became twice as enraged;
seeing his army depleted and being slaughtered by the monkeys,
he felt great distress in the battle upon witnessing this reversal of fortune.
And he spoke to Mahodara, the subduer of enemies, who stood nearby:
"O mighty-armed one, at this time my hope for victory rests in you.
O hero, slay the enemy host and display your prowess today."
"This is the time to repay the debt of your master's sustenance; fight well!
Having been addressed thus, Mahodara said "So be it" to the lord of the Rākṣasas and entered the enemy army like a moth into a fire.
Then that mighty and radiant one, impelled by his own heroism and by the command of his master, wrought a slaughter among the monkeys.
Seeing the great army of the monkeys broken in battle, he [pressed on].
Immediately thereafter, Sugrīva rushed toward Mahodara;
seizing a massive, formidable rock as large as a mountain,
the immensely powerful lord of the monkeys hurled it at him for his destruction.
Seeing that rock suddenly falling upon him, Mahodara,
remaining unperturbed, then pierced that formidable mass with his arrows.
Cut down by the flood of arrows from that Rākṣasa, it shattered into a thousand pieces.
It fell upon the rocky ground like a turbulent circle of vultures.
Seeing that rock shattered, Sugrīva, overwhelmed with rage,
uprooted a *sāla* tree and hurled it at the rākṣasa at the forefront of the battle.
And that hero, the conqueror of enemy cities, pierced him with arrows.
Then, filled with rage, he beheld a spiked mace fallen upon the ground;
brandishing that blazing mace, he displayed it to him.
With great speed, he struck the king’s excellent horses with the tip of his iron club. From that great chariot whose horses had been slain,
the heroic Rākṣasa Mahodara leaped down in a fury and seized a mace.
6.085.015 With maces and iron clubs in their hands, those two heroes met in battle,
roaring like bulls or like two clouds charged with lightning.
6.085.016 The lord of monkeys struck his mace with an iron club.
Shattered by that mace, his iron club fell to the surface of the earth.
Then the radiant Sugrīva seized from the ground a terrible iron mallet, adorned all over with gold.
Raising it up, he hurled it; he too hurled another mace.
Having struck one another, the two broke apart and fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then, their weapons shattered, the two encountered each other with their fists.
Pervaded by fiery energy and strength, blazing like two sacrificial fires,
they then struck one another and roared again and again;
having struck each other with their palms, they both fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then they both sprang up quickly and struck one another;
the two unconquered heroes hurled each other with their arms. Then [one] seized a sword that was lying nearby.
The rakshasa Mahodara,
possessed of great speed, fell along with his shield; likewise, the best of monkeys, Sugriva, who was even more impetuous, seized the great sword that had fallen together with the shield.
With their limbs overcome by rage, those two, skilled in weapons, rushed forward roaring in battle with swords raised, eager for combat;
both of them swiftly circled to the right in a defensive maneuver.
Both of them, enraged at one another, were intent on victory.
But that hero Mahodara, possessed of great speed and boasting of his own prowess,
the evil-minded one, brought down his sword upon that great shield.
6.085.027a Raising his sword, that elephant among monkeys struck with his blade at the sword [of his opponent]. 6.085.027c He seized the head, complete with its helmet and adorned with earrings.
6.085.028a As he lay fallen upon the earth with his head severed, [the enemy was destroyed].
Seeing that army of the lord of the rākṣasas, he did not remain there.
Having slain him along with the monkeys, the monkey rejoiced and let out a roar. Daśagrīva became enraged, while Rāghava shone forth, filled with joy.
When Mahodara had been slain, the exceedingly powerful Mahāpārśva agitated Aṅgada’s formidable army with his arrows;
he [struck] the heads of the foremost monkeys on all sides.

Like the wind causing fruit to fall from its stalk, he struck them down from their bodies. Highly incensed, the Rākṣasa severed the arms and shoulders of some monkeys with his arrows, while others he tore through the sides.
Afflicted by that shower of arrows from Mahāpārśva, all those monkeys became despondent, turned away in defeat, and lost their resolve. Seeing his army agitated and tormented by the Rākṣasa, Aṅgada—
The mighty-armed one exerted his force like the ocean during the change of the moon;
