seizing an iron club as radiant as the rays of the sun,
the best of monkeys struck Mahāpārśva down in the battle.
By that blow, Mahāpārśva became unconscious;
deprived of his senses, he fell from his chariot along with his charioteer onto the ground.
But the radiant king of the ṛkṣas, resembling a mass of black collyrium, [remained firm].
Rushing forth from his own herd, which resembled a mass of clouds, that one of great prowess,
filled with rage, seized a massive boulder resembling a mountain peak;
he swiftly struck the horses and shattered that chariot.
6.086.010a But after a moment, the mighty Mahāpārśva regained consciousness and once more pierced Aṅgada with many arrows.
6.086.011a He struck Jāmbavān in the middle of the chest with three shafts.
He struck the king of the bears, Gavākṣa, with many arrows.
Seeing both Gavākṣa and Jāmbavān afflicted by those arrows,
Aṅgada, overwhelmed with rage, seized a terrible iron club.

6.086.013a Angada, provoked to anger, seized with both arms that iron 6.086.013c club, which possessed a radiance like the rays of the sun, while the Rākṣasa stood at a distance; and having whirled it with great speed, 6.086.014a [he hurled it].
The son of Vālin hurled it at Mahāpārśva for the purpose of killing him. That iron club, cast by the powerful one,
felled from the hands of that Rākṣasa both his bow with its arrow and his helmet.
6.086.016a Having approached him with speed, the powerful son of Vālin,
enraged, struck him on the root of the ear adorned with an earring with his palm.
6.086.017a But he, Mahāpārśva, possessed of great speed and great luster, was filled with rage.
With one hand he seized a massive battle-axe;
that axe was polished with oil, stainless, made of the essence of stone, and firm.
Enraged beyond measure, the Rākṣasa brought it down upon the son of Vālin.
With that [axe], he struck violently against the surface of Aṅgada’s left shoulder;
Aṅgada, filled with rage, warded off that battle-axe.
Then that hero Aṅgada [hurled] his own fist, which resembled a thunderbolt.
6.086.020c Turning back, highly incensed and equal to his father in prowess,
6.086.021a knowing the vital spots, he brought down his fist— whose touch was like Indra’s thunderbolt— toward the heart of the Rākṣasa, near his two breasts. 6.086.021c He struck it down.

By that falling upon him in the great battle, the heart of the rākṣasa instantly burst asunder; struck down, he fell to the earth. When he had fallen to the ground, that army was utterly thrown into turmoil.
And a great rage arose in Rāvaṇa during the battle upon seeing the two Rākṣasas, Mahodara and Mahāpārśva, slain,
and when that heroic and mighty Virūpākṣa had also been killed.
A great rage took possession of Rāvaṇa in that great battle;
he urged on his charioteer and spoke these words:
"My ministers have been slain and the city has been besieged."
"I shall remove this suffering by slaying those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. In battle, I shall strike down the tree that is Rāma, which yields Sītā as its flowers and fruit;
Sugrīva, Jāmbavān, Kumuda, and Nala are its branches."
Making the ten directions resound with the roar of his chariot, that great Atiratha set out swiftly and turned toward Rāghava. By that sound, the rivers, mountains, and forests were filled.
The entire earth, along with its mountains, wild boars, deer, and elephants, trembled.
He discharged a most terrible and exceedingly dreadful weapon of darkness;
it incinerated all the monkeys, who fled in every direction.
Seeing those numerous divisions of Rāvaṇa shattered by the hundreds with his supreme arrows, Rāghava stood firm. Then he beheld Rāma standing there, unconquered.
Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he was like Viṣṇu with Vāsava;
leaning upon his great bow, he seemed to scrape the very sky—
broad-eyed as a lotus petal, long-armed, and a subduer of enemies.
Seeing the monkeys broken in battle and Rāvaṇa charging toward him, Rāghava, filled with joy, grasped his bow in their midst;
he then began to draw that supreme bow.
Possessing great speed and a mighty roar, as if splitting the very earth,
Rāvaṇa entered the path of the arrows of those two princes;
he appeared like Rāhu in the vicinity of the moon and the sun.
By the floods of Rāvaṇa’s arrows and by the sound emitted by Rāma, hundreds of rākṣasas then fell down. Desiring to fight him first, Lakṣmaṇa [struck] with sharpened arrows.

Drawing his bow, he released arrows resembling flames of fire. As soon as those arrows were released into the sky by the archer Lakṣmaṇa, the immensely powerful Rāvaṇa warded them off with his own arrows.
With one arrow he severed one [limb], with three three, and with ten ten,
displaying his lightness of hand;
then Rāvaṇa, the victor in battle, bypassed the son of Sumitrā.
Then he approached Rāma, who stood firm like an immovable mountain.
Having reached Rāma in battle, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
Rāvaṇa loosed showers of arrows upon the descendant of Raghu.
Then, seeing the showers of arrows discharged from Rāvaṇa’s bow falling swiftly upon him, Rāma quickly and with great haste seized his *bhalla* shafts; thereafter,
with those sharp *bhallas*, Rāghava cut down that flood of arrows.
Blazing with great speed like enraged venomous serpents,
Rāghava swiftly showered Rāvaṇa with various sharp arrows, and likewise Rāvaṇa showered Rāghava; thus they both rained down upon one another.

Unconquered in battles, they moved for a long time in various circles, both to the left and to the right, as they observed the trajectories of their arrows. As those two fought together simultaneously, all living beings were struck with terror.
Then, as those two fierce archers, who resembled Yama and Antaka,
continuously loosed various arrows, the sky became filled with them like the heavens at the end of the summer heat, crowded with clouds wreathed in flashes of lightning.
The sky became as if latticed with windows by the showers of arrows from those heroes— arrows with great velocity, sharp points, and well-feathered wings like vultures.
At that time, the two of them created a supreme and terrifying darkness of arrows.
When the sun had set, two great clouds, as it were, arose;
a tumultuous battle ensued between those two who desired to slay one another,
being unassailable and inconceivable, like the combat between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
For both were supreme archers, both were experts in weaponry,
both were foremost among those skilled in missiles, and both moved about the battlefield.
Indeed, wherever the two of them went, there followed waves of arrows.
Like waves driven by the wind upon two oceans, they surged forward.
Then Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out, with his hands locked together,
fixed a garland of iron arrows upon Rāma’s forehead.

Bearing upon his head that arrow released from the fierce bow, which possessed the luster of a blue lotus petal, Rāma did not experience any pain. Then, while reciting sacred mantras, he invoked the Raudra weapon.
Taking up more arrows, Rāma, filled with wrath,
drew his bow and released them; the valiant one of great splendor,
whose shafts were never obstructed, loosed those arrows at the lord of the rākṣasas.
Those arrows, falling upon the armor that resembled a great cloud,
caused no pain at that time to the invincible lord of the rākṣasas.
Then Rāma once again [assailed] that lord of the rākṣasas as he stood upon his chariot.

Skilled in all weapons, he pierced the forehead with a supreme missile. Having been split by those arrow-forms, they entered the earth hissing like five-headed serpents, acting as adversaries to Rāvaṇa.
Having neutralized Rāghava’s weapon, Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage,
took up another most terrible and demonic weapon.
It possessed the faces of lions and tigers, as well as others with the faces of herons and crows.

He discharged sharp arrows that had the faces of vultures and hawks, as well as those with the faces of jackals; others had the heads of hyenas, while still others had gaping mouths and were terrifying to behold— five-faced and licking their lips.

He discharged these and other sharpened arrows created through his illusory powers— arrows with the faces of donkeys, those shaped like the faces of boars, those with the mouths of dogs and cocks, and those with the faces of sea-monsters and venomous serpents.

6.087.042c Toward Rāma, the one of great splendor, enraged and hissing like a serpent, 6.087.043a that descendant of Raghu, possessed by the Āsura weapon, 6.087.043c being like fire itself, discharged with great energy the fiery weapon.

Arrows with mouths blazing like fire, as well as those with faces like the sun, those with faces like the full moon or the crescent moon, and even those with faces like comets; arrows possessing the colors of the planets and constellations, and those stationed with faces like great meteors.
He discharged other sharp arrows resembling tongues of lightning;
those terrible arrows of Rāvaṇa, struck down by the weapon of Rāghava,
dissolved in the sky and fell away by the thousands.
Seeing that weapon destroyed by Rāma of unwearied deeds,
all the monkeys, who could assume any form at will, then roared with joy.
When that weapon had been repelled, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, [acted].

He redoubled his wrath, and from that anger, he immediately unleashed a weapon. The immensely radiant Rāvaṇa then proceeded to discharge another terrible and fierce weapon, fashioned by Maya, at the descendant of Raghu.
Then, from his bow, there issued forth on all sides blazing spears, maces, and clubs, as hard as thunderbolts;
likewise, there appeared deceptive hammers, nooses, and flaming thunderbolts.
Various sharp weapons flew forth like the winds at the end of an eon.
Then the illustrious Rāghava, the most excellent among those skilled in supreme weapons and possessed of great splendor, struck down that weapon with the Gandharva weapon, the highest of all weapons.
When that weapon had been neutralized by the high-souled Rāghava,
Rāvaṇa, his eyes copper-red with rage, discharged the solar weapon (*saura-astra*).
Thereupon, great and radiant discs flew forth.
From the bow of the wise Daśagrīva, who possessed terrifying speed,
[arose arrows] by which the sky was illuminated as they flew hither and thither,
and the quarters of the horizon were set ablaze by those falling shafts, like the moon, the sun, and the planets.
With floods of arrows, Rāghava cut down those various weapons of Rāvaṇa at the front of the army.
Seeing that weapon destroyed, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, [acted].
He pierced Rāma in all his vital organs with ten arrows. Though pierced by those ten arrows released from Rāvaṇa’s great bow, the highly resplendent Rāghava did not tremble.
Then the conqueror in assembly pierced him in all his limbs;
but Rāghava, greatly incensed, struck Rāvaṇa with many arrows.
In that interval, the powerful younger brother of Rāghava became enraged.
Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, seized seven arrows. With those high-velocity shafts, the immensely radiant one cut down Rāvaṇa’s banner, which bore a human head, into many pieces.
And with an arrow, the illustrious and mighty Lakṣmaṇa struck off the head of that Nairṛta charioteer, which was adorned with flaming earrings. Furthermore,
with his arrows, he severed the bow of that foe, which resembled the trunk of an elephant.

Lakṣmaṇa struck the lord of the rākṣasas with five sharpened arrows, while Vibhīṣaṇa, leaping forward, slew Rāvaṇa’s excellent horses— which resembled dark clouds and were like mountains— with his mace.
6.088.018a Having leaped with speed from the great chariot whose horses had been slain,
6.088.018c Rāvaṇa summoned a fierce rage toward his brother. 6.088.019a Then, the one of great power took up a spear, blazing like a flaming thunderbolt.
The powerful lord of the rākṣasas hurled it at Vibhīṣaṇa;
but before it could reach him, Lakṣmaṇa cut it down with three arrows.
Then, a great roar of the monkeys arose in that battle.
Cut into three pieces, that spear adorned with golden garlands fell down,
blazing with sparks like a great meteor fallen from the sky.
Then [he struck] her who was highly esteemed and difficult even for Time to overcome.

He seized a massive spear, blazing with its own radiance. That most terrible weapon, equal in splendor to Indra’s thunderbolt, blazed up when grasped by the impetuous, powerful, and evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
In that interval, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa quickly approached Vibhīṣaṇa, who had fallen into a life-threatening danger;
drawing his bow, the hero Lakṣmaṇa prepared to liberate him.

He overwhelmed Rāvaṇa, who held a spear in his hand, with a rain of arrows. Being covered by the flood of arrows discharged by that great-souled one, Rāvaṇa’s prowess was turned back and he no longer set his mind on striking.
Seeing his brother rescued by Lakṣmaṇa,
that Rāvaṇa stood facing Lakṣmaṇa and spoke these words:
"O you who boast of your strength, since Vibhīṣaṇa has been thus rescued by you..."

Having released the Rākṣasa, this spear is now hurled at you. This spear, marked with blood, shall pierce your heart; discharged from my arm which is like a club, it will depart taking away your life.

Having spoken thus, he aimed at Lakṣmaṇa that spear— which was equipped with eight bells and emitted a great sound, fashioned by Maya through his power of illusion, unfailing, a slayer of enemies, and blazing as if with fiery energy.
6.088.031c Rāvaṇa, filled with supreme rage, hurled it and let out a roar.
6.088.032a Hurled with terrifying speed and sounding like Indra’s thunderbolt,
6.088.032c that spear fell with force upon Lakṣmaṇa at the forefront of the battle.
As that spear was falling, Rāghava addressed it:
"May it be well with Lakṣmaṇa! Become futile and have your effort frustrated!
It fell with great velocity upon the broad chest of Lakṣmaṇa.
Like the blazing tongue of the king of serpents, it possessed great splendor; then,
its heart pierced by that spear which had plunged deep due to Rāvaṇa’s force, Lakṣmaṇa fell to the earth.

Seeing Lakṣmaṇa in that state, Rāghava, who was standing nearby, became despondent at heart out of brotherly affection, for he was possessed of great splendor. Having reflected for a moment, his eyes became clouded with tears.
He became even more enraged, like the fire at the end of an eon. Reflecting that "this is not the time for despondency," Rāghava,
resolved upon the slaying of Rāvaṇa, waged a most tumultuous battle.

Then, in that great battle, Rāma beheld Lakṣmaṇa pierced by the spear, smeared with blood like a mountain covered in serpents. He also saw that spear which had been hurled by the exceedingly powerful Rāvaṇa.
Despite their efforts, those best of monkeys were unable to crush him,
even as they were tormented by the flood of arrows from the swift-handed Rākṣasa. That arrow,
having pierced the son of Sumitrā, entered the surface of the earth.
Grasping that terrifying spear with both hands, Rāma,
enraged in battle, broke it and pulled it away with great force. As he was pulling out the spear, [he was opposed] by the more powerful Rāvaṇa.
Arrows that pierce the vital organs fell upon all his limbs; yet,
disregarding those shafts and embracing Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava spoke to Hanumān and Sugrīva.
"O best of monkeys, remain here surrounding Lakṣmaṇa.
This moment for valor, long desired by me, has now arrived. Let this evil-souled Daśagrīva, whose resolve is wicked, be slain."
Like the sight of a cloud at the end of the summer heat by one longing for it, O monkeys,
in this very moment, before long, I promise you truly:
you shall see the world either without Rāvaṇa or without Rāma.
The loss of the kingdom, dwelling in the forest, wandering through Daṇḍaka,
the abduction of Vaidehī, and the encounter with the Rākṣasas—
he experienced great, terrible suffering and affliction comparable to hell.
"Today, having slain that Rāvaṇa in battle, I shall renounce everything—
for the sake of which this monkey army was assembled by me,
and for which Sugrīva was established in the kingdom after slaying Vālin in combat."
"For whose sake the ocean was crossed and the bridge was built across the sea—
that very same wicked man has today come within the range of my sight.
Having come within the range of my sight, he does not deserve to live."
"O invincible bulls among monkeys, behold me with my gaze like that of a venomous serpent; remain at ease and watch this battle between me and Rāvaṇa as we sit upon the mountain peaks."
"Today, let the three worlds— the Gandharvas, the gods, the Ṛṣis, and the Cāraṇas— behold Rāma’s true nature in my combat.
Today I shall perform such a deed that all the worlds, including the mobile and the immobile, shall witness it."
"Accompanied by the gods, they shall speak as long as the earth endures. Having spoken thus, Rāma, composed in mind, struck the Ten-necked one in battle with sharp arrows adorned with refined gold.

Then Rāvaṇa showered Rāma with blazing iron arrows and maces, just as a rain-cloud pours down torrents of water. As the arrows released by Rāma and Rāvaṇa struck one another, they collided in mutual conflict.
A tumultuous roar arose from the clashing of arrow against arrow.
Those arrows of Rāma and Rāvaṇa— pierced and scattered,
their tips blazing— fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth.
The great sound of the bowstrings of Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like a thunderous crash;
it was terrifying to all living beings and resembled a marvel.
He [Rāvaṇa], being overwhelmed by showers of nets of arrows;
Afflicted by that great-souled one who wielded a blazing bow,
Rāvaṇa fled in fear upon encountering him,
like a cloud driven away by the wind.
Having fought a tumultuous battle against the evil-minded Rāvaṇa and discharging volleys of arrows, he spoke these words to Suṣeṇa:
"Here is Lakṣmaṇa, fallen to the earth by the force of Rāvaṇa."

Like a serpent, this hero writhes, stirring up my grief. As I behold this hero, who is dearer to me than life itself and drenched in blood, what power do I have to fight with my mind so utterly distraught?
"This is that brother of mine, praised in battle and endowed with auspicious marks;
if he has met his death, what is the use of my life or my happiness?
For my valor seems to shame me, and the bow seems to slip from my hand."
My arrows falter and my vision has fallen under the sway of tears; my intense anxiety increases and the desire for death arises within me,
having seen my brother slain by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
6.089.006c He fell into utter despair and lamented, his senses overwhelmed.
6.089.007a "I have no need for battle, nor for my life, nor even for Sītā,
having seen my brother Lakṣmaṇa slain in the dust of the battlefield."
"What use have I for a kingdom, what use for life, when there is no purpose left for war,
since this Lakṣmaṇa lies here slain at the head of the battle? To Rāma, who was thus despondent, the heroic Suṣeṇa spoke these words of consolation.
"This mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity, is not dead.
His face has not changed its form; it is neither dark nor lusterless.
His countenance appears radiant and serene."
The palms of his hands are as red as lotuses and his eyes are very serene;
O Lord of the People, such a form does not exist for those whose life has departed. O Hero, O Subduer of Enemies, do not despair, for he is still alive.

"O hero, it will be told how, while he was sleeping with his limbs cast upon the ground, his heart throbbed repeatedly with a gasp as it trembled again and again. Having spoken these words to Rāghava, Suṣeṇa, who was skilled in speech, [continued].
Hurrying, he spoke these words to Hanumān, who was standing nearby:
"O gentle one, go quickly from here to the mountain of medicinal herbs, O hero; for that auspicious peak was previously described to you by Jāmbavān."
"Bring the herb born upon its southern peak,
named Viśalyakaraṇī— the auspicious Viśalyakaraṇī—
and likewise the Sauvarṇakaraṇī and the Saṃjīvanī."
"Go quickly and bring back the *saṃdhānakaraṇī* herb from there for the sake of reviving the great-souled hero Lakṣmaṇa. Having been addressed thus, Hanumān went to the mountain of medicinal herbs.
Not knowing those great medicinal herbs, the illustrious one fell into deep thought.
Then, a resolution arose in the mind of that son of the Wind-god of immeasurable power:
"I shall go back from here, taking this very peak of the mountain with me."
"If I depart without taking the Viśalyakaraṇī herb,
there would be the fault of exceeding the appointed time, and great distress would ensue. Having reflected thus, the mighty Hanumān departed quickly.
Hanumān, having seized a mountain peak, leapt up;
"O bull among monkeys, I did not recognize those medicinal herbs,
so this entire peak of that mountain has been brought by me."
6.089.022a While he was speaking thus, Suṣeṇa, the best of monkeys, having praised that son of the Wind-god, 6.089.022c plucked up the medicinal herbs and took them.
6.089.023a Then, having crushed that herb, the foremost of monkeys—
Suṣeṇa, of great splendor, administered it through the nose to Lakṣmaṇa.
Having inhaled it while still pierced by the arrow, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
was instantly freed from the shaft and relieved of his pain, rising quickly from the surface of the earth.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa raised up from the ground, the monkeys, being well-pleased, honored Suṣeṇa, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then Rāma, the slayer of enemy heroes, said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Come, come!"
With eyes clouded by tears, he embraced him with deep affection;
and having embraced the son of Sumitrā, Rāghava then said:
"By good fortune, O hero, I see you returned from death."
"Indeed, I have no purpose for life, nor for Sītā, nor for victory.
For what purpose would I have for life once you have met your death?"—
thus spoke that great-souled Rāghava.
Exhausted, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words in a faltering voice:
"O you whose prowess is truth, having previously made that vow,
you ought not to speak thus now like some light-hearted person lacking in courage."
For the virtuous, O sinless one, do not make their promises false;
indeed, the fulfillment of his promise is a great thing for Lakṣmaṇa. Therefore, O sinless one, it is enough that you have come to despair on my account.
By the slaying of Rāvaṇa today, fulfill your vow;
having come within the range of your arrows, this enemy shall not escape alive,
just as a great elephant does not survive before a roaring lion with sharp fangs.
"But I desire the swift slaughter of this evil-minded one,
before this sun, having accomplished its task, goes to its setting.
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, that descendant of Raghu [replied].

He discharged terrible arrows at Rāvaṇa at the head of the army. Standing upon his chariot, the Ten-necked one struck Rāma with most fearsome arrows resembling thunderbolts, just as a rain-cloud pours down torrents of water.
With arrows resembling blazing fire and adorned with gold,
Rāma, remaining composed, pierced the Ten-necked one in battle—
Rāma standing upon the ground and the Rākṣasa stationed in his chariot.
"The gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas say that battle is never equal," they said.
Then [there appeared] a chariot with variegated golden parts, adorned with hundreds of small bells,
resembling the rising sun, and having a pole made of lapis lazuli.
Yoked with excellent horses adorned with golden crests and white plumes— bay steeds resembling the sun and decorated with nets of gold—
is the glorious and supreme chariot of the King of the Gods, bearing a banner with a golden staff.

Descending from heaven, he approached the descendant of Kakutstha; and then Mātali, the charioteer of the Thousand-Eyed One, standing upon the chariot with the goad in hand, spoke these words to Rāma with palms joined in reverence: 6.090.007c He descended and approached the descendant of Kakutstha. 6.090.008a And then Mātali, the charioteer of the Thousand-Eyed One, standing on the chariot with the goad, spoke these words to Rāma with palms joined in reverence.

"O Kakutstha, O Great Being, this glorious chariot, the destroyer of enemies, has been given to you by the Thousand-eyed One for your victory. This too is the great bow of Indra, and armor resembling fire."
Arrows resembling the sun, as well as bright and sharpened spears—
O hero, mounting this chariot, slay Rāvaṇa, the Rākṣasa,
with me as your charioteer, O Rāma, just as Mahendra slew the Dānavas.

Having been addressed thus, Rāma circumambulated the chariot, saluted it, and then ascended it, illuminating the worlds with his splendor. Then there occurred that wonderful duel between two chariots, which caused the hair to stand on end.

O mighty-armed one, that Rāghava, the supreme knower of weapons, struck down the Gandharva weapon of the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa with his own Gandharva weapon, and the divine weapon of the king of Rākṣasas with his own divine weapon.
Then the night-stalker, the lord of the Rākṣasas, being exceedingly enraged, once again discharged that most terrible and dreadful Rākṣasa weapon.
Those arrows, adorned with gold, were released from Rāvaṇa’s bow.
6.090.016c Having become highly venomous serpents, they rushed toward the descendant of Kakutstha. 6.090.017a With blazing faces, vomiting flaming fire from their mouths,
those terrifying creatures with gaping jaws rushed toward Rāma alone.
With those snakes, whose touch was like that of Vāsuki, whose coils were blazing, and who were possessed of great venom,
all the cardinal directions were pervaded and all the intermediate quarters were completely enveloped.
Seeing those serpents rushing toward him in battle, Rāma—
He manifested the terrible and fearsome Gārutmata weapon.
Released from Rāghava’s bow, those gold-feathered arrows, radiant as fire,
became golden eagles— the enemies of serpents— and flew about.

6.090.021a Those arrows of Rāma, which could assume any form at will, took the shape of *suparṇa* birds and struck down all those extremely swift arrows in the form of serpents. 6.090.022a When his weapon was thus neutralized, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the *rākṣasas*, became enraged.
Then he rained down terrible showers of arrows upon Rāma. Having afflicted Rāma, the one of unwearied deeds, with a thousand arrows, he pierced Mātali with a flood of shafts.
Having struck down the golden banner from the chariot onto the floor of the vehicle,
Rāvaṇa slaughtered Indra’s horses with a net of arrows;
the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas, along with the Cāraṇas, were filled with despair.
Seeing Rāma thus afflicted, the Siddhas and the supreme Ṛṣis were distressed,
as were the leaders of the monkeys along with Vibhīṣaṇa,
upon seeing the moon-like Rāmacandra seized by the Rāhu-like Rāvaṇa.

Having occupied the lunar mansion Rohiṇī, the beloved of the Moon, which belongs to Prajāpati, Budha remained there, bringing misfortune to all creatures. The ocean, with its waves turning amidst smoke, appeared as if it were ablaze.
Then, enraged, he leapt up as if touching the sun;
the sun, its color like that of weapons, became harsh and dimmed in its rays,
appearing with its body severed at the waist and joined with a comet.
The constellation of the Kosalas, clearly presided over by Indra and Agni, was overtaken by Aṅgāraka, who remained stationed there in the sky, as did Viśākhā; meanwhile,
the ten-faced one with twenty arms stood grasping his bow.
The ten-necked one appeared like Mount Maināka;
but Rāma, being repelled by the Rākṣasa Daśagrīva,
was unable to aim his arrows at the front of the battle.
6.090.033a Having knit his brows in anger, with his eyes somewhat bloodshot,
6.090.033c he fell into a state of great fury, as if burning everything with his gaze.
6.091.001a Seeing the face of the wise Rāma thus enraged,
All living beings were terrified and the earth trembled;
the mountain, filled with lions and tigers, shook along with its trees,
and the ocean, the lord of rivers, became agitated as well.
And birds with harsh cries and rough sounds, portending calamity, flew about in every direction, shrieking in the sky;
for they saw Rāma filled with intense rage and those most dreadful omens.
All beings were terrified, and fear entered Rāvaṇa.
At that time, the gods, Gandharvas, and great serpents (mahoragas) stationed in their celestial chariots,
as well as the sages, Dānavas, Daityas, and the Garuḍas who move through the sky, were struck with alarm.
Then they beheld that battle, resembling the dissolution of the world,
as the two heroes fought with various terrible weapons.
All the gods and asuras who had gathered for the conflict then spoke:
Beholding the great battle, the asuras stood together and, with joyful devotion, said these words to the Ten-necked one: "Victory! Then the gods said to Rāma again and again: "May you be victorious!"
In the meantime, that evil-minded Rāvaṇa, out of anger toward Rāghava and desiring to strike him, touched his great weapon—
the thunderbolt-like essence, which roared loudly and was the destroyer of all enemies.
It was covered with peaks resembling mountain summits, terrifying to the sight;
sharp-pointed as if smoking, it was like the massed fire at the end of an eon—
extremely fierce, unapproachable, and difficult even for Time itself to overcome.
Terrifying all beings, causing them to flee and rending them asunder,
Rāvaṇa, blazing as if with rage, seized his spear.
Then, filled with supreme fury, the valiant one grasped that spear by its middle.
Surrounded in battle by many heroic Rākṣasas,
that large-bodied one raised [his weapon] and let out a terrifying roar in the fray;
with eyes bloodshot from rage, he gladdened his own army.
Then that terrible roar of the lord of the Rākṣasas made the earth, the atmosphere, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters tremble;
by that cry of such excessive volume from that evil-minded one, [the world was shaken].
All living beings were terrified and the ocean was greatly agitated. Grasping that great trident, the immensely powerful Rāvaṇa let out a tremendous roar and spoke harshly to Rāma.
"O Rāma, this spear of adamantine essence has been raised by me in anger against you;
it shall instantly take away the life-breaths of you and your brother as your ally.
Today, it shall strike down the heroes among the rākṣasas at the head of the army."
"O you who boast in battle, having slain you by my own strength, I shall make myself equal [to you].
Stay now! I shall kill you with this spear, O Rāghava!
Having spoken thus, the lord of the rākṣasas hurled that spear.
Rāghava warded off that [demon] as he rushed forward with a flood of arrows,
just as Vāsava wards off the rising fire at the end of an eon with torrents of water.
He consumed those arrows released from Rāma’s bow.
Rāvaṇa’s great spear was like fire to moths;
seeing those arrows reduced to ashes and pulverized by the touch of the spear as they remained in the sky, Rāghava was seized with rage.
6.091.024a Rāghava, the joy of the Raghus, seized with supreme rage that spear fashioned by Vāsava which had been brought by Mātali.
6.091.025a That spear, resounding with the ringing of its bells, was weighed by the powerful one.
With its radiance, it set the sky ablaze like the fire at the end of an eon.
When hurled by the lord of the Rākṣasas, it fell upon that spear;
shattered by the *śakti*, the great spear fell down, its luster extinguished.
Then Rāma pierced his exceedingly swift horses with sharp,
high-velocity arrows that were like thunderbolts;
he then pierced Rāvaṇa in the chest with sharpened shafts.
Rāghava, with supreme effort, struck him on the forehead with three feathered arrows. With all his limbs pierced by those shafts and blood flowing from his body,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, standing in the midst of his host, shone like a blossoming Aśoka tree.
With his limbs pierced by Rāma’s arrows and his body drenched in blood, that lord of the night-stalkers fell into exhaustion in the midst of the assembly.
At that moment, he became exceedingly enraged.
Then, tormented in battle by that descendant of Kakutstha out of his anger,
Rāvaṇa, who delights in combat, was seized by a great fury.
With eyes blazing with rage, that valiant one drew his bow and,
highly incensed, assailed Rāghava in the great battle;
with thousands of streams of arrows, he was like a rain-cloud pouring from the sky.
Rāvaṇa filled Rāghava with arrows as if filling a lake; yet,
though covered in that battle by the net of shafts released from his bow,
the descendant of Kakutstha did not tremble, remaining as unshakable as a great mountain.
Standing in the battle, that valiant one, warding off nets of arrows with his own shafts, received them as if they were the rays of the sun.
Then the night-stalker, swift-handed, loosed thousands of arrows.
Enraged, he struck the chest of the high-souled Rāghava. Smeared with blood in that battle, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa appeared like a massive *kiṃśuka* tree in full bloom in the forest.
Enraged by the impact of the arrows,
that descendant of Kakutstha, possessed of great majesty and radiant as the sun at the end of an eon, also took up his shafts.
Then both Rāma and Rāvaṇa became intensely enraged with one another.
In that darkness of arrows within the battle, they could not distinguish one another at that time.
Then Rāma, the heroic son of Daśaratha, overcome with fury,
laughed and spoke these harsh words to Rāvaṇa.

"O lowest of Rākṣasas, because my wife was carried off from Janasthāna by you while she was helpless and unaware, therefore you possess no true heroism. [For you did not see her] when she was separated from me, miserable, and dwelling in the great forest."
"Having forcibly abducted Vaidehī, you imagine yourself a hero. O hero among women who are without protectors, you who violate the wives of others,
having performed the deed of a coward, you imagine yourself a hero."
6.092.014a O you who have broken the bounds of propriety, shameless, and unstable in your conduct! 6.092.014c Out of pride, having brought death upon yourself, you imagine, "I am a hero.
6.092.015a [By] a hero, the brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), endowed with great forces...
6.092.015c A great deed, praiseworthy and conducive to fame, has been performed by you.
6.092.016a Now reap the very great fruit today of that action which was undertaken with arrogance, which is censurable and harmful.
"O evil-minded one, you consider yourself a hero;
yet you feel no shame at dragging away Sītā like a thief. If Sītā had been violated by you by force in my presence,"

But you shall see your brother Khara slain by my arrows; by good fortune, O evil-souled one, you have come within the range of my vision. Today, with my sharp shafts, I shall send you to the abode of Yama.
"Today, let the flesh-eaters drag away your head— adorned with flaming earrings— which has been severed by my arrows and scattered amidst the dust of the battlefield,
once you have fallen upon the earth, O Rāvaṇa."
Let them drink with thirst the blood flowing from within the shafts of my arrows;
today, let birds of prey tear at your entrails as you lie fallen, breathless, pierced by my shafts— just as Garuḍas seize serpents.
Speaking thus, the heroic Rāma, the destroyer of enemies,
covered the lord of the rākṣasas standing nearby with showers of arrows;
his valor, strength, and joy were doubled in that battle.

And as Rāma, desiring the destruction of his enemy, [prepared for battle], all the weapons of that self-knowing one appeared by their own power. Out of great joy, the one of immense splendor became even swifter of hand.
Having recognized these auspicious signs occurring within himself, Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas,
struck Rāvaṇa once more with showers of arrows from Rāghava and with masses of stones from the monkeys.
Being struck, the ten-necked one’s heart began to reel;
when he neither took up a weapon nor drew his bow,
he could no longer counteract the hero's prowess because of his distressed inner self.
Even the arrows and various weapons discharged by him did not function for the sake of battle, as he was approaching the time of death. But his charioteer, the driver, beheld him in that state.

6.092.030c Without being bewildered by the battle, he slowly drove the chariot away from him. 6.093.001a But Rāvaṇa, driven by the force of destiny and exceedingly enraged out of delusion, his eyes bloodshot with anger, spoke to the charioteer:

Like one lacking vigor, incapable, and devoid of manliness; like one who is timid, insignificant, and without fortitude; as if deprived of splendor, as if abandoned by illusions, and as if cast out by weapons.
"O evil-minded one, disregarding me, you act according to your own whim. For what reason, having shown me contempt and disregarding my will,
have you driven this chariot of mine away in the presence of the enemy?"
"O ignoble one, today you have destroyed my long-accumulated fame, heroism, splendor, and reputation,
as well as that of my enemy, whose prowess is renowned and who is beloved for his valor."

"Even as I looked on, you, who were eager for battle, have been made a coward by you! O evil-minded one, since you do not urge this chariot forward out of delusion, this suspicion of mine is proven true: you have been subverted by the enemy."

"Indeed, such an action is not found in one who is a friend desiring the welfare [of others]; it is characteristic of enemies, yet this was not well-performed by you. Turn back the chariot quickly, before my enemy departs."
"Whether you have dwelt here before or whether your virtues are remembered—
if you have been treated thus harshly by one lacking in wisdom, yet possessing a mind intent on his welfare,
the charioteer spoke these beneficial and conciliatory words to Rāvaṇa."
"I am not afraid, nor am I deluded, nor have I been instigated by my enemies; I am neither negligent, nor devoid of affection, nor have I forgotten the honor [you showed me].
But it was by me, desiring your welfare and protecting my own reputation,"

6.093.012c With a mind drenched in affection, I have done what was unpleasant [thinking it] pleasant. 6.093.013a O Great King, you ought not, on account of this matter, to find fault with me— who am devoted to your pleasure and welfare— as if I were some insignificant and ignoble person.
"Listen, I shall tell you the reason why the chariot was turned back by me from the battle, like the force of a river by its waters.
I perceive your exhaustion from the great feat of combat."
"O hero, I do not perceive in you either cheerfulness or joy. These horses drawing your chariot are exhausted;
they are dejected and scorched by the heat, like cows struck by the rain."

"Moreover, regarding those many omens that appear to us, whenever they manifest, I perceive them as inauspicious. O Lakṣmaṇa, one must understand the proper time and place, as well as the significance of gestures and facial expressions."

One must recognize the depression, joy, and exhaustion [of the enemy], as well as the strength and weakness of the chariot-warriors; the high and low ground of the terrain, as well as the level and uneven places;
the time for battle; and the detection of the enemy's vulnerabilities.
The approach and retreat, the stationing and the withdrawal—
all this must be understood by the chariot-driver stationed upon the chariot. For the sake of your rest, as well as that of these chariot-horses, [he must act accordingly].
6.093.021c Avoiding anger toward the fierce [enemy], I have acted with forbearance. 6.093.022a O hero, this chariot was not driven away by me of my own free will;
6.093.022c O Lord, this which was done by me was performed because I am overcome by affection for my master.
"Command me according to the truth, O slayer of enemies; O hero, I shall do that with a mind free from debt. Rāvaṇa was satisfied by those words of his charioteer.
Having praised him in many ways, he who was greedy for battle spoke these words:
"O charioteer, quickly turn this chariot toward Rāghava;
Rāvaṇa will not return from the field of battle without having slain his enemies."
Having spoken thus, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, being pleased,
gave him a single, auspicious, and most excellent hand-ornament.
Then, swiftly urged by the words of Rāvaṇa, [he departed].
Then that great chariot-warrior, the charioteer of the lord of the Rākṣasas, urged on the horses;
in an instant, he appeared before Rāma at the front of the battle.
The king of men beheld the chariot of the king of the Rākṣasas as it came rushing suddenly, roaring loudly, with its great banner,
yoked to black horses and endowed with fierce splendor.
Thick with banners like flashes of lightning, displaying the weapon of Indra’s bow,
and discharging showers of arrows like a rain-cloud pouring down torrents; seeing that chariot of his enemy approaching, resembling a mass of clouds—
6.094.003c A sound like that of a mountain being shattered when struck by a thunderbolt;
6.094.003e Rāma spoke thus to Mātali, the charioteer of the Thousand-Eyed One: 6.094.004a "O Mātali, behold the enemy's chariot rushing forward in a fury!"

6.094.004c Just as he was flying away with great speed in a counter-clockwise direction, he again resolved in battle to destroy himself; 6.094.005a therefore, remain vigilant and go forth to meet the chariot of the enemy.
"I wish to destroy him, as the wind scatters a risen cloud. Drive the chariot swiftly— unflinching, unperturbed, with heart and gaze steady, and with the reins held with firm control."

"Granted, you are not one who needs instruction, being as worthy of Indra’s chariot as he is; yet, being single-mindedly desirous of battle, I am merely reminding you, not teaching you. Mātali was highly pleased by those words of Rāma.
The most excellent of divine charioteers urged the chariot forward;
then, keeping Rāvaṇa’s great chariot to his left,
he overwhelmed Rāvaṇa with the dust kicked up by its wheels.
Then the ten-necked one, enraged and with eyes wide and copper-red,
struck Rāma, who stood facing his chariot, with arrows. Rāma, provoked by this assault, was overwhelmed by fury and overstepped the bounds of his composure.

He, possessed of great majesty, took up the bow of Indra, which possessed a most violent force in battle, as well as arrows whose radiance was equal to the rays of the sun. Then a great battle commenced between those two who were each desirous of slaying the other.
Like two proud lions facing one another, [the two heroes stood] like two lions facing one another.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis,
gathered together, desiring the destruction of Rāvaṇa, to witness that duel between the two chariots.
Then, terrible and hair-raising portents arose for the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the victory of Rāghava. The god rained down blood upon the chariot of Rāvaṇa.
Fierce, whirling winds began to blow in a counter-clockwise direction;
and a great flock of vultures, circling in the sky,
flew wherever the chariot went.
Enveloped by the twilight, which resembled the color of hibiscus flowers, Laṅkā appeared as if ablaze even during the day;
great meteors accompanied by thunderclaps fell with a tremendous roar.
Causing terror among the *rākṣasas*, those [arrows] were then aimed at Rāvaṇa;
and wherever Rāvaṇa moved, the earth trembled there,
and the arms of the striking *rākṣasas* felt as if they were seized.
Copper-colored, yellow, reddish, and white rays of the sun, fallen upon Rāvaṇa’s body, appear like minerals on a mountain;
and vultures follow him, vomiting fire from their mouths.
Looking at his face, the jackals howled fiercely and inauspiciously;
an adverse wind blew in battle, scattering dust and obscuring the vision of that king of the Rākṣasas.
Indra’s thunderbolts fell upon his army from all sides—
terrible and unbearable in sound, even without the roar of rain clouds—
and all the cardinal and intermediate directions became shrouded in darkness.
Due to a great rain of dust, the sky became difficult to see. Then,
sārikā birds, uttering a terrible quarrel toward his chariot,
fell there by the hundreds— fierce and making a dreadful sound.

From their haunches the horses emitted sparks, and from their eyes they shed a continuous stream of tears; thus they released both fire and water simultaneously. Such were the many portents of this kind that arose, bringing great terror.
27c. For the destruction of Rāvaṇa, terrible omens appeared; 28a. And for Rāma as well, gentle and auspicious signs arose on all sides, portending victory.
Then Rāghava, skilled in the interpretation of omens, having observed the signs occurring within himself during the battle,
experienced joy and supreme tranquility.
He displayed even greater prowess in the battle;
then there commenced that most cruel and immense duel between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, which brought fear to all the worlds.
Then the army of the rākṣasas and the great host of monkeys stood motionless, with their weapons grasped;
having seen those two powerful ones, the man and the rākṣasa, engaged in combat.
With their hearts distracted, they were all struck with supreme wonder;
their minds bewildered by their arms busily wielding various weapons,
they stood gazing at the battle and did not strike one another.
6.095.005 As the hosts of Rākṣasas gazed at Rāvaṇa and the Vānaras gazed at Rāghava with eyes wide in wonder, the army appeared like a wondrous spectacle.
6.095.006 There, Rāghava and Rāvaṇa both observed certain omens.
With their minds resolved and their indignation firm, the two fought fearlessly; Kākutstha thinking "I must conquer," and Rāvaṇa thinking "I must die.
Then, steadfast in their own prowess, they displayed the very essence of their heroism in battle.
Then, out of anger, the powerful Ten-necked one fixed arrows to his bow and released them,
aiming at the banner standing upon Raghava’s chariot.
Those arrows, however, failed to reach that banner on the chariot of Purandara.
Touching his red spear, they fell to the surface of the earth.
Then the valiant Rāma, becoming enraged, drew his bow and resolved in his mind to retaliate for what had been done against him.
Aiming at Rāvaṇa’s banner, he released a sharp arrow—
unbearable like a great serpent and blazing with its own splendor.
That arrow pierced the earth and struck the banner of the Ten-necked One.
6.095.012c That banner of Rāvaṇa’s chariot, having been severed, fell to the ground.
6.095.013a Seeing the destruction of his banner, the exceedingly powerful Rāvaṇa 6.095.013c became as if set ablaze in that battle by the fire born of his wrath.
Overcome by the power of rage and vomiting forth a great shower of arrows,
Rāvaṇa pierced Rāma’s divine horses with his shafts. Though pierced, those bay steeds neither stumbled nor did they waver.
They became composed in heart, like lotus stalks struck [by water]. Seeing that lack of agitation among the horses, Rāvaṇa then,
becoming even more enraged, released a rain of arrows once again.
Maces, iron clubs, discuses,
and pestles, as well as mountain peaks, trees, spears,
and battle-axes— he caused this rain of weapons, created by means of illusion, to fall.
Then, with tireless heart and effort, he discharged arrows by the thousands;
that great battle, consisting of many weapons, became tumultuous, terrifying, fearsome, and filled with a dreadful resonance, making it difficult to withstand.
Having surrounded Rāghava’s chariot on all sides within the host of monkeys,
he quickly made the sky devoid of any gaps with his arrows;
and the Ten-necked One released them with a heart free from hesitation.
Seeing Rāvaṇa exerting himself with total devotion in that battle,
Kākutstha, as if smiling, fixed sharp arrows to his bow;
he then released hundreds of thousands of shafts in the fray.
Seeing them, Rāvaṇa made the sky continuous with his own arrows.
Then, by the radiant shower of arrows discharged by those two,
a second luminous sky appeared as if woven with shafts.

In that battle, as Rāma and Rāvaṇa discharged their arrows, not a single shaft was without a mark, none failed to pierce deep, and none were fruitless. Thus they fought without ceasing, shooting with both their left and right hands.
With floods of arrows, the two of them made the sky seem as if it were breathless;
Rāma struck Rāvaṇa’s horses, and Rāvaṇa struck Rāma’s horses,
as they each acted in response to the other's deeds.
6.096.001 All living beings beheld Rāma and Rāvaṇa fighting in that manner in battle, with their inner selves filled with wonder.
6.096.002 In that conflict, those two were afflicting each other’s excellent chariots.

Intent on slaying one another, they both assumed terrible forms. Displaying various maneuvers born of charioteering— circles, paths, advances, and retreats— the two sons of Sūta exhibited their skill.

Rāma afflicted Rāvaṇa, and Rāvaṇa likewise afflicted Rāghava; having attained a speed of movement, they both advanced and retreated. As those two hurled nets of arrows, their respective excellent chariots [remained steady].
They moved across the field of battle like two rain-clouds pouring down showers; having displayed various maneuvers in the fight,
they then once again stood facing one another.
Then, as the two chariots stood facing each other, their poles met pole to pole, the faces of the horses met face to face, and the banners met banner to banner.
Thereafter, Rāma [struck] Rāvaṇa with sharp arrows released from his bow.
With four [arrows], he drove back the four blazing horses;
having fallen under the sway of anger at the horses' retreat,
that night-stalker released sharp arrows at Rāghava.
Though deeply pierced by the powerful Ten-necked one, O Rāghava,
he underwent no change of state nor did he even feel distressed.
And once more he discharged arrows whose sound was like the falling of a thunderbolt.
Aiming at the charioteer of the wielder of the thunderbolt,
the night-stalker discharged arrows of great velocity; yet they fell upon Mātali’s body without causing even the slightest confusion or pain in the battle.
Enraged by that insult more than by anything to himself,
Rāghava turned his enemy back with a web of arrows;
he struck him twenty, thirty, sixty, by the hundreds, and even by the thousands.
The heroic Rāghava released arrows at the enemy’s chariot;
by the clashing sounds of maces, clubs, and iron bludgeons,
and by the wind from the feathers of the arrows, the seven oceans were agitated.
All the serpents dwelling in the depths of Pātāla and the Dānavas by the thousands were distressed at the agitation of the oceans;
the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
The sun became lusterless, and the wind ceased to blow.
Then all the gods, along with the gandharvas, siddhas, supreme ṛṣis,
kinnaras, and great serpents, fell into deep anxiety.
"May there be well-being for cows and brahmins; may the worlds endure eternally. May Rāghava be victorious in battle over Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas.
Then the mighty-armed enhancer of the Raghus' fame became enraged.

Aiming with his bow, Rāma severed Rāvaṇa’s glorious head, adorned with blazing earrings, using a razor-sharp arrow resembling a venomous serpent. That head was then seen by the three worlds as it fell upon the earth.
Another head, exactly like it, rose up for Rāvaṇa;
that second head of Rāvaṇa was swiftly severed in battle with arrows by Rāma, who is quick of hand and swift in action.
As soon as that head was severed, another appeared;
that too was cut down by Rāma with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
In this very manner, a hundred heads of equal splendor were severed.

And yet no end to Rāvaṇa was seen, even as his life reached its exhaustion. Then the hero Rāghava, skilled in all weapons and the increaser of Kausalyā’s joy, equipped with many arrows, began to reflect.
"By these arrows Mārīca was slain, as were Khara and the very wicked Dūṣaṇa; by them Virādha was killed in Krauñcāraṇya and Kabandha in the Daṇḍaka forest.
All these arrows of mine have proven their efficacy in battle."
"What indeed is the cause by which [the gods] have become so feeble in spirit against Rāvaṇa?"—
thus lost in thought, yet vigilant in battle,
Rāghava rained showers of arrows upon Rāvaṇa’s chest.
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, standing upon his chariot,
became enraged and assailed Rāma in battle with a rain of maces and clubs—
[he who was] among gods, dānavas, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
While they watched that great battle, it continued throughout the entire night.
Neither by night nor by day, neither for a moment nor for an instant did the combat between Rāma and Rāvaṇa come to a rest.
Then Mātali reminded Rāghava:
"O hero, why do you follow him as if you were unaware?
O Lord, discharge this weapon of Brahmā for his destruction."
"The time of destruction that was foretold by the gods is now upon us. Then, reminded by those words of Mātali, Rāma took up a flaming arrow that hissed like a serpent.
The powerful [king] possessed that great, unerring arrow, bestowed by Brahmā, which the venerable seer Agastya had first given to him;
it was created of old by Brahmā of immeasurable splendor for the sake of Indra.
Formerly, it was given to the Lord of the Gods when he desired to conquer the three worlds—
[that bow] whose string is the Wind-god, whose two arrowheads are Fire and the Sun,
whose body is composed of space, and whose weight is equal to Mount Meru and Mandara.
Blazing with its form, well-feathered and adorned with gold,
it was fashioned with the splendor of all living beings and possessed the brilliance of the sun;
like the fire of time accompanied by smoke, it was as radiant as a venomous serpent.
He was swift in shattering multitudes of chariots, elephants, and horses;
he could break through gates, iron bars, and even mountains.
His limbs were drenched in various kinds of blood, smeared with fat, and most terrible to behold.
It was as hard as adamant, possessed a great roar, and was fierce with various kinds of arrows;
it was terrifying, causing all to tremble, like a hissing serpent,
and [filled with] herons, vultures, cranes, packs of jackals, and *rākṣasa*s.
Constantly providing food in battle, he was like Yama himself, inspiring terror;
he was the delight of the lords of monkeys and the destroyer of the rākṣasas.
He was endowed with various kinds of speed, as beautiful and variegated as that of Garuḍa.

Then the mighty Rāma, having consecrated that great arrow— which was the supreme weapon of the worlds, the destroyer of the fear of the Ikṣvākus, the stealer of the fame of his enemies, and the bringer of joy to himself— [prepared to discharge it].
6.097.014c The powerful one, according to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas, fixed [the arrow] upon his bow.
6.097.015a Greatly incensed at Rāvaṇa, he drew the bow back fully and, with supreme concentration, discharged that vital-point-piercing shaft.
Irresistible like a thunderbolt released from the arm of Vajrabāhu,
and as unavoidable as Death itself, it fell upon Rāvaṇa’s chest.
That arrow, discharged with great velocity, was capable of ending the body.
6.097.017c It pierced the heart of that evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
6.097.018a Smeared with blood, that arrow, swift and bringing an end to life,
6.097.018c taking away Rāvaṇa’s vital breaths, entered the surface of the earth.

Having slain Rāvaṇa, that arrow— its surface drenched in blood— having accomplished its task, quietly returned once more to its own quiver. From the hand of the slain [Rāvaṇa], that bow together with the arrow was quickly [seized].
6.097.020c He fell down along with his life-breaths as he was being deprived of his life.
6.097.021a Deprived of life, the lord of the Nairṛtas, possessed of terrible speed and great splendor,
6.097.021c fell from his chariot to the ground like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, the surviving night-stalkers,
their leader slain, fled in all directions, trembling with fear.
Then the monkeys, who fight with trees, rushed toward them, roaring aloud.
Having witnessed the slaying of the Ten-necked one and the victory of Rāghava,
they fled toward Laṅkā out of fear, tormented by the exultant monkeys;
with faces streaming with piteous tears, they were deprived of their refuge.
Then the monkeys, exultant and appearing as victors,
let out a roar, proclaiming the victory of Rāghava and the slaughter of Rāvaṇa.
Then, in the sky, the gentle drum of the gods resounded.
There, a most pleasant breeze blew, carrying divine fragrances;
and then a rain of flowers fell from the sky onto the earth,
scattering those rare and enchanting blossoms over the chariot of Rāghava.
From the sky, a preeminent voice of the high-souled deities was heard joined with Rāghava, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
A great joy entered the gods along with the Cāraṇas.
When the fierce Rāvaṇa, who caused terror to all the worlds, had been slain,
Rāghava, being pleased, fulfilled the desires of Sugrīva and the mighty Aṅgada by killing that bull among the Rākṣasas.
Then the hosts of Maruts attained tranquility;
the quarters became clear and the sky grew stainless.
The earth ceased to tremble and the winds blew no more.
And the sun became steady in its radiance.
Then Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and the others—
those preeminent friends— along with Lakṣmaṇa, [beheld him] at that time.
Having gathered together, they joyfully honored Rāghava, who was delightful in battle, according to the prescribed rites because of his victory; he,
however, having slain his enemies, remained firm in his vow.
Surrounded by his own kinsmen and forces, the highly powerful joy of the Raghu dynasty shone in battle like Indra surrounded by the hosts of the thirty gods.
6.098.001 Having heard that Rāvaṇa had been slain by the high-souled Rāghava,
the rākṣasīs, emaciated by grief, rushed out from the inner apartments.
6.098.002 Though restrained many times, they rolled about in the dust of the earth.
With their hair disheveled and afflicted by grief like cows whose calves have been slain,
they emerged through the northern gate along with the rākṣasas;
entering the terrible battlefield, they searched for their slain husband.
Crying out everywhere, "O noble son! and "Alas, our protector!", they fell upon the earth, which was marked by headless trunks and mired in the mud of blood;
their eyes were filled with tears, for they were overwhelmed by grief for their husband.
Like female elephants whose herd-leader has been slain, they cried out with loud wails.
They beheld Rāvaṇa, of massive body, great heroism, and immense splendor,
lying slain upon the ground like a heap of black collyrium.
Seeing their husband suddenly lying amidst the dust of the battlefield,
they fell upon his limbs like severed forest creepers.
Out of great reverence, one of them embraced him and wept.
One woman, embracing his feet, and another, clinging to his neck;
one, raising her arms, rolled upon the ground;
and another, seeing the face of the slain man, fell into a swoon.
6.098.010a One woman, placing her head upon his lap, wept while gazing at his face;
6.098.010c bathing his face with tears as if they were frost falling upon a lotus.
6.098.011a Thus, distressed at seeing their husband Rāvaṇa slain upon the ground, [they lamented].
They cried out in many ways out of grief and lamented even more:
"By him Śakra was terrified; by him Yama was terrified;
by him King Vaiśravaṇa was deprived of his Puṣpaka chariot."
He, by whom great fear was instilled in the Gandharvas, the sages, and the high-souled gods— he now lies slain in battle.
Likewise, [he who caused fear] from the Asuras, the Suras, or even the Pannagas.
He who knows no fear— this fear of his has come from a human.
He who was incapable of being slain by the gods, as well as by the Dānavas and Rākṣasas,
now lies here slain in battle by a human on foot.
"He who could not be slain by the gods, nor by the yakṣas, nor likewise by the asuras—
this very being, appearing like some insentient thing, has been brought to death by a mortal.
Speaking thus in many ways, his wives wept for him.
Afflicted by further sorrow, they lamented again and again:
"Because you did not listen to your friends who constantly spoke for your welfare,
now both we and yourself have been brought low together."
Even though your beloved brother Vibhīṣaṇa spoke words that were for your benefit,
he was treated with insolent harshness by you out of delusion, as you desired your own destruction. Had the Maithilī Sītā been restored to Rāma, [all this would not have happened].
"This terrible, root-destroying calamity would not have befallen us;
our brother Rāma would have been desirous of his own welfare, he would have become a kinsman to his friends,
and we all would not have been widowed, nor would our desires have been thwarted by enemies."
But by you, acting so cruelly and forcibly imprisoning Sītā, three things have been brought down to an equal level: ourselves, the Rākṣasas, and your own self.
O bull among Rākṣasas, this was neither an act of your free will nor a mere whim.

Fate impels everything; that which is struck down by fate is slain. This destruction of the monkeys and the Rākṣasas in battle, O mighty-armed one, has come upon you as well through the conjunction of fate.

"Neither by wealth nor by desire, neither by prowess nor by command can the course of destiny, once it has set out in the world, be turned back. Thus lamented those wretched wives of the lord of the rākṣasas.
Like female ospreys afflicted by grief, their eyes clouded with tears;
while those Rākṣasa women were thus lamenting,
the eldest wife, beloved and dejected, gazed upon her husband.
Seeing the Ten-necked one slain by Rāma of inconceivable deeds,
the wretched Mandodarī there lamented for her husband:
"O mighty-armed one, O younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa..."
Even Purandara trembles to stand before you when you are enraged;
the sages, the gods of the earth, and the illustrious Gandharvas have indeed fled to every quarter out of fear of you, as have the Cāraṇas.

"O King, O bull among Rākṣasas, having been defeated in battle by Rāma, who is merely a human, are you not ashamed? What is this, that having traversed the three worlds and being endowed with such splendor and heroism— "
"You, a mere human dwelling in the forest, have slain one who was otherwise invincible. For you,
who range in a domain inaccessible to humans and can assume any form at will,
destruction by Rāma in combat is not possible."
"I do not believe this deed of Rāma at the head of his army—
that he should have touched you, who are endowed with every excellence. Having conquered the senses in the past, you have conquered the three worlds."
"He has been conquered by his very senses, as if those senses were remembering that old enmity;
or perhaps Vāsava himself has come here in the form of Rāma,
having devised this inconceivable illusion for your destruction."
For as soon as your brother Khara was slain by many Rākṣasas in Janasthāna, he was no longer a mere mortal.
And as soon as [he entered] the city of Laṅkā, which is difficult even for the gods to penetrate—
As soon as Hanumān entered by his own prowess, we were then distressed.
This is the consequence that has now arrived because you did not heed my words when I told you, "Let no hostility be waged against Rāghava."
"O bull among Rākṣasas, you have suddenly become lustful for Sītā,
which will lead to the destruction of your sovereignty, your body, and your kinsmen—
especially since she, O evil-minded one, surpasses both Arundhatī and Rohiṇī."

"By violating Sītā, who is worthy of honor, you have indeed committed an act unworthy of yourself. Maithilī is superior to you or at least equal to you in lineage, beauty, and courtesy; yet, out of delusion, you do not realize this."

In every way, for all living beings, there is no death that lacks its defining characteristics; yet this death of yours, O King, has been defined by Maithilī. Maithilī shall dwell in joy together with Rāma, free from sorrow.
But I, of little merit, have fallen into this terrible ocean of grief;
yet I wandered together with you through Kailāsa, Mandara, Meru, as well as in the Caitraratha forest and all the celestial gardens.
I, who used to travel through various regions in a fitting celestial chariot with incomparable splendor, beholding them while adorned with variegated garlands and garments—
now, because of the slaying of your hero, I have been deprived of all sensual enjoyments.
"That illustrious brother-in-law of mine, whose speech is truth,
said: 'This destruction of the leaders of the Rākṣasas has arrived,
brought about by an addiction arising from desire and anger.'"
"By you, this entire host of *rākṣasas* has been rendered protectorless.
Indeed, you, whose strength and prowess are renowned, are not to be grieved for by me;
yet my mind turns toward compassion because of the nature of a woman."
"Taking with you both my good deeds and my evil deeds, you have gone to your own destination. I grieve for myself, distressed by separation from you—
you who resemble a dark blue cloud, wearing yellow garments and beautiful armlets."
"6.099.025c Having tossed all your limbs about, why do you lie there drenched in blood? 6.099.025e Why do you not answer me, who am afflicted with grief, as if you were fast asleep?
6.099.026a [You were] of great heroism, skillful, and one who never fled from battles."
"O daughter of a Yātudhāna, why do you not look upon me? This very [weapon],
which you use to slay enemies in battle with the brilliance of the sun— this thunderbolt, like that of the wielder of the thunderbolt— is constantly worshipped by you."
"O Parigha, you who strike down enemies in battle and were adorned with a net of gold,
you have been scattered by my arrows and shattered into a thousand pieces. Fie upon this heart of mine, which does not likewise shatter into a thousand fragments!"
"When you have met your death, it will bear fruit as the torment of grief.
In the meantime, Rāma said to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"Let the funeral rites for your brother be performed, and turn back these women."
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, who had heard the words [of Rāvaṇa], being humble toward Rāma and knowing the dharma, reflected with his intellect and replied with a response consistent with dharma and artha,
solely for the sake of complying with Rāma’s will.
"I am not worthy to perform the funeral rites for one who has abandoned the vows of dharma, who is cruel, pitiless, and likewise untruthful, and who has violated the wife of another; for this man,
though appearing as a brother, is my enemy, devoted to the harm of all."
"Rāvaṇa does not deserve honor, even though he is worthy of respect due to his seniority;
O Rāma, men on earth will call me cruel.
But upon hearing of his virtues, they will all speak instead of his great merit."
Having heard that, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma and an expert in speech, was exceedingly pleased and spoke these words to Vibhīṣaṇa, who was himself skilled in speech:
"You too must do what is pleasing to me; it is through your power that victory has been won by me."
"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, you must certainly be spoken to by me in a manner that is appropriate;
for this night-stalker, though joined with unrighteousness and falsehood,
is indeed energetic, powerful, and ever a hero in battles."

It is heard that the high-souled Rāvaṇa, endowed with great strength and the terror of the worlds, has never been defeated by the gods headed by Śatakratu. Hostilities end with death; our purpose has been accomplished.
"Let his consecration be performed; this [rite] for him is just as it is for you.
O mighty-armed one, he deserves to receive the consecration from you quickly according to the prescribed rules, O knower of dharma; you shall thereby partake in glory."
Having heard the words of Rāghava, Vibhīṣaṇa, acting with haste,
prepared Rāvaṇa for the funeral rites according to the appropriate ritual procedure.
Vibhīṣaṇa then offered the sacred fire to him in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Having spoken soothing words, he repeatedly entreated those women.
And when all the rākṣasīs had entered, Vibhīṣaṇa approached Rāma’s side and stood there humbly.
Rāma too, together with his army, Sugrīva, and Lakṣmaṇa,
attained joy after slaying his enemy, just as Śatakratu did after slaying Vṛtra.
Having witnessed the slaughter of Rāvaṇa, the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas rejoiced.
They departed in their various celestial chariots, recounting auspicious tales:
the terrible slaughter of Rāvaṇa, the prowess of Rāghava,
the well-fought battle of the monkeys, and the counsel of Sugrīva.
Speaking of the devotion and the valor of Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā,
those illustrious ones departed joyfully as they had come.
Rāghava, however, [mounted] the divine chariot given by Indra, which was radiant like fire.
Having granted permission, the illustrious one honored Mātali in return.
Permitted by Rāghava, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra,
mounted that divine chariot and ascended to heaven.
When that best of divine charioteers had ascended to heaven,
Rāghava, filled with supreme joy, embraced Sugrīva. Having embraced Sugrīva, he was then saluted by Lakṣmaṇa.
Being honored by the foremost of monkeys, he arrived at the army camp.
Then Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was standing nearby, endowed with courage and radiant with splendor.
"O gentle one, consecrate this Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā—he who is devoted, loyal, and has indeed rendered me assistance.
This is my supreme desire: that this younger brother of Rāvaṇa [should be so installed]."
"O gentle one, may I see Vibhīṣaṇa consecrated in Laṅkā.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Rāghava, the son of Sumitrā,
saying "So be it," joyfully took up a golden pitcher.

6.100.012 With that jar, the son of Sumitrā consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as king in the midst of the Rākṣasas in Laṅkā, by the command of Rāma. 6.100.013 That righteous-souled one consecrated the pure-souled Vibhīṣaṇa.
His ministers and those rākṣasas who were devoted to him rejoiced upon seeing Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, consecrated in Laṅkā;
and Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, attained the highest joy.
6.100.015 Having obtained that great kingdom bestowed by Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa,
after consoling the subjects, then approached Rāma.
6.100.016 He brought unbroken grains, sweetmeats, parched grain, and likewise celestial flowers.
Then, filled with joy, the night-stalking citizens brought those auspicious items to him;
taking them, the invincible and heroic one presented all those auspicious objects to Rāghava and to Lakṣmaṇa.
6.100.018 Having seen Vibhīṣaṇa, whose task was accomplished and whose purpose was fulfilled, Rāma accepted all of that out of a desire to do him a favor.
6.100.019 Then, [he addressed] the hero who resembled a mountain, standing at his side with palms joined in reverence.
6.100.019 Raghava spoke these words to Hanuman, the leader of the monkeys:
6.100.020 "O gentle one, having paid your respects to this great king Vibhishana,
enter the palace of Ravana and approach him with humility."
"O best among victors, O Lord of Monkeys, tell Vaidehī that I am well, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, and that Rāvaṇa has been slain by me;
having delivered this pleasant news to Maithilī, you— "
"Having received this message, you ought to return.
Thus instructed, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god,
entered the city of Laṅkā while being honored by the night-rangers.

Having entered Rāvaṇa’s residence, the one of great splendor beheld her who was like Rohiṇī distressed by the absence of the Moon. Approaching her, he bowed down, humbled and respectful, and offered his salutations.
6.101.003c He began to relate all of Rāma’s words:
6.101.004a “O Vaidehī, Rāma is well, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa;
6.101.004c the subduer of enemies, having achieved his purpose and slain his foe, inquires after your welfare.”

"O Queen, Rāvaṇa has been slain by Rāma, together with his monkey hosts and aided by Vibhīṣaṇa, through the guidance of Lakṣmaṇa. And having inquired after your welfare, the heroic Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, addresses you."

6.101.006c With his inner self fulfilled, he spoke, supremely delighted: 6.101.007a "O Queen, I tell you pleasant news; I honor you with this joy. 6.101.007c By good fortune you live, O knower of dharma, through my victory in battle."
"O Sītā, victory has been won for us; be at ease and free from distress.
That enemy Rāvaṇa has been slain, and this Laṅkā now stands under our control. Indeed, I remained awake and steadfast throughout the effort to achieve your rescue."
6.101.009c This vow has been fulfilled, having built a bridge across the great ocean.
6.101.010a You must not feel any anxiety while staying in Rāvaṇa’s abode;
6.101.010c for this sovereignty of Laṅkā has now been made subject to Vibhīṣaṇa.
"Therefore, take heart and be confident; you are moving about as if in your own home. And here he approaches, overjoyed and eager for the sight of you.
Having been addressed thus, Sītā, whose face resembles the moon, sprang up.
Overcome by great joy, she said nothing at all.
Then the best of monkeys spoke to Sītā, who remained silent:
"O Queen, what are you thinking? And why do you not address me?"
Thus addressed by Hanumān, Sītā, established in righteousness,
spoke with words faltering with joy,
being exceedingly delighted upon hearing this pleasant news concerning her husband's victory.
Overcome by the force of great joy, I remained speechless for a moment.
O monkey, though I reflected upon it, I could not find anything equal to my heartfelt welcome for you,
who have brought me this pleasant news.
"O gentle one, O monkey, I do not see anything on this earth that would be equal to giving you a reward for delivering my beloved’s message—
be it silver, gold, or various kinds of jewels."
"Even sovereignty over the three worlds does not deserve to be spoken of in comparison to this.
Thus addressed by Vaidehī, the monkey,
standing before Sītā with his hands joined in reverence, replied with these words.

6.101.020a Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of your husband, and desiring your husband’s victory, 6.101.020c only you are worthy to speak such affectionate words as these. 6.101.021a O gentle lady, these words of yours are both substantial and full of affection.

It excels even a multitude of various jewels and the sovereignty of the gods. In truth, I have attained qualities such as the sovereignty of the gods because I behold Rāma standing victorious, having slain his enemies.
"If you indeed permit it, I wish to slay all these rākṣasīs by whom you were previously threatened— those who tormented you,
a woman devoted to her husband, when you had gone to the Aśoka grove."
"Terrible in appearance and conduct, cruel, with eyes even more cruel than their deeds— these Rākṣasīs of dreadful speech, grant me this boon:
I wish to slay these most hideous women with various means of destruction."
With fists, hands, and feet, O beautiful one,
with terrible blows of the knees and the knocking out of teeth,
with the devouring of ears and noses, and likewise with the plucking out of hair;
"O illustrious lady, with their mouths severely parched and exhausted by harsh fasts— by many such various afflictions,
O Queen, I desire to destroy these women of yours who have committed this offense."
Thus addressed by the highly esteemed Hanumān, the illustrious Vaidehī, daughter of Janaka, spoke words consistent with dharma to the glorious one:
"For those who are subject to the power of dependence on a king and act under his command..."
"O best of monkeys, who would be angry with submissive female slaves?
All this that I am experiencing is due to the conjunction of adverse fortune and past misdeeds; for one must indeed enjoy the fruits of one's own actions."
"I have determined that this must be endured by me through the conjunction of my current circumstances;
though I am weak here, I shall endure it because I am a slave to Rāvaṇa.
Commanded by Rāvaṇa, these rākṣasīs have been threatening me."
"O best of monkeys, once he is slain, they will certainly not offer you threats.
However, O monkey, listen to this ancient verse concerning righteousness that was sung by a bear in the presence of a tiger."
6.101.035a One does not incur the sin of others who perform evil deeds; 6.101.035c however, an agreement must be honored, for the virtuous have good conduct as their ornament.
6.101.036a Whether they be wicked or virtuous, or even those deserving of death, O monkey—

6.101.036c A noble person should exercise compassion; there is no one who does not commit some offense. 6.101.037a Even toward Rākṣasas who take pleasure in harming the world and can assume any form at will, even if they commit evil deeds, one must never do what is unseemly.
Thus addressed by Sītā, Hanumān, who was skilled in speech,
then replied to the illustrious Sītā, the wife of Rāma:
"It is fitting that you, the illustrious and lawful wife of Rāma, [should speak thus]."
"Give me your word, O Goddess, and I shall go where Rāghava is.
Thus addressed by Hanumān, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, replied:
"O best of monkeys, I wish to see my husband."
6.101.041 Having heard those words of hers, Hanumān, the son of the Wind and possessed of great luster, spoke these words to Maithilī to gladden her:
6.101.042 "O noble lady, you shall see Rāma, whose face is like the full moon, together with Lakṣmaṇa."
6.101.042c Like Śacī to the Lord of the Thirty-three, she was one whose friends were steadfast and whose enemies were destroyed.
6.101.043a Having thus addressed Sītā, who was radiant like the goddess Śrī herself,
Hanumān, possessed of great speed, went to where Rāghava was.
Approaching Rāma, who is possessed of great wisdom and is the best among all archers, that monkey, who understood the meaning of things, spoke these words:
"For what purpose has this undertaking been begun, and from what [cause] does the fruition of these actions arise?"
6.102.002c You ought to see that queen Maithilī, who is tormented by grief.
6.102.003a For she, though overwhelmed by sorrow and her eyes clouded with tears,
attained joy upon hearing of your victory, O Maithilī.
"Based on that previous assurance, she spoke to me with full confidence:
'I wish to see my husband, who has accomplished his purpose, together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Thus addressed by Hanumān, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma—"
Suddenly he fell into deep reflection and sat there overwhelmed with tears;
sighing long and hot while gazing at the earth,
he spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa, who stood before him like a dark cloud.
"Bring Sītā here without delay— Vaidehī, with her limbs anointed with celestial unguents, adorned with divine ornaments, and having bathed her head.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa acted with haste.
6.102.008c Having entered the inner apartments, she urged Sītā along with her own women:
6.102.009a "O Vaidehī, anointed with divine unguents and adorned with divine ornaments,
6.102.009c mount the vehicle— may prosperity be yours— for your husband desires to see you."
Thus addressed, Vaidehī replied to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"O Lord of Rākṣasas, I wish to see my husband without having bathed.
Hearing those words of hers, Vibhīṣaṇa replied.
"Since Rāma is your husband, you ought to act accordingly.
Hearing those words of his, Maithilī— whose deity was her brother,
who was virtuous, and whose vow was devotion to her husband— replied, "So be it."
Then, having placed Sītā— who had bathed her head, was adorned by young women,
endowed with costly ornaments, and wearing precious garments— upon a radiant palanquin covered with the finest cloth;
